items.title: South Florida severe weather and flooding live updates
items.summary: Historic flooding across South Florida has left neighborhoods underwater, roads impassable and Broward schools closed as residents begin cleanup efforts and officials assess the damage.

scraped.title: South Florida flooding live updates: Communities struggle to recover as floodwaters linger
scraped.description: Historic flooding across South Florida has left neighborhoods underwater, roads impassable and Broward schools closed as residents begin cleanup efforts and officials assess the damage.
scraped.h1: South Florida flooding live updates: Communities struggle to recover as floodwaters linger
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 20, 2026 / 3:59 PM EST / CBS Miami

A family-owned farm in Davie is struggling to recover after this week's flooding killed about 30 chickens and caused extensive damage to equipment and animal feed.

Ashley LaStella, who owns Essential Farm to Family with her husband, said the family managed to rescue their goats and rabbits but could not save all their animals.

"It's just days later and we're still under water," LaStella said.

The latest flooding comes just two weeks after the family had to move animals to higher ground because of flooding at another nearby property.

Neighbors have been using ATVs to reach one of the farm's flooded stands, while supporters have started an online fundraiser to help the family recover.

"I thought I was at my breaking point, to be honest, like how can we recover from this?" LaStella said. "I do have my faith and we are going to rebuild, little by little, but it's heartbreaking with the loss of the animals."

Members of Congress and Hollywood's mayor got an up-close look at the damage left behind after historic flooding slammed the city and other South Florida communities this week.

Rabbi Dr. Gideon Goldenholtz told CBS News Miami that the visit by local leaders is valuable for everyone who is connected to Temple Sinai.

Earlier on Friday he led a tour for U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz and U.S. Rep. Jared Moskowitz, as well as Hollywood Mayor Josh Levy.

"They care about this community," Rabbi Goldenholtz said. "They're part of the community in every possible way. And it makes us feel like we're not alone."

Brightline says it has temporarily suspended train service from West Palm Beach to Orlando because of high water.

Officials said high water conditions and the impacts of flooding impacting the rail corridor in Orange County and Brevard County led to the decision to suspend all trains to and from the Orlando Station on Friday.

"The safety of our guests, team members and the communities we serve remains our highest priority," officials said. "Maintenance personnel are on scene, and train service will resume when conditions allow safe movement through the area."

Cleanup is underway in South Florida following historic flooding, but efforts in some areas remain stalled as residents wait for water to recede .

Because some areas are still flooded, Broward County Public Schools will remain closed Friday.

According to the Sun Sentinel, the superintendent says about 30 schools in the county have flooding or damage.

Miami-Dade County Public Schools are open on Friday, and both districts remain closed next week for Thanksgiving.

Heavy rainfall has left neighborhoods underwater, roads closed, and residents scrambling to clean up across Broward County.

With public schools closed for Thanksgiving break, some students have found creative ways to navigate flooded streets.

"They're like surfboards. We use them on the beach, but instead we're using the truck," said high school student Tristan Dunlap.

The severe weather follows as much as 16 inches of rain in Hollywood's Driftwood neighborhood, where residents are working to clear standing water and assess property damage. At a local Home Depot, residents picked up supplies to clean flood-damaged homes, including a resident whose cottage in Hollywood flooded.

In Dania Beach, residents reported being trapped by surrounding floodwaters for two days. In Davie, an Interstate 75 on-ramp was closed as water covered nearby roads, and the parking lot at the Tower Shops was left submerged.

Tami, a 20-year resident of the area, said the flooding is the worst she has ever witnessed.

"This is the absolute worst I have ever, ever seen it," she said, noting that last week's rain already trapped her at home for three days.

In Sunrise, water covered the area around Amerant Bank Arena, where crews worked throughout the day to clear it ahead of Friday evening's Olivia Rodrigo concert.

Residents have called on local leaders to address the ongoing infrastructure and drainage issues.

The City of Davie stated it is monitoring its drainage system and implementing preventative measures to ensure stormwater moves efficiently.

Storms that brought record rains to South Florida this week shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses alike.

This is supposed to be Florida's dry season, which runs from October to May.

So far, it has been quite the opposite.

"Never seen such a thing like this in Florida," said Jazmin Foster, who has lived in her Melbourne home for eight years.

This week's storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. Heavy rains and flash flooding were expected to persist through Friday, possibly moving north toward the Carolinas and the mid-Atlantic into the weekend, the weather service said.

On Thursday, the storms hit Brevard County directly. People with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.

First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.

Water inundated Foster's home Thursday, two weeks after she endured a previous round of flooding. She said an insurance claim filed for the earlier flood was denied.

"Where is FEMA? Multiple people here in Brevard need help! I know other people are worse than we are!" Foster told The Associated Press via social media.

Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

The St. Johns River near Cocoa rose above a record flood level set in 1953 and was forecast to stay at least 2 feet above flood stage through early next week, according to the weather service.

Cyndy Paulin saw a fish swimming on her flooded street in Cocoa on Thursday, and her adventurous 5-year-old granddaughter played in the water. She brought a small body board and got on it, but it sank immediately, and she got soaked.

"She had a blast," Paulin said.

The storms are an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the tropical Pacific that distorts weather patterns worldwide.

Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.

"That's what the forecast models are saying," said Yale Climate Connections meteorologist Jeff Masters. "Winter hasn't even come yet — we're still in November. And things are likely to get even more active. And with record-warm ocean temperatures both off the coast of California and off the coast of Florida, we're going to be seeing some very heavy downpours."

In July, United Nations officials warned that El Niño would add fuel to the world's accelerating climate crisis, powered by the burning of coal, oil and natural gas.

Longtime Pompano Beach resident Ken Evans said he has seen heavier rain and flooding worsen, especially over the past five years.

On Tuesday night, he was caught in his SUV on Interstate 95 north of Miami during a heavy downpour with hail, leaving many roads underwater.

"This is absolutely a whole new cycle that's going on, and a cycle that we should be very concerned about," Evans said.

A nontropical low-pressure system expected to form Friday could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf, and coastal flooding into early next week.

Broward County government offices, public libraries, and the 311 Call Center will reopen and resume normal operations Friday, Nov. 20, following severe flooding across South Florida, though a local state of emergency remains in effect.

Broward announced that county offices will reopen starting at 7 a.m. Friday, even though the local state of emergency remains active and the National Weather Service's Flood Watch was extended for southeast Florida through Friday morning.

While administrative offices prepare to reopen, Broward County Communications reported that several facilities remain impacted by standing water:

Parks and Events: All Broward County parks remain closed Thursday, and the Camelot Days medieval festival scheduled at T.Y. Park in Hollywood is expected to be canceled due to flooding. Campgrounds at T.Y. Park, Markham Park, and C.B. Smith Park remain open to registered campers.

Libraries: All Broward County libraries remain closed Thursday before reopening Friday, Nov. 20.

Shelters and Health Services: All county homeless shelters remain operational with expanded capacity at both the Central and South Homeless Assistance Centers, while the Taskforce for Ending Homelessness is providing transportation for unsheltered residents. The Broward County Addiction and Recovery Center and the Nancy J. Cotterman Center also remain open and fully operational.

Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport and Port Everglades remain open and operational, though travelers and cruise passengers are advised to check directly with their airlines or cruise lines for potential delays before arriving.

Broward County Transit is operating on or close to schedule, with localized flooding forcing detours on Routes 9, 12, 14, 16, and 30. Paratransit services continue to operate, and community shuttles are running normal schedules except in Pompano Beach and Hollywood.

Broward County Public Works crews continue to monitor roadway conditions and operate pre-positioned pumps in flood-prone areas. Officials continue to urge motorists to avoid flooded roads, obey posted closures, and never attempt to drive through standing water.

Heavy rain flooded several streets in Pompano Beach on Thursday, surrounding homes near Copans Road and leaving at least one driver stranded as residents waited for floodwaters to recede.

On Northeast 12th Terrace, resident Kevin Garvey said water rose quickly after heavy rainfall began Thursday morning. By evening, the water surrounded his home and reached a utility pole in front of it.

"I never thought I had waterfront property," Garvey said.

Neighbor Gipcy Jullmis, a mother of three, said she planned to stay home and keep her car off the road.

"You just have to stay inside as much as possible, 'cause it's not safe," Jullmis said.

Floodwaters began to recede on nearby Copans Road, where larger trucks moved through the water faster than smaller vehicles. Resident Ramon Ginguio said the flooding damaged the front of his car, but he planned to repair and move it himself.

At Powerline Road and Northwest 16th Street, another car stalled in floodwater. The driver declined to speak with CBS News Miami and remained inside the vehicle while waiting for the water to recede.

Residents said the water stayed outside their homes, though they worried that future heavy rain could push it indoors.

Days after heavy rainfall inundated South Florida, business owners and residents in Davie and Dania Beach are dealing with extensive flood damage and standing water.

At the Tower Shops plaza off University Drive in Davie, the main parking lot remained completely underwater Thursday. Customers resorted to parking in fire lanes and on sidewalks to access the few open businesses.

"It's not that busy inside because nobody can park here and I have no idea where the water is going to go," said Aubrey Strasberg, a Home Depot shopper.

A few blocks away, staff and volunteers at Nova Gymnastics worked to rip up wet drywall after nearly knee-deep floodwaters rushed into the building.

"We were moving equipment while the water was coming in, so that was very, very, very, very hard because we weren't as fast as the water coming in," said owner Andreea Bordei.

The facility serves approximately 700 families in the local area.

"We were all kind of in shock, and it didn't really hit us until we started trying to do everything we can to save everything," said Damara Tamzil, Bordei's daughter.

Bordei, who lacks flood insurance, estimated the facility sustained roughly $200,000 in structural and equipment damage. In response, community members launched an online fundraiser that raised nearly $30,000 within two days.

"So many parents don't want this to end. They love this gym as I do, as their second home, but I didn't expect this," Bordei said. "I didn't even cry for the damages because I couldn't, but I cried when I saw how many people are not letting me quit because I wanted to quit."

Meanwhile, in nearby Dania Beach, residents near Southwest 40th Avenue have remained stranded in their homes for two days due to high water levels.

"This was horrible; the water was up to here all the way; it was very ugly," said area resident Nidia Palma, noting that floodwaters completely inundated her son's vehicle parked outside their apartment. "That's my son's car; the water went inside too."

Brightline has temporarily suspended all passenger train service between Orlando and West Palm Beach for Friday, Nov. 20, due to flooding and high water along the rail corridor in Orange and Brevard counties.

The rail company announced Thursday that all trains traveling between Orlando and West Palm Beach are canceled for Friday while crews monitor flooded sections of track.

Due to continued flooding and hazardous conditions along the rail corridor in Brevard and Orange Counties, Brightline has made the decision to suspend long-haul service between Orlando and West Palm Beach for tomorrow, Friday, November 20. The safety of our Teammates and Guests remains our top priority. Our teams are closely monitoring conditions as we perform the necessary repairs and inspections. South Florida train service between Miami, Aventura, Fort Lauderdale, Boca Raton, and West Palm Beach is operating normally. Brightline encourages guests to monitor https://t.co/crYOBqkdNh, Brightline app and social media channels for the latest service updates.

South Florida service between Miami, Aventura, Fort Lauderdale, Boca Raton, and West Palm Beach continues to operate normally.

According to Brightline, rail infrastructure teams are actively monitoring water levels across the affected corridor in coordination with rail contractors and Florida Department of Transportation District 5 officials.

Once floodwaters recede, crews will inspect all tracks, signals, and grade crossings before resuming passenger operations. Brightline said it will issue an update on Orlando-to-South Florida service no later than 5 p.m. Friday, Nov. 20.

Guests with canceled reservations are being contacted directly regarding their travel options, and updated schedules are available on the Brightline website, mobile app, and social media channels.

Cleanup is underway after up to 16 inches of rain fell in the Driftwood neighborhood in Hollywood.

Floodwaters crept up front yards, leaving many residents with heavy debris even though the water stayed out of their homes.

"We're cleaning up the mess from Tuesday's heavy rain. We couldn't drive out of our driveway. We still can't, and we're just cleaning up all the dirt that came in our yard," said Flo Horn. She and her son, Michael, were helping a neighbor clean up his yard.

"Any time to help out a neighbor, especially in situations like this, whether it be the flooding, the rain, hurricanes, any kind of disaster, we usually all try to get out and help each other," Michael said.

In Hollywood's Emerald Hills neighborhood, getting around remains a challenge. Stirling Road, west of Interstate 95, is reduced to one lane in some areas.

At North 56th Avenue and Stirling Road, the water has not receded, leaving additional cars stalled and partially submerged.

The city has deployed 32 pumps and three vacuum trucks to clear the water, a process slowed by saturated ground.

The Flood Watch across South Florida has been extended through Friday morning as significant standing water and flooding persist across the region's hardest-hit neighborhoods.

While the area experienced a temporary lull in heavy rainfall Thursday afternoon, with the main focus shifting farther north, the NEXT Weather Team warns that localized bands of heavy rain are still expected to develop Thursday evening and overnight, particularly across northern Miami-Dade County and Broward County.

Although the incoming storms will be hit-or-miss, any downpours moving over communities already dealing with active flooding could trigger rapid, significant impacts. Because saturated ground and overwhelmed drainage systems cannot absorb additional runoff, even 1 to 2 inches of rain will add directly to existing pools of standing water.

With vulnerability remaining high across both counties, the NEXT Weather Team noted that the threshold for triggering Emergency Alert System weather alerts, such as a Flash Flood Warning, remains very low.

Fort Lauderdale officials announced Thursday that free sandbags will be available to residents this weekend as crews continue pumping water from flooded neighborhoods and prepare for another round of king tides.

Melrose Manors, Melrose Park, Riverland and Edgewood remain among the hardest-hit neighborhoods, with city crews working around the clock to remove standing water using vacuum trucks and portable pumps.

A flood watch has been extended until 7 a.m. Friday, with up to 2 additional inches of rain possible over the next 24 hours.

The city will distribute free, prefilled sandbags Saturday and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at five locations: Floyd Hull/Morton Center, George English Park, Holiday Park, Mills Pond Park and Riverland Park. Residents must show proof of residency and are limited to five bags per vehicle, while supplies last.

Officials are also preparing for king tides expected Nov. 22-28, warning that elevated tides combined with saturated ground could cause additional flooding in low-lying neighborhoods.

Meanwhile, garbage and recycling collection is expected to resume Friday where roads are accessible, although crews may skip flooded streets to avoid pushing water into homes.

Residents whose homes have flooded are encouraged to document the damage and submit reports through the city's FixItFTL app to help officials assess the impact.

Pop star Olivia Rodrigo's team has canceled her Unraveled Tour Experience merchandise pop-up in Sunrise due to severe weather and flooding across South Florida, though both of her scheduled concerts at Amerant Bank Arena will proceed as planned.

In a statement posted on Rodrigo's website and social media accounts, her team cited thunderstorm forecasts and an active National Weather Service Flood Warning for canceling the Thursday and Friday pop-up events.

"Sunrise, we were SO excited to see you for the Unraveled Tour Experience, but with thunderstorms in the forecast and the National Weather Service Flood Warning in effect, we have to cancel the Nov 19 and 20 pop-ups at this stop," the statement read. "Your safety comes first. Thank you for the love, and we'll see you at the next stop in Nashville on Nov 22."

The Unraveled Tour Experience pop-up was designed to allow fans to purchase tour merchandise without needing a concert ticket. While the outdoor pop-up is canceled, Amerant Bank Arena confirmed that fans can still access early tour merchandise inside Pantherland—located on the Publix Plaza just inside the arena's main doors—starting at 3 p.m. on both show days.

Know before you go to The Unraveled Tour ♡ We encourage everyone to prepare for the weather. For your comfort and safety, please do not begin lining up for the shows until one hour prior to doors. Bags up to 12″ × 12″ are permitted, subject to additional screening. Amerant Bank Arena encourages all guests to travel light to help reduce wait times at entry. Umbrellas are permitted, subject to additional screening. We appreciate your cooperation and look forward to seeing you at Amerant Bank Arena!

Rodrigo's sold-out performances at Amerant Bank Arena on Thursday, Nov. 19, and Friday, Nov. 20, with special guest Devon Again, remain on schedule. Ahead of the shows, the venue shared event guidelines on social media to help attendees navigate the wet weather:

Event Times: Parking gates open at 5 p.m., arena doors open at 6 p.m., and the show begins at 7 p.m. on both Thursday and Friday.

Lining Up: Venue officials asked fans not to begin lining up outside until one hour before doors open.

Permitted Items: Umbrellas and bags measuring up to 12 by 12 inches are permitted inside the arena, subject to additional screening.

The National Weather Service has extended a flood watch for Miami-Dade and Broward counties until 7 a.m. Friday as the threat of additional flooding continues across South Florida.

The watch was previously scheduled to expire at 7 p.m. Thursday but was extended as communities continued dealing with the effects of several days of heavy rainfall.

According to the NWS, widespread rainfall totals of 3 to 5 inches have been recorded across South Florida in recent days, with some areas receiving between 8 and 15 inches.

Additional rainfall could lead to flash flooding, particularly in urban areas, neighborhoods with poor drainage and locations where the ground is already saturated.

The NWS previously forecast an additional 1 to 2 inches of rain in areas affected by showers and thunderstorms Thursday, with isolated totals potentially reaching 3 to 5 inches.

Residents are urged to monitor weather alerts and avoid driving through flooded roads.

All Miami-Dade County courts and Clerk of the Court and Comptroller's offices will reopen Friday, following closures caused by severe flooding across South Florida.

Officials confirmed Thursday that all locations will resume their regular schedules.

The reopening comes as Miami-Dade public schools and Florida International University also prepare to resume normal operations Friday.

Florida International University announced Thursday that it will reopen Friday, with classes and university operations resuming at all locations following this week's widespread flooding across South Florida.

In a message to the university community, FIU officials said weather conditions are improving but warned that some areas could still experience localized flooding and hazardous road conditions.

Students, faculty and staff are urged to exercise caution while traveling, avoid flooded roadways and remain alert for downed power lines.

The university also asked professors and supervisors to remain flexible with students and employees who may still be affected by flooding or lingering travel disruptions.

FIU's reopening comes as Miami-Dade County Public Schools also prepares to resume normal operations Friday. Broward County Public Schools, meanwhile, will remain closed until after Thanksgiving break, with students expected back Nov. 30.

Broward County Public Schools announced Thursday that all schools and district offices will remain closed Friday, Nov. 20, because of the widespread flooding that has affected South Florida this week.

District officials said offices are expected to reopen Monday, Nov. 23, but students will not return to classrooms until Monday, Nov. 30, following the scheduled Thanksgiving break.

Schools will remain closed Nov. 23-27 for the holiday break.

⚠️ WEATHER UPDATE ⚠️ All BCPS schools and District offices will remain CLOSED Friday, November 20. Offices are expected to reopen Monday, November 23. Students are expected back Monday, November 30, after Thanksgiving break. # pic.twitter.com/nqHrGlapXK

The district also announced that the school calendar will be adjusted to account for missed instructional time, with additional details expected after Thanksgiving.

The announcement comes as Miami-Dade County Public Schools confirmed that its schools, offices and activities will resume normal operations Friday.

Miami-Dade County Public Schools Superintendent Rafael A. Villalobos announced on Thursday that all Miami-Dade County Public Schools, region offices, district offices, and school-related activities will resume normal operations on Friday.

Schools across South Florida have been closed because of the historic flooding that took place this week.

A decision regarding Broward County Public Schools will be made later on Thursday.

The National Weather Service in Miami has canceled a flash flood warning for northern Broward County that was originally scheduled to remain in effect until 2:15 p.m. Thursday.

The warning had covered several communities, including Fort Lauderdale, Pompano Beach, Margate, Coconut Creek, Oakland Park, Lighthouse Point and Lauderdale-by-the-Sea.

Before the cancellation, the NWS reported that thunderstorms had produced heavy rainfall across the warning area, with between 3 and 4 inches of rain already fallen.

Although the warning has been canceled, residents should continue to exercise caution around flooded roads and areas where standing water remains following days of heavy rainfall across South Florida.

Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Thursday that Florida is mobilizing hundreds of Florida National Guard and Florida State Guard personnel, along with more than 200 state troopers, as heavy rain and flooding continue to affect communities across the state.

In an update posted on X, DeSantis said the state's response also includes 235 Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers, 50 high-water vehicles and 60 pumps.

STORM UPDATE: As heavy rainfall impacts communities across Florida, the state is continuing our active response efforts. @FLSERT is mobilizing hundreds of @FLGuard and @FLStateGuard personnel and more than 200 @FLHSMV troopers, along with 235 @MyFWC officers, 50 high-water…

Additionally, 750 Florida Department of Transportation crew members are supporting flood response efforts in affected communities.

FWC has also prepared 28 ATVs and UTVs, 26 shallow-draft boats, 17 airboats, eight swamp buggies and a specialized all-terrain vehicle known as a Fat Truck.

The state has pre-positioned more than 6,000 feet of flood control devices, placed shelters on standby and positioned generators and vacuum trucks for rapid deployment if needed.

"Florida will continue deploying resources and working alongside local partners to protect residents and respond to the needs of impacted communities," DeSantis wrote, urging residents to follow guidance from local officials.

A Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officer helped rescue a baby who had stopped breathing after first responders attempting to reach the child became stuck in floodwaters in Broward, the agency announced Thursday.

According to the FWC, an officer responded and transported the infant to waiting emergency medical personnel. The baby recovered.

In a separate incident, FWC officers rescued a disabled veteran who was unable to evacuate after floodwaters washed away his wheelchair. Officers transported the veteran to a safe shelter for the night and recovered his wheelchair.

The rescues are part of a larger emergency response to widespread flooding across South Florida. In Broward County, FWC officers responded to a flooded apartment complex , where more than 90 residents have been evacuated, rescued or transported for medical assistance.

The agency said approximately 235 officers have been deployed to affected areas, along with 28 high-water ATVs and UTVs, 26 shallow-draft boats, 17 airboats and eight swamp buggies.

A coalition of three Broward County nonprofit organizations has activated a disaster recovery fund to help residents and businesses affected by widespread flooding across South Florida.

The Broward Cares Disaster Recovery Fund, a partnership between the Community Foundation of Broward , Jewish Federation of Broward County and United Way Broward , will raise money to support recovery efforts in Hollywood, Fort Lauderdale and other hard-hit communities.

The organizations announced Thursday that 100% of donations will go toward grants for selected nonprofits providing disaster relief, including assistance with housing, food and other essential needs.

The three organizations said they will assess the community's most urgent needs, coordinate with local governments and emergency response teams, and distribute grants to nonprofits assisting flood victims.

Broward Cares said it previously provided nearly $1 million in emergency assistance following the historic April 2023 flooding, awarding grants to more than 40 nonprofits that helped residents with housing, food, clothing, furniture and other necessities.

Residents interested in contributing can visit the ⁠ Broward Cares website to make a donation.

Nonprofits involved in flood recovery efforts can also contact the Community Foundation of Broward at info@cfbroward.org to report immediate and long-term needs.

Fort Lauderdale officials announced Thursday that the city's Light Up the Beach event has been canceled as additional heavy rain threatens neighborhoods already dealing with widespread flooding.

Some areas of Fort Lauderdale have received as much as 3.5 inches of rain since 1 a.m. Thursday, raising concerns about flash flooding in neighborhoods still recovering from the past two days of heavy rainfall, the city said.

City crews worked overnight to address flooding, deploying additional vacuum trucks and portable pumps to vulnerable neighborhoods. High-water vehicles also remain on standby to assist Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue with emergencies in flooded areas.

The flooding has also disrupted transportation services. The LauderGO! Water Trolley remains suspended, although the city's Community Shuttle is operating normally.

A flood watch remains in effect until 7 p.m. Thursday, with another 1 to 2 inches of rain expected through Friday. Isolated areas could receive 3 to 5 inches.

Officials are urging residents to avoid flooded streets and unnecessary travel, warning that vehicles driving through standing water can create wakes that push floodwaters into nearby homes and businesses.

The Town of Davie announced Thursday that several municipal services have resumed, although flooding continues to affect roads, parks and public transportation.

Town government offices and recreational facilities are open, while the Blue and SFEC community shuttle routes have fully resumed service. The Green Route is operating with one bus, and some stops remain inaccessible due to flooding. Garbage collection could also be affected in flooded neighborhoods.

Officials are assessing damage to parks and trails before determining which areas can safely reopen.

Davie has also opened a temporary horse refuge at Bergeron Rodeo Grounds, 4201 Rodeo Way, for residents whose horse stalls have been significantly affected by flooding. The service is free, with limited space available on a first-come, first-served basis. Horses can be dropped off Thursday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

A flood watch remains in effect through 7 p.m. Thursday, with 1 to 2 inches of additional rain expected across South Florida through Friday. Some areas could receive 3 to 5 inches, with wind gusts reaching 30 mph.

Residents can call the town's information hotline at 954-797-1122 for updates on services and facility closures.

The National Weather Service issued a new flood advisory for Miami-Dade County Thursday morning as additional rainfall threatens areas already dealing with widespread flooding.

The advisory took effect at 9:10 a.m. and is scheduled to remain in place until 11:45 a.m.

The new alert comes shortly after the NWS issued a separate flood advisory for Broward, in effect until 12:45 p.m.

Parts of South Florida have received more than 15 inches of rain since Tuesday, leaving roads underwater, stranding drivers and prompting widespread school closures.

A flood watch remains in effect across South Florida through Thursday evening as additional rainfall could worsen flooding in already saturated areas.

The National Weather Service issued a new flood advisory for Broward Thursday morning as additional rainfall threatens communities still recovering from widespread flooding earlier this week.

The advisory took effect at 8:44 a.m. and is scheduled to remain in place until 2:15 p.m.

Parts of Broward have already received more than 15 inches of rain since Tuesday, leaving roads underwater, stranding drivers and prompting school closures.

A broader flood watch also remains in effect across South Florida through Thursday evening, with additional heavy rainfall potentially worsening conditions in already saturated areas.

Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood says a ruptured roof drainage pipe that contributed to significant flooding inside the facility Wednesday has been repaired, and previously flooded areas are now clear of standing water.

In an update Wednesday evening, hospital officials said the pipe, which carries rainwater, was responsible for a significant portion of the flooding that affected the hospital earlier in the day.

New video footage released by the hospital showed previously flooded interior areas and the parking garage after the standing water was cleared.

Water remediation teams worked throughout Wednesday to remove water, dry affected areas and clean up the facility as hospital officials continued efforts to restore normal operations.

The hospital temporarily suspended visitation Wednesday morning because of the flooding but resumed visits for hospitalized patients later that morning.

Several cities in South Florida saw rain totals of more than a foot over the past 72 hours:

Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport saw nearly 10 inches of rain, and Coral Gables picked more than a half-foot.

The NEXT Weather Alert will continue in South Florida on Thursday as more rain moves in , and with the ground already saturated additional flooding will be possible.

Broward County Transit bus service continues to operate amid heavy rain and flooding in parts of Broward County, but some routes are seeing delays and detours as roadway conditions change.

Those current impacts include:

Passengers are being urged to check the riders alert page here , RideBCT App or call BCT Customer Service at 954-357-8400 for real-time bus information before heading to the bus stop.

The flooding situation that has been ongoing in Hollywood since late Tuesday night and Wednesday appears to be improving as floodwaters continue to recede across the city.

Some areas remain underwater, however, like Liberty Street and North Park Road. While the water levels have dropped, the road remains covered and cars have been attempting to make it through the water.

City crews and water pumps worked overtime Wednesday night to drain submerged streets in Hollywood after heavy rain and wind turned major thoroughfares into rivers, leaving dozens of vehicles stalled in high water.

Near the intersection of Stirling Road and North 56th Avenue, rows of disabled cars remained stranded along the flooded roadway. Some residents told reporters they have had to pay tow truck companies hundreds of dollars to haul their waterlogged vehicles off the street.

For longtime residents, the recurring street flooding has become a frustratingly familiar sight after intense South Florida downpours.

"I mean, it's crazy, but if you live down here, you're like, 'Oh, it happened again,' essentially," said Humberto Abrill, who lives nearby.

Another resident, Jamie Avery, said watching neighbors lose their vehicles to the floodwaters has been difficult, even though her pickup truck has had an easier time navigating the wet conditions than smaller passenger cars.

"I feel really bad for all the people that it's happening to," Avery said. "I mean, this is an issue here. I don't really know if there's anything we can do about it."

Despite driving a higher-profile vehicle, Avery said she refuses to risk crossing deep standing water.

"I just don't go through it. I just go around, if I can—turn around, don't drown, right?" she said.

Officials continue to remind motorists across Broward County not to drive through flooded intersections while pumping operations continue overnight.

Standing water showed little sign of receding across neighborhoods off Stirling Road in Dania Beach on Wednesday night, even after hours without rainfall, leaving residents stranded at home and commuters wading through submerged streets across southern Broward County.

Intersections across the region continued to disrupt travel through the evening rush hour. In Dania Beach, resident William Martin parked his vehicle on higher ground and took a ride-share to work Wednesday night after learning a costly lesson from a previous storm.

"Last time it flooded, I had to buy an all-new starter," Martin said. "It rusted it out because it's too deep of water."

Further south in the Hollywood area, workers walked home through standing water during the evening rush after major arteries became impassable. Siblings Nancy and Francisco took off their shoes to wade down flooded streets toward their parents' home.

"Sheridan is beyond flooded," Nancy said as her mother called to check on their progress while navigating the flooded roads to pick them up.

"We are trying to get to our kids now," their mother said over the phone. "We are on the way, but it's not looking nice out here."

In Dania Beach, several homeowners remained trapped inside their properties with standing water pooling just outside their back doors. Homeowner Itay Arrous, whose backyard had been dry just days earlier, said any additional rainfall could push water inside his house.

"The water you see behind you is a few feet away from our house," Arrous said. "One more day of rain, and that's it—the water is going to be inside."

City of Dania Beach officials announced that sandbags will be available again Thursday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the public services facility off Stirling Road. Most municipal operations are expected to resume normal schedules Thursday.

Hours of persistent rain left major neighborhood entrances flooded in Cutler Bay well into Wednesday night, creating hazardous driving conditions and stranding multiple vehicles even after the downpours stopped.

Water still covered portions of Southwest 216th Street between Old Cutler Road and Southwest 87th Avenue at 11 p.m., after the rain had stopped. Some larger vehicles made it through, while other drivers needed a tow. CBS News Miami saw multiple tow trucks on the street, including one hauling away a larger vehicle.

Alfred Montaner, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years, warned drivers not to underestimate the water depth along the corridor.

"Whatever you do, if you live in the Cutler Bay area, do not come down 216th Street," Montaner said. "If you have a small car, you may get flooded, and you may have to get towed out of here."

Montaner said homeowners should also keep an eye on drains in their neighborhoods.

"We have to be vigilant as homeowners to ensure that all the drains are clear," he said.

Other neighbors pointed to a lack of drainage infrastructure along the stretch as a recurring culprit whenever heavy rain saturates South Florida.

"This weather has been a mess," said resident Lasasha Swane. "There's no drain here. If we had drains, none of this would be happening."

With saturated ground unable to absorb the excess runoff, many Cutler Bay residents went to bed Wednesday night with the main road out of their neighborhoods still underwater.

Following a historic round of rainfall that left parts of Broward and Miami-Dade counties underwater, the CBS Miami NEXT Weather Team continues to track the potential for additional heavy rain. This may result in renewed pockets of flooding, especially in Broward County, where the soil remains oversaturated.

A Flood Watch remains in effect across South Florida through Thursday evening.

Additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms are expected, with periods of heavy rainfall that could produce renewed flash flooding. This is not expected to be as widespread or as impactful as storms going into early Wednesday morning.

Our greatest concern is for the communities that have already experienced substantial rainfall, particularly across eastern Broward and northeastern Miami-Dade counties, where saturated ground and standing water leave little room for additional runoff. Even a relatively modest rainfall could worsen flooding conditions. Should thunderstorms repeatedly move over the same neighborhoods, additional significant flooding is possible.

An additional 2-4 inches is possible across South Florida through Thursday, with locally higher amounts where persistent storm bands develop. If this scenario develops, highly localized and concentrated rainfall maximums may approach 8-10 inches.

Not every community will experience renewed heavy rain, and additional rainfall totals will vary greatly from one community to the next.

Periods of heavy rain will remain possible through Thursday, with a lesser chance of additional storms into Friday. However, a gradual transition toward drier conditions is expected heading into the weekend. Rain chances should decrease Saturday and Sunday, bringing much-needed relief to flood-affected communities.

Floodwaters will be very slow to recede as ground soil remains fully saturated across South Florida.

All Miami-Dade County courts and Clerk of the Court and Comptroller's offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, due to heavy rain and widespread flooding across South Florida.

In a joint statement Wednesday night, Chief Judge Ariana Fajardo Orshan and Clerk of the Court and Comptroller Juan Fernandez-Barquin said the closures were ordered to keep residents and staff off hazardous roadways.

"The safety of the community and our judges and staff comes first," Fajardo Orshan and Fernandez-Barquin said. "We do not want anyone having to drive through flooding to have to come to court."

First appearance hearings will still be held on a weekend and holiday schedule.

Court and clerk officials said they will continue monitoring weather conditions and issue updates as more information becomes available.

Both Florida International University and Broward College have announced class cancellations on Thursday due to the continued rainfall and flooding across South Florida.

Broward College issued a statement saying that all classes at all of the college's campuses and centers will be canceled due to flooding throughout Broward County. They explained that it is due to "the expectation of continued rainfall and flooding."

FIU also announced that all classes and university operations will be suspended at all of its locations, including its campuses in Sweetwater, Biscayne Bay, and Miramar. They note in a statement about the closure that the FIU Health Ambulatory Care Center site for Baptist Health and Nicklaus Children's Ambulatory Surgery Center at MMC will remain open.

"The decision to close the university is being made out of an abundance of caution, as ongoing rainfall and localized flooding continue to impact roadways and travel conditions throughout the region. The safety of our students, faculty, and staff remains our highest priority. We ask all members of the university community to take the necessary precautions and avoid unnecessary travel. Please do not attempt to drive or walk through flooded roadways, and remain alert to changing weather conditions, downed power lines, and other potential hazards. We also ask that professors and supervisors communicate with students, faculty, and staff as needed regarding any academic or work-related matters affected by the closure," FIU said in a statement to CBS News Miami.

Both schools said it is unclear whether the campuses will remain closed on Friday, with FIU adding in its statement that a decision will be made Thursday based on the latest forecasts.

Students for both FIU and Broward College are asked to check their university communications emails for updates.

Heavy rainfall moving south into Miami-Dade County left streets submerged in Key Biscayne on Wednesday evening, prompting at least one resident to paddle a kayak down a flooded roadway while motorists navigated standing water measuring up to 9 inches deep.

Along West Heather Drive near Hampton Park and roughly two minutes from Key Biscayne K-8 Center, saturated ground and intense earlier downpours left neighborhood streets inundated. Standing water measured between 8 and 9 inches deep near the curb, pushing onto lawns as passing trucks sent wakes across the pavement.

While higher-profile trucks managed to navigate the flooded stretch, smaller passenger cars struggled—including one vehicle spotted with a damaged piece hanging from its undercarriage after driving through the deep water.

Local residents warned drivers against attempting to push through the submerged streets, citing the risk of water entering exhaust systems and stalling engines.

"I think a lot of people don't realize that if your exhaust goes underwater, the gas—what waterlocks the car," one Key Biscayne resident said. "So definitely would rather just walk outside. I think the risk of walking isn't too bad, so definitely just walk, I'd rather, I'd say."

Although rainfall had paused by Wednesday evening, officials continue to urge residents in Key Biscayne and across Miami-Dade County to remain indoors and avoid driving through flooded streets until standing water recedes.

Homeowners in parts of Dania Beach say they feel trapped inside their properties as persistent floodwaters submerge neighborhood streets and an overflowing lake creeps within feet of their back doors.

Standing water along local roadways reached ankle- to shin-deep levels on Wednesday evening, rising to knee-deep just around the corner—where several drivers became stranded earlier in the day. Abandoned vehicles remained parked along flooded front streets, while residents whose cars were spared kept them stationary rather than risk driving through high water.

Behind the properties, water from an adjacent lake pushed deep into backyards that had been dry just days earlier. One resident waded through waist-deep water overnight to tie a heavy-duty outdoor table to a tree so it would not float away, noting the rising water had stopped only a few feet shy of entering his house.

"I didn't know I was going to get a free swimming pool, but yeah, that's too much," the homeowner said. "The water, as you can see behind me, is like a few feet away from my house. So like one more day of rain, and that's it—the water is going to be inside."

With roadways impassable and standing water yet to recede, residents said daily routines have ground to a halt as they wait for municipal drainage crews to intervene.

"I'm really hoping that the city will show up, because that's the only thing that can save us," one resident said. "You buy your property, you want to live a good life, and you don't expect to see this."

City officials also reminded motorists that owners of any vehicles stalled or abandoned in floodwaters are responsible for arranging to have them towed.

Hours of persistent afternoon rain flooded major roadways in Cutler Bay on Wednesday, creating hazardous conditions for evening commuters and prompting tow trucks to respond to stranded vehicles.

Along Southwest 216th Street between Old Cutler Road and Southwest 87th Avenue, passing trucks and SUVs pushed wakes across the submerged roadway as drivers returning home from work encountered deep standing water that had not been there when they left Wednesday morning.

With tow trucks spotted working the area by early evening, local residents urged neighbors—especially those driving smaller sedans—to avoid the flooded corridor altogether.

"Whatever you do, if you live in the Cutler Bay area, do not come down 216th Street—especially if you have a small car," one resident warned. "You are going to be flooded, and you might have to get towed out of here."

Another resident echoed the warning, urging drivers to stay home after high water stalled vehicles and backed up evening traffic.

"Everybody keep your cars out of the road because it is messing up with the cars and making cars smoke," the resident said. "If you go down there far enough, it got us in a traffic jam. All this rain is not okay. Stay home, relax."

While the heaviest rainfall initially targeted Broward County on Tuesday night, bands of heavy rain shifted south into Miami-Dade County on Wednesday, inundating low-lying streets across Cutler Bay and surrounding communities.

The city of Fort Lauderdale has declared a state of emergency as stubborn floodwaters remain pooled across several neighborhoods, including Edgewood, where standing water has crept inside some homes despite around-the-clock pumping operations.

According to city officials, 13 vacuum trucks and 14 portable pumps have been strategically deployed across hard-hit areas, including Edgewood, with crews working 24-hour shifts over the next two days to drain submerged roadways.

"I bought a little blowup pool to put stuff in," Anna Rysedorph said.

Rysedorph said this is the ninth time her home has flooded.

"The water in here is all contaminated; it's just gross water from the outside," she said.

Waist-deep water pooled outside her front door. She questioned why her street, S.W. 32nd Court, frequently floods.

"They should fix this; there's no reason that we should live like this," Rysedorph said.

City officials said this area of Edgewood is not yet on the new pump system, though it is on the list to be added. The public works director estimated it could take at least a year before construction begins.

"Anytime you get an event similar to what happened last night and two rain bomb events where you have an extraordinary amount of rain in a very small matter of time, it doesn't matter what kind of system you have, it's inevitable," said Bradford Kaine, City of Fort Lauderdale public works director.

Public safety leaders urged residents to remain off flooded streets while cleanup and pumping efforts continue.

Fort Lauderdale's fire chief asked residents to immediately report any downed power lines by calling 911 and warned the public—especially children—to stay out of standing floodwaters due to contamination risks. The police chief echoed that message, urging drivers to stay home and avoid flooded areas.

To help residents protect their vehicles from rising water, the city is offering free parking on the second floor and above at the Riverwalk Center Garage through 9 a.m. Friday.

The streets of Hollywood were a flooded mess Wednesday, with cars stalled and tow trucks operating around the clock following heavy overnight rains.

"We've been nonstop since last night, 11 o'clock. We've got two trucks on the road. We've been going 24/7 since last night when the storm started," a tow truck driver said.

The city received 300 calls for help from midnight to 4 a.m., including several requests for assistance for people trapped in stranded vehicles.

"It looked like an apocalypse. Everything breaking down. Got cars in the middle of the street," Hollywood resident Bryan Hart said.

The city declared a state of emergency.

"I just want everyone to know that we are fully responding to this. We have all of our crews deployed, working to try to clear floodwaters where we can," Hollywood City Manager Raelyn Storey said.

Jose Figuerroa woke to severe flooding shortly after midnight.

"At 12:15, I woke up and went to the bathroom. I put my feet on the ground. It was what I was thinking: 'Did I spill water?' I turned on the light. There was a lake in here," Figuerroa said.

Figuerroa, who has mobility issues, attempted to clean up the water before a friend arrived to assist.

"All the leaves like ran into here. Trash everywhere. The bathroom started leaking through the roof, and I was up from 12:15 till 10 o'clock, sweeping the water and pushing it out," he said.

Streets remained submerged as night fell Wednesday in Fort Lauderdale's Melrose Manors and neighboring Melrose Park, capping a day of high-water rescues and emergency pumping operations after roughly a foot of rain inundated the southwest Fort Lauderdale communities.

Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue conducted dozens of water rescues across the city, including in Melrose Park and Melrose Manors. To clear the impassable roadways, city crews deployed portable pumping stations and vacuum trucks. Along Southwest First Street, a city worker measuring standing water in the middle of the roadway recorded a depth of 10 inches.

With water pooling deep enough to flood vehicles, many residents left their cars parked in their driveways and navigated the neighborhood on foot.

Barbara White, a Melrose Manor resident who cares for a disabled family member who needs to reach medical appointments, spent the day stranded inside her house—though she expressed relief that floodwaters did not breach it.

"I thank God I have a house to stay in," White said. "I feel like they are trying to do something. It's nobody's fault. We weren't expecting this much rain, but we are alright, and I thank God for that."

While the city of Fort Lauderdale has long-awaited plans to construct a modern stormwater drainage system for the flood-prone neighborhood, construction remains years away.

The Archdiocese of Miami has announced that it will make decisions on closing Catholic schools across South Florida on a "school-by-school basis" on Thursday, they said in a statement to CBS News Miami.

"We continue to monitor the current weather situation and will make any closure decisions on a school-by-school basis depending upon local conditions," the statement said.

Parents at any closed school will be informed directly, they said.

This comes after both Miami-Dade and Broward County Public Schools announced they will close all schools on Thursday due to heavy rain causing street flooding across South Florida.

Heavy overnight rainfall left block after block submerged in Fort Lauderdale's Melrose Manors neighborhood on Wednesday, trapping residents in their driveways and with standing water creeping up to front doorsteps.

Located west of Interstate 95 off Broward Boulevard, the neighborhood was inundated by ankle- to knee-deep water after roughly a foot of rain fell across parts of the city overnight.

While water levels approached the thresholds of several homes, residents faced an immediate obstacle simply trying to leave their properties, fearing that backing out of their driveways into the submerged streets would flood and ruin their vehicles—a scenario that has already stranded numerous drivers across Fort Lauderdale.

Melrose Manors lacks a modern stormwater drainage system, making the low-lying community chronically vulnerable to prolonged standing water after intense downpours.

For newer residents unfamiliar with the neighborhood's drainage limitations, waking up to flooded yards and impassable streets came as an alarming surprise.

Yaniel Contreras, who moved to Melrose Manors with his wife a couple of years ago, said he never anticipated seeing floodwaters surround his property.

"It's kind of scary. I don't want my house to get flooded," Contreras said. "This is a no-flood zone, so we did not expect this. It's crazy."

Officials continue to advise drivers across Fort Lauderdale to stay off flooded neighborhood streets until standing water recedes.

Miami-Dade County Public Schools will close all schools and district operations Thursday, Nov. 19 , due to the threat of additional heavy rainfall and flooding across South Florida.

The School Board of Miami-Dade County made the decision during a meeting Wednesday afternoon as the region continued to deal with widespread flooding following hours of torrential rain.

The announcement comes as Broward County Public Schools also confirmed that schools and district offices would remain closed Thursday for a second consecutive day because of severe flooding.

While Broward experienced some of the worst flooding, with nearly 12 inches of rain reported in parts of the county, Miami-Dade has also seen flooded streets, stranded vehicles and water entering homes in communities including Miami Gardens.

A flood watch remains in effect across South Florida through Thursday evening, with additional heavy downpours expected before conditions begin improving Friday.

The Miami-Dade closure is a precautionary measure as officials prepare for the possibility of worsening conditions.

With both Miami-Dade and Broward public schools closed Thursday, students across South Florida will remain home as the region braces for another round of potentially dangerous weather.

Persistent rainfall inundated major thoroughfares in Miami Beach on Wednesday afternoon, slowing traffic across Miami-Dade County as more intense storms threatened the region overnight.

In Miami Beach, standing water pooled along Collins Avenue between 22nd and 23rd Street, along Fifth Street near the MacArthur Causeway entrance, and near 11th Street. High water also slowed drivers along Biscayne Boulevard near Aventura Mall and along southbound Interstate 95 heading toward downtown Miami.

Despite the soggy conditions, tourists visiting Miami Beach said they were trying to make the best of their trips amid the wind, thunder, and downpours.

"This is crazy right now," said Jolene Bill, a tourist from Arizona. "All of this is going on, and we traveled here for this vacation. This is something right now."

"The wind, the rain," said Alexia Six, another tourist from Arizona. "Oh my God, this is unbelievable."

Dave Bawden, a tourist from Plymouth, England, said: "Believe it or not, in England we are used to this. But this is not what we expected on our holiday. It restricts what you can do."

CBS News Miami spoke with them on Collins Avenue at 23rd Street, where there was street flooding. Flooding was also reported on Fifth Street.

The city of Miami Beach said it was opening ten parking garages for residents who want to keep their vehicles away from the flooded streets. The garages will be open free of charge until 8 a.m. Friday.

Wildlife officers rescued more than 70 residents and between 20 and 30 pets from a severely flooded Hollywood apartment complex on Wednesday after an Instagram post alerting authorities to stranded neighbors sparked an hours-long evacuation effort.

Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission used high-profile vehicles throughout the day to navigate deep floodwaters leading into La Vue at Emerald Pointe Apartments, located near Sheridan Street and Northwest 40th Avenue.

According to FWC Capt. Jeff Carroll, an officer initially spotted a post on Instagram from a resident reporting they were trapped by the rising water—a tip that ultimately led rescue crews to dozens more stranded neighbors inside the complex.

Carroll said torrential rain that began Tuesday night left standing water roughly knee-deep inside ground-floor units, displacing numerous elderly residents and pet owners.

"There's a lot of families that are in a very rough spot right now that have lost everything," Carroll said. "We had a bad rainfall that started last night. In these houses, you've got water at about knee height. These are a lot of elderly families; you've got a lot of animals, things like that. Not a good situation."

Residents told CBS News Miami that floodwaters had been even higher earlier in the morning, submerging vehicles throughout the complex and seeping inside ground-floor units. Dozens of cars are expected to be total losses, and first-floor residents reported losing nearly all of their personal belongings.

items.title: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by a deepening tech rout
items.summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled more than 1,200 points, putting it on track for its second-worst day of the year.

scraped.title: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by a deepening tech rout
scraped.description: The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled more than 1,200 points, putting it on track for its second-worst day of the year.
scraped.h1: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by a deepening tech rout
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 20, 2026 / 3:57 PM EST / CBS News

Technology stocks plunged on Friday, dimming investor cheer over Anthropic's high-profile IPO this week amid mounting concerns about the health of the artificial intelligence sector.

The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,241 points, or 5.2%, to 22,638 shortly before the close of trading. That puts the tech-heavy index on track for its worst day since Nov. 5, when it tumbled 5.5%. The S&P 500 declined 3.2%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 1.5%.

Both the S&P 500 and Dow entered "correction" territory, meaning the indexes have fallen more than 10% from their most recent highs. The S&P 500 is set for its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the pandemic caused investors to sell in a panic.

Investors are fretting over the value of AI stocks, which drove much of Wall Street's gains earlier this year but are now driving the slide. Microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom led Friday's losses over concerns about a possible slowdown in data center construction and over tighter federal policies on exporting chips outside the U.S.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

The S&P 500's decline into correction territory was largely driven by investors selling AI-related companies, but the underlying U.S. economic and business fundamentals remain solid, said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email.

"It's impossible to know when any selloff will run its course, but history shows most moves like this don't turn into bear markets —only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 have done so," he said, referring to when stocks decline 20% or more from the market's most recent peak.

Thursday's big market debut for Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, fizzled on Friday, along with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14, although it remains above its IPO price of $83 per share.

As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic's stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive Facebook (now Meta) saw shortly after its May 2012 IPO.

Shares of Nvidia, considered practically synonymous with the AI boom, are falling for the ninth day in the last 10, down 13% in late Friday trading.

The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI buildout, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang , its co-founder and former CEO. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has shed more than 25% of its value.

Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.4%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 2.5%.

Edited by Alain Sherter

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

items.title: Trump touts relationships with Putin and Xi after historic Asia trip
items.summary: The president met with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin.

scraped.title: Trump touts relationships with Putin and Xi after historic Asia trip
scraped.description: The president met with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Trump touts relationships with Putin and Xi after historic Asia trip
scraped.body_text:
The president met with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin.

President Donald Trump touted his relationships with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday following his trip to Asia earlier this week, during which he called Putin his "friend."

"I have a fantastic relationship with Putin. That's a very good thing. I have fantastic relationship with President Xi. That's a good thing. And our country is safe because of that," Trump said during a Friday news conference.

Immediately following the trip, Trump didn't have much to say about his meeting with Xi and Putin and didn't take questions from reporters afterward.

But he told NBC News after the meeting he thought it was a "12" on a scale of 10.

"I think it was a 12. On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12," NBC News reported Trump saying. "It went great ... Fantastic relationships built."

China's state-run Xinhua News Agency said Xi described the meeting between the three leaders as "positive, constructive and fruitful," but did not quote him directly.

It also reported that in his one-on-one meeting with Trump before the three leaders met, Xi urged bilateral cooperation on issues including artificial intelligence but also warned against the creation of "turbulence" over the issue of Taiwan.

The three leaders committed in a joint statement released after their meeting to reforming the United Nations, increasing the supply of refined petroleum products and engaging in dialogue over nuclear weapon proliferation.

Trump also met with Putin and said they had a "long discussion today," including talking about Russia's war with Ukraine, now approaching its fifth year.

"I think things are happening. I think that he -- and I hope the other side -- would like to see an end to that war," Trump said.

Trump was in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit. He first stopped in Manila, where he participated in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region and was expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

items.title: New government report sparks concern over potential cyberattack on US food supply
items.summary: A new government report is warning that the federal government is susceptible to threats to the nation's food supply.

scraped.title: New government report sparks concern over potential cyberattack on US food supply
scraped.description: A new government report is warning that the federal government is susceptible to threats to the nation's food supply.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: New government report sparks concern over potential cyberattack on US food supply
scraped.body_text:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office is warning that the nation's food sector is increasingly susceptible to cybersecurity threats.

In a Thursday report , the federal watchdog group said both the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Food and Drug Administration had "reported having limited resources to address critical cybersecurity activities, such as information sharing and cybersecurity emergency preparedness activities."

The GAO specifically noted that although the agencies "have taken steps to improve cybersecurity," they "haven't conducted emergency response scenarios to prepare for potential cyberattacks on the sector since 2024."

"Both agencies reported that a lack of resources and staffing hindered their ability to meet all the requirements," the agency said in a blog post Thursday, published in tandem with the report's release. "By assessing whether there are opportunities to reprioritize or if there is a need for additional resources, the agencies would be better positioned to provide cybersecurity-related assistance and resources to the sector and help mitigate potential disruption of the food supply chain, which could lead to significant economic and environmental impacts."

The report comes a week before Thanksgiving and following a spate of prominent tech outages , including a cyber breach affecting some JPMorganChase customers' personal information, like emails and addresses.

The country's largest bank said "third parties who provide services" to the bank "were the target of a cyberattack," and some customers' info was accessed.

Other high-profile companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, Apple, and Marriott have also reported recent, separate tech outages, as well as the National Security Agency's internal system, which sends classified messages and reported technical issues this week.

In October, cyberattackers targeted grocery stores and supermarkets in France. French authorities blamed Iran for conducting the attacks, which cranked up the temperature on supermarket refrigerators, causing food to spoil and sparking fires.

The GAO has issued recommendations for changes to the Department of Health and Human Services and the USDA. They include conducting cybersecurity emergency preparedness exercises and simulations, sharing any potential threats or vulnerabilities with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and "developing planning documents for coordinated action in the event of cybersecurity disasters or emergencies."

"The food and agriculture sector is one of the nation's 16 critical infrastructure sectors and is essential to the nation's health, security, and economy," the agency wrote in its blog post Thursday. "The sector is reliant on information technology to produce, process, and deliver products, and faces increasing cybersecurity-related risks. Cyberattacks could result in unsafe food and could erode public trust and faith in the food supply."

24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

scraped.title: Russia complains of ‘new Iron Curtain’ as Estonia shuts its borders
scraped.description: Tallinn’s decision to shut road border crossings comes after an attack on a drone manufacturer.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Russia complains of ‘new Iron Curtain’ as Estonia shuts its borders
scraped.body_text:
Tallinn’s decision to shut road border crossings comes after an attack on a drone manufacturer.

Save

Share

Moscow has accused Estonia of planning to build a “new Iron Curtain”, and promised to respond, after the small Baltic nation formally decided to close all border crossings with Russia to the east and south.

Estonia’s government on Friday approved a preliminary six-month closure of its road border crossings from December 1, and will decide next year whether to extend it.

Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova told a news briefing in Moscow that “should Tallinn proceed with these plans, our country will take the necessary political and diplomatic measures in response to safeguard its national interests.”

“Such moves are tantamount to attempts to erect a new Iron Curtain under the false pretence of some sort of threat from the East,” Zakharova added.

In Tallinn on Friday, Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna described the border closure as “an important measure”.

“It will reduce opportunities to exploit cross-border movement to recruit people, conduct influence operations, organise acts of sabotage or circumvent sanctions,” he said.

Estonia, a NATO and EU member and a staunch supporter of Ukraine, first announced the border closure earlier this month, accusing Russia of being behind an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

The Kremlin denied the accusation at the time, saying it was part of what it called a pattern of false allegations levelled against Moscow by European countries.

Estonia’s northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations ⁠Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.

Of the 760,000 people who crossed the Estonia-Russia border this year, 307,000 were Russian nationals, 175,000 were Estonian citizens and 54,000 held Finnish passports, Estonian ‌police ‌data showed.

Rail freight is not affected by the road closure, but remains subject to strict customs checks, Estonia said.

scraped.title: Israeli drone attacks kill seven Palestinians in central Gaza
scraped.description: Drones cause ‘fear and panic’ among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite ‘ceasefire’.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Israeli drone attacks kill seven Palestinians in central Gaza
scraped.body_text:
Buzzing of drones causes ‘fear and panic’ among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite ‘ceasefire’.

Save

Share

Israeli attacks have killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central part of the Gaza Strip, as attacks continue despite a “ceasefire” agreement.

Four Palestinians were killed on Friday when an Israeli drone struck the Bureij refugee camp in Deir el-Balah, medical sources told Al Jazeera.

Witnesses said the drone targeted a group of civilians within the camp.

Separately, a medical source at al-Awda Hospital reported the arrival of the body of a Palestinian killed by an Israeli drone strike in the Nuseirat refugee camp.

Two Palestinians were also killed when an Israeli drone struck civilians near the entrance to the city of Deir el-Balah.

Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said the injured were brought to hospitals in central Gaza that operate at reduced capacity due to a lack of medical supplies and staff.

Mahmoud added that drones were “causing fear and panic” among Palestinians in Gaza.

“People cannot run simple errands because of the ongoing fear of being attacked and killed on the road,” he said.

The buzzing of drones adds to the sound of explosions from home demolitions and to that of fighter jets, our correspondent added.

The Israeli army on Friday carried out demolition operations near areas under its control in the al-Shuja’iya neighbourhood in the eastern part of Gaza City using explosive-laden drones.

It also carried out three large-scale demolitions near the “Yellow Line”, east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.

By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).

Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and homes in the Gaza Strip amid ongoing military operations and disputes over the “ceasefire” line.

Israel has repeatedly violated the so-called “ceasefire” agreement that entered into force on October 10, 2025.

Since then, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza. Since the genocidal war began in October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured 176,000 others.

Separately on Friday, which marks World Children’s Day, Palestinian prisoner groups said that around 350 Palestinian children were being held in Israeli prisons, where they face torture, starvation and deprivation of medical care, education, and family visits.

The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society said dozens of children from Gaza were detained during the war, but enforced disappearance and restrictions on visits have made it impossible to determine their numbers.
