scraped.h1: Nepali cricket fans in Qatar want to see their team competing with the best
scraped.body_text:
As thousands from Qatar’s Nepali community watch their team play, they hope for the team to rise in global rankings.

Save

Share

Nepal cricket fans celebrate their team’s global rise

Doha, Qatar – On a warm Friday afternoon in Qatar, the country’s only international cricket stadium was a sea of Nepal’s uniquely triangular crimson and deep blue flags.

Nepal’s supporters arrived with flags draped across their shoulders, held them aloft to flutter in the breeze, cheering every delivery and waving them wildly in celebration of every wicket.

The events on the field seemed nearly inconsequential against the loud cheers of the thousands of fans who had filled the West End International Cricket Stadium on the outskirts of the Qatari capital, as the nation with the world’s highest mountain faced the most powerful force in cricket.

Nepal were bowling first against India A – India’s second XI – in their first group match of the Asian Cricket Council’s (ACC) Rising Star Asia Cup 2026 in Qatar.

Indian captain Tilak Varma and his batting partner Kumar Kushagra kept finding boundaries. Nepal’s bowlers faced the wrath and their fielders could barely keep up.

But the noise in the stands barely subsided.

The supporters followed every ball closely, their attention firmly focused on the team they rarely get to watch up close, especially living thousands of kilometres from home.

Qatar is home to at least 367,000 Nepalis, according to the Non-Resident Nepali Association of Qatar, making them the Gulf country’s third-biggest diaspora community.

Pradeep Kumar Yadav was one of the few thousand Nepali fans who were on a mission to provide vociferous support to their cricket team this weekend.

Yadav arrived at the stadium with seven Nepali friends, who had been planning to come as soon as the tournament’s fixtures were announced.

“This is our first time watching Nepal play outside our country,” Yadav told Al Jazeera.

For Nepal’s sizeable diaspora in Qatar, the cricket team provides a reason to gather around a national passion and often draws large crowds.

The supporters are happy to travel to stadiums to back a team that has risen through the international ranks over the past decade.

Nepal’s modern cricketing journey can be traced back to 1996, when the country became a member of the International Cricket Council (ICC) and the men’s team first competed in an international tournament.

The turning point came when the South Asian nation qualified for its first ICC event at the T20 World Cup 2014.

Soon, Nepal’s players were being noticed on the international stage and leg-spinner Sandeep Lamichhane’s selection in major T20 leagues around the world raised the country’s cricketing profile.

Back home, cricket has spread far beyond the capital Kathmandu into towns and villages, backed by efforts to build the sport’s structure at grassroots level.

For Qatar-based fan Himmat Joshi, the Nepali cricket team’s success has resulted in a sharp rise in the popularity of the sport.

“I feel a lot of happiness,” Joshi said while watching the team play against India. “In the past, fewer people followed it but it has grown over the years,” he said.

Mohammad Zahoor, who was among the thousands in the stands, sees the national team’s progress as a source of pride. He describes the Nepalis as a hardworking nation and says the country is building a domestic cricket system capable of competing with higher-ranked international teams.

“There is a lot of pride in seeing Nepali cricketers represent the country. We are a passionate people,” Zahoor said.

The ambitions extend beyond the T20 format.

Nepal’s supporters want to see the country compete against established cricketing nations and eventually earn a place among the teams playing Test cricket.

For Zahoor, defeating a Test-playing country would be an important step towards that ambition.

He also hopes cricket will become part of Nepal’s international identity, alongside its reputation for mountaineering, the Himalayas and being home to Mount Everest.

“Nepalis play the game like a festival,” Zahoor explained.

“Our expectations and hopes are that one day Nepali people are known for their cricket as they are known for their culture of mountaineering and Mount Everest.”

At the stadium in Qatar, the flags, chants and sheer number of supporters reflected that ambition.

In the end, India broke their hearts with a crushing 306-run win.

But it mattered little to the thousands cheering on their team, despite the loss.

For some, including Yadav and his friends, it offered a unique opportunity to watch Nepal play abroad.

Others were simply happy to get a chance to follow a team that has given the country, and its passionate supporters, a growing presence in international cricket.

items.title: Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation
items.summary: Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

scraped.title: Renowned Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's anti-corruption foundation
scraped.description: Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.
scraped.h1: Russian ornithologist jailed over donation to Navalny foundation
scraped.body_text:
Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

He lives in Israel , while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arctic birds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with her colleagues focused largely on science: "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

This article was originally published in Russian.

items.title: Repression against Iranian lawyers increases
items.summary: At least 135 lawyers in Iran have been subjected to repressive measures over the past year. UN experts warn that this seriously jeopardizes the right of those accused to trial in a constitutional court.

scraped.title: Iran: Lawyers increasingly under pressure
scraped.description: At least 135 lawyers in Iran have been subjected to repressive measures over the past year. UN experts warn that this seriously jeopardizes the right of those accused to trial in a constitutional court.
scraped.h1: Iran: Lawyers increasingly under pressure
scraped.body_text:
At least 135 lawyers in Iran have been subjected to repressive measures over the past year. UN experts warn that this seriously jeopardizes the right of those accused to trial in a constitutional court.

UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers. They warn that limiting access to legal representation increases the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials.

"Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts said in a statement in mid-November.

They said that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling. In January and February 2026, 23 lawyers, including five women, were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests .

A current example is the case of Amirsalar Davoudi, a human rights lawyer who was arrested in October in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, where he was defending a client in the Revolutionary Court. According to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), he was taken to hospital on November 9 after suffering a heart attack in custody.

"There is a long history to the persecution of and coercive measures taken against lawyers," Sina Yousefi, a 41-year-old lawyer and human rights activist, told DW.

In October 2022, Yousefi was arrested by security forces in Tabriz during the nationwide "Woman Life Freedom" protests . Later, he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for "propaganda against the system." He has since left Iran, and now lives in the German capital Berlin.

"The pressure was already increasing on lawyers back then, because they were undertaking the defense of people who were arrested and publicly expressing their support for the demonstrators ," said Yousefi. "The security services, judiciary, and criminal prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted mechanisms to move against independent lawyers."

Even renowned and internationally known lawyers such as Nasrin Sotoudeh, who was co-awarded the Sakharov Prize in 2012, have been affected by this repression. In 2026, Sotoudeh was awarded the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize after being repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

Yousefi said arrests and threats against lawyers working on political and human rights cases not only curtailed the rights of those accused to a defense, but also discouraged other lawyers from accepting such briefs. This, he added, compromised the fairness of trials.

Criminal proceedings have also been instigated, or other measures taken, against lawyers who undertook to represent demonstrators. Comments on social media about the violation of civil rights can also be cited as grounds for investigation and judicial proceedings.

Yousefi also warned against tightening restrictions on a person's right to choose their own lawyer. According to the note to Article 48 of Iran's Code of Criminal Procedure , for people arrested on certain charges, access to lawyers of their own choosing is already restricted during the investigation phase. Defendants must resort to lawyers approved by the head of the judiciary. In some cases, even these lawyers are not granted access to all the files and evidence.

According to Yousefi, in many cases in which charges have been brought against demonstrators, lawyers have only been granted access to the files "when the preliminary investigations have been concluded and the evidence for the prosecution has been gathered — including confessions made during their imprisonment." Even then, he said, "their access to the records is limited and they have little time to prepare the defense."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"In many cases," Yousefi added, "the judges ascribe greater importance to reports by security agents than to the defense. Verdicts are handed down predominantly on the basis of this."

Shabnam Moinipour, the program director at the Center for Supporters of Human Rights (CSHR) in the UK, sees the independence of the bar as a fundamental precondition for the effective defense of citizens. The organization monitors the situation of lawyers in Iran, documenting violations of their rights, and following up at an international level.

"A lawyer must be able to call into question the charges brought by the public prosecutor and the credibility of the security agencies' reports without fear of criminal prosecution," Moinipour told DW. "Because when a lawyer's freedom and professional activity are threatened, their client's right to defense is impaired."

In Moinipour's view, when the decision as to which lawyers are approved is made by the most senior representative of the same court authority, it raises serious questions about the independence of the bar.

"This restriction has psychological as well as legal consequences," she stressed. "For the accused, it may reinforce a sense of being unprotected, as well as feelings of fear and mistrust. It can also prevent them from disclosing details of threats, torture, and illegal behavior."

Moinipour considers this practice incompatible with Iran's obligations as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. International law stipulates that people must have immediate access to a lawyer of their own choosing, be able to communicate with them in confidence and be supplied with sufficient means to mount a defense.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Referring to a joint report by the Tehran-based Defenders of Human Rights Center and the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI), as well as the recent statement by UN human rights experts, Moinipour said: "Even without mass arrests, the actions taken against a limited number of lawyers can send a threatening message to others and restrict their professional activity. This phenomenon is described as a chilling or deterrent effect."

However, Moinipour stressed that, despite this pressure, "many lawyers in Iran continue to defend the rights of their clients and accept the risk of arrest, criminal prosecution, and professional restrictions. In doing so, they are prepared, if necessary, to pay a high price for this resistance."

This article was originally written in Persian.

items.title: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
items.summary: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

scraped.title: At COP31, disinformation and disagreements over climate facts slow action
scraped.description: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?
scraped.h1: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
scraped.body_text:
Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya , an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023 .

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next " global stocktake ," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report cover climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks , expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action . And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment."

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

items.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
items.summary: A young Canadian woman travelled to Turkey after graduating from medical school. In her last days there, she fell ill and died within hours. Authorities there blame food poisoning, but a joint investigation by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed 12 similar deaths and a different poison at work.

scraped.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else | CBC News
scraped.description: A young Canadian woman travelled to Turkey after graduating from medical school. In her last days there, she fell ill and died within hours. Authorities there blame food poisoning, but a joint investigation by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed 12 similar deaths and a different poison at work.
scraped.h1: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
scraped.body_text:
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.

A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.

But for her family, that doesn't add up.

A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.

The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.

"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."

The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)

With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.

They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.

The next morning, they woke violently ill.

The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.

She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.

"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."

They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.

‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)

That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.

"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"

Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.

"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"

Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)

The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.

As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?

Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.

"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."

The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.

Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.

Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.

But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.

Safe extermination of bedbugs

Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.

"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said

The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.

In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.

Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.

In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)

Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.

"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."

We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.

"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."

Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)

In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.

Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.

Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.

The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.

Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.

She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.

Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)

She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.

"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.

"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."

She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.

"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."

Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.

"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."

She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.

"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)

We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.

One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.

We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.

The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.

That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?

We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.

We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.

"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.

Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)

He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.

The extermination company is called Wolves.

A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.

Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.

The employee was cautious on the phone.

He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.

"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."

Deaths of Quebec women in Thailand may have been caused by pesticide

Phosphine pesticide used to kill bedbugs causes Fort McMurray baby's death

We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.

Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.

The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.

Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.

We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.

"Of course," she said.

A life without her

The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.

While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.

"Those who are gone never come back."

Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.

"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.

"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."

In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."

After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.

items.title: 2 U.S. veterans, who both survived Pearl Harbor attack, die on same day
items.summary: Two former U.S service members who were stationed at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii when Japan attacked in 1941 died on the same day last week, it has been learned.

scraped.title: 2 U.S. veterans, who both survived Pearl Harbor attack, die on same day | CBC News
scraped.description: Two former U.S service members who were stationed at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii when Japan attacked in 1941 died on the same day last week, it has been learned.
scraped.h1: 2 U.S. veterans, who both survived Pearl Harbor attack, die on same day
scraped.body_text:
Two former U.S service members who were stationed at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii when Japan attacked in 1941 died on the same day last week, it has been learned.

Gebhard (Geb) Galle, died on Saturday at his home in Moses Lake, Wash., according to his daughter, Lynda Palmer. He was 105.

Galle died the same day as the oldest known Pearl Harbor survivor, Freeman Johnson, of Centerville, Mass., who was 106.

Galle and Johnson were among the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, when Japan attacked — killing just over 2,400 Americans and drawing the U.S. into the Second World War.

The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names since the December 2025 death of Ira (Ike) Schab, who was 105.

The American Legion commended Galle and Johnson as "two members of a generation whose courage and sacrifice will forever be part of our nation's history," in a post on X.

Galle was serving aboard the battleship USS Nevada, while Freeman was with the cruiser USS St. Louis at the time of the attack, the veterans' organization noted.

Freeman Johnson looks down at his navy cap during an interview at his home in Centerville, Mass., on May 6. (Charles Krupa/The Associated Press)

Galle was born in Germany. He came to North Dakota with his family as a child and joined the U.S. navy in 1939 at age 18.

He was a machinist's mate aboard the Nevada, and was waiting below deck to be taken ashore for church services on Dec. 7, 1941. He looked out of a porthole and saw planes approaching.

A torpedo struck the ship, allowing water to enter, but officers were able to get it moving, the navy said. The ship was attacked again, causing more leaks in the hull and fires. The Nevada ran aground.

Galle could not see what was happening.

"Of course, we felt a couple jolts, and that's when we got hit with the torpedo, and we had a few bomb hits," he told the Columbia Basin Herald, a newspaper based in Moses Lake, in 2020.

"After we were beached and everything, and we got up to topside, then we saw all the mess that took place," including the capsized USS Oklahoma and the partially submerged USS Arizona, he said.

"A pretty sad lookout," Galle said.

Galle was reassigned to the USS Northampton. That ship came under fire on Nov. 30, 1942, by Japanese torpedoes during the Battle of Tassafaronga.

Galle told the Basin Herald he was ordered to leave a hatch closed behind four sailors who would've been trapped when the ship was sinking. The officer left, but Galle defied the order, opening the hatch. He closed and secured it after the sailors escaped.

"He heard those guys pounding on the roof of the hatch," Palmer said. "He went to open it up, and the senior officer walked by and said, 'No, leave it closed, because we don't want water to get in there because the ship might go down.'"

The Northampton sank, and Galle and other sailors spent more than a day adrift in life rafts before they were rescued.

Canadians mark Remembrance Day across the country

His "courage under fire" in that incident, as well as his having fought in 19 of 20 Pacific naval engagements, was noted in a 2025 letter from then-acting Chief of Naval Operations Adm. James Kilby, marking Galle's 104th birthday.

"Your humility, quick thinking and selfless actions remain a shining example of Navy valour," Kilby wrote.

In December 2016, Galle attended a 75th anniversary service at Pearl Harbor to honour and commemorate the USS Nevada and those who served on it. A total of 76 sailors and marines lost their lives as a result of that attack, the navy said.

After the war, Galle got married and opened a refrigeration and air-conditioning business in Grafton, N.D. He then served as a civil engineer with the air force and then later worked for the Army Corps of Engineers. He retired in the 1980s.

Johnson's death was confirmed by one of his daughters, Diane Johnson.

An explosion erupts at the Naval Air Station on Ford Island, as the USS Shaw explodes in the centre background during the 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor. The USS Nevada is also visible in the middle background, with its bow headed toward the left. (Fox Photos/Getty Images)

Johnson was working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack occurred. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn't hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes.

"While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn't see anything, absolutely nothing," said Johnson.

Descendants say reviving Japanese Canadian veterans' Legion rights historical wrong

Trump to Japan's PM: 'Why didn’t you tell me about Pearl Harbor?'

While Johnson didn't see the Pearl Harbor attack, he was witness to other historic moments during the war.

He helped commission the USS Iowa and recalled the battleship's preparations in November 1943 ahead of transporting President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin.

He also witnessed the war's end while aboard the Iowa. He was on its mast on Sept. 2, 1945, watching the surrender ceremonies about a mile away on the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay.

"I could see the boats coming up with the marines escorting the Japanese onto the ship and sitting around a table," he said. "It was all over."

We say goodbye to another one of our treasured heroes! Freeman Johnson, one of the oldest remaining survivors of the attack on Pearl Harbor, has died at the age of 106. Johnson passed away on November 14, 2026 at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. On December 7, 1941, he was among an estimated 87,000 military personnel stationed on Oahu when Japan launched its surprise attack on Pearl Harbor. Serving aboard the USS St. Louis, Johnson was working below deck on a boiler when the attack began. He later recalled that he heard and saw none of the chaos unfolding above him. “While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing,” he told The Associated Press in a May 2026 interview. His remarkable military career continued beyond Pearl Harbor. Johnson helped commission the USS Iowa, served aboard the battleship during its preparations to transport President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the 1943 Tehran Conference, and witnessed one of history’s defining moments: Japan’s formal surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945. From the attack on Pearl Harbor to the end of World War II, Freeman Johnson lived through a pivotal chapter in American history. Rest in peace, Sir! We thank you for your service! #WeRememberThem

For all the attention to Pearl Harbor, the gruff Johnson, who was known for his cackling laugh and mischievous smile, didn't see it as one of the defining moments in his life.

Those would have been getting married after the war to his late wife and having three daughters. He worked for years in a machinist shop, then in a convenience store and, finally, delivering meals to seniors. He finally retired from all work at age 90.

With files from CBC News

items.title: Tenants in Madrid say Toronto-based Brookfield is pricing them out of formerly public housing
items.summary: Canadian investment firms, led by Toronto-based Brookfield, have become central targets in Spain's Nov. 29 election fight over housing affordability. Long-term Madrid tenants living in former public housing allege Brookfield plans to let their rent-controlled leases expire and sell their apartments at unaffordable market prices.

scraped.title: Tenants in Madrid say Toronto-based Brookfield is pricing them out of formerly public housing | CBC News
scraped.description: Canadian investment firms, led by Toronto-based Brookfield, have become central targets in Spain's Nov. 29 election fight over housing affordability. Long-term Madrid tenants living in former public housing allege Brookfield plans to let their rent-controlled leases expire and sell their apartments at unaffordable market prices.
scraped.h1: Tenants in Madrid say Toronto-based Brookfield is pricing them out of formerly public housing
scraped.body_text:
At a Madrid apartment complex just outside the city's centre, red maple leaves hang upside down in windows along with defiant posters urging Canadian investment money to get out of their neighbourhood.

"They are pushing us out of our houses," said Rafael Cuadrado, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.

The main target of the residents' wrath is Toronto-based Brookfield Corporation.

A sign on a window of a Madrid apartment accuses Toronto-based Brookfield of treating tenants unfairly. In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield said it complies with all 'applicable Spanish tenancy legislation, including statutory tenant protections and extension requirements.' (Jason Ho/CBC)

One of Canada's premier financial and investment institutions, Brookfield owns 900 units in Cuadrado's residential complex, along with approximately 4,100 others around the Spanish capital.

Cuadrado and other residents accuse Brookfield of planning to let their leases expire and then flip their homes for market prices that few here can afford. He says several of his neighbours have already received notices from Brookfield's management company informing them their tenancies will not be extended.

CBC News has seen one letter sent to a tenant who was told their expiring lease would not be renewed and they would have to turn over the keys to their apartment.

It's not illegal, but the residents say it's unfair.

"Our daughter came here when she was two years old. This is our first house ... so this is our life," Cuadrado told CBC News in his living room.

Many of the residents are long-time tenants who moved into the buildings when they used to be part of Madrid's public housing stock. Most pay rents well below the current market rate, as a succession of lease extensions and government-mandated rent caps have kept their outlay relatively low.

Raphael Cuadrado lives in a Madrid apartment complex owned by Brookfield, one of Canada's top investment firms. He and other residents fear the company plans to flip their units when their leases expire. (Jason Ho/CBC)

Cuadrado says he pays 930 euros a month for his 800-square-foot, three-bedroom apartment. The unit would likely fetch about 1,500 euros on the open market.

"Why do we have to leave our house because there is a big investment company coming from abroad to get a profit [from] us?" he said. "No way."

Clashes in Spain as millions protest nation's housing crisis

Anger over housing in Spain has hit a breaking point.

The eviction of Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal in late September, after the 87-year-old woman was unable to pay a hefty rent increase, sent protesters into the streets. Authorities evicted her on the back of a stretcher and she died in hospital a few weeks later.

Her eviction prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an election for Nov. 29, with housing the central issue.

Spain's public unions, which allied with the tenants, are casting money from institutional investors, such as pension plans, as one of the primary villains. And some of them are Canadian.

"'Vulture funds' are what they call them," said Alicia Del Rio, who is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid (Madrid Tenants Union), one of the country's most prominent advocates for renters.

Del Rio blames a succession of cash-strapped Spanish governments for laying out the welcome mat for foreign investors, who she says have in turn treated Spanish residential properties as a commodity to be flipped, with little regard for the people living in them.

Alicia Del Rio is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid, Spain's most prominent tenants union. (Jason Ho/CBC)

"[The government] gave the message, 'Welcome to Spain, this is going to be your paradise.'"

Canadian retirement funds and investment firms are designed to seek out safe returns — wherever they can find them. And Spain is seen as an attractive place to grow that money.

Along with Brookfield, Canada Pension Plan Investments has a roughly 900-million-euro portfolio ($1.4 billion Cdn) in the Spanish housing sector, although it's focused on student housing rather than residential homes. It owns approximately 13,000 dorm-type beds across Spain and Portugal, concentrated in cities with large universities.

In a statement to CBC News, CPP said its investments help "expand the overall supply of housing available to students without removing existing homes from the conventional residential market."

HOOPP — Health Care of the Ontario Pension Plan — owns approximately 700 million euros ($1.1 billion Cdn) worth of Spanish properties, including 27 residential buildings and 2,300 Madrid homes.

The Spanish tenant unions haven't raised any specific concerns about HOOPP's activities or its properties.

Whether foreign investment firms are cornering the country's housing market has become one of Spain's most fiercely debated issues.

Numbers from the Bank of Spain say institutional investors control only a tiny share — roughly two per cent — of the country's total housing stock.

The tenant unions, however, say the fact that many of those properties used to be public, non-market housing for middle- or lower-income families matters far more than their share of the national total.

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears at a campaign rally in Palma de Mallorca on Nov. 14, ahead of the Nov. 29 general election. (Francisco Ubilla/Reuters)

They also claim that the concentration of apartments in central areas of cities gives companies like Brookfield outsized power to drive up rents across entire neighbourhoods.

Brookfield used to be chaired by Prime Minister Mark Carney, but he had left the company more than a year before it bought the Spanish homes in March 2026 from U.S. private equity giant Blackstone.

Blackstone held the buildings for 13 years. Residents claim Brookfield's intention is to sell the apartments once their existing leases finish.

Residents of the Madrid building told CBC News that when Brookfield eventually puts their apartments on the open market, they believe they could fetch upward of 600,000 euros apiece — a price few of them can pay.

"It is a constant anguish that is affecting our mental health," said Yutzy Fany Vargas Jimenez, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.

In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield says any allegation that it is forcing people out of their homes is false.

"We comply with all applicable tenancy laws and tenant protections, and allegations that we terminate rental contracts in breach of these protections are inaccurate," said the statement.

None of the residents that CBC News spoke to had suggested Brookfield had cut short an existing lease. Rather, their concerns were about what will happen when their current tenancy contracts expire.

"We are working closely with our local operating partner, to engage with residents and address their concerns, while continuing to invest in the maintenance and quality of these homes and providing opportunities for residents who wish to become homeowners," the Brookfield statement continued.

The company didn't explicitly address whether it plans to terminate leases when current contracts expire, as the residents claim. However, the company did say it will review individual tenancy matters on a case-by-case basis.

Residents of a Madrid apartment complex say Brookfield intends to force them out of their homes when their leases expire. The company told CBC News that all of its rental arrangements in Spain 'reflect the applicable Spanish legal framework, including statutory requirements governing lease duration.' (Jason Ho/CBC)

The cost of housing has become a central issue in Spain's upcoming election, although the roots of the problem can be traced back almost two decades.

Sara Herrero, vice-dean for academic planning and financial management at EAE Madrid business school, says after the 2008 global financial crisis, Spain was broke and its government turned to private capital to bail it out.

"The situation was really horrible," Herrero recalled, as governments and municipalities were forced to unload real estate they had on their balance sheets.

She said at the time, international funds were among the only buyers willing to inject billions of euros into the Spanish economy, helping banks clean up their toxic debt.

"What if they didn't come? What would have happened with these many residential houses if these supposed 'vulture funds' didn't come to Spain?" she said.

"They were doing a legal thing."

Sara Herrero is vice-dean of academic planning and financial management at EAE Madrid, one of Spain's top business schools. (Jason Ho/CBC)

But recently, property values in the country have soared, rising 34 per cent in the past five years.

"The problem is the basic economic problem of supply and demand," Herrero said. "It's the perfect storm of low salaries, high population growth and high taxes."

The Bank of Spain also estimates upward of 300,000 homes have been converted to short-term tourism rentals, further displacing long-term tenants.

The left-wing government of Prime Minister Sanchez is trying to harness the housing anger to help with his re-election bid — even though the price hikes have all happened under his watch.

People in Madrid take part in a 24-hour nationwide general strike on Nov. 11 demanding wages that allow access to what demonstrators say is decent housing. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)

Sanchez even appeared to give tacit support to the unions leading the general strike, as he passed tenant-friendly decrees that would likely be reversed if he fails to get re-elected.

His opponents on the political right, the People's Party and the far-right VOX, accused Sanchez of creating the crisis by passing legislation that made it hard for landlords to stay profitable, thereby discouraging new supply.

The latest opinion polls in Spain continue to favour a right-of-centre coalition taking power after Nov. 29, although they also indicate Sanchez's party has shown some recent momentum.

Tenant Raphael Cuadrado says he has repeatedly written to the Canadian Embassy in Madrid, hoping someone there can help residents who are worried about their future.

So far, he says he has not received a reply.

"This is day-by-day fighting, and this is not a life," he said.

In a statement to CBC News, Global Affairs Canada said any questions about Brookfield and its activities in Spain should be directed at the company.

Foreign correspondent

Chris Brown is a foreign correspondent based in the CBC’s London bureau. Previously in Moscow, Chris has a passion for great stories and has travelled all over Canada and the world to find them.
