scraped.title: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
scraped.description: The 287(g) immigration enforcement program funnels millions in federal dollars to local law enforcement with few strings attached. In Texas, cash-strapped police departments are spending the money on things like new equipment and vehicles.
scraped.author: Josh Hinkle, David Barer, Arezow Doost, Grace Reader, Dalton Huey, and Matt Grant
scraped.h1: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

Co-published with KXAN and The Texas Tribune

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

This article is co-published with KXAN and The Texas Tribune as part of an initiative to report on state and federal efforts to restrict local control.

Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing.

His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement.

“I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000.

It stands to earn much more.

Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year.

Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key incentive for local governments across the country has long been the funding that comes with participation .

The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments.

The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time spent,” he said.

And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature” could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and money for overtime.

“How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner John Moore asked.

“Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.

Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it difficult to pull away from the program in the future.

“I’m concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of these small police departments,” she said.

In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations, in addition to immigration work.

The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and “fleet purchases.”

Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our everyday job,” Fowler said.

Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets dangerous criminal offenders.

Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN’s questions about the department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by phone, email and in person.

“We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie Galloway, the only official to respond.

Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money is spent.

KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300 people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60 days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if an agreement is terminated.

That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.

Between the end of April and mid-June, it made two.

Local law enforcement agencies that join forces with ICE can choose among three models, two of which focus on identifying people already in jail who may be subject to deportation.

Trump revived the third kind, called the task force model, at the beginning of his second term. Task force agreements often worry civil and immigrants’ rights groups because of the model’s problematic track record: ICE started phasing them out in 2012, after Department of Justice investigations revealed that sheriff’s offices participating in the model had committed civil rights violations.

But task force agreements can also be lucrative.

Agencies can receive federal reimbursement for salaries, overtime and benefits for “conducting purposeful and intentional” immigration enforcement activities once the contract starts, according to a service agreement obtained by KXAN.

They can also get recurring quarterly incentive payments and one-time stipends for equipment, technology and vehicles, though federal memoranda and agreements obtained by KXAN don’t specify what agencies can purchase.

The Department of Homeland Security stopped renewing task force model agreements during the Obama administration after federal investigations revealed civil rights violations involving sheriffs’ offices in Arizona and North Carolina .

Since Trump’s return to office, the model has become the most common of the three agreement types. At least 241 task force model agreements were signed in Texas in 2026 alone, compared to just 30 combined for the other models in that time period, according to ICE participation data from September.

Smith County was among the first in Texas to sign on after the president reinstated the task force model in early 2025.

Moore, the only member of Smith County ’s Commissioners Court who agreed to speak with KXAN, explained why he thought the commissioners wanted to partner.

His first word: “budgetary.”

“Any kind of training that any of our departments need to have, or are required to have, costs money, and it’s rare that we get an opportunity to get funding for training from outside county taxes,” Moore said. “Any time we can save the taxpayers money, I’m all for it.”

Smith County got more money than any other of the 93 Texas law enforcement agencies whose funding KXAN reviewed. The sheriff’s office received nearly $2.2 million in federal 287(g) funding from January 2025 to June 2026, according to records obtained by KXAN. That’s equivalent to about 12% of its budget for fiscal year 2025.

Smith, the sheriff, told the Commissioners Court last November that although vehicles purchased with that money would be used for the 287(g) program, “that doesn’t mean, if we’re out here, we won’t run to another call or take another call that comes across the radio. We will do that. We try not to separate 287(g) from our other law enforcement duties. We do it all together.”

About 120 of 198 licensed officers in the Smith County Sheriff’s Office participated in the program. Together, they conducted 124 immigration enforcement actions between October 2025 and July. KXAN requested a list of 287(g) stops from the department, in addition to any associated charge. Smith County listed no associated criminal charge for more than 100 of these stops.

Jose Rodriguez and his 23-year-old son, Pablo Rodriguez, were among those affected.

One afternoon in late June, the pair cruised along Loop 323, a circular segment of highway in Tyler, a city of 113,000 people in East Texas. They’d spent hours working in the summer heat at a construction job and were headed to Chick-fil-A to pick up lunch for their family.

Then red and blue lights appeared behind them. The law enforcement agent said that he’d pulled their black extended-cab work truck over because of a missing license plate on the trailer attached to the pickup and a missing dual-wheel mud flap.

Body and vehicle camera footage showed the detective requesting that Jose Rodriguez get out of the truck. “Any English at all?” the detective later asked. Jose Rodriguez raised his right hand, holding his thumb and index finger close together.

“Un poquito?” the detective asked, followed by, “Are you a U.S. citizen?”

The man shook his head and answered. “No.”

Seconds later, the detective pulled Jose Rodriguez’s hands behind his back and put him in handcuffs.

He was eventually taken from the Smith County jail to an ICE detention facility, about two hours west of Tyler. His son, who is a U.S. citizen, said Jose Rodriguez was detained for about three months before being deported to Mexico.

KXAN could find no criminal convictions or arrests on his record when the Smith County detective took him into custody in June.

“Just like that, he’s gone,” Pablo Rodriguez later told KXAN. “My dad’s gone.”

Law enforcement officers, Pablo Rodriguez said, “portray us as criminals, rapists, violent people. We’re not that. We’re just regular people trying to find a better life. The only difference is our skin. That’s pretty much it.”

Elections earlier this month have left the 287(g) program’s future uncertain, at least in Texas.

While the Trump administration has reached agreements with local law enforcement to work with immigration officials, Congress has broader oversight authority. That includes decisions about funding. In January, Democrats will take over both chambers of Congress and many, including freshman Texas Sen. James Talarico, have criticized ICE tactics. It’s unclear, however, how much of their focus will be on immigration enforcement and specifically on the 287(g) program.

More locally, state Sen. Charles Schwertner, the Republican lawmaker who authored a measure in 2025 that required most Texas sheriff’s offices to participate in the program, wants to expand the mandate during the coming legislative session to include other law enforcement agencies, like police departments. So does the conservative think tank where Blair works.

But support for such legislation may be harder to get after November’s midterm election.

Schwertner retained his state Senate seat, and Republicans maintained their majority in that chamber, but Democrats took control of the governor’s mansion and the state House of Representatives for the first time in a generation. Any new bills would require legislative approval from both chambers and the governor’s signature, or enough legislative support to override a veto.

In a press release well before the election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa called on Gov. Greg Abbott to “demand accountability from the Trump administration and stop enabling ICE operations that are terrorizing communities and violating the law.” The release did not mention the 287(g) program by name. Hinojosa beat Abbott in this month’s election and will take over as governor in January. She did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

The state program could also be affected by this month’s election of Democrats Nathan Johnson , who won the race for state attorney general, and Sarah Eckhardt , who won her bid to become state comptroller.

Johnson, as a state senator, opposed the mandate that sheriffs’ offices participate in the program. He will inherit responsibility for enforcing the law, which requires most sheriffs to seek agreements with ICE by Dec. 1. Johnson said he will use his discretion in deciding whether to sue sheriffs who fail to comply if they have “legitimate law enforcement reasons for not having a 287(g) agreement.”

He also questioned the state attorney general’s continued participation in the program. Current Attorney General Ken Paxton signed a 287(g) task force model agreement in February 2025.

“The attorney general’s office has tremendous, vast responsibilities,” Johnson said. “Never included among them since the creation of this state was outsourcing your employees to a federal agency for a purpose in which we’re not trained or qualified and which distracts me from the mission of my office.”

Johnson didn’t entirely rule out working with ICE in some capacity if it allowed his office to investigate crimes committed by ICE agents in Texas.

Eckhardt, meanwhile, will take over oversight of a $20 million grant program that state lawmakers created two years ago to help sheriff’s offices cover any costs of participation in the 287(g) program not reimbursed by the federal government. By late September, the comptroller’s office had awarded more than $6.5 million to 78 sheriff’s offices, according to figures obtained by KXAN.

During her campaign, Eckhardt warned that expenses for the program could eventually fall on local taxpayers, calling it “unsustainable.” After winning her seat, she said she would “do a 287(g) audit to show how that expense is driving up property taxes.”

This story is an adaptation of an investigation by KXAN. Read the original reporting:

Even if state leaders don’t expand the participation requirement or remove the current mandate, departments can choose to keep collecting federal money to enforce immigration law.

In Fayette County southeast of Austin, Sheriff’s Lt. David Beyer told KXAN that the 287(g) funding his office had already received totaled about $800,000, which helps purchase equipment it can also use for ordinary police work.

“If they want to pay us extra to do that job,” Beyer said, “we’re more than happily going to accept those funds, because that saves our taxpayers money.”

Reporting was contributed by Richie Bowes and Chris Nelson of KXAN and Vianna Davila of ProPublica. Misty Harris of ProPublica contributed research.

scraped.title: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
scraped.description: JobsOhio gave the biotech company AquaBounty $1 million for a project that promised to create 112 new jobs. Not long after, the plan imploded. Now, the program wants a refund.
scraped.author: Anna Clark
scraped.h1: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

When a biotech company named AquaBounty Technologies announced plans to farm genetically engineered Atlantic salmon at a new plant in Ohio, local and state officials eagerly provided it with incentives. Not long after, the company paused construction and auctioned off “new” and “unused” equipment. Now, the state’s private economic development arm wants its $1 million back.

JobsOhio has requested repayment from AquaBounty by Sunday, according to a company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing also notes that, at the end of September, AquaBounty was down to three employees and $122,255 in cash.

AquaBounty said that its salmon could thrive in indoor freshwater farms and help feed the world. Announced in 2021, the new development in Pioneer, Ohio, was supposed to be its first large-scale production facility.

The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. It was believed to be the largest investment ever in rural Williams County.

But AquaBounty, which had never made a profit over its 30 years in business, faced a tangle of regulatory challenges and pushback from environmentalists.

Locals were also suspicious of how the village mayor’s personal interests were tied up in the project. Among other moves, Pioneer Mayor Ed Kidston bought land that AquaBounty wanted to build on. He then sold it to the company for $1.5 million more than he’d paid.

AquaBounty’s plan was unproven, but, as ProPublica reported last year , the company was buoyed by state and local resources — including the million-dollar grant from JobsOhio. The company received the money in August 2021, according to financial filings, shortly after the project went public.

“Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling,” said Sherry Fleming of Williams County Alliance, a grassroots environmental group. While AquaBounty had genetic engineering know-how, she said it seemed to have limited experience in production.

In response to ProPublica’s queries, a press contact for AquaBounty said it shares what it can in its SEC releases and filings, and that it’s still in discussion with JobsOhio over the repayment demand. AquaBounty’s filing said that “there can be no assurance that JobsOhio will agree to any payment schedule or other accommodation.”

“Any collection or legal action by JobsOhio could result in additional costs and management distraction,” it added.

Kidston didn’t respond to requests for comment. He said at the time that his actions involving the plant were intended only to help the community. The village administrator referred ProPublica to AquaBounty and its website.

JobsOhio operates privately but has a funding mechanism set up by the state and a board appointed by the governor. Matt Englehart, a spokesperson for JobsOhio, said in an email to ProPublica that it “operates with transparency and accountability,” but its limited disclosures have long been a sore point for Ohioans.

On its website, JobsOhio says its funding model for specialized grants is “independent” and accommodating of “unique needs.” Qualifications include, but aren’t limited to, “job creation, additional payroll, fixed-asset investment commitment, project return on investment, and project location.”

The AquaBounty grant depended on not only the creation of jobs, but also $222 million in capital investment and a payroll of more than $5.4 million by the end of 2026. It had to maintain those commitments through the end of 2028.

Less than two years after it got the money, construction stalled. Roughly 30% built, the site languished at the end of Kexon Drive, a smooth new road that Pioneer had extended for its benefit.

AquaBounty sold equipment intended for the Ohio farm in 2024 and 2025. It also sold its intellectual property for genetically engineered salmon. By the end of September, according to its filing, its primary remaining assets were unsold equipment, the land in Pioneer and the incomplete build.

JobsOhio and other economic development boosters should “take a good look at this because they’re putting taxpayer dollars at risk when they advertise to bring these industries in, and they haven’t done their homework to protect the community,” Fleming said.

Englehart told ProPublica that he can’t discuss a situation that may result in litigation. But with any company, he said, “when metric commitments are not met, we work closely with those businesses” to help them overcome challenges.

If all options are exhausted, he added, “we will claw back some or all of our dollars so they can be used for future economic development projects to benefit Ohioans.”

JobsOhio’s demand notice came in September, the financial filing said, informing the company that its equipment sales and consideration of acquisition offers for the Ohio farm were a breach of the grant agreement.

AquaBounty “provided additional information” to JobsOhio in October, the filing said, but the agency upheld its demand and requested repayment this month. If it doesn’t come, the filing said, JobsOhio may refer the matter for collections and “pursue the remedies available” under the grant agreement.

With an onerous process and uncertain outcomes, it’s “pretty rare” for JobsOhio to try to claw back money, said Kristan Wong Karinen, a research analyst with the nonprofit Good Jobs First, which tracks public subsidies in economic development. More commonly, she said, it and other agencies will renegotiate the contract — extending the time period for a company to meet commitments, perhaps, or lowering requirements.

“In this case, with AquaBounty,” Wong Karinen said, “because they haven’t done anything, they haven’t fulfilled any of the requirements, I feel like JobsOhio is being forced into this.”

scraped.title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
scraped.description: Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by scammers, affecting about 990,000 households. We spoke with experts to answer common questions about how this theft happens and what victims can do.
scraped.author: Cassandra Garibay and Eli Hager
scraped.h1: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt.

The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California.

“I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?”

If you receive SNAP benefits, Joly’s experience may sound all too familiar. Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households.

ProPublica recently published an investigation into why Congress and the Trump administration have failed to crack down on SNAP theft despite promises to tackle fraud and waste in safety-net programs. As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted.

Many of the victims we heard from had similar questions: How did this happen? How can I prevent it from happening again? Why am I not being reimbursed? And why does it seem like little is being done to prevent these crimes in the first place?

We spoke with dozens of federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, caseworkers, food security advocates and other experts to help answer these questions for you.

Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install “skimming” devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When you swipe your card, these devices capture your data off the magnetic strip on the back, as well as your PIN. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby.

Skimming is largely preventable via microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have been greatly successful in reducing fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.

In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with these scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case , a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits.

Unfortunately, due to the government’s inaction, the burden of protecting benefits from being stolen has largely been left up to you, the individual SNAP recipient. And the options are less than ideal.

Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel , allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use. These apps may also allow you to change your PIN and block out-of-state or online transactions.

But these aren’t always practical solutions, many victims told us. Remembering new PINs all the time, for example, isn’t easy, especially for older beneficiaries.

Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she wasn’t using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits.

“I was simply unable to do whatever the steps were, no matter how hard I tried,” she said.

Besides card locking and changing PINs, the Secret Service has suggested that people may be able to spot evidence of tampering with card readers at grocery stores. For example, if you look closely at the reader and see a noticeable gap between the keypad and the rest of the device, or if you see that something is blocking the light from under the keys, there may be a skimming device there.

If you’ve had your SNAP benefits stolen, you can report the theft to your state or local social services office — the agency where you applied for SNAP — or to the EBT card customer service line on the back of your card to receive a new card and change your PIN so thieves can’t continue to access your benefits.

You can also report the crime to local law enforcement and to the agency within your state in charge of investigating SNAP fraud — for example, in Texas, SNAP theft victims are advised to report it to the Texas Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. ( This map shows where to report SNAP fraud for each state).

A representative for Texas Health and Human Services said, “HHSC takes the security of our client’s benefits very seriously. SNAP card skimming has been a persistent problem across the country, including Texas.”

While there have been some large-scale investigations into SNAP theft, individual reports don’t often lead to an arrest. More than 40 of the victims we heard from said that they had reported their stolen benefits to a SNAP office, the EBT card customer service line, the police or all of the above. A handful also called the stores where they’d noticed unrecognized transactions on their card history, and two said they contacted the FBI. Most were told nothing could be done.

“I was told that I will receive another card in the mail and that I will not get the money back,” one person wrote us. “They took my statement but said they couldn’t help,” wrote another. “No one ever followed up,” said a third.

The main benefit of reporting these thefts is that doing so keeps the issue on the radar of SNAP officials. Many program administrators and caseworkers told us that they feel the urgency of this crisis precisely because so many people have been calling in about it.

In all but two states (California and Maryland), your benefits will not be reimbursed. The federal government had been reinstating stolen SNAP funds in all 50 states starting in late 2022. However, at the end of 2024, an effort to extend that reimbursement system was quashed after Elon Musk posted more than a hundred social media messages opposing legislation that included it , as the Department of Government Efficiency era began. (Musk did not reply to a previous request for comment.)

Democrats in Congress have proposed legislation to restart the reimbursement program. Following the recent midterm elections, they will take power in January.

As ProPublica has reported, the Secret Service devotes a lot of investigative resources to this issue, with teams going store to store around the country to manually check card readers for skimming devices. But that’s not a very efficient approach — it’s a little like playing whack-a-mole, multiple Secret Service agents told us.

Local cops and state prosecutors, meanwhile, are often overmatched, having neither the jurisdiction nor the technical chops to catch scammers who are constantly crossing county, state and international lines. And the feds, who do have the capacity to bring interstate conspiracy charges, haven’t always shown an interest in doing so, given that these are considered relatively low-level cases compared with the other types of crime that federal prosecutors work on.

As for caseworkers, most can’t offer concrete help. Several said that all they can do is provide a list of local food banks.

If your benefits were stolen, there’s a good chance they were skimmed. And the best solution to skimming appears to be tap-to-pay EBT cards with microchips.

In California, where chip cards were implemented independent of federal efforts, reported theft of SNAP and other benefits decreased by more than 80% within two years.

Following ProPublica’s reporting in October, the federal Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP, announced plans to require all 50 states to adopt more secure card technology. But overhauling the SNAP payment system could take years, as well as additional funding from Congress.

The chip card transition comes at a time when social benefits are being drastically cut and more of the financial weight of SNAP is being shifted to the states . Issuing these new cards is likely to cost states millions, involving complicated negotiations with EBT card companies like FIS and Conduent, which are essentially the Visa and Mastercard of SNAP. Grocery stores, bodegas and any places that accept EBT will also need to update their card reader systems. It will be mostly up to states to notify local stores about this and help them with it, which some, like California, Alabama and Oklahoma, have already tried to do.

While ProPublica is no longer gathering information about people’s experiences with SNAP theft, we are still interested in learning more about America’s changing safety net. If you work to administer SNAP or Medicaid, we want to know how the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill is shaping your work and what you are seeing and hearing from the communities you serve.

I’m an engagement reporter working on community-sourced investigations. I also speak Spanish.

I’m a ProPublica reporter who writes about issues affecting poor and working-class people across the country.

I’m interested in hearing from Social Security and SNAP officials and staff, including at the state level, as well as lower-income people and their advocates about the issues affecting them.

scraped.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
scraped.description: About 1 in 4 US adults are family caregivers.
scraped.author: Patricia Smith
scraped.h1: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people .

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.

“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.

One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.

My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion .

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.

Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 .

But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.

Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.

Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.

But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.

Professor of Economics Emeritus, University of Michigan

scraped.title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
scraped.description: Medicare and Medicaid provide limited help with caregiving for older adults – and that means unpaid relatives often bear big burdens.
scraped.author: Jane Tavares
scraped.h1: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?

The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.

While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit , limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements .

This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.

Medicaid , the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023 . The divide between these programs dates back to 1965 , when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.

However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services .

Who provides care in the meantime?

Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born .

The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025 , only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned.

When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.

Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.

Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states , for example, have launched paid family leave programs . In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers . Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage .

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance , an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.

Senior Research Fellow and Lecturer of Gerontology, UMass Boston

scraped.title: Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’
scraped.description: After slashing foreign aid for the promotion of democracy, the State Department is giving $1 million to AfriForum, an NGO that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.
scraped.author: David Campbell
scraped.h1: Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

The U.S. State Department will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum , a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.

The grant, first reported by ProPublica on Nov. 5, 2026 , would support research to document the “ hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” experienced by Afrikaners – descendants of white Dutch settlers who moved to South Africa in the 17th century.

As scholars who study foreign aid and civil society organizations , we would see U.S. support for AfriForum as a radical departure from the kinds of NGOs the U.S. has funded in the past .

The U.S. used foreign aid for decades to support efforts to build democracy abroad, enhance governance and strengthen human rights protections .

Until the second Trump administration, the primary government agencies distributing this assistance were the U.S. Agency for International Development, the State Department and the National Endowment for Democracy.

Past administrations called this assistance “ fundamental ” to the goals of U.S. foreign policy. By the end of President Joe Biden’s term, funding for democracy promotion had reached almost $3 billion annually .

Some of this money has supported NGOs engaged in civic participation and media independence. These efforts had been particularly important in fragile states and fledgling democracies, where civil society is especially at risk .

NGOs can also play an important role in reducing risks of violence between different ethnic and religious groups. By raising awareness about past atrocities, they can help stave off future violence .

The Trump administration suspended most U.S. foreign aid in January 2025 , soon after Donald Trump was sworn in as president for a second time.

It then dismantled USAID , the federal agency previously responsible for foreign aid and development assistance, and the White House compelled Congress to rescind billions of dollars of foreign aid spending . It has continued to take steps in that direction with or without lawmakers’ cooperation .

As a result, many lifesaving public health programs lost funding. This policy change has had an enormous human toll , which public health researchers have begun to quantify .

In addition, democracy assistance has been severely cut. USAID’s Democracy Fund , which funded programs dedicated to building democratic institutions and promoting fair elections and respect for human rights, was eliminated. The Department of State’s and National Endowment for Democracy’s funding and staffing for promoting democracy were also slashed .

In our research on NGOs that work on promoting democracy and the prevention of violence, we have seen and documented the benefits of these efforts . The organizations we have studied emphasize how people in South Africa and other countries with a history of identity-based violence can learn to live together across racial, ethnic and religious divides.

By contrast, AfriForum seeks to lift up Afrikaner identity and history , without any evident effort to bridge the divide between Afrikaners and other racial groups in South Africa.

It champions causes that have contributed to what South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, scholars and other analysts call a false narrative of a “ white genocide ” in that country.

In fact, researchers have found that Afrikaners and other white people in South Africa are less likely to be victims of crime and other forms of violence compared to other ethnic and racial groups in South Africa.

By funding AfriForum, the State Department would be elevating the dubious claims the group makes about the oppression of Afrikaners in South Africa.

And the Trump administration’s embrace of this false narrative goes beyond this grant for AfriForum. It explains why the U.S. has allowed thousands of white South Africans to come to the U.S. as refugees while denying admission to nearly all other refugees from the rest of the world.

Professor of Public Administration and Policy, University at Albany, State University of New York

Professor of Public Administration, Binghamton University, State University of New York

scraped.title: Trump Administration Awards First-Ever Deep-Sea Mining Exploration Leases - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: A private company bid $6 million for access to 31.5 million acres of federal waters. Environmentalists have vowed to stop the deal from moving forward.
scraped.author: By Teresa Tomassoni
scraped.h1: Trump Administration Awards First-Ever Deep-Sea Mining Exploration Leases
scraped.body_text:
In a historic first, the Department of Interior has leased more than 31 million acres of Pacific waters to a deep-sea mining company seeking to exploit mineral-rich deposits from the ocean floor off American Samoa.

“This is the first time that a lease has been issued for deep-sea mining in U.S. waters,” said Arlo Hemphill, U.S. project lead against deep-sea mining for Greenpeace USA.

Deep-sea mining is a highly contested, emerging industry that aims to extract rock-like deposits on the seabed called polymetallic nodules, formed over millions of years. They contain cobalt, copper, manganese and nickel—so-called “critical minerals” used in batteries, electronics and other devices that have historically been mined on land. To date, no commercial deep-sea mining operations have begun anywhere in the world.

Scientists, environmentalists and Indigenous peoples with strong cultural connections to the ocean aim to stop the industry from moving forward at all.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

“Once mining strips away habitat that took millions of years to form, no amount of money can bring it back,” said Hemphill in a statement. “Congress should press the administration to suspend these leases before work begins.”

The lease sale took place Thursday, during a live auction held at the Ventura County Fire Department in Thousand Oaks, California, as Hemphill and dozens of other activists from American Samoa and across the Pacific rallied, prayed and sang outside in protest.

“This is not just seabed on a map. This is our home, our livelihoods, our identity, and our responsibility to protect,” said Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, American Samoa’s youth and environment nonprofit, who traveled from American Samoa to protest the auction. “Ocean rights are human rights, and our home is not for sale,” she said in a statement.

Representatives from just two companies attended the auction, including Adepth Minerals Inc., from Norway, and Wetstone U.S. Ventures, a New York-based offshore critical minerals exploration and deep-sea mining company.

Ultimately, Wetstone bid $6 million on two areas marked for mineral exploration that lie adjacent to the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a marine protected area established by President George W. Bush in 2009 to protect more than 10,000 square miles of ocean from commercial fishing and other forms of extraction.

The bid made Wetstone the provisional winner of the auction, according to a spokesperson from the Marine Minerals Administration. The new office was established earlier this year within the Department of Interior to help promote the Trump administration’s agenda to secure critical minerals.

“A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, in a statement about Thursday’s auction. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

The areas offered for leasing will be open for exploration activities, which include mapping and surveying the seabed to locate mineral rich deposits. Actual mining would require further federal approvals. But Hemphill and others warn that exploration in itself is a dangerous step towards paving the way for an industry that could threaten ocean ecosystems and the people that depend on them.

“The industry will push to move from surveys to exploration to extraction, putting profits ahead of marine life and trampling the culture, livelihood and objections of communities that have said no again and again,” Hemphill said.

Ever since the proposed lease sale was announced earlier this year, many American Samoan leaders and communities have voiced their concerns. Several lawsuits were filed against the Trump Administration to stop it from happening.

Just a few days before the lease sale, a federal judge in Hawaiʻi ruled the Marine Minerals Administration had violated the Endangered Species Act by approving the lease sale without taking into account the potential impacts of exploration and mining on endangered species.

The areas leased are home to several dozen endangered species including the blue whale, fin whale, sei whale and sperm whale, as well as the leatherback sea turtle, oceanic whitetip shark and giant manta ray.

Many of these species are already threatened by climate change, which is altering their sources of prey and migration patterns. More than 1000 marine science and policy experts from 75 countries say deep-sea mining could further add to the stress these marine animals are facing.

“In deciding to move forward with today’s scheduled sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act,” said Chris Eaton, attorney at Earthjustice, an environmental nonprofit that represented American Samoan and Hawaiian plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” he said in a statement Thursday.

scraped.title: Blue Wave Trickled Down to Little-Known Utility Commissions - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Once overlooked, utility regulator elections drew millions in outside spending and increased attention from consumer and environmental groups nationwide, leading to some Democratic victories in red states.
scraped.author: By Ryan Krugman
scraped.h1: Blue Wave Trickled Down to Little-Known Utility Commissions
scraped.body_text:
Data centers and increased energy costs brought attention to typically low-profile utility commission races in states across the country during this year’s midterms.

Nine states, all historically Republican, held elections for their utility regulators this year. Democrats won five of the 15 contested seats, flipping four Republican-held seats and retaining one, while Republicans won 10 seats, including one flipped from a Democrat in Louisiana.

Every state has a commission responsible for regulating its utilities, with authority over decisions that affect how electricity is generated, delivered and priced. Most are called Public Service Commissions (PSCs) or Public Utility Commissions (PUCs), and their structures vary. Some have three members, others five or seven. In most states commissioners are appointed officials, while in 10 states they are elected in partisan races.

In this election cycle, the biggest shifts occurred in Georgia and Arizona, where Democrats made historic gains. In Georgia, they won control of the PSC for the first time in 30 years, while in Arizona, they ended Republicans’ 5-0 hold on their commission. Both states have seen a surge in data center development, bringing new scrutiny to electricity costs and how to meet growing energy demand.

In Georgia, Democrats Shelia Edwards won her first PSC election while Peter Hubbard was reelected to his first full term, an early endorsement of the job he did his rookie year as commissioner. Joined by Commissioner Alicia Johnson, who won a seat last year, Democrats now hold a 3-2 majority on a commission that was entirely Republican just two years ago.

In Arizona, Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill won the first Democratic seats on the commission since 2020.

Pratte also became the first Indigenous woman elected to statewide office in Arizona, bringing a unique perspective and set of goals to the utility regulator. “We’re the sunniest state in the union; we could be generating a lot of our own solar rather than relying on fossil fuels,” Pratte said. “We need to be collaborative, and reach across the aisle to help Arizonans.”

Pratte noted that in addition to fossil fuel reliance, energy costs and transparency among utilities were key issues in the state. She also hopes to make meetings more accessible for the Navajo Nation.

Of the nine states to hold elections this year, Georgia and Arizona have experienced the most data center development. All four of the elected Democrats promised increased scrutiny for data centers, ensuring they pay their fair share of energy costs and preventing unchecked expansion.

“I think data centers definitely played a role in Democrats’ success in Arizona and Georgia,” said Jared Heern, a political scientist at Connecticut College who studies utility commission politics across the country.

Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill speak at a press conference calling on the Arizona Corporation Commission to launch an investigation into how data centers are increasing utility bills for Arizona Power Service customers. Credit: Wyatt Myskow/Inside Climate News

In Arizona, concerns about data centers’ water use likely played a particularly large role, according to Heern. Hill, a scientist, campaigned on protecting natural resources, including water, an increasingly prominent issue amid concerns over the Colorado River’s declining supply.

“Incumbents who got booted out in those states can be directly tied to data center development,” Heern said. Utility commissioners have the ability to shape how data centers are powered and who pays for the infrastructure needed to serve them.

Hill and Pratte defeated incumbent Kevin Thompson in the statewide, at-large election for two commission seats. Thompson owns a consulting firm and acknowledged having a data center client.

Outside spending across the two states topped $7 million. In Arizona, Democrats received the most support, largely from a PAC called Arizonans for Affordable Energy . In Georgia, Republicans received the most outside support, much of it from a group called Powering Georgia’s Future, which supports “pro-growth” policies and a stronger industrial base. Spending in Georgia reached a record high for its PSC election.

Activists and energy watchdogs also played a big role in the elections, helping raise awareness of the little-known regulatory bodies. Grassroots groups like Georgians for Affordable Energy ran social media campaigns and distributed flyers, while national groups like the Sierra Club endorsed the Democratic candidates in Georgia and Arizona and educated members on the stakes of utility commission elections.

“The increased awareness of these bodies over the past few years has translated into frustration and anger as the public sees they are not doing their job,” said David Rogers, deputy director of the Beyond Coal Campaign at the Sierra Club. ”I think that’s what really showed up at the polls.”

While Democrats’ biggest victories came in Georgia and Arizona, they also picked up a seat in Nebraska. Former state Sen. Wendy DeBoer won Nebraska’s 2nd District, which includes Omaha, by more than 30 points, breaking Republicans’ single-party hold on the state’s PSC. DeBoer campaigned on modernizing the state’s infrastructure.

But despite Democratic gains in those red states, Republicans held onto control of eight of the nine commissions that held elections. They also flipped a historically Democratic seat in Louisiana.

The funding gap between Republicans and Democrats in Louisiana’s two PSC races was substantial, and likely played a significant role in the outcome, according to Heern. Republican candidates raised a combined $1.26 million, compared with less than $40,000 for the two Democratic candidates, according to campaign finance filings from late September. Louisiana is one of six states that allow regulated utilities to contribute directly to candidates for utility commission seats. Both Democratic candidates refused utility contributions, while Republican Stephanie Hilferty accepted substantial donations from companies and executives connected to utilities she will now regulate. Republican John Atkins, who won the other seat, also pledged not to accept contributions from regulated utilities. Hilferty did not respond to requests for comment.

In the other five states that held elections—South Dakota, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Alabama and Montana—Democrats failed to pick up a single seat in the deep-red states. But that does not mean voters weren’t interested in energy affordability.

In Alabama, voters clearly sought change amid high electricity prices, even though Democrats didn’t gain any seats on the state’s Public Service Commission. The two incumbent Republican commissioners on the ballot this year lost in their party’s primary, and the commission will undergo even more dramatic changes thanks to sweeping utility legislation passed in April.

The Alabama PSC will expand from three members to seven, including the first two Black commissioners in state history appointed by outgoing Gov. Kay Ivey.

Governor-elect Tommy Tuberville will also select Alabama’s first secretary of energy, a new cabinet-level position that will oversee the commission, set its agenda and give the governor a much larger and more direct role in regulating utilities.

For states that do not elect utility commissioners, the midterms still mattered. Governors or state legislatures appoint commissioners in those states. Democrats flipped governorships and legislatures across the country, giving them more influence over appointments in states like Texas, where the governor appoints all five members of the Public Utility Commission.

“That’s obviously a much slower process decided when seats open up,” Heern said. ”But even though the public didn’t get to directly vote on commissioners, seeing how their midterm votes will translate into new commissions is important to watch.”

In Georgia, a new majority will allow Democratic commissioners to leave an immediate mark, pursuing campaign promises, improving transparency, scrutinizing data center deals and limiting rate increases as much as possible. But even in states where they made partial gains, their performance was not insignificant, according to Heern and consumer and environmental advocacy groups.

In Arizona and Nebraska, breaking up unanimous Republican majorities will give Democrats a greater voice in commission decisions and more opportunity to challenge existing policies.

“Regardless of who won and where, one thing is abundantly clear: People are struggling to meet their basic needs, including electricity,” said Rogers. ”The candidates who won promised to address these issues and we expect them to keep their word.”

scraped.title: How the Bipartisan Permitting Bill Could Drive Up Natural Gas Exports - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: The legislation is expected to accelerate pipeline buildout and lock in future LNG projects, climate advocates warn.
scraped.author: By Nicholas Kusnetz
scraped.h1: How the Bipartisan Permitting Bill Could Drive Up Natural Gas Exports
scraped.body_text:
U.S. exports of natural gas are surging, and legislation moving through Congress could boost them even higher.

A bill that would overhaul federal permitting for a range of projects across energy, technology and other sectors is expected to unleash a wave of pipeline construction, experts say. Much of that gas could end up overseas.

Exports of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, are already the fastest-growing source of demand for U.S. gas production, which hit a record high this summer. By 2040, those exports are expected to roughly double .

If the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act becomes law, that projected increase could grow by an additional 8 percent to 15 percent, according to modeling by the Rhodium Group .

While some of the bill’s proponents say it would help reduce climate pollution by speeding construction of renewable energy and electricity transmission, many environmental groups are warning those gains would be outweighed by accelerating fossil fuel development.

Ben King, a director with Rhodium’s energy and climate practice, said the biggest winner among fossil fuels would be LNG. The group’s modeling projected a buildout of new gas pipelines, most of which would be oriented to exports, he said.

While LNG growth has faced few constraints, one of them has been a lack of new pipelines, said Mariam Al-Shamma, a director with the Bipartisan Policy Center’s energy program.

“It’s gotten really difficult to build interstate gas pipelines in the United States, and that’s obviously something you need if you want to be exporting LNG and don’t want to have an impact on gas supply domestically,” Al-Shamma said.

The permitting bill would make it harder for states and tribes to modify or reject certain permits needed for pipelines and would also restrict legal challenges by environmental groups or other opponents. These types of challenges have slowed or blocked numerous pipeline projects in the Northeast and Appalachian region.

Beyond pipelines, the bipartisan bill could free more gas for export by reducing demand for it in the United States. While domestic gas use is expected to grow in coming years, driven in part by demand from data centers and others, the bill could help wind and solar energy gain a larger share of that increased electric demand, Rhodium’s modeling found.

Yet rather than remaining underground, the modeling said, that natural gas would likely get exported.

It’s unclear what that would mean for the global climate. If LNG exports displace coal, they could, under certain conditions, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, Rhodium said. (Some studies suggest LNG is even worse for the climate than coal, because of methane leaks.) If they spur new demand or replace renewable energy, they would drive pollution higher. In cases where exports replace gas from Russia or the Middle East, they wouldn’t change emissions much at all.

“The simple fact of the matter is it’s a whole jumble of all those things,” King said.

Modeling aside, some climate advocates are warning that provisions in the bill would effectively lock in a massive wave of LNG exports that has already been approved.

The U.S. Department of Energy had authorized the export of nearly 56 billion cubic feet of gas per day as of September. For a sense of scale, that figure is equal to roughly 40 percent of current U.S. gas production . Only about two-thirds of what has been authorized is either operating or under construction.

The Trump administration has focused on expanding LNG exports. It has devoted billions of dollars in federal subsidies to help build terminals or sell gas overseas and wielded exports as leverage in trade negotiations to secure new deals with foreign governments.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

In 2024, the Biden administration paused approving new gas exports, saying it was reviewing its criteria for determining whether they were in the public interest. Provisions in the new bill would make it much harder for a future administration to do the same.

“That kind of project uncertainty is exactly what the legislation is attempting to eliminate,” Al-Shamma said.

An analysis by Public Citizen , a consumer advocacy group, argued current law allows a future administration to modify existing LNG permits if, for example, it determined exports were inflating domestic energy prices. The new bill could erect significant hurdles to this approach, the group argued, by restricting such modifications to a narrower set of circumstances.

What’s more, the bill would impose a new standard for judicial review that would allow companies to sue the government if agencies modified or revoked permits. In those cases, the agency would need to show “by clear and convincing evidence” that its action was warranted. If it failed, the government could face substantial penalties tied to the costs of construction or operations.

If an agency denied or “unreasonably delayed” a permit, and an applicant could establish it was being treated unfairly, the penalties could reach 100 percent of “reasonably expected” costs.

LNG terminals often cost tens of billions of dollars to construct, a sum that experts say could serve as a formidable deterrent to an agency that was considering modifying a permit. Once built, the terminals are meant to operate for decades.

“The project certainty provisions in this bill are quite certainly the worst provisions I’ve seen in 20 years of following congressional legislation on the environment,” said Jeremy Symons, president of the Center for Energy & Environmental Analysis, a think tank. “They are a blank check to industry.”

Symons added that under the Natural Gas Act, “the Department of Energy has a responsibility to determine whether or not these facilities’ exports are in the public interest, and this provision stomps on that.”

Al-Shamma said her reading of the bill suggested it would be unlikely to prevent the Energy Department from using its authority under the Natural Gas Act. One of the allowable reasons for modifying or revoking a permit is if the action were taken “pursuant to any applicable law or regulation.”

Others have argued that permits have not presented a constraint on LNG exports—some of the proposals that have won approval to export gas have yet to secure investors to finance construction. By this argument, the permit certainty provisions may have little practical effect.

LNG exports rose by nearly 25 percent in the first half of this year. And bill or no bill, they are expected to keep climbing next year.
