scraped.title: Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states
scraped.description: In at least four states, hyperscale facilities account for 10 percent or more of the electricity sold.
scraped.author: Clayton Aldern
scraped.h1: Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Δ

In at least four states, hyperscale facilities account for 10 percent or more of the electricity sold.

It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet translating “a lot” to real numbers pinned to individual facilities requires usage data, something that data-center operators are loath to disclose.

A Harvard-led study published this week in Nature Sustainability gets us closer to these numbers. Researchers extracted locations and building footprints for as many U.S. hyperscale data centers as possible, ultimately cataloguing 403 of the warehouse-sized facilities across the country. Translating power capacity to theoretical electricity usage, the authors estimated these facilities gobble up roughly 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes. They suggest this electricity is associated with about 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

The 82-TWh estimate corresponds to about 2 percent of U.S. electricity. Though noteworthy in its own right, that figure shrouds high state-to-state variability, with many states boasting data-center electricity shares in the double digits. When viewed as a fraction of the retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) in 2024, Oregon’s studied data centers used the equivalent of 18.6 percent of the electricity sold in the state. In Virginia and Iowa, data centers consumed 15.5 and 13.1 percent, respectively.

While data-center electricity consumption remains a national issue, electricity prices and utility planning look very different from state to state. And the speed of hyperscale buildouts mean these figures can change quickly.

In Oregon, for example, the state’s data-center share of electricity use grew from about 3 percent in 2015 to about 23 percent in 2025, according to analyses presented to the state by energy economics firm ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia. The group estimated that data centers were associated with approximately 96 percent of the state’s electricity sales growth between 2020 and 2025.

Data centers can “no longer be understood as a marginal component” of Oregon’s electricity demand, the authors wrote — and in the Wild West of hyperscaling, it’s a component poorly matched to current regulatory structures. In its most recent biennial energy report , the Oregon Department of Energy noted that the state “currently lacks a policy mechanism to address emissions from data center load growth.”

Many states are grappling with the ramifications of recent data-center buildouts. Because the Harvard study was limited to hyperscale facilities the authors could verify, its electricity-use estimates are likely undercounts. In Virginia, for example, the study’s 142 included facilities account for about 15 percent of the state’s electricity sales — itself a staggering sum. But Dominion Energy, the largest seller of electricity in the state, has estimated that data centers purchased 28 percent of the electricity its Virginia subsidiary sold last year.

Currently, there is no federal apparatus to track or check these figures, as surveys of utilities’ sales tend to label customer segments as merely residential, commercial, industrial, or transportation-related. In March, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley wrote to the EIA, arguing: “Without this data, policymakers, utility companies, and local communities are operating in the dark.” The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the infrastructure permitting bill currently under consideration in the Senate, would direct the agency to explicitly measure data-center electricity usage.

Hyperscale electricity can also be understood in terms of the plant-warming gases emitted during its generation. Together, the facilities catalogued by the Harvard researchers emit more annually than the carbon-dioxide equivalent of countries like Jordan, Kenya, and Guatemala.

State context matters here, too, since emissions estimates depend on a given state’s grid, which vary by energy mix. The Nature Sustainability study’s authors used federal power-plant data to estimate the average per kilowatt-hour emissions for each confirmed data center. The resulting rates range from Washington’s hydropower-heavy 10 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour to Virginia’s fossil-fuel-backed 325.

Yet even grid averages fail to capture the growing phenomenon of on-site power plants. Frequently gas-fired, these generators are built at or near hyperscale campuses to generate electricity directly for the data centers themselves. Electricity usage from on-site power can be harder to measure, given it is often “behind the meter” — that is, the electrons might never touch a public grid. As of June , about 2 GW of gas generators powered four data centers around the country, including Elon Musk’s xAI sites in Memphis, Tennessee. There are 143 GW of gas plants currently proposed to power data centers around the United States, according to the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP), a watchdog group.

Most of this proposed on-site power could push the hyperscale buildout outside the Harvard study’s map. West Virginia, for example, hosts exactly zero of the data-center campuses confirmed by the Nature Sustainability study. Yet the state is second only to Texas in proposed on-site gas capacity, with more than 15 GW tagged by EIP.

If built, these projects could reshape the geography of U.S. data centers — and make their electricity use less visible in utility-sales and grid-demand data. Behind-the-meter power doesn’t show up as utility purchases.

It’s possible many of these proposed plants will never actually break ground; only about two dozen of the 74 proposed plants tagged by EIP are currently permitted for construction under the Clean Air Act. Yet if the recent supercharged data center build-out offers any indication, applications for new on-site facilities will continue to roll in.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the Nature Sustainability study, in a statement. Forget 2 percent: The electricity and emissions estimates offered by his team “could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

scraped.title: Is it OK to want a ‘normal life’ during the climate crisis?
scraped.description: A home, a family, a vacation — therapist Leslie Davenport weighs in on how to reconcile life goals with guilt and fear about climate change.
scraped.author: Leslie Davenport
scraped.h1: Is it OK to want a ‘normal life’ during the climate crisis?
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

“I would love to be a parent, but I worry it is unethical to bring children into a world that is wrecked by climate change.”

“It feels kind of silly to be bothering with working a normal job and planning for retirement in some distant future, given the overall circumstances.”

“Sometimes I feel hypocritical, working toward a better, more sustainable future while not fully reflecting those values in my own daily choices.”

“My partner and I are thinking about buying our first home together and becoming parents. How can I make plans for the future in a world that is unravelling?”

In the many questions we’ve received through the Ask a Climate Therapist form , I’ve noticed a theme running through several of them. People longing to have children, but grappling with the ethics of that decision. People wanting to enjoy occasional travel or an omnivorous diet, but feeling the sting of guilt. People hoping to plan for retirement or home ownership, but unsure how to reconcile those long-term visions with their fears and doubts about our climate future.

I’d sum it up like this: Knowing what we know about the climate crisis, and knowing that we each must do our part to contribute to a liveable future, is it OK to want to enjoy life, too?

Climate change is a systemic problem, but the choices we make in our own lives still matter as we push for large-scale change. Some choices are more impactful than others — but it’s important to remember that guilt isn’t a very discriminating guide.

Pick one or more of the decisions that’s been bothering you or causing guilt. Sit with it for five quiet minutes and then ask:

When a choice comes out heavy in impact and light in meaning, it’s worth changing. When it comes out light in impact and full of love, put the guilt down. Most choices land somewhere in between, and that’s where question five supports you the most. Keep what matters and adjust what you can: Buy the house and plan its first upgrades around efficiency. If you have kids, let raising them bring your family into your community’s climate efforts. When you’ve stopped agonizing over the decision, you can put the energy you’ve freed up where it counts the most: advocating within your sphere of influence, showing up for local policy meetings, voting, and talking honestly about climate with the people in your life.

A warming world asks you to pursue your dreams more intentionally. It doesn’t require you to abandon them. A home, a family, time away — these things already look different for everyone, and what counts as “normal” or aspirational may shift, but the wish for a place to belong and people to love is an ancient human drive.

I’d even go so far as to say that life is what we’re fighting to protect when we work for a healthier, safer, and more just future.

Rest, joy, and your love of life are what will make a lifelong commitment to the planet possible. In my experience, the people who stay engaged for decades always make time for what matters most to them. So take the trip and let yourself relax and rejuvenate. Love deeply. Then come home and continue to defend our planet, where your dedication will help shape the future for all of us.

In this with you, Leslie

scraped.title: Even the 'good guys' of AI are locking in fossil fuels
scraped.description: Anthropic claims to be developing AI safely. So why doesn’t its own impact on climate change make the cut?
scraped.author: Kate Yoder
scraped.h1: Even the ‘good guys’ of AI are locking in fossil fuels
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Anthropic became one of the most valuable companies on the planet on Wednesday, valued at $1.5 trillion after its IPO. Known as one of the “good guys” of AI , Anthropic was founded by employees who left OpenAI over disagreements about ethics and safety. But despite the company’s emphasis on responsibility and preventing AI from killing everybody, one thing you don’t hear Anthropic talking about much is its contribution to climate change.

Ahead of the initial public offering this week, Greenpeace accused the company of “asking average investors to join them in throwing the planet into the climate furnace.” AI data centers are causing electricity demand to soar and fueling a surge in natural gas plants . A recent report found that the biggest data centers in the United States emit about as much carbon dioxide as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark. Anthropic is contributing to that: It reportedly signed a $3.4 billion deal with the Texas-based company OnePWR Solutions in September to power data centers with gas-fired engines — the largest known single purchase of its kind by an AI lab.

“It signals what direction they’re taking very clearly,” said Charlie Cray, a senior strategist at Greenpeace USA. The company is locking in fossil fuels at a time when scientists say the world is certain to overshoot the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees C . Anthropic’s reputation for being the most responsible of the AI giants means it should be minimizing its climate impact, Cray argued: “Show the world that you can do it better.”

The company has been lauded for focusing on safety and “alignment,” trying to ensure that AI acts in accordance with human values — or as its website puts it , “training Claude to be helpful, harmless, and honest.” Earlier this year, Anthropic got into a dispute with the Pentagon when it refused to give the Department of War unrestricted use of AI for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. This summer, Dario Amodei, its CEO, called for the government to regulate the industry and for AI development to slow down . But Anthropic’s actions are decidedly less “aligned” with efforts to preserve the stable climate that allowed complex human civilizations to grow and flourish .

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

In the hundreds of pages of its IPO filings, the maker of Claude mentioned climate change sparingly , laying out a number of ways that the warming planet could threaten its business. One risk is higher operating costs : Anthropic said that higher temperatures “can increase the power consumption and water usage required to cool equipment at the facilities on which we depend.” In addition, fires, hurricanes, and floods amped up by climate change could disrupt its operations, it noted.

Environmental policies pose another set of risks to the company’s resource-intensive business. Anthropic acknowledged that some investors may choose not to invest in the company if its sustainability measures are seen as inadequate. On the other hand, implementing such goals “could be difficult to achieve or costly to implement,” it wrote in the filings, adding that navigating various climate and sustainability disclosure laws in California, the European Union, and the United Kingdom could require “significant time and resources.”

That good-guy reputation might also take a hit. The filings suggest that AI’s environmental harms could hurt Anthropic’s image, as its brand is “subject to heightened scrutiny with respect to perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety-related impacts.”

“At least they admit that climate change is a threat when they say it’s a risk to their own operations,” Cray said, “but they’re not taking responsibility for their own contribution.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

In the broader public discussion about AI, concerns about global warming have been drowned out by a more immediate existential threat. One of Anthropic’s researchers, Jacob Coxon, accused the company of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives” when he resigned in September ; then the lead of its alignment division , Evan Hubinger, said he thought there was a greater than 10 percent chance that “AI could kill all humans” within the next decade.

Assuming humans avert an AI apocalypse, we’ll have to contend with the reality of living on a rapidly warming planet. Some experts are trying to bring sustainability into the conversation about how to use AI responsibly. “The entire sector needs to be scrutinized closely as to what choices they make and how much transparency is in their reporting — which in this case, is not a lot,” Cray said. A recent analysis from the firm Integrum ESG compared Anthropic to 14 peer companies across the AI supply chain and found that all of them except Anthropic and SpaceX reported their direct greenhouse gas emissions and the indirect emissions from the energy they purchase (called Scope 1 and 2 emissions in energy wonk-speak).

Anthropic has pledged to cover the electricity price increases from its data centers so the public wouldn’t have to pay those costs and committed to “being a responsible neighbor” and addressing its environmental impacts, such as by deploying “water-efficient cooling technologies.” In June, it joined other major corporations in backing the carbon removal industry . (Anthropic did not respond to a request to comment.)

Cray has ideas for how Anthropic could apply its ethical standards to the problem of climate change. In addition to greater transparency, the company could commit to a timeline for powering its data centers with only renewable power and set firm climate targets. “They shouldn’t be building data centers that are powered by natural gas without a timeline for phasing that out and replacing it,” he said.

WASHINGTON —The MAHA Institute, a nonprofit launched last year to support Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health agenda in Washington, burned over $1 million in 2025, leaving it with little cash on hand to continue operating, tax documents obtained by STAT show.

The group started 2025, its first year in operation, with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, but ended the year with just $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed this week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year.

scraped.title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
scraped.description: Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates before applying the pay cuts and sudden ghosting that data workers have faced.
scraped.h1: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
scraped.body_text:
Ideas

Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates, but then use the same tactics of pay cuts and sudden ghosting that have plagued global data workers.

Julián Posada is an assistant professor at Yale University and the author of “Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence.”

The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania.

Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers , and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions.

They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on.

I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day.

For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold.

This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on . Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out.

The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else.

An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books , artists’ works , all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S.

Outlier’s terms let the company delay or suspend payment during an investigation of a worker’s tasks and withhold “some or all amounts accrued” where it finds a violation “in the company’s sole determination.” The company may also deactivate an account “immediately without prior notice for any reason.” The same language appeared word for word in the Remotasks terms that Rogelio’s family worked under in 2021.

Earlier this year, Josh Dzieza reported on the laid-off lawyers , scientists , and screenwriters now filling these platforms. Of the more than 30 workers he interviewed, nearly all described the same arc: Demands increased, target times shrank, and pay fell as a project went on. One designer was tagging videos for Meta at $21 an hour when the project ended for “scope changes.” Days later, the same job reappeared under a new name at $16 an hour — the same sequence that Rogelio’s family went through five years earlier.

Of course, workers can leave, and many do. But the ones who stay are often those who can’t leave. One woman I interviewed was confined to her home during the Covid-19 pandemic by a health condition and couldn’t risk losing the job. “This is my only source of income,” she told me.

The rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it.

None of this is unknown within the industry. In a 2024 meeting convened by the nonprofit Partnership on AI and the Fairwork project which rates platform companies, I sat with representatives of AI companies and the outsourcing firms that supply them. The AI companies said they didn’t employ the data workers; the outsourcing firms said their operations were determined by the prices the AI companies expected. Everyone agreed pay should be better, but when the question of representation came up, the room went quiet as no workers were present.

Workers have still acted. In March 2023, a judge in Kenya temporarily halted the dismissal of 260 Facebook content moderators, prevented Meta from moving their work to another contractor, and barred Meta and contractor Majorel from blacklisting workers. As workers fought in Kenya, Meta moved the work to West Africa.

American courts are also grappling with this issue. Claims by workers on Scale AI’s platforms led to a proposed settlement that has received preliminary approval in San Francisco. The company denies wrongdoing. A separate class action suit alleges Mercor misclassified more than 30,000 lawyers, doctors, and engineers while setting their pay and reviewing their work. Mercor’s clients have included OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, but they are not named as defendants. The case is ongoing.

A cardiologist who is offered a three-digit hourly rate is not in the same position as Rogelio and his family. What connects them is the fact that the rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it.

The work will keep moving, and the rules will continue to be set by the companies that commission it, wherever the next worker logs on, whether in Kenya, Venezuela, or the Philippines.

The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.

MinoHealth researchers in Ghana jailbroke their own LLM as a test. What emerged were thousands of toxin recipes—and an urgent push for regulation.

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

scraped.description: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. scraped.h1: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
scraped.body_text:
METR’s latest report finds that AI models are still improving at a rapid clip, but they show some weaknesses in tasks that require judgment.

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

scraped.body_text:
Plus: Trump has fired his cyber director after a wave of tech outages.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars. In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand .

Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

Read more:

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Trump has fired his cyber director after a wave of tech outages Pentagon official Kirsten Davies will replace Sean Cairncross. ( NBC News ) + The outages disrupted flights, banks and security systems. ( Reuters $) + They’ve fuelled fears of a wider collapse. ( WP $) + AI agents are expected to drive even more outages. ( Politico ) + We need to monitor AI agents in real time. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 The US approved sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China Many went to firms the Pentagon links to China’s military. ( CNBC ) + California is investigating Nvidia’s links to China. ( Politico ). + New US export rules are set to hinder Chinese AI. ( WSJ $) + Nvidia is eyeing Arm chief Rene Haas as its next CEO. ( FT $)

3 The US Senate has passed a bill to fast-track energy projects It would cut red tape but weaken environmental protections. ( Axios ) + The bill could advance Trump’s fossil-fuel agenda. ( New Yorker $) + But it could also unlock more clean energy. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Taiwan says China is using Threads to sway next week’s elections It has flagged nearly 2,700 suspected accounts to Meta. ( Reuters $) + Taiwan’s “silicon shield” is weakening. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Google’s AI push is hurting its search ad business Advertisers are shifting spending as AI answers displace ads. ( NYT $) + The agentic web is here. ( MIT Technology Review )

6 Apple is building its own AI agent It would browse the web, work across apps and write code. ( Verge ) + Apple’s longtime iPhone camera chief has retired. ( Bloomberg $)

7 UN climate talks are set to call for carbon removal technologies It could reverse warming, but the systems remain unproven. ( WP $) + Is carbon removal in trouble? ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Global cooling needs have overtaken heating for the first time Higher temperatures are driving a surge in air conditioning. ( Bloomberg $)

9 GTA 6 has become the biggest entertainment launch ever First-day sales were estimated at a record $2.3 billion. ( BBC )

10 Physicists sent a message through a wall using gravity and an old lift Unlike radio signals, gravitational fields can’t be blocked by walls. ( Gizmodo )

Quote of the day

—Dingsheng Li, an environmental health professor and Anthropic investor, tells The New Yorker why he's buying into a company whose technology threatens to make human workers obsolete.

One more thing

—Amit Katwala

A couple of weeks ago, at a $50 million arena built in a casino parking lot in Las Vegas, I witnessed a libertarian thought experiment come to life. The inaugural Enhanced Games were the first sporting competition where participants were encouraged to take performance-enhancing drugs.

For the event’s supporters, the Enhanced Games offered a glimpse of a future where medical advances push the human race to new heights—and they never have to get old. As I watched the games unfold, two questions bounced around my head: Were they right? And what does that mean for the rest of us?

Read the full story to understand the answers .

scraped.body_text:
Plus: Anthropic has raised $81 billion in the biggest-ever IPO.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.

They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive .

—Antonio Regalado

After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion.

The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition.

Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry .

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Separating AI reality from hyped-up fiction isn’t always easy. That’s why we’ve created the AI Hype Index—a simple, at-a-glance summary of what’s shaping the industry right now.

The latest edition tracks AI’s spread across everything from literary prizes and cyberattacks to a Grok-ified version of The Odyssey . See where it all landed on this month’s index .

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Anthropic has raised $81 billion in the biggest-ever IPO It eclipsed SpaceX as the largest stock-market debut. ( Bloomberg $) + Its stated mission could conflict with shareholders’ interests. ( NYT $) + The IPO comes amid new safety fears about its AI advances. ( FT $) + Its performance will test the strength of the AI boom. ( BBC ) + What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review )

2 China is reportedly seeking Nvidia chips for AI-powered weapons Beijing is trying to circumvent US export controls. ( CNBC ) + Alibaba tapped Nvidia to support a military-linked lab. ( NYT $) + When the US military implemented AI, civilian deaths rose . ( Intercept ) + “Humans in the loop” in AI war is an illusion. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 Elon Musk has joined Silicon Valley’s retreat from Trump He called his midterm spending “foolish” and broke with MAGA. ( FT $) + OpenAI and Palantir leaders have also struck new tones. ( Gizmodo ) + Silicon Valley got the midterms badly wrong. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Ukraine used relay drones to strike Putin’s bridge without Starlink The strike showed how it’s learning to fight without SpaceX. ( Ars Technica ) + Musk has denied Kyiv’s claims about restrictions on Starlink. ( CNBC )

5 A major cyberattack has hit the European Commission It may have exposed large amounts of staff personal data. ( Politico ) + Trump has blamed Minnesota for water system hacks. ( ABC )

6 Trump may force US firms to disclose their use of Chinese AI The proposal aims to discourage reliance on Chinese models. ( Reuters $)

7 The US has slashed funding for biomedical science abroad It’s also weakened oversight of foreign grants. ( Economist $)

8 AI datacentres are set to drive a 70% rise in emissions by 2030 The US and China are turning to fossil fuels to power AI. ( Guardian ) + The climate case for AI has not been made. ( MIT Technology Review )

9 Grand Theft Auto 6 has become the best-reviewed game ever It scored 99 out of 100 on review aggregation site Metacritic. ( BBC ) + Schools and businesses are bracing for “GTA Flu” season. ( NYT $)

10 A new underwater research station aims to protect coral reefs Aquanauts there will monitor struggling ecosystems. ( New Scientist $)

Quote of the day

—Thomas Nagel, a philosopher and professor emeritus at NYU, tells Wired why he objects to Anthropic giving Claude more independence, just as the company makes its record-breaking stock-market debut.

One more thing

Sitting in the courtyard of his house in China’s Henan province last October, Dong Hui decided to try holding a pen. Six years after a car accident left him paralyzed from the neck down, he slowly wrote his name, “Thank you,” and the date.

The breakthrough was made possible by a brain implant called NEO. In March, it became the world’s first invasive brain-computer interface approved for use beyond clinical trials. The approval is expected to accelerate China’s push to become a global leader in brain implants.

Here’s how China reached the milestone—and what it means for the future of BCIs .

—You Xiaoying

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

At the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026, Marren Akeyo, addressed world leaders on their responsibility to take real action to stop climate change. “Climate change does not ask for your birth certificate before affecting you. So, why should we wait until we’re adults to protect our planet?” said 8-year-old Akeyo. “We are ready to grow food. We are ready to take care of our planet. But we need you to give us opportunities. Don’t just tell us, ’You’re the leaders of tomorrow.’ Let us lead something today. Start with what you have.”

AMY GOODMAN : We now turn to a little girl, 8-year-old Marren Akeyo of Kenya, holds the title Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026.

MARREN AKEYO : Good morning, COP31. Good morning, Your Excellencies, distinguished guests, professors, teachers, parents and all the very important people here today.

My name is Marren Akeyo. I am 8 years old. Yes, only 8. I know some of you are wondering what this small girl is doing at COP31. Yes, I might be small, but my dreams are taller than some of the trees you have planted.

I am Little Miss Environment Kenya, overall Mini Miss Kenya, a model, a climate champion and the founder of Akeyo Foundation. But please, don’t be confused by my crown. I am not the queen of sitting pretty; I am the queen of getting my hands dirty.

My farm, my classroom. Near my home is a wonderful place called Impact SMART Solution demo farm. That is where I teach children how to plant food and take care of our planet. Some children love playing with their phones. Me, I love playing with soil. And guess what: My vegetables don’t need Wi-Fi; they need water, sunshine, good soil and a little love. At the farm, I learn how to grow food and take care of our planet.

And also, why I started Akeyo Foundation, ladies and gentlemen, I have discovered something very important. You don’t need to be big to solve big problems. That is why I started Akeyo Foundation. My dream is to help children discover their talents, learn smart farming, protect nature and become environmental champions.

I invite my friends to the farm so that we can learn and plan together, because when I teach one child and that child teaches another child, soon we’ll have a whole generation of climate champions.

And let me tell you something: Climate change does not ask for your birth certificate before affecting you. So, why should we wait until we’re adults to protect our planet? We children are ready to plant.

My crown has a job. I also love modeling, dancing, singing, poetry, swimming, skating and cycling. Yes, I have many talents. Sometimes I even think my talents need a timetable. But my biggest dream is not to collect crown and trophies. My biggest dream is making my talents useful to the world, because a crown on my head is beautiful, but a tree growing because of my hand is much more beautiful.

My challenge to the world, now I have a question for all the big people here today. You have big offices, big cars, big meetings, and sometimes very big speeches. But tell me: How big is your action for our planet? We children are ready to plant. We are ready to grow food. We are ready to take care of our planet. But we need you to give us opportunities. Don’t just tell us, “You’re the leaders of tomorrow.” Let us lead something today. Start with what you have.

Now I need your help. When I say “COP,” you say “31.” COP !

AUDIENCE : Thirty-one!

MARREN AKEYO : COP !

AUDIENCE : Thirty-one!

MARREN AKEYO : When I say “little hands,” you say “big change.” Little hands!

AUDIENCE : Big change!

MARREN AKEYO : Little hands!

AUDIENCE : Big change!

MARREN AKEYO : And finally, I am Marren Akeyo. I am only 8 years old. I may be not old enough to drive a car, but I am old enough to drive change.

Thank you, COP31. Let us make our planet green again. I am representing the voice of children, not to just speak for — not to just speak for phones, not to just speak for electronics, but I am speaking for our environment and climate. Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN : So, that’s Marren Akeyo, 8-year-old Kenyan activist, holds the title of Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026. She spoke at COP31, the climate summit, on Thursday.

Special thanks to everyone with the Associated Press team here: Pablo Delbracio, Ka Chin Chen, Zoran Jankovic, Andrei Klassin, Julian Jones, Filiz Bozkurt Kaplan and Berfin Kaplan. And our Democracy Now! team here in Turkey: Nermeen Shaikh, Anjali Kamat, Nicole Salazar, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Hany Massoud and Denis Moynihan, And in New York, Mike Burke and Deena Guzder and Messiah Rhodes and María Taracena and John Hamilton, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, also Julie Crosby. I’m Amy Goodman. Thanks so much for joining us from Turkey.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change.

“This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on Democracy Now! by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries.

“At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, [are] saying is, 'There is no money at home.' But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from Turkey on the final scheduled day of the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31.

Climate advocacy groups and Indigenous organizations from across the world have slammed this gathering as the “worst COP ever” and rejected the latest draft text as a “disaster,” urging developing countries to reject the latest draft text.

Meanwhile, at a news conference just before our broadcast, Panama’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro has threatened to block any final agreement if it doesn’t include a cap on oil production. Earlier this week, he spoke out forcefully against the role of what he described as the “petroleum mafia.”

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO : I do not bear good news. We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.

AMY GOODMAN : And this is Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s environment minister, speaking just before we went to air, flanked by representatives from Finland and Vanuatu, Belgium, Ivory Coast, France, Guatemala and other countries.

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO : We have come together because we feel that the COP can still be saved if we focus on six key issues for our final declaration that clarifies for the world where we must go.

The first is that science must be the foundation. Everything we do must be based on science.

Second, we need a clear transition away from fossil fuels. It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly. We must transition away from fossil fuels in an orderly manner, if we are to confront climate change.

The third point for us, which is very important, is that fair contributions to climate finance must come from those with greatest responsibility. You pollute, you pay. It’s actually rather simple. You cause the problem, you must help to fix it. If you are the biggest emitter of CO2, if you are the biggest producers or consumers of petroleum, then you must contribute to solve this problem and these issues.

AMY GOODMAN : Earlier today, in a packed room for the press, the Climate Action Network, which encompasses over 2,500 civil society groups worldwide, as speakers detailed the failures of the COP , there were activists in the room, journalists and many others representing this COP31. The activists on the stage called out the European Union and other developed nations for their obstruction. The room repeatedly broke out into chants of “shame.” The moderator of CAN called the draft text a “disgrace” and introduced speakers.

DANNI TAAFFE : Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International.

TASNEEM ESSOP : There is nothing on the table that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. … This COP has had the highest number of lobbyists — fossil fuel lobbyists, AI lobbyists, CCUS lobbyists, CDR lobbyists. So, what we’re leaving this COP with is decisions made to actually promote the interests of those culprits.

DANNI TAAFFE : Avantika Goswami from CSE India.

AVANTIKA GOSWAMI : The European Union have, in a way, taken on the mantle that the U.S. has left the vacuum of, the blocker that the U.S. was. Unfortunately, we expected them to be leaders, but they have disappointed us. … And these are the parties that posture the most in the media. They say they are committed to climate multilateralism, and they are concerned about 1.5°C and the breach of the Paris Agreement goals. … So, we want to let them know that we see them and the games they’ve played, and we will not stand for it.

DANNI TAAFFE : Anabella Rosemberg from CAN International.

ANABELLA ROSEMBERG : The COP is not dying. The COP is being killed, not because it’s bloated, not because it’s inefficient or useless. It’s being killed because it’s the last space where civil society, where developing countries can hold developed countries accountable. … We are now asked to accept more empty words. We say no. We will fight back. And we say thank you for nothing. … So, this is also an appeal for all of us, for all the movements, to keep working together and change the faces of who’s representing developed countries in this place.

DANNI TAAFFE : And Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa.

MOHAMED ADOW : I can tell you, without any doubt, that this has been the worst COP ever.

AUDIENCE : Shame! Shame! Shame!

MOHAMED ADOW : Communities living in drought, floods and failed harvest were promised action. They cannot survive on an annual renewal of promises. We’re effectively pushing poor, vulnerable countries into further debt to protect themselves from a crisis they did little to cause.

TASNEEM ESSOP : I want to just say two things. One, when you come into a COP and a commissioner of a very important regional bloc says, “We’re not coming with any finance. Finance is dead in the water,” think about that, “dead in the water.” For us in the Global South, dead in the water is very literal. So it’s a shameful way to come to a COP where we are going to be fighting for adaptation finance to protect people from being dead in the water.

Secondly, the pledges that they brought to this COP for adaptation finance, you would have seen totaled around $50 million, which we said in our ECO is half the cost of an F-35 Lightning fighter jet.

AUDIENCE : Shame! Shame! Shame!

TASNEEM ESSOP : And we’re not even going to measure that $50 million in relation to the $3 trillion that rich nations are spending on wars, a genocide and conflicts across the world. Put that into perspective.

AMY GOODMAN : That was Tasneem Essop, the executive director of CAN , Climate Action Network International, and others speaking at a news conference earlier today. She is from South Africa.

For more, we’re joined by several leading environmental justice advocates.

Harjeet Singh is strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, a social justice organization, also global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign.

Nafkote Dabi is the climate change policy lead for Oxfam International, where she works at the intersection of climate and inequality. She’s from Ethiopia, where the next COP , COP32, will be held, in Addis.

And Meena Raman is with us, head of programs at Third World Network and president of Friends of the Earth Malaysia.

We thank you all for being with us. We’re going to start with Harjeet. You, as well as Nafkote, were holding up a sign behind the speakers that said, ” ECO . End the Genocide,” with big letters, ” SHAME !” There was rage in this room. It was the most packed news conference I had seen, packed with activists. Talk about where we are at on this last scheduled day, though it’s clear it’s going to go further.

HARJEET SINGH : Well, it is a matter of shame, Amy. This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction. We have spent more time on talking about electrification, without any details whether it’s going to be green or is going to be accessible to people. We have removed the reference to —

AMY GOODMAN : Wait. Just to explain that, “electrification” is sort of the watchword here.

HARJEET SINGH : Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : And the idea was renewable electrification.

HARJEET SINGH : Exactly.

AMY GOODMAN : But that seems to be — “renewable” — being dropped.

HARJEET SINGH : Absolutely. And otherwise, why are we talking about electrification in this space, if it is not green? That’s the question we should be asking. We do not see any reference to fossil fuel phaseout. Now, only the words are not enough, and I can explain that later, but that being dropped from the previous draft is just not acceptable. Adaptation finance, there was a clear agreement to scale it to $120 billion annually for developing countries.

AMY GOODMAN : No one knows what “adaptation finance” means.

HARJEET SINGH : OK. So, adaptation means helping communities prepare to deal with climate impacts. It’s about retrofitting their homes. It’s about building dikes. It’s about making sure that their agriculture is resilient and we are food-secure. And if you do not provide money — let’s take the example of Nepal. The reason they faced such a catastrophic disaster, because they were not prepared. When we see people in Ethiopia —

AMY GOODMAN : More than seven — what? About 7,000 people dead or missing?

HARJEET SINGH : Exactly. That’s the number.

AMY GOODMAN : Because of a glacier that melted?

HARJEET SINGH : Absolutely. So, it was a glacial lake outburst floods. And the numbers are important. They lost — the destruction was to the tune of $2.6 billion, and they will need now $5 billion for recovery and rehabilitation, which is 10% of their GDP . Imagine.

AMY GOODMAN : Why should the wealthy countries give it to them?

HARJEET SINGH : Because glaciers melted because of the burning of fossil fuels, and they did not provide money to Nepal for adaptation, and they are facing now loss and damage. So, Nepal, we should see it as a report card of the climate inaction that we have seen over the last 30 years. We did not phase out fossil fuels in time. That resulted in melting of glaciers. And we did not even have a plan or support to Nepal to deal with these climate impacts. And it shows that how we are failing to deal with climate impacts. And that’s why we say “shame.”

AMY GOODMAN : Meena Raman, you are head of programs at Third World Network, head of Friends of the Earth Malaysia. You have been to so many of these conferences. You, too, have expressed rage on each panel you are at. What do you want to see happen here?

MEENA RAMAN : Well, at this particular point in time, it’s relatively empty. The most important aspect of the COP is money, whether it’s for emission reductions, whether it’s for adaptation, whether it’s for loss and damage. The developing world came together, and they said, “We need money on the table of provision of finance.” What the developing countries demanded was actually to ensure that we talk about this. It was about talking about how the developed world is going to do that.

But all we came here as, you know, the EU commissioner was saying anything about finance is dead in the water. Now, that is horror, because we just came out of Nepal, as we know, and you say, “dead in the water.” People are literally dying due to the historical —

AMY GOODMAN : In the water.

MEENA RAMAN : “Dead in the water.” That’s what Hoekstra said. It was — it was for us —

AMY GOODMAN : The EU negotiator.

MEENA RAMAN : The EU commissioner. The EU commissioner. So, even before this COP , he said it. So, when you go to the negotiating halls, what you saw was finance was dead in the water, nothing on finance. So there’s no point talking about having higher ambition in terms of emission reductions or developing countries having to do fossil fuel phaseout or having more targets on electrification. They’re not going to be able to do this, if what they say is the means to implement that is not available. So, this is where this COP always becomes a problem.

AMY GOODMAN : You are wearing a sign — you are wearing a sticker, Nafkote Dabi, on the back of your ID here that says “Make rich polluters pay.” You have said — you’ve talked about inequality. Oxfam International is known for their report , “Disaster Divide.” The richest 0.1%, or 8 million people, have more emissions than the bottom 3.5 billion people, and that their carbon emissions contribute to the increase of climate disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and food crises. Can you explain how you feel this can be remedied? And how close to a tipping point are we?

NAFKOTE DABI : So, at the heart of the negotiations right now lies money, because, ultimately, you know, to support communities to adapt to the climate crisis, they need finance. And what rich countries, especially the EU, is saying is, 'There is no money at home.' But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities. You know, just private jets alone, you can raise $45 billion a year. From the excess of profit of fossil fuel companies, you can raise $400 billion. So, this money is available, and you can support communities at home, whether in Europe or the U.S. And then you can commit to your international climate finance obligation and support communities in the Global South, especially, you know, in Africa, that are faced with droughts, floods, displacement and death.

AMY GOODMAN : You know, we just had a headline on a vote on war in the U.S. Senate, and the amount — the billions of dollars that are being spent on the war in Iran, which has also led the entire world to understand how dependent we are on fossil fuels.

NAFKOTE DABI : Exactly. You know, emissions from military is about 5%. This is something that we’re not talking about. There’s huge money, as you said, Amy, going towards militarization, when communities around the world are actually literally dying from escalating extreme weather events. For the first time, by the way, Amy, I’m feeling really desperate, because we’re being told next year is going to be the hottest year on record. It’s going to go up to 1.7. Right now as we’re speaking, communities around the world are faced with the worst El Niño on record, and there is no support. These are communities that have done the least to cause the climate crisis, but they’re being left alone to deal with this situation. So, it’s a very shameful COP .

AMY GOODMAN : Now, what are the NGOs going to do? We just have two minutes before we end with an 8-year-old child who spoke out. A few years ago, it was Greta Thunberg, when she was 15 years old. Now we’re going to Little Miss Environment Kenya, who is 8, who has something to teach her elders. But one last statement. Harjeet, where we go from here? Are the NGOs going to reject the text? And what does it matter? What role do you play?

HARJEET SINGH : So, we have already rejected the current text. And what we would like to see: the developing countries really standing up and reject this text. And we keep saying developing countries are here to represent their own citizens. They can’t accept a text which will not enable them to implement climate action back home because there is no money on the table. And that’s exactly the reason developing countries have now — need to be very loud and clear in saying this COP outcome is not going to help us, unless developed countries open their pockets. It’s all about money.

AMY GOODMAN : Meena, how can it be this is the largest COP , and you’re talking about it being the greatest failure? Pick up that mic.

MEENA RAMAN : Yeah. The problem is that when you have the developed world come here and say that they don’t have national budgets to put on the table, and they talk about leadership, I think it is really imperative that we work with our Global North to actually put the pressure on the developed countries. We can’t have COP after COP backsliding. We let alone scaling up our resources. The U.K. has cut its pledge to the Green Climate Fund. The Global Environment Facility, the worst replenishment ever. So, when they are backsliding, here we are asking for more top up.

AMY GOODMAN : And finally, Nafkote, if you can talk about next year? We’re going to Ethiopia for COP32. What is the point of these COPs?

NAFKOTE DABI : You know, Ethiopia is faced — is at the frontline of the climate crisis. Ethiopians know what it means to face drought. Ethiopians are the most resilient people. They have been through many droughts, droughts after droughts. Right now, as I said, we’re faced with El Niño. Next year, the Ethiopian COP presidency needs to deliver justice for communities at the frontline of the climate crisis.

AMY GOODMAN : We have to leave it there, Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International, Harjeet Singh of Fossil Food Treaty Initiative, Meena Raman of Third World Network.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.
