scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

The world’s top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s Rohingya Muslim minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 refugees into Bangladesh. The landmark ruling is the first time the International Court of Justice has held a nation directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. “This is a vindication of what Rohingyas have been saying for the last almost 50 years, since 1978, when the first wave of genocidal expulsion was conducted by the very same perpetrating institution,” says Burmese dissident scholar Maung Zarni. By recognizing Myanmar’s “identity-based group destruction” of the Royinghas, he says, “the court vindicated [the] Rohingya’s collective articulation, memory and suffering.”

“For the first time in its history, the court has set up a process for restitution and reparation for the members of the Rohingya community,” explains Philippe Sands, an international human rights lawyer who served on the legal team for The Gambia, which first brought the legal case against Myanmar to the ICJ six years ago. Sands discusses next steps for restitution and reparations to Rohingya victims, as well as what the Myanmar judgment means for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, also before the ICJ .

AMY GOODMAN : Later in the broadcast, we’ll speak with three leading environmental justice advocates, from Malaysia, from Ethiopia and from India. But right now we go to this top story out of The Hague. This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

In a historic decision, the International Court of Justice in The Hague has ruled Myanmar, also known as Burma, committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims during a 2017 military crackdown that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. It’s the first time the court has held a nation directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. The presiding judge of the International Court, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, read the ruling.

JUDGE YUJI IWASAWA : For these reasons, the court, one, by nine votes to six, finds that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. … The court has also determined that the estimate of 10,000 Rohingya violently killed during those clearance operations is supported by the evidence. … On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.

AMY GOODMAN : The genocide case against Burma, or Myanmar, was brought by The Gambia, the smallest country in mainland Africa. Gambia’s Justice Minister Dawda Jallow spoke in The Hague after the ruling.

DAWDA JALLOW : Today, the International Court of Justice confirmed what Rohingya have said since 2017: What was done to them was genocide, and Myanmar is responsible. The court has found that Myanmar breached the 1948 convention, Genocide Convention, and has ordered to make reparations. This is the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide, the crime of crimes. The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived, they testified, and today they were believed.

AMY GOODMAN : The International Court of Justice, ICJ , case was closely followed in Bangladesh, where more than 1.2 million Rohingya Muslim refugees live after being forcibly displaced from their homes. Rahama Khatun is a 43-year-old Rohingya widow living in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh.

RAHAMA KHATUN : [translated] My husband was killed in the Rakhine area. I want justice for his murder. Following this verdict, I am now demanding exemplary punishment for those who killed my husband. I hope the perpetrators will receive the punishment they deserve. …

We hope to return to Myanmar one day. However, for a safe and dignified return, our homes and lands must be restored, adequate compensation must be provided, and our fundamental rights and citizenship must be guaranteed. Our children must also be given access to education.

AMY GOODMAN : While Bangladesh is home to the most Rohingya refugees, there are also sizable populations in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, United Arab Emirates, India and here in Turkey. Earlier today, Malaysia announced it’ll resettle 10,000 Rohingya refugees in Turkey.

Thursday’s historic ruling comes as the International Court of Justice is also in the process of determining whether Israel committed genocide in Gaza, in a case brought by South Africa.

We’re joined now by two guests. Philippe Sands served on The Gambia’s legal team. His piece in The New York Times today is headlined “Can a Country Be Guilty of Genocide? Finally, the Answer Is Yes.” Philippe Sands is a professor of law at University College London and a visiting professor at Harvard Law School. He’s also the author of East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity .

We are also joined in London by Maung Zarni. He’s a Burmese dissident and co-author of the 2014 study headlined “The Slow-Burning Genocide of Myanmar’s Rohingya.” He’s a human rights activist and scholar of genocide.

Maung Zarni, let’s begin with you. Can you respond to the ICJ decision, the first time the court has held a country responsible for genocide?

MAUNG ZARNI : Yes. This is a vindication of what Rohingyas have been saying for the last almost 50 years, since 1978, when the first wave of genocidal expulsion was conducted by the very same perpetrating institution, Myanmar military. The Rohingyas were the first to actually frame their experience, those who survived the first wave, under the false pretext of illegal immigration crackdown in February 1978, as genocide. But they have not been believed. And many of us who started looking at this from a both historical and sociological, not just legal, perspective of genocide, which is a coordinated process of group destruction based on identity, have been saying it.

And so, yesterday, the court ruling simply vindicated what Rohingyas have known for decades to be a genocidal persecution of their group simply because of their identity. They are killed, their community is uprooted and destroyed, simply because they are Rohingya. Genocide is an identity-based group destruction. And so the court vindicated Rohingya’s collective articulation, memory and sufferings.

AMY GOODMAN : If you could, Zarni, describe the condition on the ground, both in Bangladesh, that has more than a million Rohingya who have fled their country, Burma, and the conditions on the ground in a country that the ICJ , the International Court of Justice, has determined has committed a genocide against the Rohingya.

MAUNG ZARNI : Well, in Bangladesh, the, like you said, Amy, 1.2 million Rohingya genocide survivors — they are not simply displaced people from Myanmar, as the Bangladeshi government described it — that they live in, you know, semi-Gaza-like situation, except without the daily bombings and cutting off deliberately of food rations and access to humanitarian aid. I’ve been there a number of times, and, like, just a month after they were driven out, about 700 — over 700,000 were driven out in the months of August, September and October in 2017. And, you know, they have no future. You know, the resettlement is not an option. They are trapped in these refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar.

Inside Myanmar, about half a million Rohingyas are living under military occupation, not of — not the Myanmar military, but another anti-Muslim, anti-Rohingya Buddhist racist group called Arakan Army, representing Buddhist Rakhine in the region of Rakhine state, which is shared by both Rohingya, predominantly Muslims, and Rakhine ethnic group, largely Buddhist. And, you know, they’re under military occupation.

And then you’ve got another population of diaspora in Malaysia, about 100,000. They are subject to all kinds of hate mobilization by the Malaysian groups.

And so, you know, when we talk about Rohingya, we need to look at, like, three different populations that have survived and suffer all kinds of hardships and, you know, repression: in diaspora, refugee camps and still inside Myanmar.

AMY GOODMAN : I want to turn to Philippe Sands, who is on The Gambia’s legal defense team at the International Court of Justice. First of all, Philippe, why The Gambia? Why did they bring this case? And number two, talk about the significance, again, of this being the first country that has been convicted of genocide, and what that ultimately means.

PHILIPPE SANDS : Sure. Well, it’s lovely to be back on with you after a gap of about 15 years, Amy.

The Rohingya case was brought by The Gambia basically on the initial instance of a single individual, Ba Tambadou, who was the attorney general of The Gambia, who went on a visit to Cox’s Bazar, the place that’s just been described, spoke to a lot of the people who had fled Myanmar, heard stories, and because he had been previously a prosecutor in the Rwanda Criminal Tribunal in The Hague, in Arusha, understood that the stories that he was being told told a story of genocide. He persuaded the government of The Gambia, of which he was a member, to bring a case to the International Court of Justice. One of the reasons that happened is because both Myanmar and Gambia were parties to the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of Genocide, and The Gambia is predominantly a Muslim country concerned about the mistreatment of a Muslim community in Myanmar.

So, that was the basis on which, in 2019, the case began. It’s run for seven years. It’s been fiercely litigated. Myanmar participated very actively. At one stage, Aung San Suu Kyi, was the former Nobel Prize winner, was the head of their delegation in one of the early phases of the case.

And the judgment was handed down yesterday by the International Court of Justice. And by a majority, as you said, of 9 to 6, the court found, for the first time ever — it’s a historic judgment — that a state, Myanmar, was responsible for perpetrating acts of genocide. And this has enormous significance, because it essentially breathes life into a convention that was adopted in 1948 at the instance of another single individual, Raphael Lemkin, a Polish jurist, who invented the concept of genocide in 1945.

AMY GOODMAN : So, it was a 9-to-6 ruling. How does it get enforced? And then, as we begin to wrap up, talk about what this means for another case brought before the International Court of Justice by an African country, by South Africa, against Israel. They are charging Israel with genocide for what’s happened in Gaza.

PHILIPPE SANDS : Well, the judgment of yesterday is binding and final, so there is no appeal. It will be enforced through U.N. bodies and, presumably, will go to the Security Council of the U.N. for some sort of authorization. But more significantly, for the first time in its history, the court has set up a process for restitution and reparation for the members of the Rohingya community. It’s given Myanmar two years to report on the steps it’s going to take to allow full restitution for the homes — but a lot of them have been destroyed, so it’s very difficult to see how that’s going to happen — and return of the Rohingya — and they may not want to return. And after two years, The Gambia will be able to go back to court and ask for reparations, not for itself, but for the individual members of the Rohingya group. So, a process is now in train and is now underway in relation to the process.

In terms of the implications of the case for other cases, including the one brought by South Africa against Israel, the court has basically adopted the standard it has always adopted. To prove genocide, you have to show genocidal conduct, conduct in which the only reasonable inference is that it was motivated by an intention to destroy a group in whole or in part. And so, the burden will be on South Africa to do that with its own evidence. I’m not expressing a view as to whether that evidence meets the burden or not. But the court in the Rohingya case did go out of its way to make clear that every case will turn on its own facts. So, following this judgment yesterday, the door remains open to the South African case. It has not been shut, nor has it been opened more widely. It will be for South Africa to persuade the judges on the basis of the evidence.

And just so that your viewers are clear, this case is not going to finally come to court for the major hearing for three or four years, because it’s on a very slow-track process. So don’t expect any action until 2030 or 2031.

AMY GOODMAN : Finally, if you could talk about the U.S. and the China response to this decision, Philippe Sands.

PHILIPPE SANDS : I mean, the initial U.S. response, the State Department put out a perfectly reasonable statement saying that they were going to study the judgment and then consider what their reaction is to it. There had been previously a tweet, I think it was, put out by the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, warning the court — almost seen by some as a threat to the court — that if it lowered the standard, it would face the same kinds of sanctions and difficulties, or might, that the International Criminal Court has faced.

My own view is, as I said in the op-ed piece in The New York Times this morning, is the standard has not been lowered. The case simply turned on its own facts. It’s the same “only reasonable inference” standard. And we will have to wait and see.

As for China, I’m not aware of what the reaction has been. One of the six who voted against the judgment was the Chinese judge, Madam Xue. The American judge voted in favor —

AMY GOODMAN : Philippe Sands, I want to thank —

PHILIPPE SANDS : — of the judgment.

AMY GOODMAN : I want to thank you so much for being with us, Philippe Sands, human rights lawyer, served on The Gambia’s legal team in The Gambia v. Myanmar case at the International Court of Justice. We’ll link to your New York Times piece , “Can a Country Be Guilty of Genocide? Finally, the Answer Is Yes.” And Maung Zarni, Burmese dissident and co-author of the study , “The Slow-Burning Genocide of Myanmar’s Rohingya.”

Coming up, today is the last scheduled day of the U.N. climate summit here in Antalya, Turkey. There is a great deal of controversy, advocates saying the draft agreement text is a failure and should be rejected. And the minister of Panama has said he may block the agreement if Panama’s limited demands are not met. We’ll hear from him and host a discussion with environmental justice advocates. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “Polluters Must Pay” protesters dressed up as peanuts, holding up giant pennies that spell out “pay up” here at COP31 in Antalya earlier this week.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

The exact truth behind Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia remains murky. But one thing’s for sure: it’s been a huge boon to China hawks like Marco Rubio and other enormous AI firms.

Because of a combination of the way we’ve structured our economy and Washington corruption, one man’s horniness can risk bringing down the US economy and ramping up conflict with China. (Alex Kraus / Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Our winter issue is out soon. Subscribe today to get your copy in our first mailing.

O ften, when people cheat on their spouses, they get kicked out of the house and strain their families. Not many can say they wiped out $1.8 trillion worth of share value and made the economy wobble.

Yet this is exactly the case with ousted Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang and the scandal surrounding his various infidelities, including to a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy. (Or is she?)

The uncertainty around that question is part of the general murkiness of this entire affair (no pun intended), one tied into a knot of three separate political threads: the economy’s outsize reliance on the artificial intelligence industry, ruthless corporate anti-competition, and the simmering new Cold War with China.

While Huang had a number of infidelities, it’s his affair with business executive Alice Huang that is central to both the global attention this has drawn and to his ouster from the company he had founded over a Denny’s meal with only $40,000 of capital, thanks to his paramour’s alleged role as a spy for the Ministry of State Security, roughly China’s equivalent to the Central Intelligence Agency. Even as the infractions piled up, it’s hard to imagine Huang — a widely admired , politically connected CEO who commanded intense loyalty from his employees — being pushed out of his own company over infidelity if not for the possibility, leaked to the press, that he fell for a Chinese government honey trap.

So it’s notable that no one seems to really know whether or not Alice Huang truly was a spy. CNN reports that US intelligence agencies aren’t actually sure, with some officials viewing media reports alleging that she is as overstating the reality. At the same time, Donald Trump , Vice President J. D. Vance , and Attorney General Todd Blanche have all publicly claimed uncertainty about this central allegation. The Singaporean government went out of its way to explicitly deny The Wall Street Journal’s reporting that its officials had been concerned about her alleged spying for Beijing and investigated it.

Most explosively, T he Washington Post reported that the spy claim came from one official in particular: China hawk Marco Rubio, who personally reshaped the CIA’s more ambiguous intelligence into a memo forcefully making the spy allegation and circulated it around the administration all the way back in May, to little effect.

Let’s take a moment now to note how odd it is that the details of that memo then somehow made their way to the press. Let’s also take a moment to note how odd it is that neither this administration, which has zealously investigated and thrown the book at leakers, nor Rubio, who has called leakers “criminals” and once tried to throw some in prison for a decade, seem to particularly care about this leak.

S o what exactly is going on here? It’s too early to say for sure. But one thing we can say with certainty is that Huang was long given the side-eye by Washington’s China hawks owing to his unabashed advocacy for doing business with China, his closeness with the president, and the fact that he had used that closeness to get Trump to let Nvidia skirt US export controls and sell its chips to China. For those hawks, who Huang publicly lambasted as carrying a “badge of shame,” this was a grave offense and a threat to national security, with the possibility that China could use the advanced chips to win the “AI race” that this crowd is obsessed with.

Another certainty is that these same hawks have wasted no time in seizing on the affair to push for harder-line policies against China, at a time when Trump had been edging toward a more conciliatory posture with the country, drawing growing pushback from Washington. The Trump administration has now tightened export controls on AI chips in the wake of this scandal, and a consensus is now e merging in Congress to go beyond this. China hawks are making a renewed push to tighten them even further, with parts of a fourth bill doing so now set to be added to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for 2027.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, reportedly the main figure within the administration resisting a crackdown on the export of Nvidia chips, is being publicly undermined by one of his own fellow cabinet members, facing the possibility of being investigated , and may see his head roll over the episode, all as lawmakers demand he clamp down on the chip exports. China hawks “are thrilled right now” and are “gonna win the day,” one Trump official told T he Washington Sun , while an economist who backs the stricter controls told the outlet that with Lutnick and Nvidia “sidelined, the center of gravity has shifted to Rubio-world,” since they “were the main opposition to any sort of export controls.”

C hina hawks aren’t the only ones who stand to benefit from Huang’s ouster. The battle over China’s access to high-end AI chips is, in part, a proxy for a whole other battle being fought within the industry.

The removal of Huang is viewed as a blow to the movement behind open-source AI models — those that the general public can download and tinker with, as opposed to closed-source models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude, where the developer has exclusive control but chooses to make the model available for public use. Open-source models also happen to be mostly the kind developed by Chinese companies, whose cheaper models US companies are increasingly turning to .

Huang also happened to be a major champion for — and, more importantly, financial backer of — such models, probably because the proliferation of more AI models also means more business for Nvidia. One venture capitalist who invested in some of the same start-ups as Nvidia told the Financial Times that Huang getting the boot means “we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers.”

That put him at odds with companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, whose commercial interest lies in trying to dominate the AI market and preventing the spread of open-source models that would make people less reliant on their products. Anthropic has long been an outspoken proponent of the export controls on AI chips that Huang chafed against, breaking from other industry players over the issue by backing the three restrictionist bills included in the NDAA for 2027.

OpenAI, meanwhile, pulled back on its advocacy for export controls, both as Huang’s dealmaking saw it become more financially intertwined with Nvidia and to align more closely with Trump as he came under Huang’s influence, costing China hawks what they had counted as an important industry ally. But Huang’s ouster has “loosened them up a bit,” a source told Politico , with OpenAI now back to arguing in favor of those same three export control bills in the defense authorization bill for next year.

In fact, it goes much further than this. Because filings show that both of these closed-source firms have thrown a small mountain of money into lobbying various arms of the federal government on this issue, including the very two organs — the State Department and the National Security Council (NSC) — that happen to be headed by Marco Rubio, China-hawk-in-chief and the main figure responsible for the spy claims about Huang’s mistress.

Starting from the third quarter of this year, dating from July to the end of September — the period that came after Rubio reportedly circulated his spy allegation memo in May — OpenAI spent a whopping $1.5 million lobbying on issues that included “foreign AI capabilities and national-security risks,” lining up with Politico’s reporting that the firm had started voicing its support for export controls to Congress in recent months. This was a notable shift from 2025: that year, OpenAI’s in-house lobbying outfit had spent substantially less than this amount per quarter and hadn’t lobbied the State Department, nor does that phrase appear as a lobbying issue in that year’s filings.

In other words, it’s not just that OpenAI started pushing for restricting the export of chips right after Rubio circulated his questionable memo linking Nvidia’s CEO to Chinese spying, and that it was that CEO’s removal that had “loosened them up” to do it. They also lobbied Rubio’s own department, and did it just months before that memo mysteriously leaked to the press, forcing his ouster.

There is a similar pattern with the other closed-source AI giant, Anthropic, which, in that same July-to-September period paid several Trumpworld lobbying firms to work on this matter.

One was Navigators Global, which that very same quarter started lobbying Congress on behalf of the AI firm on the export control provisions in the NDAA. Navigators Global’s cofounder happened to be Rubio’s very first chief of staff when he was a senator, while one of the lobbyists who worked on this issue is Andy Keiser, who for fourteen years served in various roles for ex-congressman Mike Rogers, the Trump ally who ran for Michigan’s Senate seat this year and in 2024.

Sit for a moment with the fact that Anthropic was pushing this issue using a lobbying firm closely connected to the very figure arguably most responsible for driving Huang’s ouster.

It’s a similar case with Ballard Partners, founded by a longtime Florida lobbyist who counts Rubio as a friend and where Trump’s recently ousted chief of staff Susie Wiles was managing partner for years before joining up with Trump in 2019 — a firm so connected that one departed Trump official has charged it “controlled” White House policy. In the third quarter, it started lobbying for Anthropic on “advocacy regarding US policy regarding AI” to the tune of $380,000, including at Rubio’s NSC, for which it employed two recently departed Trump national security personnel, one of whom had just worked at Rubio’s State Department.

Another specifically Rubio-connected lobbying firm used by Anthropic for this was Continental Strategy, one of whose managing partners is Alberto Martinez — a “trusted advisor” to Rubio who worked in various roles for the former senator over the course of a decade, including chief of staff and senior strategist on his first Senate race — and which promoted Wiles’s daughter a day after Trump hired her. Martinez was among the lobbyists Continental used to lobby agencies that included Rubio’s NSC (from April to the end of June) and then Rubio’s State Department (in this just-passed third quarter) on “AI development and national security,” for which it was paid a total of $300,000 by Anthropic for these periods. Both Ballard and Continental’s roles were first reported by ZeroHedge , but this is based on my own separate analysis of Anthropic’s 2026 lobbying disclosures.

It’s remarkable that at the same time the interests of Rubio-led China hawks and firms like Anthropic were crossing over, the company was literally employing Rubio’s own former loyalists to lobby the government bodies he was in charge of.

This is on top of the $230,000 that Anthropic paid over the past year’s three quarters to Fierce Government Relations — a firm with a couple of Trump-connected employees — to lobby Congress and the Office of the President on export controls and the NDAA bills; another $180,000 over the same period to Aquia for the same issues; $60,000 to the Democratic firm Avenue Solutions to lobby Congress on the NDAA starting in the third quarter; and the nearly $6 million it spent in-house in that period to lobby on issues that included these topics. In that last case, it used a longtime staffer of Sen. Patty Murray, who had been demanding in recent months that Trump impose these stricter export controls.

So in summary, the two closed-source AI firms that view China’s AI industry as a threat to their own bottom line have done the following: lobbied heavily for these China-squeezing export controls this year; appear to have in some cases ramped up their lobbying on this after Rubio circulated the sensational but unproven claim that led to Huang’s booting; hired former staffers from Trumpworld to do that lobbying; and in particular, hired lobbying firms and used lobbyists with long-standing connections to Rubio specifically to do it.

The picture that emerges is of the unmistakable — some might say convenient — convergence of interests between Washington’s China hawks and AI giants, and the downright eerie overlap between the offices and personnel of what are in theory meant to be two different entities. Even more convenient, all of this has come to a head just as one of these AI giants, Anthropic, was set to embark on its initial public offering, which it did yesterday, raising $81 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record.

Like I said: convenient.

L ess convenient is another thing we can say for sure, which is that, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO aside, this entire saga is causing heart rates to spike.

That’s because Nvidia — and, owing to his domination of the company and personal role in every deal it struck, Huang himself — is a load-bearing force for an industry straining to stay standing up, passing out the necessary capital for flagship AI firms, start-ups, the building of data centers, and the neo-cloud firms that provide the computing power for firms that can’t build their own. In fact, Nvidia effectively came to the rescue of one of those neo-clouds, CoreWeave, when its bonds recently entered distressed territory after skeptical investors started dumping the company’s debt en masse.

Huang’s ouster throws the industry into uncertainty as it waits to see, first, if any one person is able to actually fill Huang’s shoes, and second, if the person who does has the same kind of appetite for risk that he did. So far, indications are that the interim CEO does not , and with the firm about to be dragged through an acre of thorns in the form of congressional hearings and other scrutiny, it would not be surprising if it embarks on a more conservative approach going forward.

That doesn’t necessarily mean that the AI industry is headed toward an imminent crash. But this is all spectacularly bad timing given the spate of setbacks and growing investor doubts it’s been weathering, the last one being an incoming US Congress dominated by politicians who ran and won on restricting the data centers that AI firms need to keep being built to stay financially viable.

At this point, you might stop to marvel at the absurdity that — because of the way we’ve structured our economy, the way it’s intertwined with US foreign policy, and the corrupting distortion of the Washington revolving door and influence-peddling — one man’s horniness threatens to bring down the US economy and ramp up conflict between two nuclear-armed powers. It’s just one of several layers of absurdity to a situation and industry that, without ever being consulted on it, we have all as a society been roped into staking our collective future on.

Huang is not the first or last CEO who will have a personal scandal that can be exploited by shadowy forces with their own ulterior motives. But because of the nature of the AI industry, whichever executive draws embarrassing headlines next, it’s gossip that we’re all going to have to care deeply about.

Branko Marcetic is a Jacobin staff writer and the author of Yesterday’s Man: The Case Against Joe Biden .

scraped.title: Billionaires Always Want to Maintain Control
scraped.description: California’s billionaire tax was defeated this time. But Mark Zuckerberg’s deal with Meta in anticipation of Proposition 40 teaches us two things: billionaire wealth can be converted into cash, and tech elites value control even more than wealth.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

California’s billionaire tax was defeated this time. But Mark Zuckerberg’s deal with Meta in anticipation of Proposition 40 teaches us two things: billionaire wealth can be converted into cash, and tech elites value control even more than wealth.

The Meta deal struck by Mark Zuckerberg in the face of California’s proposed billionaire tax can help us understand the obstacles that the movement to tax the ultrarich’s wealth faces, beyond even their massive spending against Proposition 40. (Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images)

Our winter issue is out soon. Subscribe today to get your copy in our first mailing.

I n October, Meta released a filing saying that Mark Zuckerberg had threatened to leave California in anticipation of Proposition 40 , the billionaire wealth tax on the 2026 state ballot, which was defeated 53 to 47 percent. According to the document, Zuckerberg told the board he was “evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California,” and that any steps toward doing so, including listing his residential real estate on the market, “would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees.”

In response, the board quickly mobilized to negotiate a deal: Meta agreed to issue a new class of nonvoting (“Class C”) stock, which will be distributed to all shareholders in January 2027. This would have allowed Zuckerberg to sell his shares to convert a portion of his wealth into the billions in cash he would need to meet his potential tax liability, without losing his near-supermajority voting share. In exchange, he agreed to stay in the state for at least eight years and keep his $1 annual salary.

Conveniently, the new stock will also allow Meta to raise capital for artificial intelligence investments without changing the decision-making composition of the company. In the fallout of the proposition’s defeat, it’s useful to reflect on what the Meta deal can help us understand for the long-term movement to tax the ultrarich’s wealth.

P rop 40 was designed as a onetime 5 percent tax, payable over five years, on the net worth of California residents with over $1 billion who lived in the state as of January 1, 2026. The proposition was written by legal and economics faculty and introduced by the health care workers’ union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers (SEIU-UHW). The goal of the tax was to raise around $100 billion, which would offset roughly 90 percent of the federal budget cuts to health programs, including Medi-Cal, since the beginning of the second Trump administration — and in particular, since the passing of the 2025 “Big Beautiful Bill,” which takes effect this January.

According to research by economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, California’s billionaire wealth reached around $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, which is roughly equal to the total income reported by every Californian in a year. This wealth is both extremely concentrated and recent: it’s increased by 144 percent in just three years. The approximately 250 billionaires who would qualify only pay about 0.2 percent of their wealth in California income tax each year, representing 2.4 percent of total California income tax revenue. The four richest billionaires, Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang, pay only 0.07 percent of their wealth.

If Proposition 40 had passed, it would have been the first tax of its kind and the culmination of decades of advocacy by policymakers and researchers across the world working to expose how dramatically economic inequality has grown and the degree of billionaires’ tax avoidance. This is particularly salient in California, the fourth-largest economy in the world and home to fifty-eight of the Fortune 500 companies. Companies in the Bay Area alone represent 35 percent of the market cap of the world’s top hundred companies. This makes the state an ideal place to experiment with taxing the ultrawealthy.

T he initiative failed for myriad, well-documented reasons. Primarily, it faced a concerted and incredibly well-funded opposition campaign. Its opponents, mostly ultrawealthy donors, spent $378.4 million against the measure (compared to the yes campaign’s budget of $33.5 million). Google cofounder and Donald Trump supporter Sergey Brin alone donated $102 million, and also funded two additional Propositions (41 and 42) designed to block the tax if it passed. California Governor Gavin Newsom opposed the measure and endorsed Proposition 42, stating , “Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level.”

According to Rigel Robinson, former Berkeley city councilmember and Democratic public policy consultant,

It would be a mistake to see the electoral outcome of Proposition 40 as a clear rejection of its goal from voters. There was the enormous and well-funded opposition campaign, and competing and confusing ballot measures designed to nullify the measure. Proposition 42, which was put on the ballot to prevent Proposition 40 (and future versions of it) from taking effect even if it did pass, was sold to voters as a protection for retirement savings.

However, in California and across the country, candidates won on a message of seizing power from billionaires and championing affordability. In many ways, this is the sort of message Bernie Sanders tried to bring to the Democratic agenda a decade ago.

Voters across the country have demonstrated that redistribution and economic justice are clear priorities, and we cannot let the outcome of this proposition diminish the ground won.

There were also concerns about the legality and mechanics of the legislation — in particular, that it was introduced as a onetime proposition, was not national, and was technically a retroactive tax, since it applied to anyone living in the state as of January 2026. And as Fred Glass explained in Jacobin , California’s labor and progressive forces were unable to form a unified front in support of the measure.

While disappointing, it’s helpful to historicize the initiative and the broader movement to tax the assets of the ultrawealthy alongside other fights for redistribution. The federal income tax, for example, took several attempts before successfully passing. It took the Sixteenth Amendment passing in 1913 to make it permanent. SEIU-UHW has already said it plans to try again in 2028, and Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna have introduced a bill at the federal level this spring.

F rom the Meta deal, we can learn two things. First, it is possible for tech leadership to convert their wealth into liquidity. One of the most persistent arguments against taxing the ultrawealthy is that their money isn’t “real,” since it’s mostly in shares of companies whose value rises and falls with the market. Because of this, it shouldn’t be treated as income.

Stocks are legal claims on future production whose prices are set by expected returns. It is not uncommon for the companies who issue them to have not yet produced anything profitable or concrete. SpaceX’s shares were the most valuable in history at the time of their initial public offering (IPO), even though its AI division had lost $2 for every dollar of revenue it earned in 2025.

In other words, a stock is a title of ownership to a slice of the surplus value a company will produce. In the Marxian sense , this is an example of fictitious capital and inherently speculative. However, “speculative” does not mean unreal. As Dimitris P. Sotiropoulos, John Milios, and Spyros Lapatsioras write in A Political Economy of Contemporary Capitalism and its Crisis: Demystifying Finance , fictitious capital is not detached from real production but a necessary phase within its totality, and claims on future income can become commodities in their own right. These can be traded, priced, and converted into money at any time. A stock is not just a promise of future wealth; it is wealth (and command over the labor of others) today.

Modern finance for the AI sector also has a remarkable capacity to innovate and reinvent itself, and the financial engineering to create the Class C share is another demonstration of the sector’s remarkable capacity to adapt to secure endless capital for the AI rush.

S econd, tech executives are most concerned with losing control of their companies. As economist and tax expert Gabriel Zucman told me, “the existence of super-voting shares and the Zuckerberg and Proposition 40 episode more generally highlight that what matters most to billionaires, even more than their wealth, is their power to exert control over the giant businesses they own. This is indeed their greatest power.” He also commented on X that the opposition to the wealth tax could not be driven by concerns about losing money, since the onetime 5 percent liability would “merely bring billionaire’s fortunes back to where they stood a few weeks ago, at the beginning of September.”

Meta is not an isolated case, and a dual-class share system (which allows companies to sell shares to the public, while a small group keeps most of the votes) has been on the rise. When SpaceX went public, Elon Musk floated only 3–4 percent of the company and retained 42 percent of its shares, but 85 percent of its voting share through his “super-voting stock.” Anthropic’s IPO includes five types of stock, which specifically gives the cofounders the ability to keep a say over the controlling vote even if they give away 98 percent of their shares. The most valuable companies in the world are increasingly owned by a handful of individuals insulated from markets, shareholders, and other public mechanisms of accountability.

As Fred Glass wrote , Proposition 40 is a lost battle, not a lost war. Amid the manufactured panic over the tax, Zuckerberg seized the political moment to negotiate a deal with his company. The outcome of their agreement deepens our understanding of how to anticipate and oppose the coordinated class response against taxing extreme wealth. First, the shares of future value held by tech billionaires are not just abstractions but real money today, necessary to the current cycle of reproduction. And second, billionaires will fight hardest to protect not their fortune but their control.

The Left’s political project has to include a new front of contestation beyond fighting for shares of the returns tech companies produce. Countering the enclosure of the AI economy will require reclaiming democratic control over the infrastructures of this intelligence in the first place.

Sophie Bandarkar is a writer, organizer, and PhD student in economics. She is based in Paris.

scraped.title: What the Ottomans Tell Us About Plunder and Capitalism
scraped.description: Did colonial plunder create capitalism? Ottoman history suggests not.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Did colonial plunder create capitalism? Ottoman history suggests not.

Capitalist relations emerged from within Ottoman feudal society between 1550 and 1650, long before the Industrial Revolution and Western domination. (Heritage Art / Heritage Images via Getty Images)

Our winter issue is out soon. Subscribe today to get your copy in our first mailing.

V ivek Chibber’s recent interview on the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism and Vijay Prashad’s response in Monthly Review have reopened fundamental questions about capitalism’s origins, colonialism, and the transition from feudalism to capitalism in world history. Drawing on my research into Ottoman history, I want to make the case that societies beyond Europe belong in this history not simply for their contributions to the rise of capitalism in the West but for their own internal transformations.

The origins of capitalism and its subsequent development through colonialism are distinct historical problems. Ottoman history allows us to draw this distinction by examining a transition beyond the northwestern European cases at the center of this debate.

On the central question of this debate, I am closer to Chibber: I support his distinction between the emergence of capitalism and colonial plunder, and his insistence on looking to the internal transformation of feudal society for an explanation. I also accept Robert Brenner’s account of the English transition. My disagreement concerns whether capitalist relations could also emerge from within other feudal societies, before Western economic domination and along different historical paths. I agree with some of Prashad’s criticisms of political Marxism, but that agreement does not extend to his account of capitalism’s origins.

In the Ottoman Empire, too, capitalism developed out of the internal dynamics of feudal society without relying on colonial plunder, and before Western economic domination and the Industrial Revolution. This process transformed both society and the state, later laying the groundwork for internal colonization. Ottoman history thus brings into focus the distinctions between capitalism’s emergence, its colonial expansion, and the rise of the West — processes that Prashad folds into a single explanation.

C hibber’s starting point is that the accumulation of wealth and the emergence of capitalist social relations are distinct processes. A society that possesses vast financial resources does not necessarily organize its production along capitalist lines. Nor does the wealth that colonizers plundered create capitalism on its own.

Chibber acknowledges that once capitalist relations have emerged, such wealth can accelerate their development. Supporting his argument about capitalism’s origins therefore does not require denying colonialism’s importance in its subsequent history. On the contrary, it allows us to ask within which social relations, and at what historical stage, colonialism acquired that importance. The crucial advance we need to preserve in the debate over capitalism’s origins is the shift from explaining it through the quantity of wealth to explaining it through the character of the relations of production.

Here the meaning of primitive accumulation becomes clear. Before asking how enough money accumulated to finance investment, we need to explain how producers’ relationships to their means of subsistence and production changed. Capital’s power over production and labor depends on social relations that allow money to function as a social power. The emergence of those relations involves dispossession, coercion, and class struggle.

But we cannot equate all these processes with colonialism. Transformations within feudal society have their own history of dispossession and struggle. To treat colonial plunder as capitalism’s necessary starting point is to subsume the very history we need to explain under a different process. The value of Chibber’s intervention lies in bringing this social transformation back to the center of the debate over capitalism’s origins.

Just as trade existed before capitalism, so did plunder, invasion, and conquest. Their existence alone cannot explain the emergence of capitalist social relations.

We should also note that Chibber does not locate capitalism’s early development exclusively in England. He also includes Holland and other parts of the Low Countries in his account of the transformation of northwestern Europe. I accept Brenner’s account of the emergence of capitalism in England. My objection is not to its validity for England but to ruling out the possibility that capitalist relations could also emerge from feudalism’s internal dynamics in other societies.

Such transitions need not reproduce England’s historical trajectory or institutional forms. Different paths need not contradict political Marxism’s definition of capitalism: the social relations that define capitalism can emerge under different historical conditions and take different forms. This is the case I am making by bringing Ottoman history into the debate. I am not rejecting the explanation of the English transition but challenging the use of its specific forms as a yardstick that excludes other histories of capitalist development.

Chibber also points to northwestern Europe’s stronger growth as one reason to locate capitalism’s early development there. Here too we need to be clear about what the evidence allows us to conclude. It is one thing to explain why certain societies grew faster by pointing to capitalist relations; it is another to claim that capitalist relations existed only in those faster-growing societies. The second proposition does not follow from the first.

A society can become capitalist without becoming a leader in capitalist development. To identify capitalism, we need to establish whether capital accumulation has come to govern production and the conditions under which producers secure their livelihoods. Faster economic growth may be a consequence of capitalist relations, but it is not what defines them.

Nor can we equate the development of productive forces with economic growth or its pace. It involves changes in productive capacity, including productive techniques and the organization of labor, which we cannot reduce to increases in output. Northwestern Europe’s stronger growth therefore cannot by itself establish that slower-growing societies remained feudal or exclude the possibility of capitalist transitions elsewhere. The distinction between capitalism’s emergence and economic supremacy that we defend against Prashad must also hold when we assess Chibber’s account.

H ere I agree with Prashad’s critique of political Marxism’s explanatory framework. We cannot confine the history of capitalism to the history of English agriculture. But moving beyond that limit requires more than bringing in societies outside Europe solely for their contributions to Europe’s capitalist development.

In such an account, the rest of the world enters the explanation, but the transformation it sets out to explain remains Europe’s. Changes in those societies’ own relations of production disappear. Overcoming Eurocentrism requires more than adding examples of what the rest of the world supplied to the West. We must also investigate the emergence of capitalism within these societies’ own histories.

Prashad does of course discuss the transformation of labor and social reproduction in colonized societies, so I am not reducing his account to a tally of the wealth that colonizers transferred to Europe. My objection is to making colonial connections the overarching framework for explaining the emergence of capitalism. Explaining transformations under colonial domination does not also explain transitions in which domination played no constitutive role. Colonial relations cannot be the only way we connect societies in a global explanation.

Prashad makes clear that he does not see colonialism as mechanically producing capitalism. His argument is that we cannot understand capitalism as it historically developed — industrial, global, racialized, and imperial — apart from colonial dispossession. Nor does he discuss only accumulation after the Industrial Revolution: he also examines early plantations and transformations in colonial production.

Prashad writes: “If you ignore colonialism and the machine, you do not get the genesis of industrial capitalism, only the emergence of certain social relations.” Yet the Industrial Revolution was itself a historical outcome of capitalist development, and industrial capitalism a further stage in that development. These developments transformed capitalist relations that had already emerged; they cannot serve as the defining criteria for capitalism itself.

Explaining the emergence of those relations therefore addresses the question of capitalism’s origins. It is not simply an incomplete explanation of industrial capitalism. By making a later stage of capitalist development the measure of capitalism itself, Prashad shifts the question from how capitalist relations emerged to how they subsequently developed.

The emergence of those social relations is itself the transformation we need to investigate. We must distinguish their subsequent combination with colonialism, or their development into a new phase through mechanized production, from the causes of their emergence. When that distinction is precisely what is at issue, substituting capitalism’s entire subsequent history for the question of its origins does not resolve the disagreement.

My question for Prashad, then, goes beyond whether capitalism is conceivable without colonialism. The capitalist transformation I identify in the Ottoman Empire is not a thought experiment about what might have happened had colonialism never existed but a historical process we need to explain. Why should capitalist relations that developed without colonialism fall outside an account of “capitalism as it actually emerged”?

Defining the West’s colonial and industrial development as capitalism’s real history, while excluding other paths to capitalism, does not resolve the question of origins. It narrows the history we set out to explain.

The same problem arises in the relationship between primitive accumulation and colonialism. Colonial dispossession can be one means of separating producers from the means of production and accumulating capital. It does not follow that we must define primitive accumulation, as an explanation of the emergence of capitalist relations, through colonialism.

We need to distinguish the establishment of capitalist relations from their subsequent expansion into new areas and their reproduction. Colonialism can play an enormous role in this second process. But projecting that role backward changes the explanation of capitalism’s origins.

My objection to Prashad is not that he discusses colonial dispossession, but that he places this connection at the center of the question of origins. The social conditions under which capitalism emerged without colonialism then drop out of the explanation.

We therefore cannot treat the emergence of capitalism, the West’s global dominance, and the Industrial Revolution as different names for the same problem. The first asks how new relations of production emerged; the second, how the West established its dominance on a world scale; the third, how the technical and social organization of production changed radically. These processes shape one another, but an explanation of one cannot substitute for an explanation of another. Colonialism’s importance to the West’s rise or industrialization does not establish that capitalism originated in colonialism.

We are challenging the use of later developments as founding causes of relations that had already emerged. The early appearance of colonial practices does not establish this causal link either. The fact that two processes unfolded at the same time does not show that one produced the other.

Establishing that requires us to identify the mechanisms through which colonial appropriation brought capitalist relations of production into being. The strength of the Ottoman case lies in shifting the debate from a hypothetical world without colonialism to the question of how these relations actually emerged.

M y argument is that capitalist relations in the Ottoman Empire emerged from within feudal society between roughly 1550 and 1650. After 1650, these relations reinforced one another and became increasingly decisive in shaping social reproduction. This chronology rules out explaining the origins of Ottoman capitalism as a consequence of the West’s later economic domination. It also prevents us from treating the absence of large-scale mechanized industry as proof of capitalism’s absence.

What we need to investigate is the transformation of Ottoman society from within during this period. In this light, we see not a feudal society standing still in the face of a capitalist West but a history in which productive forces developed, relations of production changed, and a new social structure took shape through class struggle.

Recent contributions to Ottoman economic and social history include Mehmet Kuru ’s work on Izmir’s regional economy, Mehmet Ali Çelik ’s research on çiftliks and agrarian labor, and Önder Eren Akgül ’s study of capital accumulation and dispossession in western Anatolia. These studies help illuminate changes in Ottoman production, property, and class relations across different periods.

What drives this transformation is not the first appearance of trade or money, both of which already existed in feudal society. What changes is the relationship between the conditions that allow producers to continue producing and control over the surplus. When merchant capital begins to organize production through credit, the supply of raw materials, and control over output, the movement of capital comes to govern the continuity of production. Producers’ relationship to the market can shift from merely selling what they have left over to depending on it to sustain their livelihoods and production.

The interpretation I am developing in ongoing research concerns how changes in property, credit, and labor relations increasingly placed the continuation of production under capital’s control. Demonstrating this requires more than evidence of expanding trade or growing indebtedness: it requires tracing how class struggle transformed producers’ access to the means of production and subsistence. Competitive pressure is one mechanism to investigate within this process, but we cannot reduce the transformation to producers losing their holdings because they could not compete.

It is in this transformation that I look for the emergence of Ottoman capitalism. The starting point of this explanation is not wealth that colonial plunder brought in from outside but changes within existing social relations. Those changes concern not only who controls the surplus but also how it flows back into reproduction.

As the expansion of production, control over labor, and access to markets intertwine, accumulation begins to determine the conditions of social reproduction. Capital thus confronts producers not simply as a power that buys their output but as a social relation that governs the conditions under which production can continue.

The existence of trade does not prove the existence of capitalism. But it does not follow that merchant capital cannot reorganize production or help transform feudal class relations. An increase in the volume of trade is not the same as the subordination of production to capital. This is not a story of capitalism emerging spontaneously from the continuous expansion of markets but a history of qualitative change in capital’s relationship to production.

The development of productive forces is also part of this transformation. A deeper division of labor, a larger scale of production, connections between different branches of production, and the reorganization of labor all increase society’s productive power even before mechanization. This development proceeds alongside changes in relations of production and struggles over control of the surplus. The conflicting interests of peasants, artisans, merchants, local ruling elites, and the state shape the direction and form of the transformation.

To speak of feudalism’s internal dynamics is not to tell a story of technological progress unfolding on its own. It is to understand capitalism’s emergence as a history in which productive forces and relations of production develop and reshape one another through class struggle. Producers’ efforts to preserve their access to land and means of subsistence come up against the ruling classes’ attempts to extract a larger surplus. The terms of debt, taxation, and control over production take shape through these conflicts.

The outcome of the transition is not a destination that feudal society contained from the outset, but the historical product of struggles to preserve and transform existing relations. The development of productive forces, then, is neither an engine operating independently of class relations nor an outcome that appears only after capitalism has emerged, but part of the social process that explains the transition itself.

The Ottoman Empire’s fiscal transformation is part of this same history. Three changes increasingly tied control over the surplus to relations of capital and credit. The tımar system (rights the state granted to collect agrarian revenues, often in return for military service) changed, tax farming ( iltizam ) expanded, and the state later introduced lifetime tax farms ( malikâne ).

None of these institutions, taken on its own, proves the existence of capitalism. But when we examine them alongside changes in production, property, market dependence, and accumulation, they show that the state itself was changing within the same social process. This moves us away from viewing capitalism as a sphere that emerges within society after the state retreats, as much of the literature assumes. The struggles that reorganize relations between producers and those who appropriate the surplus also transform the state’s sources of revenue and its social foundations.

This history does not require the Ottoman Empire to replicate the institutions of the English transition. When we turn England’s specific forms of property and labor into universal criteria for capitalism, we fail to recognize capital’s command over production in other societies.

Treating the transition from feudalism to capitalism as a problem of world history does not mean equating capitalism with trade wherever it occurs. To speak of a transition to the same mode of production is not to insist that every society follow the same historical path. This distinction also challenges the assumption that, once capitalism had emerged, it could take root in other societies only through external diffusion.

Of course, speaking of the Ottoman Empire’s internal dynamics does not mean treating it as a society isolated from the world. Trade, war, and flows of money are part of this history. But the existence of external connections does not show that the West introduced capitalism or that colonial plunder gave birth to it. What we need to explain are the social relations within which those connections operated.

Placing the Ottoman capitalist transformation before the West’s decisive economic influence does not write the outside world out of the story; it changes the direction of causality. The West’s later influence acted on capitalist relations that had already begun to emerge. Nor does their subsequent development under conditions of external dependence prove that their origins lay elsewhere. Dependency cannot substitute for an explanation of origins.

For the same reason, late industrialization is a separate issue. If we measure the existence of capitalism by the prevalence of mechanized production, we end up defining Ottoman relations of production in terms of a technological gap with the West. Yet capitalist societies do not develop at the same pace, occupy the same international position, or enjoy the same opportunities for accumulation. Colonialism can play a decisive role in widening these inequalities and securing the supremacy of particular capitalist states.

Here we move from the question of origins to that of uneven capitalist development, where the colonial accumulation and industrial transformation that Prashad emphasizes acquire explanatory force. But this explanation does not erase histories in which capitalist relations emerged earlier and without colonial plunder. Accepting Prashad’s emphasis on colonialism does not require abandoning Chibber’s distinction concerning capitalism’s origins.

The fact that Ottoman capitalism did not originate in colonial plunder does not mean that the empire stood outside later wars and struggles over the division of the world. Its participation in those struggles and wars as a capitalist state does not show that it owed its transition to capitalism to resources it extracted from colonies abroad. We need to distinguish the state’s later political position from the origins of society’s capitalist transformation.

The same distinction applies to the empire’s long history of conquest. Earlier conquests and relations of taxation do not prove that capitalism emerged from colonial plunder. Empire and capitalist colonialism are not the same historical category. We must reassess the relationship between them as relations of production and the social character of the state change.

T he transformation of the Ottoman state into a capitalist state is therefore the next step in the argument. Capitalism does more than create new sources of profit for particular sections of society. Through control over property, labor, and the surplus, it also changes how the state reproduces itself.

What makes a state capitalist is not that its rulers become merchants or that it builds factories but that social relations become organized around the requirements of capital accumulation, with class struggles unfolding on that basis. Capitalist relations emerging from within Ottoman society deepen alongside the state’s fiscal and administrative transformation. The form of state that emerges from this transformation also begins to view the empire’s vast domains in a new light and to reorganize them accordingly.

It is in the wake of this transformation that I situate internal colonization — the process I call self-colonialism . The Ottoman Empire did not owe its transition to capitalism to the plunder of colonies abroad; as the state became capitalist, it already ruled vast territories and diverse communities toward which it could direct its colonial practices. Its territories in the Balkans, the Middle East, Anatolia, the Caucasus, and North Africa became the terrain on which it established new internal relations of domination. Holding these territories is not the same as reorganizing them as internal colonies, which involved a capitalist state transforming earlier imperial rule to serve new purposes within a new set of social relations.

In this transformation, the state ties civilizing rhetoric to remaking peripheral communities into populations it can govern and tax and whose labor can be controlled. Scholars have explored Ottoman colonialism from different perspectives: Nilay Özok-Gündoğa through resource extraction in Kurdistan, İlkay Yılmaz through security policies in the eastern provinces, and Ella Fratantuono through immigrant settlement. Selim Deringil and Ussama Makdisi examine the colonial outlook and civilizing claims of Ottoman elites. My question here is how these forms of domination relate to capitalism’s origins.

I argue that internal colonization follows the capitalist transformation of society and the state; as it unfolds, it can intensify dispossession and open up new opportunities for accumulation. We can thus establish the causal sequence without denying the relationship between colonialism and capitalism. Internal colonization did not create Ottoman capitalism; a capitalist transformation already underway laid the social and political groundwork that made internal colonization possible.

I am not proposing a single historical sequence valid for all societies, only specifying the direction of the causal relationship we need to explain in the Ottoman case. Here the question is not how colonialism created capitalism but how capitalist transformation reshaped state domination and laid the groundwork for colonial practices.

This sequence does not imply that capitalism emerged without violence. The dissolution of feudal relations and the formation of capitalist relations involved conflicts over producers’ rights to their means of subsistence, their labor, and the surplus they produced. But treating every act of dispossession as colonialism prevents us from distinguishing changes in class relations from the specific history of colonial domination. We need to distinguish capitalism’s origins from colonialism not to downplay colonial violence but to explain the historical connections between different forms of domination.

In the Ottoman case, this distinction allows us to trace the capitalist transformation first, then examine how it extended into internal colonization through state action. Recognizing colonialism’s immense importance to capitalist development does not require locating capitalism’s origins in it. This is the fundamental distinction on which I agree with Chibber and part ways with Prashad.

In the Ottoman Empire, capitalism emerged from within feudal society and transformed both society and the state, and internal colonization followed. This history shows that accepting the analysis of the English transition does not require ruling out capitalism’s origins in other societies.

Writing a world history of capitalism requires us to explain more than the world’s contributions to the making of the West. We must also explain how the world itself changed. We therefore cannot reduce the transition from feudalism to capitalism to an English or European story. Capitalism’s origins belong to a world history broader than the history of Western domination.

Y. Doğan Çetinkaya teaches at Istanbul University and Istanbul Free University. His publications include The Young Turks and the Boycott Movement: Nationalism, Protest and the Working Classes in the Formation of Modern Turkey .

scraped.body_text:

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Politics

Uncontrolled burns, false claims, and federal highway funds.

John Ross | 11.20.2026 3:30 PM

Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit , a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.

Victory! Millions of Americans want and need low-FODMAP foods, which are low in certain sugars that can cause debilitating stomach issues, aggravate irritable bowels, and worse. Fortunately, this week (following the Ninth Circuit 's revival of our First Amendment challenge), the FDA lifted its ban on producers truthfully labelling their products "Low-FODMAP." Says IJ client Michelle Przybocki, who abides by a strict low-FODMAP diet after nearly dying from digestive complications, "I'm thrilled that the federal government is going to allow companies to start labeling their products as 'Low-FODMAP,' because this makes it easier for me to find foods that I know will not cause me digestive issues." Click here to learn more.

New on the Short Circuit podcast : Fancy some Elevenses? Serving up Eleventh Circuit refreshments in our #12Months12Circuits series. There's excessive bail in Alabama and excessive bar fees in Florida.

Friends, if a federal official violates your constitutional rights, your options for being made whole by money damages have been all but extinguished in recent years, leaving the feds with something akin to absolute immunity for all kinds of misconduct and misdeeds. But there has to be some avenue for accountability. So here at IJ, we're pushing back, not only on the late-lamented Bivens cause of action, but also on the too-narrowly construed Federal Tort Claims Act. And then, of course, there's the traditional source of accountability that the Founders would have recognized (and that the Supreme Court's Bivens skeptics preferred): state law causes of action, like California's traditional tort system and the state's Bane Act. All of which were on the table at oral argument in the Ninth Circuit this week, where we're happy to report we had an engaged, cross-ideological panel. Click here to learn more.

John Ross is the editor of the Short Circuit newsletter and the producer of the Bound By Oath podcast, two incomparable projects of surpassing importance from the Institute for Justice.

scraped.title: Will Democrats end New Hampshire's seat belt freedom?
scraped.description: For decades, New Hampshire has held out as the only state without a seat belt mandate. A new Democratic majority in the Legislature could bring that libertarian tradition to an end.
scraped.author: Ryan Curtis
scraped.h1: Will Democrats End New Hampshire's Seat Belt Freedom?
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Nanny State

Ryan Curtis | 11.20.2026 3:30 PM

This month's " bluenami " rippled down the ballot in many states, including New Hampshire, where Democrats captured 293 of 400 House seats and 15 of 24 Senate seats, flipping the GOP's control of the Legislature. T he Democrats' overwhelming party control could signal the end of a vestigial point of pride for many New Hampshirites: the state's uniquely libertarian seat belt laws.

Honoring its motto of "Live Free or Die," New Hampshire is the only state in the country that does not require adults to wear seat belts (though minors must wear them). After New York became the first state to mandate seat belts in 1984, a cascade of new laws followed across the rest of the country. By 1996 , New Hampshire alone stood on its principles. Left-leaning lawmakers in the state have routinely tried, and failed, to implement the regulation. The first bill in 1979 was voted "inexpedient to legislate" by the state Senate, a verdict that legislators have decreed nine more times since , most recently in 2023 .

New Hampshire lawmakers have cited personal freedom as one reason for opposing seat belt laws. In 1986, then-U.S. Rep. Judd Gregg (R–N.H.) wrote a letter to Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole, saying: "New Hampshire citizens have made it clear that they prefer this matter left to the discretion of the individual." After all, why should the government punish you for not keeping yourself safe?

Gregg worried the Transportation Department would withhold federal highway funds to pressure states into compliance (a tactic it had used before to implement a national speed limit and raise the minimum drinking age to 21). His concerns were well founded, as the department began in 1991 to condition the disbursement of some highway funds in states without seat belt laws. It also began providing extra benefits to states with mandates.

After voting to reject a proposed seat belt mandate in 2007, state Sen. Robert Clegg (R–Hudson) told The New York Times that he voted against the restriction because , "it preserves New Hampshire's way of not succumbing to the bribes of the federal government."

For some contemporary lawmakers, the issue is a question of the legitimate role of government. State Rep. Ted Gorski (R–Bedford), the current vice chairman of the state House Transportation Committee, tells Reason that a seat belt mandate "would infringe on [New Hampshirites'] privacy rights and their natural rights." Though some may think it is an unusual hill to die on, Gorski says, "with even the smallest issues you have to defend liberty, else it will be taken away from you, slowly but surely."

Gorski believes that with the Democrats back in power, the Legislature may try to approve a mandate in the next two years. The closest a seat belt bill came to passing was in 2009, when Democrats held a majority in both chambers of the Legislature. That proposal made it through the state House but died in the Senate after four Democrats sided with 10 Republicans.

While the Democrats' newfound majority might make it easier to pass a seat belt mandate, several obstacles remain—including a lack of political appetite from lawmakers. State Rep. Daniel Veilleux (D–Amherst), who sponsored the 2023 bill, tells Reason he did not plan to introduce a "similar adult seat belt mandate in 2027." While this pledge is promising, party leaders like House Speaker Alexis Simpson (D–Exeter) voted in favor of the 2023 mandate. That, along with the state Democratic Party's history of trying to regulate seat belt use, makes it hard to take Veilleux's words as a firm guarantee.

If the Legislature does pass a bill, Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who handily won reelection, could veto it. "Even with a Democratic majority, passage is not guaranteed," says Veilleux.

Wearing a seatbelt is a wise choice. It will probably save your life . But people should be allowed to make their own decisions about safety and risk, rather than having the government decide.

New Hampshire Public Radio investigated the seat belt debate in 2017, asking people on the streets of Concord what they thought about that year's proposed mandate. When asked if being the exception to the rest of the country was a problem, one passerby said: "I think it's fine…The state motto and all."
