scraped.title: Turkey climate change conference dubbed ‘worst COP ever’
scraped.description: Despite 31 U.N. climate change conferences, greenhouse gas emissions and atmospheric concentrations continue to rise, as do global average temperatures.
scraped.author: Ronald Bailey
scraped.h1: Turkey Climate Change Conference Dubbed 'Worst COP Ever'
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Climate Change

Ronald Bailey | 11.20.2026 3:05 PM

"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," says longtime climate activist Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa in DW News . Considering the sorry, ineffectual history of the United Nations' annual pre-Christmas climate carnivals, Adow is probably right about the 31st Conference of the Parties ( COP31 ) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) currently limping toward the customary ineffectual close in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 will most likely conclude this weekend with the usual conference decision filled with vague admonitions to governments urging them to enhance climate change action and increase climate finance. The former means drastically cutting back on their greenhouse gas emissions, largely carbon dioxide emitted from burning oil, gas, and coal. How drastic? Aggressive cuts by 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035, and 69 percent by 2040. The latter consists of demands that rich countries funnel through 2035 at least $305 billion annually to poor countries, ostensibly to help them adapt to climate change.

Despite 31 U.N. climate change conferences, greenhouse gas emissions and atmospheric concentrations continue to rise, as do global average temperatures.

The UNFCCC was adopted in 1992 with the aim of reining in globe-warming greenhouse gas emissions; they have instead continued their steady increase .

Rising emissions have consequently increased the concentration of globe-warming carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

The 2015 Paris Agreement on Climate Change 's aim was to hold "the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels" and pursue efforts "to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels." To achieve this goal, greenhouse gas emissions were supposed to peak before 2025 and decline by 43 percent by 2030. That obviously didn't happen.

Concomitant with rising atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, the average global temperature has been increasing.

In fact, the Paris Agreement's 1.5 degrees Celsius benchmark was breached when 2024 became the hottest year in the instrumental record. In its latest update, the independent open-source climate data group Berkeley Earth reports that "October 2026 was the warmest October on record, with a global average of 1.80 ± 0.12 °C (3.25 ± 0.22 °F) above the 1850–1900 average, about 0.12 °C above the previous record set in October 2023." Berkeley Earth also finds that it is "now virtually certain that the 2026 annual average will exceed 1.5 °C (2.7 °F) above the 1850–1900 average, with a likely annual range of roughly 1.55–1.64 °C." This level would exceed the previous record in 2024, making 2026 the warmest year in Berkeley Earth's record.

The European Copernicus Climate Change Service also projects that global average temperature in 2026 will exceed 1.5 C above the preindustrial level.

Global temperatures have been boosted this year by the super El Niño phenomenon in which very warm water sloshing periodically over into the eastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of South America releases massive amounts of heat into the atmosphere.

The United Nations now acknowledges that the "chance of holding global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels…is now gone." BusinessGreen reports that COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen said that "it falls to COP31 to be the first COP to acknowledge the world will not meet the covenant laid out in Paris 11 years ago to hold the world to 1.5C of warming".

Given the futility of U.N. climate change negotiations, what is the likely trend in global average temperatures? The U.N. suggests that warming could rise by as much as 2.6 C to 2.8 C above the preindustrial level by the end of this century. As I reported last year, climate researcher Roger Pielke Jr. and his colleagues, using more plausible emissions scenarios, projected in 2022 that global average temperatures would rise above the preindustrial baseline (1850–1900) to "between 2 ° C and 3 ° C of warming by 2100, with a median of 2.2 ° C."

"Even though projections of future climate change have moderated considerably in recent years," correctly observed Pielke, "the human influence on climate remains real and poses risks to our collective future." After 31 years of COPs, U.N. climate change negotiations have still not done much to ameliorate those risks.

scraped.description: State of the Union: The AI firm’s multi-billion dollar market debut made it one of the world's most valuable companies.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
The AI company Anthropic went public Thursday in the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record. With a market capitalization of around $1.8 trillion dollars, Anthropic—famous for its “Claude” AI models—is now one of the world’s most valuable companies. Initially listed at $83 per share, Anthropic’s stock price fluctuated throughout the trading day, closing at just above $97. Nearly 850 million shares of the stock changed hands Thursday.

Founded in 2021, Anthropic has seen its revenues explode in recent months, taking in $33 billion in the first three quarters of 2026—a 1,200 percent increase from the same period last year. It is the first of the major “frontier labs” to go public, beating out rival OpenAI (which has postponed its own IPO until next year).

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

scraped.title: Iran War Day 266: Houthis Threaten Major Attacks on Saudi Arabia
scraped.description: State of the Union: Senate Republicans rejected legislation directing President Trump to stop the war.
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
Yemen’s Houthis, an Iran-aligned group, threatened to attack Saudi ports on the Red Sea if their own ports came under attack by Saudi-backed forces. The group also threatened to strike a power station in southwestern Saudi Arabia and the financial district in Riyadh, the capital. Earlier, two power stations in Yemen were reported to have come under attack by Saudi air strikes.

On Thursday the Houthis struck Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, damaging several floors of the building.

The government of Iraq reached a compromise with the country’s Iran-backed militia, Kataib Hezbollah, after the prime minister had threatened to deploy security forces against the group. Government forces are expected to move into the group’s stronghold territory Friday while Kataib forces will move to other areas. An Iranian military commander arrived in Baghdad earlier this week to help defuse tensions between the government and the militia.

In the U.S., Senate Republicans on Thursday rejected a war powers resolution directing President Donald Trump to end the Iran War or obtain congressional authorization to continue it. The legislation had passed the House of Representatives but was defeated in the Senate by a 51–48 vote. Three Senate Republicans—Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, and Rand Paul of Kentucky—joined nearly all Democrats in supporting the resolution.

Democrats argued their party’s sweeping victories in the midterm elections earlier this month showed the deep unpopularity of the war and its economic effects.

Oil prices remained elevated on Friday with Brent crude opening at $92.38 per barrel. The average price of regular gasoline in America was $3.69 per gallon, continuing a decline. Analysts this week have noted a dip in the flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for the global energy trade. Iran claimed on Thursday that two more tankers had hit sea mines in the waterway.

Trump has weighed restarting major hostilities against Iran but on Thursday signaled he’d wait until the new year to finalize a decision. “We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” Trump told Axios. Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged Washington to attack Iran, and Israeli opposition leaders warn he aims to restart the war in a bid to hold onto power.

items.summary: Industrial titans don’t get to break the law, even if it’s stupid. The post The Question That Matters in the Huang Tangle appeared first on The American Conservative. Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Did Jensen Huang break the law? This is the central question largely obscured by all the uproar about the ousted Nvidia executive...

scraped.title: The Question That Matters in the Huang Tangle
scraped.description: Industrial titans don’t get to break the law, even if it’s stupid.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
Industrial titans don’t get to break the law, even if it’s stupid.

Did Jensen Huang break the law?

This is the central question largely obscured by all the uproar about the ousted Nvidia executive’s sexual extracurriculars and his consequent expulsion into the outer darkness.

A brief review of the facts: Jensen Huang appears to have been dallying with one Alice Huang, a Chinese national and former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company. In addition to leaving the holy vows of marital fidelity in shambles, this affair has sent editors into despair about how to handle second mentions when both agonists share a surname; we will here adopt the expedient of calling them Speedy Alice and Poor Jensen.

Per reporting, Speedy Alice is under some sort of American counterintelligence investigation for possibly serving Chinese intelligence services. Also per reporting, Megaspeed may have been acting as a shell for moving high-end Nvidia chips to the Chinese market, despite American export controls on such hardware. Journalists reporting from Megaspeed’s offices in Singapore, Malaysia, and Australia have found little to suggest that any actual business is happening there—one listed office turned out to be a newspaper vendor, and some of the others were dingy storefronts.

That was bad enough, but then reports of a second Poor Jensen affair broke, this one with a subordinate. Nvidia’s board ousted Poor Jensen from his perch atop one of the world’s most valuable firms—indeed, depending on the day and the markets, the world’s uncontestedly most valuable firm.

Blockbuster stuff. But separate and accidental elements of the story have taken on lives of their own.

One line, adopted particularly by those who would like to see Poor Jensen back on top of Nvidia so that the markets’ tech-backed bull run can continue (such as President Donald Trump ), is that the spying suspicions about Speedy Alice are flimsy or defective. Perhaps they are, although I would submit that those who dismiss out of hand the idea that Speedy Alice was in some way connected to Chinese security services just don’t know much about corporate China. Yet the exact parameters of the connection, if any, are also to some degree beside the point: If Poor Jensen was getting around export controls on a freelance basis without any input from Xi and the boys, that is still a violation of the law.

Another line is pure Kremlinological analysis. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly jazzed up the CIA report on Speedy Alice’s alleged state connections. L’affaire Huang(s) has come at a time when Rubio is rising to new prominence: The administration has adopted his preferred policy on the Iran War, of which he has emerged as a defender after largely avoiding the subject publicly for some months; at a November 13 Federalist Society confab, he delivered what may well be regarded by future historians as his first campaign speech of the 2028 presidential race. These coincidences have led some to speculate that Rubio and the China hawks are making some sort of power play—which, of course, has led people who aren’t keen on Rubio to incline toward Poor Jensen’s part. Others entertain questions about Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s role in apparently slow-walking Megaspeed’s designation for export controls, particularly in the quarters where the constant rumble of complaint about the administration’s self-dealing are heard. This all is no doubt politically interesting, but the questions of whether backing Poor Jensen is pro- or anti-Rubio, pro- or anti-Trump, must take the back seat to whether or not he broke the law, even purely analytically: It says something very different about Rubio et al. if Poor Jensen is innocent than if he is guilty.

The final line of irrelevancy is the theory that Poor Jensen was ousted by some conspiracy of wokesters and/or hostile corporate interests, like the newly IPO’d Anthropic, a doomsday cult that sells chatbot subscriptions. (Anthropic would like to cartelize artificial intelligence development, so Poor Jensen’s willingness to sell chips to anyone who will buy undercuts the AI firm's sinister schemes.) Adherents point to the fact that the board booted him only after the second affair was announced. This is susceptible to the same criticism as the Kremlinological approach. Did Poor Jensen break the law or not? And, further, does a CEO dallying with his employees create real legal exposure that could become a liability for the company? (I suspect most compliance lawyers you ask would say “yes,” in which case the board arguably had an obligation to fire Poor Jensen. The corporate governance aspect of this entire case is a nightmare—see, for just one delightful facet, this Financial Times report about Nvidia’s woeful D&O insurance coverage.)

Export controls on high-end chips may or may not be a good policy; the devil is in the details, and there are prudential arguments for both sides. Poor Jensen, for his part, contends that getting China hooked on American chips is in fact good for America; he believes that chips are basically different from other industrial products, and the usual risks to manufacturers of doing business with China do not obtain. (This, incidentally, mixes up the China dove–China hawk heuristic that would simplify the political analysis of the episode.) Others disagree . As a good protectionist, I do observe that export controls are basically a protective measure on behalf of the opposite party’s industries; indeed, China itself has put limitations on Nvidia imports in order to cultivate its indigenous chipmakers.

But this all is somewhat beside the point: A stupid policy doesn’t mean you get to break the law, and breaking the law is still breaking the law, irrespective of whether an external party was the prime mover. I think sanctions on Iran are stupid; that doesn’t mean I can start smuggling oil out of the Persian Gulf. Allowing team sports along various axes to become the dominant factors in analysis puts the cart before the horse. Did Poor Jensen break the law? Everything else depends on the answer.

Jude Russo is the managing editor of The American Conservative and a contributing editor of The New York Sun . He is a 2024–25 James Madison Fellow at Hillsdale College and was named one of the ISI Top 20 Under 30 for 2024.

scraped.title: Schumer doubles down on hawkery despite Van Hollen's anti-war test
scraped.description: 45 years of being a pro-Israel Democrat is a hard habit to break even after the people have demanded a change
scraped.h1: Schumer doubles down on hawkery despite Van Hollen's anti-war test
scraped.body_text:
45 years of being a pro-Israel Democrat is a hard habit to break even after the people have demanded a change

In some of his first remarks on the Senate floor since his leadership of the Democratic caucus was formally challenged, Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York blasted President Donald Trump for pursuing an insufficiently hawkish foreign policy.

“Trump calls the trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin ‘historic’. Yes, it’s a historic embarrassment that people will remember long into the future,” Schumer said on Thursday. “It’s a betrayal of the United States.”

Schumer went on to criticize the President for not securing any concessions from his counterparts, including on curbing Chinese espionage or preventing Beijing and Moscow from helping Iran target American troops.

The emphasis of Schumer’s remarks was striking given that dissatisfaction with Trump’s foreign policy and its economic ramifications helped propel Democrats back into the Senate majority earlier this month.

As Democrats debate whether their electoral victory presents an opportunity to rethink the party's foreign policy, Schumer's remarks suggest that some of its longtime leaders remain wedded to an older approach.

That tension is also emerging as a central dividing line in the contest to lead the new Democratic majority. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who announced last week that he would challenge Schumer, has made their disagreements over foreign policy, and in particular over how to approach the issues in the Middle East , as central to his pitch.

The two senators represent competing visions of the Democratic Party’s future. Faiz Shakir, a senior advisor to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has supported Van Hollen’s challenge, recently described him to NPR as a“pragmatic progressive” who is “going to know what the people of this country are asking us to do at this moment” and “can bring a lot of factions of the party together.”

Much of the debate is over how Democrats should approach using their power of the purse to cut off funding for the war in Iran before the new Congress is seated in January. Van Hollen and a number of his Democratic colleagues have called on the party to insist on a government funding bill that excludes money for the Iran war, which they say will force Trump and the Republicans to decide whether to risk a shutdown to continue the war. Other Democrats argue that a shutdown would be politically risky for the party, and that Democrats should wait until they are in the majority to force the issue.

Schumer, for his part, has not clarified his stance, as he continues to say that the war must end and a shutdown must be avoided.

Schumer's reluctance to say that he will prioritize ending the war has renewed scrutiny on his longstanding hawkishness toward Iran. Many foreign policy analysts and congressional critics have highlighted his place as one of a few Democratic opponents to the Obama-era Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), commonly known as the Iran nuclear deal, as one clear example.

Van Hollen has made this contrast central to his leadership campaign. “I don't see how after an election like this where ending the war and bringing down prices was a priority, we can cast a vote to fund the war,” he said recently. “And of course, Senator Schumer was one of the folks who originally opposed President Obama and the JCPOA, but I think the caucus wants to bring this war to an end,”

Progressives have also condemned Schumer’s approach in the lead-up to the war, during which he attacked Trump’s diplomacy with Tehran and, critics say, did not act quickly enough to slow the president’s march to war in February.

On Thursday, during his floor speech, Schumer questioned what “commitments” Trump made and what he “gave away” over dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, echoing his controversial June 2025 accusations that Trump was negotiating “side deals” and “folding on Iran.”

The disagreements extend beyond Iran. Van Hollen has taken a leading role in the effort to remove provisions of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that would deepen military and intelligence cooperation between the United States and Israel .

“The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology,” Van Hollen and 11 Senate colleagues wrote in a recent letter to congressional leadership. “If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement.”

The letter further argues that the provisions would shift U.S. military assistance to Israel to more “opaque, less discernible avenues,” which the Senators call particularly troubling given Israel's conduct in Gaza, the West Bank, and elsewhere in the region.

Schumer has not publicly commented on these provisions, but is seen as one of Israel’s strongest supporters in Congress. In 2025, he told the New York Times that his “job...is to keep the left pro-Israel.” He has repeatedly called himself a “guardian of Israel” throughout his congressional career, which spans 45 years.

Their perspectives on the U.S-Israel relationship appears to be a key dividing line between the two senators. Van Hollen was first elected as an establishment-supported, Israel-friendly candidate, but his views have shifted. “Times have changed in a lot of ways, where the Democratic base has changed in a lot of ways, and he has changed along with it,” Yousef Munayyer of the Arab Center recently told The Intercept. “I don’t know that the same can be said for a lot of other folks, like Chuck Schumer.”

Independent trackers show that the sitting minority leader currently has more support, though the tallies remain close. The vote for majority leader is expected to take place in a secret ballot on Dec. 1.

United States Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (Democrat of New York), left, and US Senator Chris Van Hollen (Democrat of Maryland), right, depart a press conference on the potential national debt crisis at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., Thursday, Feb. 2, 2023. (Credit: Julia Nikhinson / CNP/Sipa USANo Use Germany.)

scraped.title: A gross misreading of 'Yalta' undergirds lame critique of trilateral
scraped.description: Not only does the 1945 comparison fall flat on its face, it exposes an ignorance of history that is unfortunately common in today's mainstream discourse
scraped.h1: A gross misreading of 'Yalta' undergirds lame critique of trilateral
scraped.body_text:
Not only does the 1945 comparison fall flat on its face, it exposes an ignorance of history that is unfortunately common in today's mainstream discourse

Representatives of the transatlantic establishment were quick to liken the trilateral summit in Shenzhen to the supposed Anglo-American “ betrayal ” of Poland and other Eastern European states at Yalta in February 1945. Yalta ratified — but did not create — the division of Europe into spheres of influence that later became frozen into the dividing lines of the Cold War.

A less apoplectic strain of the same underlying sentiment holds that President Trump’s willingness to meet his Russian and Chinese counterparts is in itself an unnecessary concession to Russia and China that merely signals weakness and does nothing to advance U.S. interests; as if the avoidance of nuclear war with China were not a vital U.S. interest.

The “Yalta 2.0” narrative is not just wrong, though it is that, too, but premised in a gross historical misreading that must be confronted lest it further pollute Western policy discourse. There has been a growing tendency since the Soviet collapse to liken Yalta and the Potsdam conference that succeeded it to a kind of modern-day Treaty of Tordesillas-- an exercise between two great powers of yore, Spain and Portugal, in divvying up distant lands .

The reality is different. As it became clear toward 1945 that the second world war was moving toward complete allied victory, the leaders of the three great allied powers —Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin — naturally devoted more of their attention to the delineation and security architecture of postwar Europe. Understandings reached on the postwar status of European countries occupied respectively by the Western allies and the Soviet Union served mostly to ratify existing facts on the ground.

It was a concession to reality, not to Stalin, to acknowledge that the Soviet army, by defeating the German army in the East, had already gained control over most of Eastern Europe whether Western leaders recognized this control or not — and, alas, whether the populations of eastern Europe liked it or not.

Short of a new war with the USSR — that U.S. and British populations and soldiers would have categorically rejected and that they would probably have lost — FDR and Churchill had no ability to challenge, let alone attempt to reverse, Moscow’s assertion of a sphere of influence in Eastern Europe. Recognition of that assessment should therefore be seen not as a betrayal but as both inevitable and an act of prudence. Yalta was a first step towards establishing the geopolitical guardrails that later helped prevent the Cold War in Europe from spiraling into open and cataclysmic conflict and laid the foundations for U.S. containment strategy that prevented further Soviet expansion without recourse to war.

The Yalta comparison is also a false, and even ridiculous description of what is being discussed today. Russia would be completely incapable of occupying eastern Europe, even if it had any desire to do so, which it does not. The Russian army has proved incapable of conquering most of Ukraine. The only Russian demand for additional territorial control is the 2,000 square miles of the Donbas still occupied by Ukraine. That really does not compare to Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and the other states subjected to Soviet communism after World War II.

Nor is China in any position to imitate the U.S. in 1945 and occupy Japan, South Korea and the Philippines. The cliche "if you're not at the table, you're on the menu” that so often accompanies the contemporary “Yalta 2.0” discourse is therefore obviously untrue.

Even during the Cold War, Yugoslavia, India, as well as swathes of Africa and the Middle East were able to practice non-alignment — effectively opting out of having to choose a side in the bipolar competition — without being carved up by Washington or Moscow. That is very much the desire, and the ability, of most states in the world today, including for example former Soviet states in Central Asia, which have no desire at all to choose between Russian, Chinese or U.S. hegemony. Their declared strategy is a “multi-vector” one.

Let us grant, for the sake of argument, the fantastical notion that the White House is keen on somehow “handing over” former Soviet and Warsaw Pact countries to Russia or East Asian states to China. Who in these two regions would possibly go along with such a scheme, and how can they be compelled to do so in the absence of military conquest?

The Russian demand for the withdrawal of NATO forces to the lines they occupied in the 1990s does not require the new NATO members of eastern Europe to leave NATO, or to disarm their own forces, let alone that they submit to regime change and Russian political control ( in any case a ridiculous idea, for anyone who knows the Poles and the Balts).

It should rather be seen as the first move in a new disarmament process; and NATO, instead of rejecting it out of hand, should come back with proposals of its own whereby limits in NATO forces on Russia’s borders should be matched by strict reciprocal limits on Russian forces in Belarus and Kaliningrad.

The model and inspiration should be seen not as “Yalta” but the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaties of the 1990s. The common NATO line is now that “Russia has no say in European security.” No sane person would have said that during the Cold War, and today, alas, hundreds of thousands of dead in Ukraine also demonstrate the opposite.

In any case, the Trilateral summit in Shenzhen did not talk about any of these issues. The official statement that followed the talks contained just two elements, both of which should be seen as valuable for humanity. The summit’s call for new nuclear limitation agreements, however vaguely formulated, should be seen as a tentative first step to a restoration of the treaties agreed by the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. in the later years of the Cold War — not to end that war, but to try to ensure that it did not escalate into universal catastrophe.

More generally, the summit symbolized a truth of vast significance: that if basic peace and order in the world is to be secured, then this will depend above all on reasonably peaceful relations between the world’s most powerful states, secured by agreements regulating those relations.

So if there is a legacy of the Cold War to which we should look, it is that of great powers assuming a degree of shared responsibility for maintaining a stable, working international system to be passed down to future generations. The Shenzhen summit represents a significant first step in that direction.

Finally, on the score of spheres of influence, it is perhaps worth noting that one is tacitly accepted by virtually the entire world, including China. Nobody is challenging the U.S. insistence on absolute military hegemony in Central America and the Caribbean, because they know that any attempt to do so would bring ferocious U.S. retaliation. Nor have the Europeans, for all their supposed commitment to a “rules-based order” pushed back in any way against the extreme hardening of the Monroe Doctrine under Donald Trump, as witnessed with regard to Venezuela , Cuba , and alleged drug traffickers.

Fortunately, there is no chance whatsoever of Russia or China being able to follow this particular U.S. rule.

scraped.description: Otherwise there wasn't much for Washington in this much anticipated meeting of Trump, Xi Jinping, and Putin in China
scraped.h1: The biggest takeaway from trilateral is the nuclear piece
scraped.body_text:
Otherwise there wasn't much for Washington in this much anticipated meeting of Trump, Xi Jinping, and Putin in China

The first trilateral meeting of Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin, held on November 19 in Shenzhen, was worth holding for one reason above all. The United States has a clear interest in reducing nuclear risks with both China and Russia , and the three leaders agreed to discuss how to do so .

Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine.

The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. What Shenzhen adds is Xi’s public commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation in a dedicated three-way format. That is a meaningful opening, especially since New START expired in February.

However, the joint declaration sets no timetable or agenda and contains no commitment to negotiate limits on arsenals.

The other results of the summit were thinner. The leaders endorsed U.N. reform and greater supplies of refined petroleum products without specifying what reforms they wanted or how much additional fuel they would supply. Beijing says they discussed Ukraine, the Middle East , and the Korean Peninsula, but the declaration identified no concrete next steps. Its language on immunity for state officials and alleged jurisdictional abuse by the International Criminal Court (ICC) had a clearer political payoff. It aligned with the Trump administration’s position and benefited Putin, who faces an ICC arrest warrant.

Xi also brought a familiar proposal into the three-way meeting by calling for crisis communication and prevention mechanisms. Although the joint declaration contained no agreement to establish them, Washington and Moscow should nevertheless take up the proposal and see whether Beijing will agree to practical steps, such as establishing and regularly testing emergency contacts.

On balance, Shenzhen was long on symbolism and promises and short on results that advance global stability or U.S. interests. That judgment could change if the three governments schedule nuclear talks and agree on measures that reduce the risk of miscalculation. The summit gave them an opening. Whether they use it is another matter. I won’t hold my breath.

items.summary: Most Republicans could tell you exactly what Democrats wanted to do with a majority but couldn't say what Republicans would do.

scraped.title: GOP Bashed Dems But Failed To Offer A Conservative Agenda
scraped.description: Republicans could tell you exactly what Democrats wanted to do with a majority but couldn't specify what the GOP would do to help Americans.
scraped.author: Brianna Lyman
scraped.h1: Republicans Gave Voters A Reason To Hate Democrats But Not A Reason To Vote For GOP
scraped.body_text:
Most Republicans could tell you exactly what Democrats wanted to do with a majority but couldn’t say what Republicans would do.

Scott Colom’s victory has been described as the “ Mississippi Miracle .” His shocking victory, in which he beat incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and became the first Democrat to hold a Senate seat from the state since 1982, came amidst a blue tsunami in which Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress.

But what makes Colom’s victory — like so many other Democrat wins on Election night — even more surprising is that Mississippi “flipped … with almost no growth in the Democratic vote,” an analysis from Quantus Insights found.

While Democrats captured races in what were once considered Republican strongholds like Mississippi, Iowa, Texas, and Georgia, they didn’t do it because they managed to convince independent or Republican voters writ large.

Quantus Insights found that “of every 100 Trump 2024 voters, about 63 voted Republican, 4 voted Democratic, and 33 stayed home. Of every 100 Harris voters, about 85 voted Democratic. Very few people switched and about a third of one side sat out.”

In states like Texas, Mississippi, and Iowa, the Democrat turnout was roughly the same (or beat) the Democrat turnout for Kamala Harris in 2024. But Republican turnout paled in comparison to Republican turnout in the 2024 presidential election.

Republicans spent the campaign season warning their voters what would happen if Democrats took power, but the voters stayed home anyway because at the end of the day, voting against something clearly doesn’t drive turnout the way voting for something does.

House Republican Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain gave Fox News Digital a preview of the party’s closing pitch.

“[Democrats] want open borders. They want to defund the police, they want to take more money out of your pocket and give it to somebody else. They believe in bigger government. We believe in people. … So those are the things that we’re really hammering home during this election.”

Republicans were reportedly encouraged to talk about “putting more money back in Americans’ pockets and creating more opportunities to get ahead through hard work, ownership, and economic freedom.”

All of that sounds nice. But what bills were Republicans promising to put on the floor in January? What could a voter expect a Republican Congress to do for him that it hadn’t already done? If the Republican-controlled Congress couldn’t pass something as basic as the SAVE America Act — which would’ve required documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and photo ID to actually vote — what could a Republican Congress do?

McClain, like most Republicans, could tell you exactly what Democrats wanted to do with a majority but couldn’t specify what concrete action Republicans would take to improve life for Americans and fell back on pointing to the dangers of electing Democrats.

But giving voters legitimate reasons to vote for Republicans does work, just ask Newt Gingrich. Gingrich led Republicans to a historic victory in 1994 not because they simply ran as the opposition to President Bill Clinton and Democrats but because Republicans gave Americans the Contract with America, a list of bills they promised to bring to the floor in the first 100 days. Voters had concrete reasons to vote for Republicans because they knew what that would mean legislatively.

But even if Republicans successfully convince voters that a Republican is more deserving of a vote than a Democrat, that doesn’t guarantee a Republican victory. For years Democrats have treated mail-in voting as the main event, while Republicans still treat Election Day as the main event.

In states that report party registration on returned ballots, registered Democrats beat Republicans in the early vote by more than 10 percentage points, according to USA Today. An analysis by VoteHub found that Republicans “did not win a single day of early voting” in the states it tracked.

Once a ballot is banked, it can’t be undone. It doesn’t matter if there’s a late October surprise or a last-minute motivational push. While Democrats were locking in a coalition weeks before Election Day, Republicans didn’t really do the same. Elections are decided by who casts ballots and increasingly those ballots are cast before Election Day — and overwhelmingly for Democrats.

scraped.title: Sources: Cornyn Lobbies Dems To Tank Wesley Hunt's Nomination
scraped.description: Sources say John Cornyn has been the lone GOP holdout on approving Wesley Hunt as ambassador, hiding behind Dems to 'do his dirty work.'
scraped.author: Breccan F. Thies
scraped.h1: Sources: John Cornyn Is Quietly Lobbying Democrats To Tank Wesley Hunt’s Ambassador Nomination
scraped.body_text:
‘This is an entirely personal vendetta,’ a committee source told The Federalist. ‘It makes a mockery of whatever pretense to decency or statesmanship Cornyn has left.’

Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, has been the lone Republican holdout on approving Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Texas, as ambassador to Saudi Arabia, hiding behind Democrats to “do his dirty work for him,” according to multiple Senate sources familiar with the matter.

Since his primary race defeat, wherein Hunt was a challenger to the incumbent senator, Cornyn has been making a name for himself by obstructing President Donald Trump’s nominations to various positions, including judgeships and even now-Attorney General Todd Blanche. His latest gambit tanked the nomination of Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Counsel T. Elliot Gaiser to a federal district court in Texas.

Cornyn claims he refuses to support Gaiser because he is not from Texas, but if that is the criterion, then there is no real excuse for his apparent behind-the-scenes dealings with Democrats to kill the Hunt nomination.

Hunt was born and raised in Houston, and while Cornyn sometimes cites “qualifications” for his non-support of certain nominees, Hunt did three tours of duty in the Middle East, which included one tour as an Army Apache Helicopter Pilot and two tours as a diplomatic liaison officer in Saudi Arabia. He was nominated to the post on Sept. 14.

“Cornyn has gone to all the Democrats and has whipped them and asked them to vote against Hunt, and every other Republican on the committee is like, ‘This is crazy. Wesley’s qualified,’” a Senate Foreign Relations Committee source told The Federalist. “He’s former Army, he’s actually been stationed in Saudi, he understands the military — the intel component of that. He’s uniquely qualified, and we don’t have ambassadors in other parts of that region; we need it. So, from a U.S. national security standpoint, this is a big deal.”

Hunt’s Texas roots and tailor-made qualifications for ambassador to Saudi Arabia are why Cornyn has been forced to tank the nomination using Democrats instead of opposing it out in the open as he did with Gaiser, according to Senate Foreign Relations Committee sources. Cornyn has been the single vote in the Republican majority to not approve Hunt to advance out of committee and to the full Senate for a vote.

Cornyn informed committee Chairman James Risch, R-Idaho, on Nov. 7 that he would not vote for Hunt, and by Nov. 10 started lobbying Senate Democrats like Chris Coons, D-Del., Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Tim Kaine, D-Va., to not support him as well, the source said. Shoring up Democrat ranks was the way to make sure no Democrat could make up for Cornyn’s resistance. Cornyn also attempted to win over Republicans John Curtis, R-Utah, and Steve Daines, R-Mont., though he was “met with severe resistance.” On Nov. 18, Risch said that Hunt’s nomination had been held over by a senator until Dec. 1.

For nominees like Gaiser, “Cornyn’s publicly saying why he’s opposed, and there’s criteria. Well, you try to apply that same thought process to Wesley, and it doesn’t apply, and he knows that,” another Senate Foreign Relations Committee source said. “This is more just being vindictive, and sour grapes, and an angry old man as he’s being escorted out the building.”

The best bet for Cornyn is to kill Hunt’s nomination without having to go on record voting against him in committee, a source said.

When asked about this accusation and whether he would support Hunt, Cornyn’s office told The Federalist, “I’ll let you know if I have anything for you on this.” The office did not have a response by the deadline.

Committee sources believe that Cornyn’s animosity toward Hunt is an outgrowth of his being a primary challenger earlier this year in a race both Cornyn and Hunt ended up losing to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Cornyn’s whipping of Shaheen seemed to be fruitful enough that she asked Hunt during a Nov. 10 confirmation hearing about comments Hunt made about Cornyn during the primary campaign, calling him “Sharia John.” Sources familiar with the matter believe that line of questioning was placed directly by Cornyn as a way to get back at him.

Another source said Hunt got a call from both the State Department and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who introduced Hunt to the committee and is supporting him, saying Cornyn is the hold-up.

“This is an entirely personal vendetta,” a committee source told The Federalist. “It makes a mockery of whatever pretense to decency or statesmanship Cornyn has left.”

items.summary: President Donald Trump said that people who veer from MAGA “don’t do very well,” and he’s right — Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in a massive blue sweep after Trump started a new war that caused gas prices to skyrocket while Americans at home struggled with affordability. scraped.title: Trump Is Right: Veering From MAGA Costs Republicans
scraped.description: Trump said people who veer from MAGA "don't do very well," and he's right -- Republicans lost both chambers of Congress after Trump started a new war.
scraped.author: Brianna Lyman
scraped.h1: Trump Is Right: Veering From MAGA Costs Republicans
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump said that people who veer from MAGA “don’t do very well,” and he’s right — Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in a massive blue sweep after Trump started a new war that caused gas prices to skyrocket while Americans at home struggled with affordability.

The president was responding to Elon Musk, who said on Wednesday that he doesn’t consider himself “MAGA.”

“I’m not MAGA … Well, at least I’m not like … I’m not sure what MAGA means,” Musk said “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

Trump responded to the comments — which were made by Musk while he was traveling with the president — saying “He’s a friend of mine … there are a lot of definitions out there. MAGA, to me means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.”

As The Federalist CEO and co-founder Sean Davis said, “Trump is right. The election results prove it. When Republicans veer from MAGA, for example by starting new Middle East wars that jack up gas prices, Republicans get punished by voters.”

Trump used his farewell address in 2021 to tout the peace deals his administration negotiated in the Middle East.

“I am especially proud to be the first president in decades who has started no new wars,” the president said .

Four years later, Trump was still making the case. In his 2024 victory speech , he recalled the warnings that he would start a new war during his first administration: “I’m not going to start a war,” he said. “I’m going to stop wars.”

Trump also has previously bragged about not sending Americans to die in “stupid foreign wars.”

Trump allies who shared his opposition to new foreign wars feared in 2025 that the strikes against Iran that summer would turn into longer commitments in the region. But after months went on with no escalation, Trump was applauded for withstanding the pressure from the military-industrial complex and its adherents on both sides of the aisle. Then, in early 2026, pro-war factions lobbied Trump hard to reignite the conflict in Iran, with interventionists like the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and former George W. Bush speechwriter Marc Thiessen personally making the case to the president, as the Wall Street Journal reported. In the end, the neocons got the war they wanted, and American voters felt that the war dragged the Trump administration and its energy away from the MAGA priorities and promises they voted for in 2024.

The war caused gas prices to skyrocket. The president also said that critics of Mark Levin’s support of the war “ARE NOT MAGA, I AM.”

Prior to the war in Iran, American were paying an average of $2.94 for gas. But after the war disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, gas prices were, on average, $4.15 a gallon the day before the election.

A Pew Research poll from October found 64 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of the war, while the AP Voter Poll found roughly six in 10 midterm voters thought it was the wrong decision to strike Iran. Many of these voters backed the Democrats in the midterms.

During his first term and leading up to his second, Trump gave a rather clear idea of what MAGA meant — especially when it came to new wars. And Trump was right, veering away from that did cost the GOP in the midterms, and soon Congress will be controlled by a party that wants to destroy America and tear down the Trump administration.

scraped.title: Matt Taibbi: The 2028 Race Has Already Begun. Plus…
scraped.description: In today’s Front Page, Matt Taibbi on the start of the 2028 race. A federal judge on the redefinition of genocide. How the right made itself uncool again. And more.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
It’s Friday, November 20. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: Judge Roy Altman on the United Nations’ genocide ruling. River Page tackles “chud fatigue.” What Trump could learn from Reagan. And much more.

But first: Our new reporter at large on 2028.

Republicans face a post-Trump crossroads. Democrats are poised for civil war between the socialist left and the moderates, with both claiming the midterm triumph as their own. Few times in American history has the gap between visions of our political future seemed so vast. Are we headed for democratic socialism in the White House, a refashioned MAGA, or something entirely different?

Who better to make sense of it than Matt Taibbi ? Matt has been covering presidential elections for more than two decades, and he has done so with radical honesty and verve. He’s someone who thinks for himself—belonging to neither the blue or the red team—and whose perceptive eye has, time and again, spotted where our politics is heading ahead of the pack. We’ve long admired Matt, who worked with The Free Press on the Twitter Files in 2022 . That’s why we’re thrilled that Matt is joining these pages as The Free Press ’s reporter at large for this presidential cycle, delivering regular dispatches from the campaign trail as the country decides on its next chapter.

For his inaugural piece, Matt reports on the “Elvis” candidate wooing moderate Democrats in 2028, asks why everyone in the party seems so glum, and is booted from a Democratic Socialists of America meeting in Boston. —Oliver Wiseman

Yesterday, for the first time in its history, the International Court of Justice found a country guilty of a genocide, ruling that Myanmar had committed it against its Rohingya Muslim minority. To reach its verdict, the ICJ loosened its long-standing definition of genocide, Judge Roy K. Altman writes, at the urging of countries and activists eager to build a case against Israel. “Armed with these amorphous concepts,” he warns, “any enterprising judge can now turn any war into a genocide.” So what exactly did the court change? Read Altman’s piece to find out.

Two years ago, after podcasters like Joe Rogan and Theo Von helped Donald Trump win over young men, River Page predicted conservatism’s newfound cool wouldn’t last. He warned that the online right was going the way of the woke left: insular and terminally online. After a midterm election in which many men who had voted for Trump lurched back to the left, River says it has all unraveled even faster than he expected. The culprit is “chud fatigue”: exhaustion with the online right’s AI slop and trolling, much of it coming from the Trump administration itself. Read River on the phenomenon—and whether a post-Trump GOP will be able to shake its image problem.

Ronald Reagan believed that military strength was the surest path to peace. President Trump has embraced the same strategy—but is it working? In the latest episode of “School of War,” Aaron MacLean sits down with Roger Zakheim, author of Peace Through Strength, to explore how Reagan transformed the American military in the final years of the Cold War. From Washington’s budget battles to the rising threat of China, they discuss what Reagan’s legacy can teach Trump as he enters the last two years of his presidency.

One of the biggest stories of the past week wasn’t a single event, but a string of them. For days, it felt like a new tech outage hit every few hours: Microsoft Outlook, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, Apple, and even the National Security Agency.

Was it all a coincidence, or something more sinister? Moments like this invite speculation, so we asked experts in cybersecurity, geopolitics, and national defense how seriously we should take the possibility of a coordinated cyberattack. Don’t miss H.R. McMaster , Tyler Cowen , Michael Shermer , and others on what the outages might—and might not—tell us.

If this week’s news felt like the plot of a spy thriller, Niall Ferguson thinks that’s because it is. With Robert Pattinson newly cast as 007, Niall argues that our world of cyberattacks, honey traps, and a new Cold War with China looks a lot like James Bond’s. “As Cold War II intensifies,” he writes, “James Bond is not just relevant. He is so back.”

The outages have also fueled a run on generators and bottled water. Jon Stokes has some advice: Don’t bother. He spent years as a professional prepper, testing survival knives and water filters for a living, and he now regrets nearly every dollar he poured into it. So why is he now telling us not to panic?

Meanwhile in New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Monday that he’s disbanding the NYPD unit trained to handle violence and terrorism at protests and replacing it with mostly unarmed de-escalation teams. “We are trading a tested unit for an untested promise,” writes Saritha Komatireddy , a former prosecutor who launched an unsuccessful bid for New York attorney general this year. She warns that the move will leave the very New Yorkers the unit was built to protect vulnerable when the next riot comes.

Frontotemporal dementia is, as River Page puts it, “a disease that kills the self first.” He should know, because it took his grandmother. What he also knows is that in some cases, it’s passed down—and a test could tell River whether the same fate awaits him. All of which raises a question more of us may soon face as genetic testing advances: Would you want to know a future you can’t change?

Last but not least, Suzy Weiss and Dan Ahdoot sat down with Rob Lowe for a conversation about his surprising new role as a professor tortured during Stalin’s Great Purge in Confession , a film written by Ben Shapiro. They also talked about his faith, sobriety, marriage, and why so much of Hollywood is, in Lowe’s view, “paralyzed by preciousness.” Don’t miss Suzy’s column, and watch their full conversation on this week’s episode of Second Thought .

How many Lowe's would Rob Lowe rob if Rob Lowe could rob Lowe's?

So happy to see Matt Taibbi here. Now all they have to do is get Catherine Herridge and they will be totally unnbeatable.

scraped.title: How the Campaign Against Israel Rewrote the Law of Genocide
scraped.description: Genocide is the crime of crimes, and it requires a heightened level of proof. In its Myanmar ruling, the ICJ abandoned that standard, writes Roy K. Altman.
scraped.author: Roy K. Altman
scraped.body_text:
Yesterday’s long-awaited ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ)—finding Myanmar guilty of genocide in a case brought by the Republic of The Gambia—may have imperiled the court’s s own legitimacy. Along the way, the ICJ—the branch of the United Nations’ judicial system that adjudicates disputes between states—has violated some foundational precepts of our Western tradition in ways that may expose any government, including our own, to arbitrary genocide prosecutions in the future.

The ICJ’s finding was long awaited not because anyone had shown much interest over the last 10 years in Myanmar’s brutal campaign against its minority Muslim population, known as the Rohingya, in a war that started in 2016. The outsize attention has had little to do with either Myanmar or The Gambia and a great deal to do with the watered-down definition of genocide the court was being asked to adopt. If you guessed that this may have something to do with the international community’s obsession with the world’s only Jewish state, you’d be right.

scraped.title: Matt Taibbi: Welcome to the 2028 Democratic Primary
scraped.description: The presidential campaign starts earlier every cycle. Matt Taibbi, our new reporter-at-large, hits the road to handicap the race.
scraped.author: Matt Taibbi
scraped.body_text:
Republicans face a post-Trump crossroads. Democrats are poised for civil war between the socialist left and the moderates, with both claiming the midterm triumph as their own. Few times in American history has the gap between visions of our political future seemed so vast. Are we headed for democratic socialism in the White House, a refashioned MAGA, or something entirely different?

Who better to make sense of it than Matt Taibbi? Matt has been covering presidential elections for more than two decades, and he has done so with radical honesty and verve. He’s someone who thinks for himself—belonging to neither the blue or the red team—and whose perceptive eye has, time and again, spotted where our politics is heading ahead of the pack. We’ve long admired Matt, who worked with The Free Press on the Twitter Files in 2022 . That’s why we’re thrilled that Matt is joining these pages as The Free Press’s reporter-at-large for this presidential cycle, delivering regular dispatches from the campaign trail as the country decides on its next chapter.

For his inaugural piece, he reports on the “Elvis” candidate wooing moderate Democrats in 2028, asks why everyone in the party seems so glum, and is booted from a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) meeting in Boston. —Oliver Wiseman

At the “What’s Next?” organizing conference in Denver last Thursday, the unofficial launch of the 2028 presidential campaign cycle opened with a kick to the groin.

“Get this,” said strategist Stephanie Valencia. “Close to half of eligible Latino voters today, something like 16 million people, were not even old enough to vote when Barack Obama was first elected. Hope and Change does not mean anything to them. They were busy getting potty-trained and doing their homework.”

A nervous laugh shot through the crowd. You could read it on a hundred faces: “Jesus, are we that old?”

They used to call this time the “ invisible primary .” In the months between midterms and the first presidential stump speeches in January in half-empty diners in Iowa and New Hampshire (it’ll be South Carolina and Nevada now), party leaders huddled to line up money and endorsements behind a creature vanished from American politics: the “presumptive favorite.” That process took place away from the press in mostly closed conferences—the proverbial smoke-filled room , whose loss has at times been lamented in the Trump age by pundits like Andrew Sullivan—and was nearly 100 percent predictive. The “invisible primary” winner almost always became the nominee.

Now, everything is up in the air, total chaos. In both parties, we have fewer of Don Rumsfeld’s “known knowns” than at any time since 1968. The myriad possibilities of democracy no longer being locked away would have been a definite thrill once, but after the last 10 years, the benefits of seeing behind the curtain are murkier. The Great Oz might be drooling and insane. I went to look anyway.

scraped.title: Effective Altruism’s big payday
scraped.author: Kathleen Stock
scraped.h1: Effective Altruism’s big payday Philanthropy won’t save their souls
scraped.body_text:
You wanted to feel like a titanic superhero; so why do you feel nothing at all? (Finn Gomez/Getty)

You wanted to feel like a titanic superhero; so why do you feel nothing at all? (Finn Gomez/Getty)

What will John Stuart Millionaire do next? Anthropic employees have just become stinkingly rich — at least on paper — and one wonders what the utilitarians among them will do with their stock. After years of discussion on effective altruism blogs about the most rational forms of wealth distribution, the thought experiment has finally been actualized, though the numbers involved — not just billions but trillions — remain unreal. For those who have talked a bold philanthropic game in the past, it is time to walk out onto the pitch.

Being an effective altruist is not compulsory at Anthropic — but it probably helps. Several of the AI company’s bosses have historical and personal ties with the movement, though CEO Dario Amodei denies current affiliation. A former employee recalls being asked in an interview whether he would commit two-thirds of his equity to charity, feeling unclear whether a job offer was conditional on his answer. (He said he would, but then resigned before he actually received any holdings. I imagine this has been a somewhat challenging week.)

As Amodei told us in January, Anthropic founders have themselves each pledged to give away 80% of their personal wealth, while staff lower down the chain have also “individually pledged to donate company shares worth billions”. And it seems that most are sincere — or at least pretending to be for the benefit of passing journalists. The New York Times reports that “the money is secondary” for many worker “Ants”, as they are known. Apparently, the more common topic of conversation among newly minted magnates is exactly where to donate.

Still, one wonders whether some will allow themselves a little ethically sourced ass’s milk on the side. For the wonderful thing about utilitarianism as a practical creed is that it is often possible to convince yourself that self-serving actions are for the general good; and especially so when the main conduit of benefit is supposed to be money. As critics have pointed out , the movement’s preferred “earning to give” strategy has already justified the buying of mansions and the frequenting of luxury vegan restaurants, under the banner of luring yet more rich people to the cause. Think of it as doing a Reverse Mother Teresa, but for radical wealth not poverty: only a rich person can truly comprehend others who are in that same state. And if you convert just one billionaire to altruism by projecting an image of excess yourself, then all those private jets and Gucci manbags will have been totally worth it.

Accordingly, some in the UK are salivating at the prospect of more tech wealth entering the prime housing market. The famous Rodeo Drive shopping scene in Pretty Woman has had a 21st-century reboot: now it involves a nerdy-looking bloke in Asic trainers and a fleece, expressing interest in a Hyde Park penthouse to skeptical estate agents. Another sector said to be getting a boost is that of matchmakers and dating coaches, catering to the socially challenged tech founder keen to find a high-status mate while avoiding Chinese spies. Here, too, vast expense can presumably be justified in rigorously ethical terms, even leaving aside the benefit bestowed on future generations by finding an appropriate vessel for your genes. Hours spent fruitlessly browsing dating sites or making awkward small talk in coffee shops is a horrible waste, compared with all the vitally improving stuff you could be doing with your laptop instead.

And some investors really do have plans to change the world. A recent set of recommendations from Coefficient Giving — a “philanthropic adviser and funder” beloved of effective altruists, co-founded by Daniela Amodei’s husband — includes ending diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis, and Strep A; pulling sub-Saharan Africa out of poverty; developing early pandemic detection tools; teaching more kids to read; and lobbying the pig farming industry to stop putting sows in small crates. A lot of this is crowd-pleasing stuff, indistinguishable from goals that established charities have championed for decades. It would seem churlish to point out that if global unemployment or biological warfare were to also unfold, thanks to Claude and pals — as Dario Amodei admits they might — then all the do-gooder stuff is going to look as relevant to an overall assessment of Anthropic’s social contribution as Jimmy Savile’s work did on behalf of the NHS.

In any case: even if some ethical goals have remained constant, the evaluative landscape conjured up by a supposedly rationalist approach to philanthropy is a distinctly weird one. Unlike approaches focused on personal virtue, the contemporary altruist seems interested only in analyzing what makes a good deed, and has no complicated account of what makes an admirable person. Though there is grudging talk of traits like fairness and empathy leading to better outcomes, being good is mainly a boring matter of aggregation. That is: you climb the leader boards by causing large enough effects of the right kind. The most admirable people are those who do the most, single-handedly, to reduce suffering or enhance happiness on a global scale.

And since we are talking about a consequentialist approach, interested only in effects, there is no particular requirement here that your own intervention be hands-on. You don’t have to scrub up in the leper hospital or the animal sanctuary yourself. You don’t have to be the last link in the causal chain before the magical transformation of another person’s life occurs. Indeed, if you are the one patiently doling out the vaccines or digging the wells or whatever, then there is a sense in which you can only be a minor player. For whatever your well-meaning intentions or the skill and sensitivity with which you execute them, you are only helping a few people at a time.

By Arif Ahmed

In contrast, the further away you retreat from the scene of action, the more influential you can be. The person who organizes vaccine distribution is more “high impact” — as EA jargon would have it — than the person who merely dispenses; and the person who funds distribution in several places is higher still. At the top of the scoreboard perch the benevolent multimillionaires and billionaires, streaming huge amounts of dosh out across the universe all at once. In the old Christian tradition, alms-giving at a distance came second to acting as a loving presence in a suffering person’s life; yet the new religion decrees this was quite the wrong way round.

In our gamified, commodified world, this might seem a natural way to think; yet I wonder how well it scratches the original itch. Giving money away is not difficult when you have millions left to wallow in. Perhaps strangely, in the context of a movement that places such emphasis on making a difference to sentient experience, the multimillionaire need barely register his benevolent acts at all. The lack of effort involved in cash transfers, coupled with the causal distance, must make it all seem surreal. You wanted to feel like a titanic superhero; so why do you feel nothing at all?

And the near-total reliance upon AI agents as intermediaries with every anticipated project is not going to help with this. Victorian utilitarians could get joyfully stuck into their pet obsessions — both intellectually and practically — and claim any glory accordingly. Think of Edwin Chadwick ’s endless compiling of mortality tables on behalf of a better sewage system, or Rowland Hill’s gleefully creative invention of the Uniform Penny Post . The spiritual heirs of these quirky, inventive men, now captaining the AI industry, can only ever work at a distance. They can make robots and they can make piles of money, but the glory that comes with any longed-for outcomes will not really be theirs.

Of course, this aspect also has its useful side. If you cannot take much personal credit for something, then you cannot really be blamed for failure either — a point for tech bosses to cling to, given that the story of robot innovation is only a few pages in. But if they do end up being blamed for some tragic human ending or other, there is another Christian tradition available to fall back upon: seeking plenary or partial indulgences, by carrying out elaborate works of mercy. Really, things haven’t changed as much as we might think.

scraped.title: Did Xi just cuck Putin?
scraped.author: Seva Gunitsky
scraped.h1: Did Xi just cuck Putin? Russia is losing its sphere of influence
scraped.body_text:
Putin plays with doctored maps; XI and Trump with real ones. (Doug Mills/Getty)

Putin plays with doctored maps; XI and Trump with real ones. (Doug Mills/Getty)

It must have sounded great in the Kremlin: three leaders of nuclear powers coming together to carve up the world. A Yalta 2.0, in which Russia finally receives its due and formalizes its sphere of influence. Putin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, billed the three-way meeting with Trump and Xi as the highlight of the trip and said its significance and symbolism “can hardly be overestimated”.

As has happened to Putin so often lately, reality turned out differently: this was not a second Yalta. If Putin thought he was meeting the leaders of China and America on equal terms, he was mistaken.

Xi met Trump personally at the foot of Air Force One, the first time he has ever greeted a foreign leader at the airport. Meanwhile, Putin was met by Cai Qi, a senior party official. When the three leaders were photographed, Putin was standing awkwardly next to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan. And at the banquet, he was seated away from the head table where Xi entertained Trump. Kremlinology began as the art of reading who stood where atop Lenin’s mausoleum; Xi’s protocol slights have given the new Kremlinologists plenty to discuss.

By Wolfgang Münchau

The original Yalta brought together confident victors at the height of their powers; Shenzhen brought together two leaders mired in unpopular wars and a host whose economy is slowing. They met for about 90 minutes, held no press conference afterwards, and issued a declaration that repeated a 1985 formula on nuclear war and promised “stable energy flows”. The carve-up will have to wait, even if Putin got his photo-op.

Only a week earlier, Moscow had been demanding a new global order outright. At the close of talks with Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, Russia’s negotiator went on state television to declare that “wherever the foot of our Russian soldier has stepped, it’s ours”. Russia still wants all of the Donbas, a veto on Ukraine’s membership in Nato, and caps on its army. Oh, and also “a new, modern Yalta and Potsdam”, or a great-power settlement that would roll back the European order of the last three decades.

Putin might have wanted a new Yalta, but he forgot to win the war first. By Michael Kofman’s assessment, the Russian army is having its worst year since early 2023. The ISW counts a net Russian loss of territory in four of the past eight months due to Ukrainian counteroffensives. Meanwhile the budget deficit keeps growing, the sovereign wealth fund keeps shrinking, and a big span of the Kerch bridge, which connects Crimea to the Russian mainland, has been struck by missiles multiple times this week. The country’s elites are coming to think the war is unsustainable.

Why is Russia making maximalist claims as things deteriorate? For one, Putin might not actually believe his position is getting worse. This is partly a product of an information bubble, but as Tatiana Stanovaya argued this summer, the problem is less with bad intelligence and more with a decision process fixed by one man with a stubborn and unshakeable picture of the world. In that picture the West is divided and decaying, Ukraine is falling apart, and Russian victory is inevitable. If that’s the world you live in, increasing your demands only makes sense. Certainly no one in your inner circle will object.

It helps when you can produce an alternate reality of Russian soldiers waving flags over villages the army has not reached. The FT and ISW found dozens of these AI-generated videos ; in one, from the Defense Ministry, the flag of a town that generals claimed they had taken flips to the other side mid-frame. Whether Putin believes the doctored maps or only uses them as propaganda is hard to say; ISW reads them as a bargaining tactic . But a ruler convinced the general trend favors him will discount bad news either way.

Most importantly, Russia’s price might be rising because they think they can extract more from the Americans — which makes sense, since the Americans keep signaling that more is available. Putin says it was Steve Witkoff who proposed widening the agenda to European security, and Trump has described a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Xi may have slighted Putin at the summit, but Trump called him “my friend” and clapped excitedly when Putin joined him at the podium.

Meanwhile Washington has been squeezing Kyiv, ordering caps on Ukraine’s Starshield terminals and disabling its interceptor drones. A Ukrainian official said Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to cut off US intelligence during talks in Miami in October. Under these circumstances, how could Putin not be expected to take advantage?

And yet when Putin finally reached the big boys’ table, he was offered nothing. Xi kept Ukraine off the three-way agenda; weeks earlier he had told Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the German president, that “the Europeans must also be at the table” for any such discussion. Trump said afterwards that his separate meeting with Putin had focused on the war, and Kyiv has reason to worry what was said there — especially since, just hours after the trilateral summit, Trump was delivering a “tirade” over the telephone to the Coalition of the Willing concerning their plans to fund Ukraine. But Stalin, at Yalta, this was not. After all, Stalin didn’t need doctored maps; he was too busy redrawing the real ones. Putin can’t do that now.

In Robert Bolt’s play, A Man for All Seasons , Thomas More’s son-in-law William Roper declares he would cut down every law in England to get after the Devil. More replies with one of the great warnings of political drama:

“And when the last law was down, and the Devil turned round on you — where would you hide, Roper, the laws all being flat? … D’you really think you could stand upright in the winds that would blow then?”

Vladimir Putin has spent two decades raging against the devil of the liberal international order. Now, thanks to Trump’s foreign policy, he is getting his wish: the dismantling of the US-led system and its replacement with a world where powerful states act freely in their self-proclaimed peripheries with no regard for liberal pieties. A Concert of Europe applied on a global scale: cuius regio, eius imperium ; whoever is ruler of the realm gets to set the rules.

But the same rules that constrained Putin’s ambitions also constrained a rising China, deterred French sailors from boarding his oil tankers, prevented the US from kidnapping his clients, kept regional powers in check, and gave Russia the predictability it needed to navigate the world as a middling power that rattled its nukes and fiddled with gas switches and did little else. In fact, Russia did quite well out of the liberal order. Its nuclear arsenal and permanent Security Council seat enabled it to punch above its weight. It could play the victim of Western hypocrisy and rail against the bindings of a system that also constrained its enemies.

By Seva Gunitsky

In a true spheres-of-influence world, what does Russia have? A slowing economy, a military bleeding out in Ukraine, and no room at the head table. The liberal order’s constraints shackled Russia’s imperial ambitions, but they also protected it from the full implications of its own decay. Securing Western non-interference in Ukraine and the Baltics will come at the cost of letting China dominate Central Asia, Turkey dominate the Caucasus, and regional powers exploit the vacuum left by American disengagement from Europe.

Shenzhen offered a preview of that world. The Kremlin had sold the summit as a meeting of three equals, but — if it was a second Yalta — then Russia found itself in the position of the British at that conference: an increasingly insignificant power, valued only for the personality of its leader. That was evident in how Xi arranged and treated his guests. He was making it clear that if anyone is to carve up the world, it will be China and America. In 2022, Putin made a bet that he could cut down the liberal order’s laws and stand upright in the winds that blow. He has since doubled down on that bet. And that’s a risky proposition for a petrostate with a shrinking population and a broken army. For, what happens when the devil turns round?
