scraped.title: The end of Polish democracy
scraped.author: Thomas Fazi
scraped.h1: The end of Polish democracy Liberals are weaponizing the ‘Rule of Law’
scraped.body_text:
Protesters from both sides gathered outside the tribunal. (Woktek Radwanski/Getty)

Protesters from both sides gathered outside the tribunal. (Woktek Radwanski/Getty)

In Poland, what started as a constitutional crisis, is quickly evolving into an all-out institutional civil war. It all began on 30 October, when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska — a judge elected to the Constitutional Tribunal earlier this year by Donald Tusk’s pro-EU parliamentary majority, but whom President Karol Nawrocki, elected by popular vote last year with the backing of the national-conservative Law and Justice party (PiS), had refused to swear in — declared herself in charge of the court and suspended its president and vice-president, appointed under Nawrocki’s PiS-aligned predecessor, Andrzej Duda. From there, riot police were sent to surround the building: officially to protect judges and staff, but in practice to make sure the Tribunal’s leadership couldn’t get back in.

While all this was happening, Nawrocki himself was flying to Senegal for an official state visit. Once he heard the news, though, he ordered his plane to fly back to Warsaw. In the early hours of the following morning, he forced his way into the Tribunal amid crowds of protesters. Since then the two camps — Tusk’s government on one side, Nawrocki and the PiS-led opposition on the other — have been locked in a bitter standoff, each accusing the other of violating Polish law and the constitution. The opposition has called it a coup d’état — or, at least, given that the situation is still unfolding, an attempted one. Tusk, for his part, insists purging the court is necessary to “restore the rule of law”. Which rule of law, though? As we shall see, behind the domestic power struggle lies a much larger battle over sovereignty in the EU — and over who, ultimately, gets to decide what the “rule of law” means.

The standoff has since escalated even further. On 10 November, the Supreme Court overturned the suspension of the Tribunal’s president and vice-president. Two days later, when they both arrived at the Tribunal with the ruling in hand, the police refused to open the gates. Korwin-Piotrowska declared that the Supreme Court’s decision had “no bearing” on the suspensions, while the justice minister argued that the chamber that issued it was itself illegitimate. In other words, the government isn’t just overriding the Tribunal’s decisions but the Supreme Court’s as well. Meanwhile, on Monday, the central bank — headed by Adam Glapiński, who has longstanding ties to PiS — suspended payment orders involving the Tribunal’s accounts, citing doubts about who was legally authorized to represent the institution. The decision has drawn strong criticism from the government.

By Thomas Fazi

The latest chapter in the country’s long-running constitutional crisis began in March, when the Sejm (Polish parliament) elected six new judges to fill vacancies on the 15-member Tribunal — seats Tusk’s coalition had refused to fill since taking office. It argued that the Tribunal had been “captured” by PiS — every sitting judge had been appointed during the party’s eight-year tenure, which ended with Tusk’s victory in 2023 — and was no longer a proper court, and that electing its own judges would have meant recognizing a court it considered illegitimate. Moreover, a seat can only be filled once its holder’s nine-year term expires, and in the coalition’s first years in office that meant just a handful of vacancies: not nearly enough to tip the balance. The coalition’s preferred plan was to reform the Tribunal through legislation and reset it wholesale, but that plan ran into Duda — and then into Nawrocki. At that point, Tusk switched to plan B — judicial appointments — especially since by this year the number of vacant seats had risen to eight, enough to shift the balance.

Nawrocki, however, refused to accept the oaths of five of the eight new judges, citing irregularities in their election, as well as the political nature of some of the nominations. The government accuses Nawrocki of acting on political grounds: if all the new judges took their seats, the PiS-era members would become a minority, losing control of a court that can strike down government legislation. Tusk also argues that Nawrocki’s refusal is unconstitutional, since the constitution gives the president no role in vetoing judges elected by parliament.

On this point, the government can count on some heavyweight backing. The Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on constitutional matters, has said that the president’s role in the swearing-in is purely ceremonial; in May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered Poland to remove the obstacles preventing the new judges from taking up their seats. The Tribunal itself, however, reached the opposite conclusion: in a ruling issued that same month, it found that the president is under no absolute obligation to swear in judges elected by parliament. The point here is that Poland’s judicial question is legally contested — and that the government chose to settle it not through political mediation but with riot police.

Throughout its time in power, PiS was accused — both by the Tusk-led opposition and the EU — of politicizing the court and undermining its impartiality and independence. Indeed, most accounts trace the origins of the current crisis to PiS’s decision, in 2015, to appoint judges to three seats that had already been filled by the outgoing majority — a coalition led, then as now, by Tusk’s Civic Platform (before winning in 2023, Tusk had previously been prime minister from 2007 to 2014). What these accounts usually leave out is that PiS was itself responding to a move by the outgoing Civic Platform-controlled Sejm, which had elected five judges to the Tribunal just weeks before the parliamentary election. The Tribunal later ruled that three of those appointments were valid, but that two were unlawful, as they filled seats falling within the incoming parliament’s term; the new PiS majority, however, declared all five void and elected five replacement judges of its own.

In many ways, then, what is happening now is a replay of those events, with the roles reversed. For all the accusations leveled at PiS of “politicizing” the court, it is hard to see how the current government’s conduct is any different. Coming from a PiS-backed president, Nawrocki’s complaints about the political nature of the new appointments may be hypocritical, but they are hard to dismiss when one of the new judges served in Tusk’s cabinet until this summer and is described by Tusk himself as his “right-hand man”. The hypocrisy, it would seem, runs both ways.

Indeed, Tusk’s pro-EU government may well be right that Nawrocki is bending the rules by refusing to swear in the judges, but its own appeals to the rule of law ring hollow, given its own evident willingness to bend the rules. Even legal scholars who have spent years denouncing PiS’s judicial policies, and who have no sympathy for Nawrocki, have argued that Korwin-Piotrowska’s decision to suspend the Tribunal’s president and vice-president has “no legal basis” and “violates at least five provisions of the Polish Constitution”. One thing is clear: this is not a battle over the rule of law, but over replacing one form of political control with another — by any means necessary. Courts, prosecutors, the police, the presidency, even the central bank: every arm of the state has been drawn into the fray — a reminder of how quickly democratic norms can unravel once politics becomes an existential fight for power.

Yet this is also about much more than a showdown between government and opposition. To see why, one needs to understand why the Tribunal matters so much. It is not just the arbiter of whether the government’s laws are constitutional; it is also the body that decides, in the last instance, how the Polish constitution relates to EU law — and therefore whether Poland’s legal order can be overridden from Brussels. At its core, then, this is a battle over sovereignty in its most fundamental form: when the two collide, which legal order should prevail — the Polish constitution or EU law?

In the past, the Tribunal has ruled that the final word lies with the Polish constitution, something Brussels has never forgiven it for. The supremacy of EU law over national law is not enshrined in any of the treaties; it was created by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) itself, in its 1964 Costa v ENEL ruling. From there, it has become the engine of EU “integration through law”: by constantly creating new “laws” through its rulings, almost always in favor of “more Europe”, the ECJ has effectively become the bloc’s most important constitution-writing body, hollowing out national constitutional and legal systems from above.

A national constitutional court that rejects this principle poses an existential threat to Brussels. This is the real reason the EU was so implacably hostile to Poland under its previous government (and to Viktor Orbán’s Hungary, for the same reason). The landmark moment came in October 2021, when the Tribunal ruled that key provisions of the EU treaties, as interpreted by the ECJ, were incompatible with the Polish constitution, insofar as they allowed EU law to override it and EU judges to rule on how Poland organizes its own judiciary. In effect, the court declared that, in matters reserved to the constitution, the final word lay in Warsaw, not Luxembourg. Brussels responded with infringement proceedings against Poland and financial blackmail, freezing tens of billions in EU funds, officially over the PiS government’s judicial reforms. It later took the case to the ECJ, which, unsurprisingly, ruled in December 2025 that the Tribunal had violated EU law by rejecting the primacy of the latter — and, for good measure, that it was not even a valid court. In other words, a national constitutional court was declared illegitimate by a supranational one for daring to defend its own constitution.

This, ultimately, is what Brussels and Tusk mean when they accuse the previous government, and the Tribunal itself, of violating the rule of law: that they dared to challenge the rule of Brussels’s law. This is the law Tusk wants to restore. It also explains why Brussels has thrown its weight behind Tusk. The Commission has insisted that parliament must be free to appoint new judges: effectively demanding Nawrocki validate them. The Tribunal, said Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath, must operate “in accordance with the Polish constitution and the case law of the Court of Justice of the EU”. Meaning: the latter must take precedence over the former. Unsurprisingly, McGrath had nothing to say about a government sending riot police to take control of the country’s highest court.

By Michal Kranz

In broader terms, what is happening in Poland is part of a wider trend that one may call “liberal authoritarianism”: pro-EU governments using every means at their disposal, including blatant violations of the rule of law, to entrench their grip on power and keep the opposition out of it. Since coming to power in late 2023, Tusk’s coalition has shown scant regard for constitutional norms and institutional independence: it has seized control of the public broadcasters by ministerial fiat, bypassing the media regulator, and ignored the Tribunal’s rulings, refusing even to publish them in the official journal as the law requires.

Tusk’s move against the Tribunal should also be seen as a way of pre-emptively tying the hands of a future national-conservative government. Polls suggest the Right could return to power in the autumn 2027 election; backed by a sovereigntist president and Tribunal, it could resist further EU centralization. Taking control of the Tribunal now is one way of making sure that doesn’t happen. In the shadow of Poland’s constitutional crisis, meanwhile, the Sejm has just passed a bill that would allow it to sanction anyone deemed to support “foreign interference and manipulation in the information environment” — with breaches of sanctions punishable by up to 12 years in prison.

All this has been met with silence in Brussels, when not openly applauded. As a former president of the European Council and staunch pro-integrationist, Tusk, it seems, enjoys a near-total exemption from the scrutiny Brussels reserves for its critics. Nor is Poland an isolated case. From Hungary to Romania, appeals to an abstract and hypocritical “rule of law” have barred candidates and overturned elections, even as the AfD in Germany lives under the constant threat of a ban. Across Europe, the pattern is the same: the rule of law is invoked to suspend the rule of law, while democracy is dismantled by the very EU establishment that claims to defend it.

Thomas Fazi is an UnHerd columnist and translator. His latest book is The Covid Consensus , co-authored with Toby Green.

scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Did Claude Just Solve Math's Most Famous Problem? Even Anthropic's Mathematician Admits The Timing Is 'Horrible'
scraped.body_text:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's staff, announced on Friday that he and Claude have found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis , the 1859 conjecture on how the prime numbers are spread out and one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven $1 million Millennium Prize problems.

" I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis ," Alpöge wrote in a four-page note on his website. He said the method "easily extends much further," settling the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis as well, and that he expects the Extended Riemann Hypothesis to follow "with more time."

BREAKING: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he & Claude may have proved the Riemann Hypothesis, a $1 million math problem that has remained unsolved since 1859.

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) November 20, 2026

Instead of a paper, Alpöge released the proof written in Lean, a language in which a computer checks every step of an argument , split into 14 downloadable archive files. "Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions," he wrote, adding that the argument "is incredibly long at the moment."

He said he chose to publish only the Lean code because "it being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of 'slop', I decided to only present Lean." In a footnote he admitted he had tried anyway: "I of course amused myself, and hit 250,000+ pages."

As of Friday, no outside mathematician had vouched for the result. - and number theorists still have to confirm that the theorem at the end of the code really is Riemann's hypothesis, as Scientific American notes.

Alpöge, a number theorist, wrote that he had been planning for this problem since his student days, and gave Claude the decisive turns. "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

He said he steered the work toward the right setting and that Claude then supplied the step he expects to make mathematicians "fall out of their chairs" : a chain of "theta lifts" about as long as the square root of the size of the prime sum being bounded, each lift standing in for the "multiplicity" that the classic argument over function fields relies on and that is hard to find over the whole numbers. A timeline he says Claude compiled runs from Oct. 6, the "Stepanov determinant," to Nov. 16, with a single entry: "GRH."

Why does it matter? Take the first trillion whole numbers. A standard formula predicts about 37.6 billion primes and misses by just 38,262 . If the proof holds, mathematicians would have a guarantee on how far that estimate can stray, even at numbers far too large to check by counting. Results that depend only on Riemann being right would become theorems. For Anthropic, the bigger prize would be evidence that Claude contributed an original idea that helped crack a problem mathematicians have chased since 1859.

Alpöge's claim landed a day after Anthropic's first day of trading, with the stock sliding toward its $83 IPO price on Friday morning. He addressed the timing in his note - writing: "It is obvious to me that I should remark on the following." " The precise timing is horrible, " adding that it all came together late Sunday night, when he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, "Hypothetically, if I were to have ...", "eventually asking about my ability to announce."

"We went and figured it out and the fact is that there was a constraint to respect," he went on, adding that he was "clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer." "There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false, and I am pleased that I am in circumstances where it is obviously false."

In August, Anthropic said an unreleased version of Claude had raised the share of the zeta function's zeros known to satisfy the hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%, in work that Alpöge and fellow Anthropic mathematician Ralph Furman validated. The company wrote at the time: "We don't expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis." In July, Alpöge posted a Claude-generated counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture.

Even if the proof holds, the money is years off: under Clay's rules , a solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, wait at least two years and win "general acceptance in the global mathematics community" before the institute will consider it.

Bettors aren't sold yet:

26% chance the Riemann Hypothesis is officially declared solved by end of year. https://t.co/OEQc1VKVrb

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) November 20, 2026

Alpöge says he will write the argument up properly and expects it to shrink fast. "My intuition insists it will be massively simplified, likely immediately," he wrote. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

scraped.h1: Russia Shoots Down Kushner: Article 5 For Ukraine "Unacceptable"
scraped.body_text:
Moscow on Friday shot down Jared Kushner's claim that Washington had gotten Russia "comfortable" with NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine , a day after Trump's son-in-law and envoy made it in Berlin.

"I'd like to say that even coming up with the formula of NATO quasi-membership for Kiev or seeking a 'creative' solution in this sphere is unacceptable to us," Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov told reporters in St. Petersburg. "We discuss security guarantees primarily in terms of ensuring the security of our own country."

"As for Ukraine, let them recognize that our demand that this country must not join NATO is non-negotiable," Ryabkov said. "Once that happens, I think the issue of security guarantees can be discussed one way or another."

Kushner made the claim at a joint press conference at the German chancellery on Thursday, closing out a Coalition of the Willing summit attended by Volodymyr Zelensky. Calling it "a very big development," he said: "I think we've gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5."

Jared Kushner: "I think we've gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on [NATO's] Article 5." pic.twitter.com/93KyU4ubcK

— Scott Robertson (@sarobertson_) November 19, 2026

Kushner himself conceded "there's a lot of skepticism and disbelief on that concept in Russia," and said Washington hasn't signed on either: "From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal." Trump is "open to" it, he said, "but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that."

After Trump's Alaska summit with Putin in August 2025, fellow envoy Steve Witkoff told CNN : "We got to an agreement that the United States and other European nations could effectively offer Article 5-like language to cover a security guarantee."

Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in September there could be no talks on any options that would effectively replicate NATO membership for Ukraine , in an interview with Channel One. When the coalition, Ukraine and the US signed a declaration on security guarantees in Paris in January, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Western troops and military sites in Ukraine would be "legitimate military targets" and called the document "extremely far from a peaceful settlement." Putin has told Witkoff and Kushner that foreign troops in Ukraine would threaten Russia's security and are unacceptable.

Zelensky has called Article 5-style guarantees an "absolute minimum," and he told Ukraine's Novosti.Live channel that only US and European forces and bases on Ukrainian soil would count: "Without that, it's not Article 5 or any other article."

Ryabkov's remarks came a day after French President Emmanuel Macron said in Berlin that the question of Ukraine's NATO membership should be reopened: "Today, this question arises even for us Europeans." Ryabkov said Moscow sees "little difference between NATO and the EU," and that if British, French and German envoys accept Putin's invitation to Moscow, "it would not mean the group joining the so-called trilateral format," he added .

Zelensky said last week that US negotiators had asked, for the first time, whether Ukraine would leave Donbas in exchange for NATO membership , as we reported . Kushner came to Berlin straight off the Trump-Xi-Putin summit in China, days after Putin aide Yuri Ushakov poured cold water on bringing the Europeans into the talks.

Ukraine has hit the bridge linking Crimea to the Russian mainland three times in a week, most recently overnight into Thursday, and Putin vowed in Shenzhen: "We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that."

scraped.h1: Internal Memo Reveals What Trump's IRS Has Been Doing To Left-Wing Groups
scraped.body_text:
The Trump administration's hunt for the money behind Antifa has reached the tax man. The IRS has opened at least four criminal investigations as part of the crackdown on Antifa and the left-wing networks the administration says are funding political violence , according to an internal status report circulated among leaders of the agency's Criminal Investigation unit and reviewed by the New York Times .

The memo, which covers the unit's work from March through July, says special agents and analysts also referred at least four tax-exempt groups to the IRS's civil side for audits , were assigned to nine grand juries, and helped the FBI comb nonprofits' Form 990 filings for problems. One focus is people who dox or threaten government officials. The memo does not name the targets or say where the cases stand.

The push traces back to the assassination of Charlie Kirk on Sept. 10, 2025. Twelve days later Trump designated Antifa a "domestic terrorist organization," calling it a "militarist, anarchist enterprise" that hides its funding sources from law enforcement, and ordered investigations and prosecutions of "those who fund such operations."

Three days after that came a national security memorandum , NSPM-7, which named self-described "anti-fascism" as the banner over the violence and pointed to the so-called "anti-fascist" engravings Kirk's alleged assassin put on his bullets. It ordered the IRS commissioner to make sure no tax-exempt entity was "directly or indirectly" financing political violence or domestic terrorism , and among the warning signs it lists is "extremism on migration, race, and gender."

About a dozen IRS officials were detailed to the FBI-led task force that grew out of it, according to the memo. After protesters repeatedly clashed with ICE at Delaney Hall, the immigrant detention center in Newark, New Jersey, IRS officials combed through financial records, including subpoenaed Venmo data, of people arrested at the protests and of businesses they believed were funding them. At one point they used facial recognition and tattoo-analysis databases to identify people. The White House counted the dozens of May arrests at the Newark facility among its blows against what it calls the "Antifa terrorist network."

The task force also worked the shooting at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in the spring and a May shooting at a mosque in San Diego. It was involved in the UFC event on the White House lawn in June as well, though what the IRS did there is unclear.

Officials discussed an expedited audit process that would strip tax-exempt status from organizations whose leaders had been indicted. IRS lawyers raised concerns about its legal rigor, and the agency has not put it in place.

An IRS spokesman said the criminal unit has worked with federal partners, including the FBI, to "investigate individuals and entities that may be funding domestic terrorism or political violence."

The administration has been promising to follow the Antifa money for more than a year. In February, FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau had uncovered Antifa's funding sources , with agents examining whether the money ran through US nonprofits with tax-exempt status. Days after Kirk's killing, a senior Justice Department official directed US attorneys to draw up plans to investigate George Soros's Open Society Foundations, as we reported at the time; the foundation answered that it does not fund terrorism. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised a crackdown on the dark money behind the protests, and the State Department added four European Antifa groups, Germany's "Hammer Gang" among them, to its terror list in November 2025.

Criminal Investigation, the IRS's roughly 3,000-person law enforcement arm, has been stretched in other directions too. A Treasury inspector general report found its agents logged more than 353,000 hours on ICE support and the crime surges in Washington and Memphis between May 2025 and March 2026, about $40 million in labor and travel and the equivalent of some 313 tax investigations, according to Accounting Today 's account of the report.

Inside the task force, the memo's authors complained of "continual turnover" in the FBI's leadership and a "culture of lack of information sharing." Some IRS agents ignored the task force's emails or never mentioned they were already working a case, and some possible financial crimes went unpursued "because there was no specific threat directed at a government entity, its property or a government employee."

Their fix: a broader mandate for "investigating the misuse of 501(c)(3) organizations and/or individuals with nexus to terrorism."

scraped.body_text:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched a retaliatory drone strike on al-Riffa Helicopter base in Bahrain, followed by a wave of missiles that triggered air defense fire. On this Monday’s edition of The Target, Mint Press News’ Robert Inlakesh looks at the latest developments in all the theatres of the ongoing regional war in West Asia.

The US has started to commit routine strikes on southern Iran, including missile and drone attacks against Sirik, Bandar Abbas and Qeshm Island. Iranian retaliatory fire has since targeted a US Radar facility on an island off the coast of Oman, including a much broader wave of attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, with the counter-measures now escalating into direct fire on US bases.

US CENTCOM now has the largest number of aircraft carriers under its chain of command than has occurred since the invasion of Iraq in 2003, as the USS Theodore Roosevelt joined both the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. In the stream we look at how significant this move is and what it indicates, especially about the status of American bases throughout the region.

Meanwhile, American President Donald Trump has been expressing his outrage on social media in a new segment published by ‘60 Minutes’, which investigated Iranian attacks that resulted in casualties during the war. Despite the new owners of the programme, the company of Larry and David Ellison, having been accused of injecting pro-Trump bias, the leader is still not happy. In a rant posted to the ‘Truth Social’ platform, Trump claimed that only one Iranian missile and two drones had hit their targets and caused casualties, a statement that is demonstrably false.

In Yemen, the Ansarallah-led government forces have just taken over roughly 3,000 square kilometers of territory along the southern coast of the country, driving out Saudi-backed militant groups operating in the area. This adds to a larger offensive across the south that has resulted in the successful liberation of around 7,100 square kilometers of land in the Taiz and Lahij Provinces.

Saudi Arabia suffers set back after set back, lashing out against densely populated areas across Yemen and even launching airstrikes against their own proxy forces when they decided to retreat on the battlefield. ARAMCO oil targets also continue to take significant hits, putting enormous pressure on a nation that is almost entirely reliant on its oil revenue.

In this episode of The Target, Robert Inlakesh goes on a deep dive into the sectarianism pushed in order to sell Riyadh’s Yemen war narrative, while addressing the latest controversy that Syrian leadership are facing.

scraped.body_text:
The same Israeli military-intelligence Unit responsible for providing actionable targeting data that made the Gaza genocide possible is now directly supporting Saudi Arabia’s war effort against Yemen. Israel’s infamous Unit 9900 who built target banks for the IDF in Lebanon, Syria, Gaza, Iraq and Iran – are performing the same role for Riyadh.

Over the past week, airstrikes carried out across Yemen by the Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF) have increasingly targeted densely populated civilian centres. On Saturday, 44 civilians were killed in a Saudi double-tap attack that leveled homes in the village of al-Shariya, located within the Bani Hashish district of Yemen’s Capital City Sana’a. This followed another series of airstrikes that included the targeting of the Waziyah Marketplace in Yemen’s Taiz province – killing at least 30. The vast majority of the dead were women and children.

Despite a lack of international media coverage of the ongoing daily aerial bombardments, the atrocities have gained increasing attention on social media. However, it is less well known that Israel is playing a prominent role in the RSAF’s ongoing war efforts.

While previous reports confirmed that Israel was providing targeting support to the Saudi military, precise details were not released – that was until an Israel admitted the Unit directly tasked with performing the role.

Israel’s elite Unit 9900, a division under the IDF’s Intelligence Directorate (Aman), is directly responsible for providing the Saudi military with actionable targeting data, enabling Riyadh to develop a broad target bank to strike.

“Two main points need to be made about this. First, it serves Israel’s interests quite well because it wears down the military strength of an Israeli enemy that is preparing and planning to harm us in the future. In addition, we are monitoring and observing methods of operation and tactics, and learning a great deal from what is happening there, including about weapons that are not necessarily manufactured by the Houthis,” an Israeli military official informed the Jerusalem Post.

Unit 9900 is the sister division of the infamous Unit 8200, specifically performing the role of utilising satellites, manned-aircraft and drone reconnaissance data to generate detailed 3D topographic models and terrain overlays. These models can be directly loaded by Saudi airforce pilots into aircraft navigators, just as the Israeli airforce does.

Israel’s Unit 9900 also serves to provide precise coordinates for strikes, allowing for the IDF to strike targets in locations like Gaza, Lebanon, West Bank, Syria, Iraq, Iran and previously also in Yemen. Now it is performing the same role for Saudi Arabia, also gaining additional access to information to bolster its own target bank inside Yemeni territory too.

The Unit 9900 has also greatly contributed to the four major AI systems infamously used to commit the Gaza genocide, enabling targets to be chosen in less than a minute to strike, these being:

Unit 9900 is also notably a much smaller and specialised division than the more well known Unit 8200 (believed to employ between 5,000 to 10,000 people) – meaning that those Israeli military-intelligence operatives, who provide the Saudis with help to target sites across Yemen, are almost certainly the same individuals who provide data that leads to civilian massacres in Gaza.

This aid provided by Unit 9900 appears to have produced tangible results for the RSAF. Since Israel started supporting the air campaign against Yemen, there has been a dramatic increase in the total number of daily strikes carried out throughout the country.

For comparison, between March of 2015 and April of 2022 when the Saudi-Yemen ceasefire was announced, a total of 25,054 total air raids – comprising around 75,000 individual airstrikes – averaged around 10 total raids per day. scraped.h1: Coalition of California Prosecutors Move to Block Newsom’s Decision to Commute Every Death Sentence in the State
scraped.body_text:
A coalition of 28 district attorneys have filed a petition asking the California Supreme Court to block Governor Gavin Newsom’s deeply unpopular decision to commute the death sentences of 548 inmates to life in prison without parole.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF), a Sacramento-based crime victim advocacy group, reportedly organized the lawsuit, with the support of the California District Attorneys Association, the Peace Officers Research Association of California and several victims’ advocacy organizations.

Newsom announced on November 5 that he planned to commute every existing death sentence before leaving office, stating that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”

The prospect of a mass commutation for cold blooded murderers drew an immediate outcry from state law enforcement officials, as well as the victim families and victim advocates.

The lawsuit argues that Newsom abused his executive power by bypassing statutory requirements, such as providing notice to prosecutors and victims before acting. The challengers contend that the governor failed to conduct an individualized review of each case and that his blanket commutation disregards the will of California voters who have previously upheld the death penalty.

The petition seeks an immediate stay preventing Newsom and the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation from implementing the proposed commutations while the court considers the legal challenge.

It also asks the justices to declare invalid any commutations issued without compliance with the statutory procedures that the petitioners contend govern executive clemency.

“Only this Court can stop the Governor’s disregard of the law—his abuse of power,” the group wrote in its petition.

Newsom’s office maintains that he has the constitutional authority to grant clemency on his own initiative without prior notice, a stance that legal experts say will likely hold up. However, the commutations are not yet final, as the California Supreme Court must also approve the sentences for the 382 inmates convicted of multiple felonies, while the remaining 166 with single felony convictions can be commuted unilaterally by the governor.

The coalition includes Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman, Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho, Riverside County District Attorney Michael Hestrin, San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan and Kern County District Attorney Cynthia Zimmer.

The rest of the participating prosecutors represent Amador, Butte, Calaveras, El Dorado, Fresno, Kings, Lake, Madera, Merced, Modoc, Monterey, Placer, San Bernardino, San Luis Obispo, San Mateo, Shasta, Solano, Stanislaus, Sutter, Tehama, Tulare, Ventura and Yuba counties.

“We stand firmly with the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation in challenging this arbitrary commutation that sidelines victims’ families and disregards the will of California voters, juries and judges,” Hochman said in a Nov. 12 statement.

In a separate filing, Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer has submitted an amicus curiae brief challenging the governor’s proposed commutations of 382 of the death row killers, arguing their felony convictions require additional review by the California Supreme Court.

“Our criminal justice system does not bend with the political winds, and one man—even if he is the governor—does not get to put his thumb on the scales of justice simply because he does not like the law,” Spitzer said.

While Californians voted to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016 ballot measures, no one has been executed in the deep blue state since 2006.

The most notorious convicted killers currently on California’s death row include Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, dubbed the “Scorecard Killer” because he kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s.

“This lawsuit is about protecting the constitutional rights of victims, defending the rule of law, and ensuring that no Governor is above the law,” said CJLF head Anne Marie Schubert in a statement announcing the litigation.

“The Governor’s clemency power does not authorize mass commutations that disregard constitutional safeguards, legally required procedures, or victims’ rights,” Schubert, the former Sacramento County District Attorney, continued. “By predetermining the outcome for every inmate on death row, the Governor has abandoned his responsibility to exercise meaningful discretion.”

Newsom’s commutations, if allowed, will represent the largest mass clemency in American history and reduce the U.S. death row population by nearly 30 percent, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Debra Heine is a conservative Catholic mom of six and longtime political pundit. She has written for several conservative news websites over the years, including Breitbart and PJ Media.

scraped.h1: Census Bureau: Online Shopping Reaches All-Time Quarterly Record in Retail Sales
scraped.body_text:
Online shopping reached an all-time record of 17.9 percent of total U.S. retail sales during the third quarter of 2026, despite cooling growth, according to a U.S. Census Bureau Quarterly E-commerce sales report.

The Census Bureau announced Thursday that retail e-commerce sales rose 1.6 percent in the third quarter to $347.3 billion after seasonal adjustment, down from a revised 3.7 percent gain in the second quarter.

However, E-commerce still made up 17.9 percent of total retail sales, up from 17.8 percent in the second quarter and marking the highest share since Census began tracking it in 1999.

Retail e-commerce sales · Census Bureau Q3 2026 · released Thu Nov 19, 10:00 AM ET

HEADLINE: E-COMMERCE RETAIL SALES AS A PERCENT OF TOTAL SALES • Q3 17.90% • Q2 17.80% (revised from 17.10%) • Q3 2025 17.10% • Change +0.10 pt

IN THIS RELEASE • E-Commerce Retail Sales $347.3b, +$5.6b

REVISIONS (Q2) • E-Commerce Retail Sales $340.2b → $341.7b

VS ITS HISTORY • Highest on record (records go back to Q4 1999) • Up 6 quarters in a row • Above its 5-yr avg of 15.79% • Higher than 100% of quarters in 5 yrs • 5-yr range 13.70% to 17.80% • Pre-pandemic avg 8.75% (2015–19)

— Puget Point Capital (@PugetPointCap) November 19, 2026

Online sales were up 10.4 percent, compared with a year earlier, while total retail sales rose 1.1 percent from the second quarter to $1.94 trillion and were up 5.6 percent from a year ago.

The Census Bureau counts an order as e-commerce if it was placed online, although payment does not have to happen online.

According to Comtrex , the denominator is all retail, including cars, gasoline, and restaurants, categories that barely sell on Amazon or Walmart.

High-volume online categories globally, consistently include apparel and clothing, beauty and skincare, electronics and mobile accessories, home and kitchen organization, and everyday essentials/groceries.

The Census Bureau also revised its quarterly figures using its annual business survey, lowering earlier estimates of total retail sales, according to Breitbart.

Those revisions dropped the second-quarter growth rate for e-commerce to 3.7 percent from 3.8 percent.

items.title: Morning Greatness: Made in China, Swallowed in America
items.summary: Chinese companies will “box out” U.S. competitors and leave American patients exposed if Beijing cuts off treatments. Source

scraped.title: Morning Greatness: Made in China, Swallowed in America › American Greatness
scraped.description: Chinese companies will “box out” U.S. competitors and leave American patients exposed if Beijing cuts off treatments.
scraped.h1: Morning Greatness: Made in China, Swallowed in America
scraped.body_text:
Good Friday morning.

Here is what’s on President Trump’s agenda today: 7:00 AM THE PRESIDENT participates in Executive Time 8:45 AM THE FIRST LADY participates in a live interview with Fox and Friends 9:30 AM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Policy Meeting 10:00 AM THE FIRST LADY participates in a live interview with Varney and Co. 12:00 PM THE PRESIDENT hosts a News Conference 1:00 PM THE PRESIDENT participates in Signing Time 3:30 PM THE PRESIDENT hosts a Reception 5:15 PM THE FIRST LADY participates in the All-American Christmas Tree Lighting and a live interview with The Five

Two minutes of hate:

On Thursday, Congress’s own National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology warned that China is working to control the drug supply chain from the factory floor all the way up to the lab bench. The commission reviewed 57 deals since 2023 between the 15 largest U.S. drugmakers and Chinese biotech firms. The up-front payments are rising. The deals are shifting from licensing a single drug to co-developing around a Chinese company’s entire discovery platform. Some deals simply funnel American investor money into Chinese startups.

The commission’s conclusion: if the trend continues, Chinese companies will “box out” U.S. competitors and leave American patients exposed if Beijing cuts off treatments.

Beijing has already written the plan down. In September, it published a pharmaceutical follow-on to its five-year plan that treats the industry as a national security priority. In October, it proposed restricting exports of its most advanced drug discovery technology. China isn’t hiding the goal.

We’ve seen this movie before. It was called COVID.

In March 2020, as the virus spread, the state-run Xinhua news agency floated the idea that China could restrict pharmaceutical exports and plunge America into “the mighty sea of coronavirus.” At the same time, American nurses were reusing masks and wrapping themselves in garbage bags because the factories that made our protective gear were in China. When Beijing decided its own needs came first, our hospitals waited.

As epidemiologist Michael Osterholm put it, “They wouldn’t even have to fire a shot.”

The danger isn’t only that China could shut the spigot. It’s what comes out of it.

In 2007 and 2008, contaminated heparin made in China killed at least 81 Americans . Someone had cut the blood thinner with a cheaper chemical that mimicked the real thing well enough to pass standard tests. When FDA inspectors finally reached the factory, they found serious manufacturing violations.

In 2018, the FDA recalled the blood pressure drug Valsartan after it was found contaminated with NDMA, a probable carcinogen. The tainted ingredient was traced to Zhejiang Huahai Pharmaceutical in China. It had been in American medicine cabinets for years, and no routine inspection caught it. As the FDA’s own Janet Woodcock admitted, the inspection field is “stretched.”

That’s the problem with oversight half a world away. American inspectors can’t walk into a Chinese plant the way they walk into one in Ohio. Foreign inspections are often announced in advance. During the pandemic, they nearly stopped altogether. We are trusting the quality control of a government that doesn’t let its own scientists speak freely.

The new biotech deals take that risk and move it upstream. It’s not just the cheap generics anymore. It’s the next cancer drug, the next breakthrough, the discovery itself. The commission’s earlier report imagined China withholding a cancer cure during a fight over Taiwan. The new analysis calls that scenario “fiction today,” and says the gap is closing.

Picture a war over Taiwan. Picture an American patient whose last good option was invented in Shanghai.

Drug companies have their reasons. Chinese trials run faster and cheaper, and shareholders like quick approvals. But a company’s quarterly earnings are not a national security strategy. Better to streamline U.S. drug approval process.

The administration is moving in the right direction. Treasury has proposed screening deals with Chinese biotech firms, and the White House wants production of 86 essential medicines brought home within 18 months. Congress should finish the job. Fund domestic manufacturing. Require real, unannounced inspections. Make American drugmakers prove that a deal with a Chinese partner doesn’t hand Beijing a veto over American medicine.

Next time, it won’t be masks.

scraped.body_text:
As outages hit across America, the hosts speculate that the president is taking revenge over the 'blue wave.'

When technology outages hit, apparently the first place “The View” hosts look for answers isn't a foreign adversary — it's President Donald Trump.

“You have all of these outages that are happening. You have all of these weird, like, are we getting hacked? Is this a foreign adversary? This seems weird. We’ve got all Microsoft and then the FAA ground stop and then all of these other companies," BlazeTV host Sara Gonzales begins.

“And so the worthless shrews over at 'The View,' well, they’ve come up with some of their own theories," she continues. "Whoopi Goldberg, to be precise. She is now speculating that this is an intentional act not from a foreign adversary like China or Iran, but actually from our very own president."

Goldberg suggests that Trump could be retaliating against Americans over the so-called “blue wave.”

“How long ago was the blue wave?” Goldberg asked.

- YouTube

“I’m just posing a question,” she added.

“The View” co-host Sunny Hostin then chimed in.

“Alyssa said something yesterday that really resonated with me. I think you said something like, ‘I just don’t trust the information that’s coming to me from the government’ … and I sort of started thinking about that last night, and I was like, the government is telling us actually it's not connected, but then when you dig down and you look into industry experts, they are saying that it isn’t a coincidence," she said.

"We are being asked to not believe the very things our eyes are seeing," she added.

“We are being gaslighted,” Joy Behar agreed.

“I love how they always call us right-wing conspiracy theory nut jobs and then they go out and spew this and have no self-awareness," Gonzales says. "They lack the self-awareness to understand that maybe the conspiracy theorists are you."

To enjoy more of Sara's no-holds-barred takes on news and culture, subscribe to BlazeTV — the largest multi-platform network of voices who love America, defend the Constitution, and live the American dream.

scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump held a press conference on Friday and laid out his post-midterm legislative agenda.

President Donald Trump held a lengthy press conference on Friday following his return from Asia and told reporters that voters are unhappy with how Republicans have treated him.

After summarizing forthcoming "super intelligence" policy as well as the many trade deals he struck while in Asia, Trump turned his ire on Senate Republicans. The president claimed that conservative voters were displeased with how he'd been treated by Congress' upper body and noted that he may have an easier time passing legislation with Democrats in charge.

'We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.'

"If I were on the ballot, it would have been a whole different story. But I wasn't on the ballot, and people thought that I was not treated well by the Republican Party 'cause they didn't get the things that I wanted passed," Trump said. "They couldn't get it through the Senate. But hopefully they will now — our military and all of the other things, air traffic control. We've got to get that."

Trump expressed tempered optimism when asked about working with Democrats in the new year, emphasizing his veto power while also slamming Senate Republicans for obstructing his agenda.

"They're gonna send things my way, and I'm gonna veto them. And then they're gonna send more things, and I'm gonna veto them," Trump said. "And they could go two years and one month 'cause that's what we have. ... But I think after a month or so, they're gonna send things, and I'm gonna say, 'I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.'"

"If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too," Trump emphasized.

President Trump doubled down on his criticism of congressional Republicans

"There are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with," Trump said, referencing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) in particular.

"But we had some Republicans — I think you can have some — there's a real possibility, because of the power of the veto, there's a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially in health care.

"I'm open to great health care. Now, can it be what they [Democrats] want? No," Trump said. "But it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great health care in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans."

Trump moved on to discussing the possibility of an immigration deal with congressional Democrats.

RELATED: Here's what Trump, Xi, and Putin agreed to in China

"Probably one of the earliest things that Democrats are gonna see me [about] are gonna be very hardworking people [migrants] that came in — in some cases years ago," Trump said. "And what are we gonna do? And they work well, and they work hard."

Trump more or less left it at that, but continued discussing Democrats and his relationship with their likely leadership .

"They want to talk to me about two things in particular: health care, because we can do something with health care together — maybe easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation," Trump said. "They want to talk to me about health care, and they want to talk to me about immigration."

"I think that [Rep. Hakeem Jeffries], I think he's smart, and I think [Sen. Chuck] Schumer's smart," Trump said. "They're all smart."

Trump called Jeffries "a street-wise guy."

Trump also reminded the audience that he launched Schumer's political career after the Minority Leader solicited a donation from him for his first run in New York.

"I gave Chuck Schumer's first contribution many years ago," Trump said. "He doesn't talk about that. ... I gave him $500. ... I was one of his backers."

scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: 'We're closing Rikers once and for all': Mamdani plan will end NYC's largest jail — but there's a catch
scraped.body_text:
NYC Mayor Mamdani claims to be closing down Rikers Island, but his plan actually keeps it open longer.

The socialist mayor of New York City has announced a plan to shut down the jail on Rikers Island "once and for all" — but the truth behind his proposal is far more complex.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) revealed the plan Friday in a video on social media alongside NYC Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards, who was once an inmate at Rikers.

'They will house thousands fewer New Yorkers, which will help correctional staff better protect those in custody.'

Mamdani has previously suggested that prisons should be shut down, but in this case his plan would actually keep Rikers open for another five years — despite an existing deadline , first set in 2019, to shut down the jail complex next year.

"We're closing Rikers once and for all," he posted to X Friday.

He called Rikers Island one of the "most violent" detention centers in the country and said his goal is to build "a city where we ask ourselves what a person needs, not just what they're accused of."

To replace Rikers, Mamdani said the city will open "four borough-based jails," beginning with the first in 2029 and the rest by 2032.

"These jails will be closer to public transit, so New Yorkers can reach family, legal counsel, and court faster," Richards added.

"They will house thousands fewer New Yorkers, which will help correctional staff better protect those in custody," Richards continued.

Mamdani claimed that the city will also provide "hundreds of therapeutic beds" to deal with cases of serious mental illness.

The plan will need to be approved by the New York City Council before implementation.

In a podcast interview from 2020, Mamdani seemingly agreed that prisons are "obsolete."

"I mean, what purpose do they serve, right?" Mamdani said at the time. "I think we have to ask ourselves that, which is that, you know, I think a lot of people who defend the carceral state, they defend the idea of it and the way it makes them feel."

RELATED: Mamdani-endorsed candidate deleted posts about seizing private property and abolishing police, prisons

The New York Post editorial board pointed out that the new borough jails are nowhere near close to being opened by the current shutdown deadline.

"His term (and maybe a second term, if he wins one) will end before all four 'borough-based' jails get built," the board wrote.

And because Mamdani's plan would involve only 4,100 inmate beds while Rikers could hold 6,650 inmates, "under state law the city can’t close Rikers even when (if) they are all built," according to the board.

According to the board, demands to close Rikers are just "fantasy" ideas from liberals who want to let all the dangerous and violent inmates inside "walk free."

"'Close Rikers' is a huge waste of time and money; the only way forward is to build new, modern jails on the same island as the old ones," the board argued.

Carlos Garcia

items.title: For trans liberation, our horizon must be beyond the ‘Blue Tsunami’
items.summary: We have a duty to defend all oppressed groups under attack, most especially when it is unpopular, and to challenge that bigoted ideology tooth and nail.

scraped.title: For trans liberation, our horizon must be beyond the ‘Blue Tsunami’
scraped.description: The Democrats’ victory in the Nov. 3 midterm elections was dramatic. They swept into majorities in both houses of Congress, took several key state gov
scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: For trans liberation, our horizon must be beyond the ‘Blue Tsunami’
scraped.body_text:
The Democrats’ victory in the Nov. 3 midterm elections was dramatic. They swept into majorities in both houses of Congress, took several key state governorships and handed a stunning rebuke to the hateful, warmongering, pro-billionaire program of Donald Trump. A dozen transgender candidates won their state legislative races too, including in “deep red” states like Mississippi, Florida and Montana; and Rep. Sarah McBride (D-DE), the only trans lawmaker in Congress, successfully defended her seat in a legislative body where she isn’t even allowed to use the bathroom of her gender.

In spite of the far right’s attempts to suppress the vote, stir up hatred against minority groups and divide the working class against itself, the working people of this country are primarily concerned about the material issues that determine their lives. The gulf between the U.S. working class and the capitalist class was put on display for the world to see.

The Republicans campaigned heavily on anti-trans hatred: more than $400 million was spent on anti-trans ads, with billionaire and trillionaire backers like Elon Musk and Miriam Adelson pouring money into backing anti-trans Republican candidates and demonizing their opponents for supporting trans rights. From the White House, Trump hurled anti-trans slurs at cisgender (that is, non-trans) candidates, mirroring the way he has used “Palestinian” as an insult against his adversaries.

Yet in the same election, even in some of the same states that elected transgender lawmakers, voters approved popular referenda that restricted trans rights. Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state all banned trans youth athletes from participating in sports of their gender, and Colorado voters also chose to ban medical professionals from providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth.

This unexpected conservative victory has put wind in the sails of anti-trans bigots, perhaps because they happened in more liberal states. “We hope to pass these measures in more states and legislatures, and, where available, on state ballots as well,” Craig DeRoche, president and CEO of the anti-LGBTQ Family Policy Alliance, told MS NOW now a week after the election. He and others told the outlet they intended to target states like California, where Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, has also indicated his support for restricting trans rights.

Despite the triumphal rhetoric about “Woke 3.0” that came with the Democrats’ midterm victory, the Democratic Party has increasingly shown its willingness to compromise on the question of trans rights.

Thirty-two candidates backed by the Democratic Party in the recent election espoused anti-trans rhetoric in their campaigns, including high-profile winners like Texas Senator-elect James Talarcio. While Talarico rhetorically rejected the demonization of trans people and attacks on their rights, he also told Fox News he supported anti-trans athlete bans on issues of “fairness” — an unnecessary concession to discrimination that accepts the false premise that trans women athletes pose a danger to cisgender women athletes and to the integrity of women’s sports.

Other examples include Josh Turek, the Democrats’ nominee for U.S. Senate in Iowa, who said in an ad that he’s “against taxpayers paying for sex changes.” Rep. Marcy Kaptur, who has represented Ohio’s 9th Congressional District since 1982, declared in a September TV ad : “I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of schools.” Reps. Kathy Castor (D-FL), Henry Cuellar (D-TX) and Vicente Gonzalez Jr. (D-TX) also either voted for anti-trans bills in recent years or ran explicitly against trans rights in their reelection campaigns.

Democrat Nancy Lacore, who won her race for South Carolina’s First Congressional District, proudly declared she would “protect girls’ sports” on the campaign trail. The Congressional Democratic Caucus happily paid for ads carrying this message as well as those of Rep. Kaptur and others.

What does it mean for transgender people, whose existence the Trump administration has declared to be a form of extremism , to see our rights being attacked in the same way by the very people who claim to be challenging Trump’s political regime?

This shift by the Democrats is not new: for years, Liberation News has documented this steady betrayal of their claimed commitments to defend trans rights. The Democratic Party only added trans people to their national platform in 2016 after decades of waffling on the issue, and only after LGBTQ acceptance had already been on an upward trajectory for quite some time. Since then, there has been a concentrated anti-trans crusade by the far right that the Democrats have by and large failed to rise and meet in defense of trans lives.

Steady pressure from below, as grassroots activists confronted anti-LGBTQ prejudices in U.S. society and got pro-LGBTQ measures passed in cities and states across the country, compelled the Democrats to adopt positions in favor of LGBTQ rights on a national level. Still, their behavior often told a different story: in 2006, the Democrats won majorities in both houses of Congress, and the following year moved to pass the Employment Non-Discrimination Act (ENDA). This bill would have banned employment discrimination against LGBTQ people.

However, aware that bigotry against transgender people was still much stronger than against gay, lesbian and bisexual people, Democratic lawmakers separated ENDA into two bills: one for LGB people and another just for transgender people, hoping that by throwing trans people under the bus, the bill would become more palatable to other lawmakers. In the end neither bill passed, and trans people learned a painful lesson about just how far the Democratic Party’s loyalty went.

As of November, neither ENDA nor its successor bill, the Equality Act , have been passed despite multiple Democratic majorities in Congress. When Marriage Equality became the law of the land in 2015, it was through a U.S. Supreme Court ruling, not legislation. The Respect for Marriage Act was signed into law in 2022, but this fell short of truly codifying marriage equality in U.S. law. Instead, it repealed the anti-LGBTQ Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) and it requires the U.S. government and U.S. states and territories to respect the validity of legal marriages without making them legal itself.

The Republicans have always been hostile to LGBTQ rights, but after the gains made in 2015-2016, far-right forces launched a new effort to halt the growing acceptance of LGBTQ people. The first shot was North Carolina’s SB2, the first of the modern “bathroom bans” against trans people, which was passed in 2016, but by 2017 massive popular resistance to the law, including a devastating boycott that cost the state economy billions of dollars, forced the North Carolina legislature to repeal it. Trump’s first presidential term, from 2017-2021, saw major attacks on trans rights, and after Joe Biden became president in 2021, only a few of those were somewhat reversed by executive order – again, no permanent legislation enshrining LGBTQ rights into law.

After Trump’s 2024 presidential election victory, elements of the Democratic Party began to more openly fracture on the issue, blaming “pronouns” and supposed over-militancy on trans rights for the election loss. But we have never accepted their claim that the electorate “swung to the right,” or the faulty logic that our politics must only ever reflect what seems to be popular at the moment. We have a duty to defend all oppressed groups under attack, most especially when it is unpopular, and to challenge that bigoted ideology tooth and nail.

There is a sign that the anti-trans propaganda is still having an effect on our class and must be fought. Colorado now has an incoming state legislature with a Democrat majority: they must vote to repeal Proposition 134 and 135 immediately! Proposition 134 bans transgender athletes from competing on sports teams of their gender, and Proposition 135 bans doctors from performing gender-affirming surgeries on trans youth under the age of 18, and bans federal health programs like Medicaid from covering such procedures. Such surgeries are exceedingly rare, but the issue has been used by anti-trans activists as a wedge to justify such bans against adults receiving those procedures, and to unfairly demonize trans rights advocates as supposedly “preying” on vulnerable youth.

Wherever such a bill or amendment is proposed, we must organize the masses against it, and make clear to them the harmful and divisive nature of the attack not just against trans people, but against the entire working class. The same bigots pushing these bans against trans people are also cutting their pensions, enabling the construction of AI data centers in their communities and giving billions to a war machine that is driving up the costs of living.

These harmful ideas are fueled by persistent misinformation as well as pseudo-scientific claims about biology – attitudes that run deep in capitalist ideology and the consciousness of the working class thanks to lifelong exposure to sexist propaganda. It will take a concerted educational campaign to confront these attitudes, show their harmful and mistaken nature, and truly pull them up by the root.

As a counter to the overt attacks on trans peoples’ access to healthcare, an increasing number of pro-trans Democratic candidates and figures have begun to adopt a libertarian, government-hands-off position.

Sam Forstag, a Democrat who won his congressional race in western Montana, summarized this position in a debate last month when he said “government has no business sticking its nose into our personal lives. Whether that’s a gun safe, whether that’s a doctor’s office. I don’t want a politician anywhere near it.” A similar comment came from Abdul El-Sayed, who won his U.S. Senate race in Michigan. In October, he said in a debate: “I don’t think the government gets to have a say about what health care is provided in what circumstances and why.”

To be clear, El-Sayed and Forstag defended trans rights within the framework afforded by the capitalist system. However, both candidates are wrong: the government should be deeply invested in whether or not trans people get the medical care they need. The privatized, for-profit capitalist health care industry is not any more neutral than the rest of the capitalist system: it is anti-trans and anti-worker. Only a socialist state that has nationalized and socialized the health care industry, placing it in the hands of the working class and turning it into a public service freely available to all who need it, can guarantee that everybody is able to get the care they need.

This means the government must militantly confront anti-trans prejudices in the industry and across all of our society — something that will never happen while the billionaire class remains in charge.

Everything about the capitalist system is built for one purpose only: for the capitalist class to extract maximum profits, cut its costs and make a tiny group of people filthy rich while leaving the rest of us struggling to survive. The entire working class gets the short end of this deal because we own nothing but our own capacity to labor – for specially-oppressed and marginalized groups like trans people, that’s even more true.

Patriarchy undergirds the entire system of capitalist production: by dividing humanity along purportedly biological lines into producers and reproducers, and secluding responsibility for reproductive labor inside the family and the home, the costs of daily and generational reproduction are effectively privatized and the burden placed on the shoulders of women. This system doesn’t just justify the exploitation of women, it also constrains LGBTQ expression by demonizing us as “unnatural,” violating the falsely-claimed scientific basis of women’s inferiority.

On these principles, the Democrats and Republicans fundamentally agree, because they are nothing more than two political factions that serve the interests of the same capitalist class. Thus, neither party can ever truly deliver trans liberation or the liberation of any oppressed group.

Even before the far-right launched its anti-trans crusade during Trump’s first presidential term, rolling back the few protections trans people had won through decades of struggle, the situation for trans people in this country was dire. Dozens of trans people were murdered every year, poverty, homelessness, and survival sex work were common features of life, and the fact that trans people even existed was itself a punchline. Gender-affirming care was only obtainable on either the black market or through bigoted, gatekeeping doctors, who relied on narrow diagnoses of mental illness before prescribing trans people medication that wouldn’t even be covered by health insurance.

Decades of struggle by trans people and our allies resulted in the removal of Gender Identity Disorder from the DSM-5, the expansion of medical access and even anti-discrimination protections, and the steadily growing acceptance of the idea of trans equality among the working class. For nearly all of this fight, the Democratic Party was not our ally, but our enemy. The first victories for LGBTQ protections came not through them, but through our labor unions – that is, from the solidarity struggles of the working class against all forms of attack by the bosses.

Without converting political power into permanent seizure of control from the ruling class, transgender workers can scarcely expect more than these conditions of deep exploitation and abuse. Only with the working class in charge can we shut down the bigots and the exploiters and begin to pull up this oppression by the roots, and guarantee an end to the persecution of trans people and all workers forever.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: What’s really behind the Jensen Huang scandal?
scraped.body_text:
Last week, after more than 30 years as CEO, Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, the $3.8 trillion chip manufacturer he co-founded in 1993 and second biggest company in the world. Huang’s resignation follows reports of an extramarital affair with an alleged “Chinese spy.” But is this the real scandal or just a distraction from what’s happening behind the scenes?

How are Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Huang’s tech rivals and China hawks in the U.S. government using Jensen Huang’s affair to escalate the confrontation with China?

Who benefits from Huang’s resignation?

For several years, Jensen Huang has advocated for Nvidia to be able to sell chips to China as a means of keeping them reliant on U.S. technology, warning that otherwise China would develop its own advanced chip industry. On the other side of this debate are Huang’s tech oligarch rivals, Dario Amodei (Anthropic CEO) and Sam Altman (OpenAI CEO), who are fighting for tighter export restrictions in an attempt to monopolize the global AI industry. Amodei and Altman also strongly oppose Huang’s advocacy for open-source models, which would be good for his chip business, but threatens to ruin theirs — since their business model relies on charging customers for API access and subscriptions.

Amodei and Altman’s views are amplified by the “China hawks” in both parties of the U.S. government, who will do anything to slow China’s economic rise. Rubio went so far as to personally rewrite a CIA memo about the Nvidia CEO’s affair in “more assertive” terms to insinuate a Chinese plot to loosen U.S. policy on chip exports. But it’s not just Republicans — this was a cornerstone of the Biden policy too.

What now?

Anthropic has been a consistent advocate for three bipartisan chip export control bills that target Nvidia. On the same day that Huang resigned from Nvidia, OpenAI also threw its weight behind the bills. As they continue to gain momentum, it is becoming increasingly likely that these bills make it into the annual defense package.

Jensen Huang, one of the few moderating voices from the billionaire class on U.S.-China relations, is out. The hawks and their tech oligarch allies, thanks to a conveniently timed New York Times article using anonymous intelligence sources, are better positioned to execute their anti-China and pro-monopoly agenda.

What does all this mean for working people? Even as Washington conducts diplomacy with China, with all the pageantry and appearance of good relations, the U.S. ruling class — including the AI tycoons and military-industrial complex — have set the country on a collision course with China, towards “great power conflict.” That path is one of war, climate catastrophe, economic crisis and massive job destruction.

We must fight for a different future — the survival of humanity and the planet depend on it!

items.title: Interview with the Communist Party of Turkey: “We reclaim the republic stolen from us” – for a Republic of the Working People
