scraped.author: Jasper S
scraped.h1: Interview with the Communist Party of Turkey: “We reclaim the republic stolen from us” – for a Republic of the Working People
scraped.body_text:
The following is a Liberation News interview with Gözde Kök, a member of the Party Council of the Communist Party of Turkey (TKP), on the current political situation in Turkey as well as the ongoing mobilizations in Europe.

1. In your recent statement marking the 103rd anniversary of the Republic, the TKP argued that the Republic was “stolen” by monopolies and that its destruction cannot be halted by looking to imperialist powers or bourgeois opposition. How does the party analyze the specific class character of this “theft”? Why does the TKP insist that no political force operating within the capitalist framework can serve as a genuine alternative to the ruling AKP?

We cannot explain the dismantling of the Republic’s achievements solely in terms of the ideological preferences of the AKP government, as many tend to do. For a long time, the capitalist class in Turkey has been eroding the Republic’s historical achievements, such as public ownership, secularism and independence, in line with its own interests. The AKP government has brought this process to its logical conclusion. Apart from its particular ideological characteristics, what fundamentally distinguishes the AKP from previous governments is its remarkable “success” in transferring public assets to capital through privatizations, stripping working people of their rights, restructuring all state institutions according to the needs of capital, and pursuing neo-Ottomanist expansionism in concert with imperialism.

This is why our party emphasizes, first and foremost, the class basis of the dismantling of the Republic. We argue that no genuine alternative to the AKP can emerge within the limits of the capitalist system, because all political actors within this system seek to preserve the rule of capital. Precisely because the interests of capital weighed heavily in favour of keeping the AKP in power for years, the AKP was able to carry out its transformation of Turkey without encountering serious resistance from the opposition parties of the existing system. Conversely, in the course of the political transformation it undertook in accordance with the needs of capital, the AKP also transformed the opposition. It made all parties resemble itself. There can be no return to the conditions that existed before the transformation carried out under the AKP. Overcoming this transformation is possible only if working people take political power and the country is rebuilt on a socialist basis.

2. Following mass marches across Ankara, İstanbul, and İzmir on the anniversary of the foundation of the Republic, held under the banner “We reclaim the republic stolen from us,” the TKP called for a renewed “Republic of the Working People.” What does this vision entail in concrete political and economic terms, and how is the party working to build class unity on the ground—especially given that mainstream opposition parties like the CHP or Kurdish opposition remain tied to NATO and capital?

The republic of the working people is a socialist republic in which private ownership of the means of production and the domination of monopolies have been brought to an end, the economy is planned according to social needs, and secularism, independence and the equality of citizens are guaranteed. We do not regard this goal merely as a programme for the future. Through our organizing efforts in factories, workplaces, neighbourhoods, high schools and universities today, we are struggling to make working people an independent political force. The unity of the working class can be built on the basis of the common interests of working people of different identities against the capitalist system.

Today, if you travel across Turkey from east to west, from the largest cities to small towns and villages, you encounter one reality everywhere: the poverty of working people has reached levels unprecedented in the history of the Republic. Not long ago, workers lost their lives in a horrific workplace killing at the HABAŞ iron and steel plant in İzmir. Unfortunately, this kind of violence has become commonplace in Turkey. The cry of an elderly Anatolian woman who lost a relative at this factory shows that working people are beginning to see more clearly the causes of the conditions to which they have been reduced. She cried out: “Save us from the rich! Enough of the rule of the holding companies!” There is absolutely no possibility that the CHP or the Kurdish nationalist movement, within their present political limits and intentions, can offer a genuine response to this cry. We are working to ensure that the illusions they have created disappear more rapidly. For years, they have kept society waiting by promising solutions through the ballot box. Under the present circumstances, it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to continue doing so.

3. Turkey has seen intensified pressure at the hands of the ruling AKP against the social-democratic opposition, including the removal and jailing of elected mayors, judicial pressure on the CHP, and the emergence of new political formations like “Yeni Parti.” How does the TKP evaluate these developments, and what do they reveal about both the ruling bloc’s tactics and the crisis within the bourgeois opposition?

The AKP government’s attacks on elected mayors and opposition parties are the latest examples of its use of the state apparatus to sideline its political rivals. We oppose these attacks primarily because they are aimed at depriving the people of their right to vote and to stand for election. At the same time, it would be wrong to reduce the political crisis in Turkey to a struggle between the government and the opposition. The AKP has been in power for a long time and has made considerable progress with its pro-capital project of destruction. In doing so, however, it has triggered a major social crisis and failed to win over a substantial section of society to its project. Although attempts have been made in various ways to absorb the anti-AKP energy emerging in society within the political sphere, the reflexes of a significant part of society to defend the old republican regime remain strong. As the AKP struggles to bring its counter-revolutionary programme to a conclusion, its own support base is also losing enthusiasm. It is worth noting that a considerable section of the AKP’s social base is among those hit by growing poverty. Add to this the vast and tangled network of interests and plunder that has developed over nearly 25 years of AKP rule, and the internal power struggles it has generated. The recent investment fund fraud scandal has offered a particularly revealing glimpse into this network.

For some time, this situation had accelerated the capitalist class’s search for an alternative to the AKP, and political actors aspiring to take power in the post-AKP period began to emerge. While the AKP tries to convince the ruling circles that it remains the best party for capital and that there is no alternative to it, mounting domestic and external pressures have led it to wield the state’s coercive power against its opponents with increasing frequency and intensity, largely without a coherent strategy and with an increasingly disoriented approach. Yet, as it uses these methods to neutralize political actors who already lack a serious programme and strategy and who have themselves been tainted by the decay in the bourgeois politics, the conflicts and disintegration within the AKP itself have intensified enormously, both in their severity and their pace.

4. The TKP has characterized recent attempts at a new Kurdish “solution” or “peace process” as a capital-driven initiative and a neo-Ottomanist design to reshape Turkey—and its foreign policy—along ethnic and religious lines. Which specific class forces are driving this effort, why does the party view an ethnic framing as a trap for working people, and what dangerous implications does this project hold for wider regional stability and anti-imperialist struggle in the Middle East?

The fact that the new “peace process” has, from the very beginning, been conducted through negotiations concealed from the public tells us a great deal about its class character. So does the fact that its content makes not the slightest reference to the problems of impoverished Kurds, while those involved persistently invoke the slogan of Kurdish-Turkish Islamic unity in an effort to categorize and divide the working people of this country along ethnic and religious lines. Added to this is the emphasis by both sides that the “brotherhood” to be achieved through this process will make Turkey stronger and greater. We can also add another element which, although seemingly more symbolic, is revealing: the prominence given to representatives of the wealthy Kurdish classes as negotiators. As your question suggests, this process has a regional background. It is impossible to consider the renewed peace process in Turkey independently of regional developments and plans. At the outset, the governing coalition spoke of strengthening unity at home against Israeli aggression. Both sides made statements about strengthening Turkey’s hand in the region, beyond its rivalry with Israel. The leader of the Kurdish nationalist movement, Öcalan, is promising his support to the Turkish government in pursuing its regional ambitions, amid a rivalry fuelled by both imperialist and regional powers. Yet we have already been experiencing the consequences of policies aimed at extending political, economic and military influence beyond Turkey’s borders for some time. Now, at a time when major wars with uncertain outcomes are continuing in the region, the kind of “strong Turkey” promised by the “peace process” could mean Turkey becoming directly involved in these ongoing armed conflicts, while leaving the country vulnerable to intervention by imperialist powers along the fault lines created by categorical divisions defined on ethnic and religious grounds.

5. The TKP warns that political processes grounded strictly in ethnic or religious identity risk further dividing working people. How does the party approach national and sectarian oppression in Turkey, and how do you fight for the democratic rights of Kurdish people while maintaining a unified, class-based revolutionary strategy?

We approach the Kurdish question on the basis of certain truths that, for us, are beyond dispute. First, the Kurdish question cannot be resolved within the limits of a capitalist system built on exploitation, inequality and injustice. The Kurdish question is, first and foremost, fundamentally a class question, and it can be resolved through the common struggle for equality and freedom waged by working people of different ethnic backgrounds living in Turkey. The TKP fights against the divisive practices that have accumulated throughout the history of the Republic, alienating Kurds from the country, as well as against the prejudices that have taken root in society. Both stand in the way of united action by working people.

Moreover, we are confident that, under conditions in which capitalism is overcome and the construction of a socialist system begins, we will be able to implement policies that recognize and develop cultural identities, drawing on historical experience and scientific evidence, and thereby strengthen the desire to live together. Strengthening class-based politics among the Kurdish population is the only way forward. And we can see that this path is open. Recently, strikes and resistance have been carried out with the support of TKP in workplaces employing predominantly Kurdish workers. These struggles, and the many Kurdish workers who joined the party through them, show us that this path is indeed open.

On European & International Movements

6. In your international analysis, the TKP observed that mass protests across Europe signal that “capitalism is stalled,” yet noted that spontaneous anger alone is not inherently anti-systemic. What lessons should the international communist movement draw from these uprisings, and how can spontaneous mass discontent be transformed into a conscious, organized struggle for socialism?

The significance of the mass protests in Europe for the international communist movement lies in the fact that they have emerged at a time when European imperialism is still in the early stages of its transition towards a new phase of rearmament and a war economy. What is also striking about these mobilizations is that class anger is coming to the fore, rather than the identity politics that liberal politics has sought to promote for years. There are important signs that class struggles could enter a new phase, drawing broad masses of working people into the struggle in ways that Europe’s ruling classes would certainly not welcome. There is also a serious possibility that such a class movement could turn against the war policies of European imperialism. However, we should not forget that the efforts of Europe’s ruling classes to frighten people and secure support for their security-oriented policies, first by invoking the threat of jihadist terrorism and now the threat of Russia, have found a certain degree of resonance in society. It would therefore be wrong to characterize the current protests as an anti-war or socialist movement at this stage. This wave of mobilization also offers an important opportunity for the left in Europe, which has long been under the influence of identity politics, to reorient itself towards class contradictions and for revolutionary forces to gain strength. Communists must therefore seize this opportunity to emerge from this process stronger both organizationally and politically, to link the concrete demands of working people with an organized struggle against imperialist rivalry and the capitalist order, and to transform anger directed at the existing system into the energy of struggle for a new social system, socialism.

items.title: Australian unions distance themselves from Labor in Victorian election
items.summary: The bureaucrats that are now refusing to endorse Labor have spent years ramming through the government’s cuts to real wages and conditions and suppressing workers’ opposition to its attacks.

scraped.title: Australian unions distance themselves from Labor in Victorian election
scraped.description: The bureaucrats that are now refusing to endorse Labor have spent years ramming through the government’s cuts to real wages and conditions and suppressing workers’ opposition to its attacks.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Amid mounting anger among workers over cuts to wages, jobs and public services, several Victorian unions have declared that they will not endorse Labor in the November 28 state election and are withholding campaign funds and polling place volunteers.

Their supposed opposition to the increasingly hated Labor government is a complete fraud. None of these bureaucracies have any substantive differences with Labor or the political establishment as a whole. They have spent years ramming through the government’s cuts to real wages and conditions and suppressing workers’ opposition to Labor’s attacks.

The metaphor that inevitably comes to mind is of rats fleeing a sinking ship, though even rodents in such straits are far more decisive that the union officials.

Under conditions where the Labor government is despised in the working class, for having presided over the meltdown of public healthcare, education and other essential services, and for imposing the brunt of the cost-of-living crisis on ordinary people, the union officials have confined themselves to the most tepid statements.

The social impulse they are responding to, moreover, is from above, not from below. The frustrations of the bureaucrats dovetail with a sense in the corporate elite that Victorian Labor is a squeezed lemon, incapable of presiding over the massive austerity measures that are being demanded. It is discussed, not only in the corporate publications, but in the Labor Party itself, that the most likely outcome of the November election will be a massive defeat.

The unions engaged in the distancing operation are primarily focussing on Premier Ben Carroll, under conditions where such a defeat would almost certainly spell the end of his political career, leaving completely open the possibility of them hailing the next Labor leader.

At the same time, while the ruling elite is considering new mechanisms for attacking the working class, sections of the union bureaucracy are themselves considering new political patrons.

The United Firefighters Union (UFU) is running a prominent campaign, including newspaper and billboard advertising and manning polling booths, urging voters to “put Labor last,” and has openly promoted the far-right One Nation.

UFU Victorian Branch secretary Peter Marshall told Politico, “[One Nation’s Victorian leader] Warren Pickering has made some significant statements about firefighter safety—and we support those who support us.”

Marshall’s statement is obscene. One Nation is an extreme right-wing, anti-working class organisation. Aside from venomous attacks on immigrants, who constitute a major section of the working class, One Nation’s entire pitch is that it will completely gut regulations, boost business profits and lower wages. The idea that such a deregulation blitz will improve “safety” sounds like a sick joke.

One Nation is being promoted by sections of the ruling elite to intensify the attacks on the working class that have been spearheaded by Labor. The UFU’s turn to the far-right outfit is a warning that it is fully on board with such a stepped-up offensive.

It is a deepening of the union’s role in a protracted dispute, during which professional firefighters in Victoria have not had a pay increase since January 2021. In six years of enterprise bargaining, the state Labor government has refused to offer more than its sub-inflationary public sector wage rise cap. Moreover, they are working with an ageing, breakdown-prone fleet, two-thirds of which is past its service life.

For the first two years of this dispute, the UFU did not even permit a strike ballot. Instead, the bureaucracy conspired with management and the state Labor government to impose more than $200 million (according to the union’s own figures) worth of “efficiencies”—that is, cuts to firefighters’ conditions and entitlements.

When Labor still refused to offer a nominal pay rise over 2 percent per annum, firefighters twice voted overwhelmingly to strike, but the UFU bureaucracy prevented all but the most limited work bans and symbolic gestures.

In July 2023, the union went further and asked the Fair Work Commission (FWC) to declare the dispute “intractable,” barring all industrial action and placing workers in the hands of the anti-worker tribunal. More than three years later, firefighters are still waiting on the FWC.

The UFU’s campaign is the most open and overtly reactionary, but it is part of a broader shift. The Electrical Trades Union (ETU), which spent more than $1.6 million backing Labor in 2022, resolved on October 28 not to run a campaign this time.

The Australian Services Union (ASU) is running advertisements declaring “Ben lied. Labor lies” in Carroll’s seat and those of senior ministers, over the cap on council rates that it says holds down council workers’ pay.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU), the Australian Education Union (AEU) and the Health and Community Services Union (HACSU) have all said they will not campaign for Labor.

None of these organisations is putting forward an alternative. This is exemplified by the Victorian Trades Hall Council, which is telling voters to “put One Nation and the Liberals last”—directing workers’ votes back to Labor via preferences, while ostensibly distancing itself from the hated government.

The fact is that not only were the unions instrumental in getting the current Victorian Labor government elected—in 2022, the VTHC mobilised 700 volunteers to staff 76 polling booths for Labor—the bureaucracy is equally culpable for the deepening attack on workers’ wages and conditions, which could not have been imposed without its collaboration.

From 2021 until April 2023, Labor’s wages policy capped public sector pay rises at 1.5 percent a year, while inflation reached 7.8 percent. The cap was then raised to 3 percent, still well below the cost of living.

In 2022, the AEU struck a four-year schools agreement that lifted base pay by just 1 percent every six months, when inflation was already 5.1 percent. This year, after two statewide strikes, and two rejections by educators of AEU-endorsed deals, the union bureaucracy finally wore workers down and pushed through another sellout agreement.

The CPSU’s 2024 public service agreement delivered 3 percent a year, exactly the government’s cap. The union told members it had worked to “squeeze out the best possible outcome in the context of the government’s pay policy.” This cleared the way for Labor to slash some 1,000 public service jobs.

In public mental health, HACSU abandoned workers’ claim for rises of at least 5 percent a year and pushed through a 2025 agreement giving allied health workers 3 percent.

The sellouts continue, even as the bureaucrats attempt to distance themselves from the detested Labor government.

At a recent meeting of more than 1,000 council workers, the ASU bureaucracy used a rigged sequence of motions to pressure workers into abandoning their wage claim, forcing a re-vote of the three councils that refused and then celebrating the railroading on social media as “member-led union democracy.”

The opposition to Labor raised by the unions is explicitly conditional and limited in scope not just to Victoria, but to the premier as an individual. ASU Victorian secretary Tash Wark told the Guardian , “Nobody at the ASU wanted to be running ads against Labor MPs, and we don’t have to if the government does the right thing.”

CPSU Victorian secretary Jiselle Hanna said: “If Ben Carroll’s government won’t commit to no job cuts in the public service, then our union cannot support him,” as if the CPSU had not been facilitating Labor’s attacks on the public sector for years.

The unions’ refusal to campaign for Labor is entirely compatible with their continuing service as an industrial police force, enforcing the austerity agenda of big business and government, whichever party takes office after November 28.

This is because the unions are not workers’ organisations at all, but an arm of the capitalist state. They are led by a bureaucracy whose privileged existence depends on the suppression of the class struggle.

To the extent that these organisations are now distancing themselves from Labor, they are doing so to pull the wool over workers’ eyes, cover over their own flirty record of betrayal and, above all, to prevent the development of a struggle against Labor and the political establishment.

Contrary to the campaigns of the union bureaucrats, what workers in Victoria confront is not unique to Carroll or the state. The wage caps, job cuts and attacks on conditions are the program of the entire Australian ruling class. The Albanese government has pursued the same agenda federally—real wage cuts, the gutting of public services and the suppression of strikes—while integrating Australia ever more deeply into US-led war preparations.

Whatever the outcome, the election will resolve nothing for workers. Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all pledged to deepen the cuts to jobs, wages and social spending. Across Europe and around the world, workers confront the same combination of austerity, militarism and repression, and the same betrayal by the union and social-democratic apparatuses that claim to represent them. The struggles of Victorian teachers, health workers, firefighters and council workers are part of an emerging international movement of the working class.

The fight to build rank-and-file committees, independent of the union apparatus, is central to this struggle. These committees are the means by which workers break free of the bureaucracies that have suppressed their struggles and begin to formulate their own demands, share information and unite action across workplaces and industries. The building of such committees is inseparable from the building of a revolutionary party, armed with a socialist program and an international perspective, capable of uniting the struggles of workers in every industry and country and leading the working class in the fight for political power.

The SEP is standing candidates in this election—Morgan Peach and Peter Byrne in Northern Metropolitan—to advance that fight, for the international unity of the working class and the socialist reorganisation of society.

Attend the SEP’s final election meeting this Sunday, November 22, at 2:30 p.m., at the Djerring Flemington Hub in Flemington or via Zoom. The meeting will address the burning political issues excluded from the leaders’ debate. Register now!

Authorised by Cheryl Crisp for the Socialist Equality Party, Level 1/457-459 Elizabeth Street, Surry Hills, NSW, 2010, Australia.

items.title: Thousands of non-academic workers in Sri Lankan universities strike over government’s refusal to meet pay demands
items.summary: The one-day strike was part of a wave of struggles against the Dissanayake government’s IMF-driven austerity policies.

scraped.title: Thousands of non-academic workers in Sri Lankan universities strike over government’s refusal to meet pay demands
scraped.description: The one-day strike was part of a wave of struggles against the Dissanayake government’s IMF-driven austerity policies.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Tens of thousands of non-academic university workers across Sri Lanka held a one-day strike on November 18 to protest the government’s refusal to address their wage and other demands in its 2027 budget.

Presented to parliament on November 12, the third austerity budget since the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna/National People’s Power (JVP/NPP) came to power contains massive IMF-dictated spending cuts and pro-business restructuring. It offers no substantial across-the-board wage increase to compensate public-sector employees for the continuing erosion of their purchasing power.

Workers, who had been misled by trade union bureaucrats into expecting the budget to provide immediate relief from their worsening conditions, quickly took action following its presentation.

The Association of Public Service Engineers launched a nationwide work stoppage on November 13. The Irrigation Technical Assistants Association began industrial action on November 16. On November 17, the All Ceylon Disaster Relief Services Association decided to withdraw its members from all disaster relief duties, while the Government Veterinary Officers’ Association staged a stoppage with members collectively reporting sick. More protests by workers in other sectors are expected to follow.

On November 18, more than 1,000 non-academic workers from the universities of Moratuwa, Colombo, Sri Jayewardenepura and the Open University, all in the Colombo area, demonstrated outside the University Grants Commission. Similar actions, including picket lines, were reported at the Sabaragamuwa, Rajarata, Vavuniya, Eastern and South Eastern universities, paralysing the university system.

Protesters displayed placards and shouted slogans demanding: “Immediately increase the monthly compensation allowance,” “Fill vacant non-academic staff positions,” “Pay the slashed 20 percent allowance,” “Ensure a fair pension for all,” “Resolve salary anomalies” and “Protect workers’ rights.” The strike was called by the Joint Committee of University Trade Unions (JCUTU).

The JCUTU leaders, like the rest of the union bureaucracy, have repeatedly called limited protests over the past several years, including one shortly before the budget’s presentation, claiming that such pressure would compel the government to meet workers’ demands. The austerity budget has exposed the bankruptcy of these claims.

In July 2024, JCUTU leaders betrayed a courageous 75-day strike by non-academic workers across the universities, who were demanding a 15 percent wage increase and a 20 percent increase in the Monthly Compensation Allowance (MCA). The union promoted illusions in the promises made by an expert committee appointed by former president Ranil Wickremesinghe and later by the JVP/NPP government.

Despite none of these promises being fulfilled, the union leaders organised no protests for the next 18 months under the JVP/NPP government, which came to power in late 2024 backed by the unions. Their silence demonstrated their support for the government and its IMF-dictated program. Not a single trade union leader has raised opposition to the IMF program during the recent protests.

Despite the brutal austerity measures contained in the JVP/NPP’s budgets for 2025 and 2026, the union bureaucracy suppressed any protests by workers until early 2026, when they called a token lunch-hour protest over cuts to allowances. The union appealed for the resumption of talks with the government, which had broken down in September 2025.

Meanwhile, the unions all continued to describe the JVP/NPP government as “worker-friendly” and praised its meagre salary increases, which fell far short of compensating for the soaring cost of living.

Openly admitting that they had suppressed workers’ protests to help the JVP/NPP, Chanaka Rodrigo, a leader of the Executive Officers’ Union, stated that the 75-day strike in 2024 was “brought to an end because the government that was about to take office made promises to us.”

Speaking ahead of the November 18 strike, JCUTU co-chairperson Dhammika S. Priyantha said Prime Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake and Deputy Finance Minister Anil Jayantha Fernando had agreed during earlier discussions to address university employees’ grievances in the budget. Instead, he told the Aruna newspaper, the budget had “created further problems.”

Priyantha did not participate in the November 18 action, claiming that he was attending a discussion of the Public Sector Salary Anomalies Commission. Priyantha was among the union leaders who betrayed the 75-day strike in 2024 and worked hard to bring the JVP to power.

Ranga Meegoda, president of the Inter-University Trade Union Federation (IUTUF), declared following the November 18 protests that the unions would launch a “major struggle” to paralyse the university system and win workers’ demands from the government. In fact, the unions are seeking to contain workers’ anger and prevent them from launching a unified struggle based on an independent, socialist political program.

University workers cannot win their demands by appealing to pressuring the government, which is intensifying its attacks on the working class and accelerating the implementation of the IMF program.

Addressing a recent conference of the JVP-led trade union collective, the National Trade Union Centre (NTUC), President Dissanayake insisted that the proposed economic transformation required “breaking the old rust of the economy” and overcoming “old divisions and old attitudes.” He argued that existing laws that “obstruct the new transformation” must be amended.

The government is preparing a new “hire and fire” system that will dismantle even the limited legal protections workers currently have against arbitrary dismissal and attacks on their rights. This will facilitate the restructuring of state-owned enterprises and destruction of jobs.

The government also intends to make further cuts to social assistance, increase electricity tariffs and prices for fuel and other essential goods and services in line with IMF demands.

Dissanayake told the union delegates that they would be “the bearers of the burden of this transformation” and insisted that the trade union movement “must be transformed to suit the purpose.” In other words, the unions must enforce the government’s economic agenda and suppress resistance from the working class.

At the same time, the government is preparing to meet opposition from workers with new repressive laws. The Protection of the State from Terrorism Act and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill grant sweeping powers to the military and the police to harass, surveil and detain workers and criminalise strikes and protests.

Workers cannot defend their rights and win their demands through trade union bureaucracies that function as appendages of the capitalist government and international finance capital.

To wage a genuine struggle, the Socialist Equality Party (SEP) calls for the formation of action committees of university workers, students and academics. These rank-and-file committees must be independent of the trade union bureaucracy and all capitalist parties.

Such committees are essential not only to fight for workers’ legitimate demands but also to defend free education against government attacks and unite university employees with workers in every industry in a common struggle against austerity. This fight must be guided by a socialist program to put an end to the profit system and to reorganize society to meet human needs.

Get email updates on workers’ struggles and a global perspective from the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees.

items.title: Hillary Clinton demands escalation of US-NATO war against Russia
items.summary: Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state and the Democratic Party’s presidential candidate in 2016, on Thursday demanded that the Trump administration escalate the US-NATO war against Russia in Ukraine.

scraped.title: Hillary Clinton demands escalation of US-NATO war against Russia
scraped.description: Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state and the Democratic Party’s presidential candidate in 2016, on Thursday demanded that the Trump administration escalate the US-NATO war against Russia in Ukraine.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state and the Democratic Party’s presidential candidate in 2016, on Thursday demanded that the Trump administration escalate the US-NATO war against Russia in Ukraine. Clinton made the demand in a guest essay in the New York Times , published hours after US President Donald Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.

Clinton called on Trump to expand US support for Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia, a nuclear-armed state. “Another way to stop Mr. Putin’s ballistic missiles is to help Ukraine strike missile launch sites inside Russia,” Clinton wrote.

Clinton proposed that the Democrats use their majority to escalate the war against Russia. “In January, the new Congress should go further and pass additional support for Ukraine to help it win this war,” Clinton wrote.

Clinton called on Democrats to use Trump’s demand for a $1.5 trillion military budget—under conditions in which the Democratic Party supports an expansion of military spending—as “leverage” for an escalation of the US-NATO war against Russia. “Democrats are rightly working to use this leverage,” Clinton wrote. “They should also work with serious-minded Republicans to make winter support for Ukraine an additional condition of passage.”

The essay states the real content of the Democratic Party’s opposition to Trump. For 10 years, from Clinton’s 2016 campaign through Trump’s first impeachment to the present, the Democrats have criticized Trump from the right on foreign policy, and their central demand has been a more aggressive policy against Russia.

Clinton’s essay constitutes a set of marching orders to the Democratic Party. The Democrats intend to completely repudiate the outcome of the 2026 election, which showed widespread opposition to war, inequality and the domination of American society by the oligarchy.

The Democrats have made clear in a series of actions, including their sabotaging of the impeachment charges against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the nomination of right-wing House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker and their votes to advance a pro-corporate permitting bill gutting environmental regulations, that they agree with large portions of the administration’s domestic policies and its right to wage criminal wars of aggression all over the world.

At the Majority Democrats conference in Denver last week, attended by Jeffries and at least a dozen prospective Democratic presidential candidates, Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas urged his colleagues to work with Trump. “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” he said. Such an alliance will produce nothing but horrors for the American and world working class.

The Democrats have demonstrated that where they do differ from the administration—in demanding an ever more aggressive escalation against Russia as well as China—they will be absolutely ruthless in pursuit of their agenda. They intend to use the majority they obtained under false pretenses in the election, which was a popular repudiation of imperialist war, into a means of enabling the hated Trump administration to wage war all over the world, including with nuclear-armed states.

The only cost of the war against Iran that Clinton named was the depletion of the Patriot air defense missiles she wanted sent to Ukraine. “This problem is a lot harder to solve because the Trump administration has severely depleted America’s own stockpile of Patriots in its ill-fated war with Iran ...,” Clinton wrote.

On domestic policy the Democrats have no significant differences with the administration. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York voted three times between November 9 and November 18 to advance the permitting bill, demanded by Trump, that would exempt whole classes of projects from federal environmental review.

At the Munich Security Conference in Germany in February, Clinton said that Democratic presidents had deported more immigrants than Trump. “More people were deported under my husband and Barack Obama ... than were in the first Trump term or this first year of Trump’s second term,” Clinton said.

The Democrats’ demands are the latest stage in the decade-long escalation of the US-NATO war against Russia. The war began with the Maidan coup of February 2014, in which the United States backed the overthrow of Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych.

“We’ve invested over $5 billion to assist Ukraine in these and other goals that will ensure a secure and prosperous and democratic Ukraine,” Victoria Nuland, the assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian affairs, told a conference of the US-Ukraine Foundation in Washington on December 13, 2013.

Russia responded to the coup by annexing Crimea, and the United States began funding and equipping Ukraine’s armed forces. Clinton ran in 2016 on a program of escalating the war with Russia, a policy that was widely rejected by the population. At the second presidential debate, on October 9, 2016, the Democratic candidate called for a no-fly zone in Syria, where Russian warplanes were supporting the government.

That led to the election of Trump, and Clinton could not lead the escalation she had campaigned on. The Democrats attributed her defeat in part to Russian “meddling” and made the charge that Trump had colluded with Moscow the center of their opposition to the new president.

“Vladimir Putin himself directed the covert cyberattacks against our electoral system, against our democracy, apparently because he has a personal beef against me,” Clinton told donors on December 15, 2016, according to audio obtained and posted by the New York Times .

The Democrats used the allegations to demand a harder line against Moscow. Congress voted new sanctions on Russia in July 2017 by 419–3 in the House and 98–2 in the Senate.

On the eve of Trump’s meeting with Putin in Helsinki in July 2018, Clinton wrote on Twitter: “Question for President Trump as he meets Putin: Do you know which team you play for?”

Despite the Democrats’ accusations that he was a “Siberian candidate,” Trump massively intensified the arming of Ukraine. The Trump administration told Congress on March 1, 2018, that it would sell Ukraine 210 Javelin anti-tank missiles and 37 launchers, lethal weapons that the Obama administration had declined to supply.

“I gave you the Javelins to take out all those tanks. Obama gave you sheets” (medical supplies), Trump told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House on February 28, 2025.

Demanding an even further escalation, House Democrats impeached Trump on December 18, 2019, for withholding military aid from Ukraine in order to press Zelensky to announce an investigation of the activities of former Vice President Joe Biden and his son Hunter in Ukraine.

Democratic Representative Adam Schiff of California, who led the prosecution, told the Senate on January 22, 2020, that, “as one witness put it during our impeachment inquiry, the United States aids Ukraine and her people so that we can fight Russia over there and we don’t have to fight Russia here.”

This arming of Ukraine massively intensified under Biden. “The United States has committed $2.5 billion in support of Ukraine’s forces since 2014, including more than $400 million this year alone,” the White House said on September 1, 2021, announcing another $60 million in military aid that included Javelin missiles.

The conversion of Ukraine into a frontline state for a proxy war against Russia prompted the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Four days after the invasion, Clinton told MSNBC that “a very motivated and then funded and armed insurgency basically drove the Russians out of Afghanistan. ... But I think that is the model that people are now looking toward.”

Biden used Putin’s invasion to massively expand the arming of Ukraine against Russia. “We are going to support Ukraine as long as it takes,” Biden said at the NATO summit in Madrid on June 30, 2022.

During Biden’s presidency Congress voted $174.2 billion in five emergency bills between 2022 and 2024 in response to the invasion. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said on May 31, 2024, that Biden had approved Ukraine’s use of American weapons against Russian forces inside Russia, across the border from Kharkiv. In November 2024, Biden authorized Ukraine to fire American long-range missiles into Russia.

When the Democrats’ attacks on working-class living standards and their policies of global war, including the Gaza genocide, led to their defeat in 2024, Trump returned to office. Trump, despite his efforts to make the European powers bear the cost of the war, has continued the escalation against Russia.

On November 11, the top Democrats on the House and Senate armed services committees and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said of Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: “They and Trump are working for Putin, not for the benefit of the people of the United States.”

Clinton’s essay makes clear, once again, that the Democratic Party is a party of war and austerity, completely hostile to the interests of the working class. In the interests of intensifying the war against Russia and the trade war against China, both nuclear-armed states, the Democrats are perfectly willing to work with Trump in attacking fundamental social programs like Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security.

The Socialist Equality Party is organizing the working class in the fight for socialism: the reorganization of all of economic life to serve social needs, not private profit.

scraped.description: The campaign for the CUNY Fired Fourth continues, and so does our ongoing coverage of the fight to reinstate the fourth adjunct lecturer from Brooklyn College fired for her Palestine activism.
scraped.author: Olivia Wood
scraped.body_text:
The campaign for the CUNY Fired Fourth continues, and so does our ongoing coverage of the fight to reinstate the fourth adjunct lecturer from Brooklyn College fired for her Palestine activism.

Olivia Wood

Friday morning November 20, approximately 60 faculty, staff, students, and community allies at the City University of New York (CUNY) gathered in downtown Manhattan for a rally to support a colleague, known publicly as the Fired Fourth, during the second arbitration hearing of her case.

The Fired Four are four adjunct faculty members from Brooklyn College who were dismissed from their positions after attending a student-led campus protest for Palestine on May 8, 2025. Three of them have since been reinstated, and the Fourth — the only one who was “fired” instead of “non-reappointed” due to technicalities related to her summer employment — continues fighting for her job. She is represented in arbitration by her union, the Professional Staff Congress (PSC-CUNY, AFT Local 2334).

Click here to read more about the background of the Fired Four campaign.

The university is allowed to retract the firing and remove the Fourth’s name from the do-not-hire list at will. While the union lawyer is fighting for her reinstatement in the arbitration room, PSC members, CUNY students and alumni, and community allies are continuing to fight in the streets, demanding a settlement offer from the university to get the Fourth back into the classroom faster than the lengthy arbitration process.

In addition to the PSC president and the co-chair of the Brooklyn College chapter of the union, speakers at theoday’s rally included a student from John Jay College who is helping to organizing a Students for the Fired Fourth coalition, and Chenjerai Kumanyika, vice president of the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and professor of journalism at New York University (NYU).

The student speaker connected the struggle for the Fired Fourth to repression against other academic workers fighting for Palestinian liberation, anti-ICE activists like the Minnesota 15, the immigrants being terrorized by ICE, and the e-bike delivery drivers recently fired in New York by Amazon as part of the company’s campaign against the Delivery Protection Act. They also connected the Students for the Fired Fourth organizing to the powerful student movements that have rocked Europe this semester.

The outcome of this case has stakes for the fight against repression around the country. This includes other students and academic workers targeted for their Palestine activism, to those fired for other political reasons such as teaching about LGBTQ+ topics, attending socialist conferences, or criticizing Charlie Kirk, to the many activists facing criminal charges for organizing against ICE. It is a matter of academic freedom, but also a matter of protecting the right for everyone, both inside and outside of university settings, to speak out against oppression. Winning the Fourth’s job back is important, but it’s also important to build a strong movement around her, to build a culture of fighting back, a culture of collective resistance and solidarity.

scraped.description: A statement from the Youth of the Current for Permanent Revolution.
scraped.author: Youth of the Current for Permanent Revolution
scraped.body_text:
A statement from the Youth of the Current for Permanent Revolution.

Youth of the Current for Permanent Revolution

Across Europe, radical youth have surged onto the scene since early October, shattering capitalist normality and shaking up governments. From the revolutionary day of October 17 in France to Italy, and from Albania to Germany, Belgium, and Spain, we have joined thousands of other young people in the struggle for the most fundamental demands: decent conditions to study, and an end to mind-numbing discipline and academic pressure. We have taken a stand against racism and police violence, against budget cuts to public services, and against real estate speculation. Raising these issues in every country means confronting the central policy of European states and bourgeoisies: rearmament at a cost of hundreds of billions and the preparation of society for war.

Across borders, these struggles converge both because of the hatred and repression they provoke among our rulers and because of their common goals. Young people in Italy are calling for action “like in France”; in Germany, the tactics of blocking high schools and universities have been adopted from France and Italy. On November 20, at the call of a broad coalition of European organizations, young people in struggle across Europe are called to a youth strike against militarism, following the example of the German high school student mobilizations over the past year against the reintroduction of military service. This date must serve to show not only the face of a youth in struggle against its government but also that of a generation at war against an entire system.

For if our struggles are so subversive, it is because they are not limited to mere youth demands; they express a comprehensive anti-capitalist politicization and serve as the voice of anger throughout society. We have seen in Gaza what the weapons produced by the imperialist powers are used for, and we have seen how our governments support genocide and repress all those who dare to denounce it. In every country, we see governments attacking working conditions, forcing people to go to work while sick, raising the retirement age, and dismantling the eight-hour workday — all while bosses gorge themselves on dividends and public funds. It is to pay for war preparations, the bosses’ profits, and the cops who protect them that workers are killing themselves on the job just to barely fill up their cars or pay their rent — that hospitals and public transportation are collapsing, and our schools are falling into ruin. As our comrades in Germany sing, “The rich want war; the youth want a future.”

Faced with a capitalism in crisis that promises nothing but war and climate destruction, a future can only be won through a relentless struggle for socialist revolution — for the overthrow of the capitalist order and the building of a communist society. To achieve this, it is not enough merely to overthrow a government or overcome repression; we must overthrow the political and economic power of the capitalists, wrest control from them over the banks, industry, housing — in short, over the entire economy and the whole of society. The power to decide everything must return to those who keep this society running: the working people.

It is with this perspective in mind that, together with the youth organizations of the Permanent Revolution Current, we are fighting wherever we are to unite the struggles of the youth with those of the working class as a whole, so that the energy and radicalism of the youth can inspire the labor movement. In France, Italy, and Spain, the youth movement has already forced union leaderships to call for general strike days during the month of November. In Spain there had not been a joint strike by the major labor federations in 14 years; the outrage sparked by the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal — an 87-year-old driven from her home by real estate speculators — forced union leaderships to break out of their passivity.

These strikes marked the first convergence between the radicalism of the youth and hundreds of thousands of workers in the workplace. Nevertheless, the union bureaucracies have done everything in their power to prevent these strikes and are seeking to use them to negotiate crumbs with the governments. They are also determined to isolate the strike days to prevent the working class and the youth from organizing, developing ties, and going beyond their plans.

The union leaderships’ policy of class collaboration has sparked widespread debate within youth movements across Europe: Should we uncritically fall in line behind the union bureaucracies’ policy, or should we sever ties and demonstrate and fight separately? This debate is taking place on November 20 in Italy, in response to the CGIL’s call for a strike, but also in Germany, where Gen Z demonstrations will at times be separate from the Schulstreik (school strike) protests. It is also evident in France in the separation between the Saturday demonstrations — which seek to re-create the events of October 17 — and routine union strike days. The same was true in Spain during the November 11 strike, which some union bureaucrats even sought to frame as support for Sánchez’s socialist government.

This debate ultimately pits the masses against radicalism, as well as riotous protests against general strikes, and leads radicalized youth to turn away from unions and the workplace. Yet that is precisely where power lies in a capitalist society. As the Italian dockworkers and workers across Europe have shown, it is they who have the power to block arms shipments and paralyze the economy. A general strike is not merely a call for different sectors to go on strike; it is the primary political tool for paralyzing the ruling class and the economy and for inflicting a defeat on our governments and the bourgeoisie. That is why, as revolutionary communist youth organizations, we believe that mobilized youth have an immense responsibility to forge links with the labor movement — with both unionized and nonunionized workers — so that together we can overcome their leaderships, which seek to collaborate with the state and the bosses.

These links will not fall from the sky but must be consciously built through efforts at coordination and grassroots organization. To achieve this, we need activists organized in revolutionary parties within workplaces, neighborhoods, schools, and universities. Activists from the Permanent Revolution Current are working everywhere to develop solidarity between workers and students and to foster democratic coordination among the sectors engaged in struggle. Thus, in France, we have opened our universities to interprofessional assemblies bringing together union activists, college students, and high school students to give the strike days an active character. The same is true in Spain, where we have built united strike committees that have taken on the task of maintaining picket lines and carrying out blockades in solidarity with the strikers on November 11.

The union bureaucracies act as agents of capitalist policy within our class. They defend militarization as a source of jobs and pit workers against one another across national borders by defending “national” production alongside their countries’ bosses. The struggle against these bureaucracies is an essential task: neither bypassing them nor blindly following them — young people must bring their radicalism to the labor movement and fight alongside it.

This is the only way for the labor movement to assert itself as a class-based alternative in the face of the capitalist crisis. Otherwise, it will be the Far Right that capitalizes on the situation by relying on nationalism, its social demagoguery in response to the social attacks by traditional parties, and the sense of powerlessness in the face of the ruling class. Reformist parties propose moderate militarization and a few social concessions through illusory compromises with the bosses. They are the electoral counterpart of the union leaderships, and as such they promise nothing more than to continue the cycle of electorally co-opting struggles — a cycle that leads to demobilization and disillusionment, which in turn allows the international Far Right to thrive.

Building a powerful revolutionary movement is the only way today to halt the rise of the Far Right and the march toward war!

On November 20 and beyond, we will go on strike and take to the streets to fight militarization: Not a single euro, not a single life for their wars! We are fighting to end austerity cuts and to establish massive budgets for education and public services! To sever all ties between our educational institutions and the State of Israel and arms companies!

We are also fighting for a 400-euro wage increase for everyone and for the expropriation of arms manufacturers, major energy conglomerates, and real estate speculators.

This struggle can only succeed through the organization of a genuine general strike and the building of powerful revolutionary organizations. To defend this program and these perspectives, join the international struggle of the Permanent Revolution Current!

scraped.body_text:
This blessing for the youth — first given at a recent Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), Detroit Shabbat dinner– honors this historic season of struggle through international, anti-imperialist solidarity applied with revolutionary political strategy.

Rita Singer

Blessing the youth forms a traditional passageway into a day of rest for the Jewish holiday Shabbat, recited from the older generation to the younger. At this moment in the world, nothing could be more important than to gather our whole hearts and minds — all the generations of all countries — in enthusiastic support and critical connection with young people. For the world over , youth are rising up to demand a better life for themselves and future generations.

Blessings to the youth of Madagascar, Nepal, Bangladesh, Peru, Morocco, and Kenya , who shook the status quo and set the stage for uprising in recent seasons past.

The spearhead of advancement is France, where since October high schoolers have taken to the streets, first in the working-class suburbs of Paris, Black and Brown youth, demanding resources for their education: decent facilities, class sizes, and other basic material for a proper education. Bless the students of Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne and across the nation, for their boldness and courage. And for the students from wealthier, whiter schools, and university students, a blessing it was taking the streets in solidarity, declaring the necessity of equal access to proper education, not just for some but for all. In support and protection, the workers joined the students in struggle, the yellow vests and beyond, surrounding the students and locking arms to form a chain of protection . The massive mobilizations also overwhelmed the armed forces of the state — no small feat. In the midst of it all, the young people sing and dance in principled rebellion, further growing the organization of the movement, shaped by many struggles already in their young lives: the yellow vests, pension reform, rearmament, and of course, for Palestine to be free.

May the French students continue to build stronger and more coordinated self-organization, to join in assemblies to discuss and debate from the bottom up, and may the workers deepen their involvement with collective action and expansion of strike actions into a general strike capable of bending that old imperialist system.

In Albania the youth and workers are making a stand, initially against Trump and Kushner’s imperialist plan to expropriate land by one of Europe’s last wild river ecosystems for a fancy resort. How it has blossomed, into a student-led protest movement that has boldly disrupted government operations despite debilitating repression .

May the Albanian youth build stronger democratic self organization linked with worker power to make this movement transformational for the greater good of the planet and her people.

The youth in Germany are rising up against militarization, and the spirit of the French students infused German mobilizations around austerity and funding for education, amid rising fuel and living costs, constant repression over support for Palestine, and escalation of the climate catastrophe.

Bless the German youth for making these systemic connections , standing militantly against the violence of that old imperialist state at home and abroad, and bravely organizing for a better future. With wide support , may the young people self organize from below and may workers link in solidarity and support of democratic assemblies and grassroots democracy.

In Italy, the youth and workers have been showing the way, congealing in a general strike carrying the energy of last year’s “Blocchiamo Tutto/Block Everything” for Palestine, resurfacing in a massive youth climate strike and resistance to a racist cap on foreign students, against the Far Right, in resistance to militarism and austerity in an old power.

May the Italian youth and workers — especially the dock workers who shut down all the main ports in Italy and beyond in Europe, the US, even India — concentrate their forces by building resilient bodies of self-organization, linking in democratic class independence from the grassroots.

Spanish youth pull the housing crisis to the fore, tied to the movement of students and teachers to defend public education. Intergenerational solidarity with Maricarmen, a grandmother whose death following violent eviction spurred many thousands more to the streets, showed the housing and cost of living crisis demands standing strong against capital and militarism, against the vulture funds, banks, and speculators profiting while workers and youth face dire prospects.

May the youth and student unions, the labor movement, tenant unions, and neighborhood committees in the Spanish state march together, and make room for the differences among them to fuel principled discussion and debate in democratic assemblies and bodies of self-organization, holding the differences as important and worthwhile, unite so as to strike together with all their might .

In Portugal, Belgium, Serbia , and across Europe too, youth have taken the streets for housing justice, to defend education and democratic demands, and defy repression and austerity measures.

May the self organization from below in Portugal and Belgium link with the power of labor to prevail in defense of democratic freedoms against the forces of real estate speculation that harshen the prospects for future generations, all the lives of workers and oppressed. May the new balance of power in Serbia bring the self-organization from below needed to unify the democratic demands of students with the economic and social demands of workers, and leverage the methods of the working class to take the struggle forward with the political independence needed to fight corruption, organize workplaces, and socialize control of education and public services.

In the heart of European imperialism, radiate blessings upon the youth, who are rejecting the logic of capital and demanding material means for the seeds of liberation to grow.

And for the youth of every country on every continent injured at any time in Europe’s colonial history, may this season of revolt bring the rumblings of change to stoke over seasons ahead.

In Brazil, the youth were central among the masses who refused to allow the dominance of the Far Right to prevail, remaining critical of Lula given his capitulation to imperialism, while rising up in massive mobilization to defeat Bolsonaro, who fled the country in defeat. With assemblies at universities, this follows the hard fought defeat of the grueling 6-day work week .

May the Brazilian youth link with working sectors to form new prospects for democratic self organization to fight yankee imperialism and protect resources and democratic prospects for future generations.

In massive marches in Chile, students united to defend education from cuts and strengthen resistance to the Right.

May the Chilean student movement congeal bodies of self organization from below and link with the labor movement to form a new balance of power in defense of resources for education and broader needs.

Let us not forget the brave youth of India, whose creative resistance under the banner “ Cockroach ” forced Modi’s Far Right government to back down, challenged ingrained social hierarchies of sexism and the caste system, and waged a fundamental struggle for education and democratic rights. Despite authoritarian crackdown and violent repression, the Cockroach movement of Indian youth is a joy and inspiration that continues to make a way.

May the Indian youth build vast webs of self organization supported with working class power in this historic fight for freedom, a leading light for the region and beyond.

Youth in the United States searching for a political alternative to capitalism are rising up. College students mobilize against patriarchy and rape culture for survivors to feel safe and protected. High school students stage walk outs to denounce the racist murder of Nolan Wells and to make Black Lives Matter all the time, everywhere. They continue the movement for Palestinian liberation, despite persecution and repression. They fight against ICE tearing away their neighbors. Youth in the U.S. are rejecting the chauvinism and bigotry of the Right and are demanding space for the Left to grow liberatory alternatives, in the DSA and beyond, being drawn to socialism in vast swaths.

In the belly of the imperialist beast, bless the youth. May they build councils for democratic self organization to grow up in schools, communities, and workplaces. May U.S youth learn to struggle in the interest of and with the methods of the working class and oppressed.

To the youth of Palestine, blessings. The Palestinian youth, who are forced to show the greatest perseverance of life, instill in the youth of all countries courage for liberation. Joy amid suffering which words cannot convey; Palestinian youth, you are an untold treasure to our generation. We must mourn with all our hearts and souls the youth lost to genocide. A generation of youth, lives cut short. Heartfelt blessings to the generation of survivors, young psyches put through inhumane tragedy and bodies mangled, realities of rubble and certain violence in uncertain times.

For the Palestinian youth, we wish blessings upon blessings. For the youth of all countries must take responsibility to make Palestine free.

Blessings upon the dissenters, the refuzniks of Israel, who refuse military conscription, reject occupation and genocide, and the brave young artists who expose the violence of imperialist backed occupation and create solidarity in principled resistance.

To Israeli youth, may this movement break the grip of Zionism and nationalism on your generations to come with a Jewish-Arab workers movement that fights for socialism.

For any of us to be free, for today and future generations, across international borders, the workers and oppressed must stand strong and ready to strike with one fist — against imperialism, amid instability, for self organization from below to grow and democratically mold politically independent revolutionary organization by and for workers and oppressed.

May today’s youth planting seeds of liberation find the solidarity of workers the world over through self organization and democratic assemblies to protect and cultivate these seeds so that they bear the delicious fruits of freedom.

Europe

France

Students demonstrations

Pete Hegseth’s arrival in Caracas on November 18 shows the subjugation Venezuela has endured since the U.S. kidnapped President Nicolás Maduro on January 3. The Pentagon chief who led the incursion is consolidating U.S. control and plundering the nation’s wealth.

Milton D'León

Kast’s approval has fallen to 18 percent amid fuel hikes, soaring prices and unemployment, yet business leaders remain upbeat as banks, pension funds and arms firms profit. A truckers’ strike showed where the pressure to stop Finance Minister Quiroz’s plan could come from.

Antonio Paez

Striking garment workers did not limit themselves to the closing down of factories: tens of thousands occupied the streets in massive protests and blockaded many of the most important highways connecting the textile industrial hubs to the capital, Dhaka, as well as the main highway connecting Dhaka to Chittagong.

Sarah Micoski

The deployment of Salvadoran troops in Haiti marks a new phase of imperialist intervention in the Caribbean. Under the guise of fighting gangs, Bukele is exporting his repressive model and aligning himself with Washington’s strategy to militarize the region, deepening Haiti’s subordination.

Milton D'León and Sandra Romero

A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk isn’t what we would call “fun,” but Gibney’s film about the world’s richest man is an occasion for class rage.

Olivia Wood

Opening Cuba up to foreign investment and privatizing key sectors of the economy are not ways to advance toward socialism, but rather to retreat toward capitalism. Only working people — not the bureaucracy or imperialism — can guarantee Cuba's independence.

Sam Cadenas

Mamdani’s overhaul of the brutal police unit reflects a longstanding demand of New Yorkers, but the proposed changes merely give repression a new name.

James Dennis Hoff

To recapture the spirit of the October 17 mobilizations across France, workers must be drawn into the fight, bureaucracies bypassed from below, and cross-industry assemblies built to organize a general strike.

Leon Bengochea

scraped.title: Sault Tribe Citizens Approve Historic Three-Branch Government
scraped.description: Overview: Sault Tribe citizens have approved a historic constitutional amendment creating three independent branches of government designed to strengthen tribal sovereignty, accountability and transparency. Citizens of the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians have voted overwhelmingly to adopt an amended tribal constitution, marking a historic shift in how the tribe will govern itself. The […]
scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Sault Tribe Citizens Approve Historic Three-Branch Government
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Sault Tribe citizens have approved a historic constitutional amendment creating three independent branches of government designed to strengthen tribal sovereignty, accountability and transparency.

Citizens of the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians have voted overwhelmingly to adopt an amended tribal constitution, marking a historic shift in how the tribe will govern itself.

The results of the secretarial election, finalized Thursday evening, showed 2,697 votes in favor of the amended constitution and 990 opposed. The ballots were counted by the Secretarial Election Board at DreamMakers Theater at Kewadin Casino in Sault Ste. Marie.

The amended constitution establishes three separate, co-equal branches of tribal government: executive, legislative and judicial. Each branch will have distinct powers and responsibilities, creating a system of checks and balances designed to strengthen accountability, transparency and protections for tribal citizens.

The new constitution will take effect once the election results receive approval and certification from the Secretary of the Interior.

Under the new governmental structure, the legislative branch will be responsible for making laws, the executive branch will oversee government operations and implement those laws, and the judicial branch will interpret laws and resolve legal disputes.

Sault Tribe Chairman Austin Lowes called the vote a historic achievement following nearly two decades of advocacy by tribal citizens seeking greater separation of powers.

“This historic moment has been a long time coming,” Lowes said. “The overwhelming support for this amendment reflects something our citizens have understood for a long time — our government must be accountable to the people it serves.”

Your contribution is appreciated.

Lowes said the amendment will fundamentally change the relationship between citizens and their government by expanding individual rights, establishing meaningful checks and balances, and preventing any single branch from holding unchecked authority.

He described the constitutional change as a generational shift that will benefit tribal citizens for decades to come.

Tribal Court Chief Judge Caroline LaPorte also emphasized the importance of incorporating Anishinaabe teachings into the implementation of the new constitution, particularly the responsibility to one another and to the next seven generations.

LaPorte said the passage of the constitution creates an opportunity to strengthen tribal sovereignty while carrying forward the responsibilities of the Anishinaabe people.

She added that the judiciary recognizes the significant work ahead and will approach its responsibilities with humility, gratitude and respect for those who spent years advocating for constitutional change.

Director Tyler LaPlaunt, vice chairman of the Sault Tribe Board of Directors, highlighted the Anishinaabe concept of Gidinawendimin , meaning “we are all related,” in reflecting on the election results.

LaPlaunt said the decision represents an important step toward greater accountability, transparency and balance while honoring the tribe’s history and preparing for future generations.

He also pointed to provisions recognizing the Baaweting Anishinaabek of the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians and formally recognizing the Mackinac Band’s right to citizenship as important elements of the constitutional change.

Ahead of the election, the Sault Tribe Board of Directors approved a Constitutional Implementation Plan on Sept. 22 to guide the transition to the new governmental structure.

The plan establishes an 18-month timeline for updating tribal laws and creating the framework necessary to implement the three-branch system while maintaining government operations and services.

During the transition, current leadership, departments, programs, budgets and existing legal obligations generally will remain in place, subject to the amended constitution and applicable law.

The Sault Tribe adopted its original constitution in 1975, establishing the governmental framework that remained in place for decades. Under that structure, much of the tribe’s governing authority was concentrated within the Board of Directors.

Article X of the original constitution outlines the process for constitutional amendments, allowing the Board of Directors to initiate a secretarial election through an approved resolution.

Interest in establishing a government with a clearer separation of powers had been building among tribal citizens and board members for nearly 20 years.

In fall 2025, the Sault Tribe Election Commission mailed a survey to tribal citizens seeking input on the tribe’s governmental structure. A majority of respondents supported amending the constitution to establish separate, co-equal legislative, judicial and executive branches.

On May 19, 2026, the Board of Directors unanimously approved a resolution to begin the secretarial election process and submitted the proposed amended constitution to the Bureau of Indian Affairs for review.

The BIA subsequently worked with tribal representatives to administer the election, including voter registration, ballot distribution and tabulation.

Although tribal citizens have approved the amendment, the results remain subject to federal approval and certification before the new constitution can take effect.

Once certified, implementation will proceed under the amended constitution and the tribe’s 18-month implementation plan, providing time to update tribal laws and establish the new governmental structure.

The election marks a significant milestone in the Sault Tribe’s history, setting the stage for a new era of tribal governance built around shared authority, accountability and the long-term interests of its citizens.

For additional information about the secretarial election and constitutional amendment, visit saulttribe.com/government/secretarial-election .

The U.S. Senate late Thursday night, November 19, 2026, passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), legislation […]
scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Despite Strong Tribal Opposition, U.S. Senate Approves BAAJA in Late-Night Vote
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

The Senate's passage of BAAJA, despite strong opposition from Tribal Nations, advances sweeping permitting reforms that Tribal leaders warn could weaken Tribal consultation requirements and threaten protections for sacred sites and cultural resources.

The U.S. Senate late Thursday night, November 19, 2026, passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), legislation that Tribal leaders view as a major threat to Tribal sovereignty because, if enacted, it would weaken Tribal consultation requirements involving sacred sites and culturally significant places in Indian Country.

The Senate approved the legislation, S. 5653, by a vote of 62-33, sending it to the Republican-controlled House of Representatives for consideration.

Proponents say the legislation will accelerate the construction of energy infrastructure, modernize the nation’s electric grid and address rising electricity costs. It also includes provisions requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs associated with the electricity infrastructure needed to support their operations.

Your contribution is appreciated.

U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-CA), a member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources and Environment and Public Works Committees, issued the following statement after voting against the BAAJA:

“I have long supported commonsense permitting reform and this bill includes many provisions that I support and even authored, particularly to streamline the permitting of transmission infrastructure. Unfortunately, it also contains provisions that would irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized Tribes who call California home.

“The bill threatens Tribal sovereignty, and I am deeply concerned that it could allow the destruction of ancestral lands, sacred places, and cultural resources without adequate legal recourse for the communities that have relied on them for generations. It also asks us to rely on assurances from President Trump, who just weeks ago said he would not approve any wind projects – and lacks the enforceable safeguards to ensure renewable energy projects will be judged and approved fairly by the Trump Administration and that oil and gas drilling will not resume off the coast of California.

Much of the opposition from Indian Country centers on Division B, Title III, which would amend Section 106 of the Nation advancing sweeping changes to federal energy permitting and environmental review laws despite sustained opposition from tribal nations, environmental organizations and other critics.

The National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) has repeatedly called for the withdrawal of Title III, arguing that the legislation fails to adequately protect Tribal sovereignty and the government-to-government relationship between the United States and Tribal Nations.

Fourteen Democrats joined Republicans in voting for final passage, while 28 Democrats voted against it. Independent Sen. Angus King (Maine), who caucuses with Democrats, also voted yes.

The following 14 Democratic senators supported the legislation:

Independent voting YES:

– Angus King (Maine)

The legislation heads to the House of Representatives who are currently on Thanksgiving recess and are scheduled to return on Monday, November 30, 2026.

scraped.title: Heinrich Took Tribal, Energy Money while Negotiating a Bill that Threatens Sovereignty, Lands
scraped.description: Overview: Sen.
