Sen. Martin Heinrich is cosponsoring the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) […]
scraped.author: Suzette Brewer
scraped.h1: Heinrich Took Tribal, Energy Money while Negotiating a Bill that Threatens Sovereignty, Lands
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Sen. Martin Heinrich’s support for BAAJA has drawn criticism from Tribal Nations and state officials who say the legislation could weaken Tribal sovereignty, undermine historic-preservation protections, and impose costly consultation requirements despite his claims that the bill will improve the process.

Sen. Martin Heinrich is cosponsoring the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) as a way to lower energy costs and speed infrastructure projects. But critics—including tribal leaders, national organizations and a group of 17 state attorneys general—say its historic-preservation provisions could weaken sovereignty and burden the very offices responsible for consultation.

In a Nov. 17 press release , Heinrich said he had worked to incorporate feedback from Tribes and New Mexicans. He argued that the bill would improve consultation by requiring federal agencies to consult at multiple stages of the historic-preservation process. He also said faster permitting and grid connections could help lower electricity bills.

But tribal organizations say that his remarks amount to gaslighting and equivocation on his position regarding Title III, a provision that would cause a severe erosion of Tribal sovereignty and protections for their lands.

Your contribution is appreciated.

“Once again, Senator Martin Heinrich and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse are lying to Indian Country. Right now, the law ALREADY requires agencies to consult with Tribal Nations on all projects that affect Tribal lands, as well as ceded, ancestral, and aboriginal lands,” the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers said in a statement. “BAAJA would so severely restrict the types of projects, as well as the harms those projects might cause, on which Agencies must consult with Tribes, that it effectively eliminates consultation for most federal projects. Senator Heinrich is so desperate to sell BAAJA, he continues to play snake oil salesman, when he could have avoided this altogether if he had consulted with Tribes and listened to them in the first place.

Related by Suzette Brewer: Fast-Tracked BAAJA Puts Tribal Sovereignty, Lands at Risk

“Every single point he made [in the release] isn’t just bending the truth,” concurred a tribal policy analyst who requested anonymity to discuss the legislation. “It’s a flat-out lie.”

Campaign finance records, however, suggest Heinrich was soliciting both sides, accepting contributions from both energy interests and tribal governments as he continued working in secret to undermine Tribal sovereignty.

His filings list $120,500 in itemized contributions to Heinrich for Senate campaign through Sept. 30 from PACs and committees associated with energy, utilities, and renewable energy. This figure comes from reviewing organizations identified by name; it includes a $5,000 contribution from the Pattern Energy Group Inc. PAC as a PAC contribution.

A review of FEC filings also identified $80,400 in tribal contributions to Heinrich’s Senate campaign from Jan. 1, 2023, through Sept. 30, 2026, from 17 tribal entities from 11 states. That total includes $10,800 in 2025–26 contributions from the Chickasaw Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe and the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe.

Separately, the Heinrich Victory Fund reported $28,000 from seven tribal entities through Oct. 14, 2026. Together, the records show $108,400 in identified tribal contributions across the periods reviewed; the Victory Fund is a joint fundraising committee, and its receipts are not all retained by Heinrich’s campaign.

States’ Objections to BAAJA Gaining Steam

Objections to BAAJA’s provisions now extend beyond tribal organizations, drawing strong pushback from states as well. In a Nov. 9th letter to Senate leaders from 17 state attorneys general said the revised bill contains unfunded mandates that would add requirements and shorten deadlines for state and tribal historic-preservation programs while eliminating guaranteed funding.

Additionally, they argued that underfunded, understaffed offices could struggle to meet the new requirements, risking suspension of their funding and, in some cases, federal takeover of state programs. The attorneys general warned that the result could be more delay, not less.

The letter also said that the amendment to Section 106 restored mandatory consultation but left federal agencies broad discretion over key decisions, including whether adverse effects to historic resources could be outweighed by other considerations, which complicate Heinrich’s claim that the amendment’s consultation provisions resolve the central concerns.

“…[A]lthough we appreciate the constructive engagement over the past few weeks, we continue to have substantial concerns,” they wrote. “As detailed below, and among other defects, BAAJA would harm states’ and tribes’ abilities to protect water, historic, cultural, and natural resources under the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the Endangered Species Act, and would impinge on state and tribal sovereignty.”

In the meantime, Tribal opposition remains unequivocal. NCAI has called for Title III to be withdrawn, saying its proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act would undermine tribal sovereignty and strip protections for sacred sites. It says more than 70 Tribal Nations are represented among more than 215 entities whose letters, resolutions, statements and other materials oppose BAAJA and the proposed Section 106 changes.

Heinrich’s political records show money from energy interests and tribal governments. The accountability question is whether BAAJA’s consultation process gives tribes meaningful influence—and whether its preservation offices will have the resources to do the work the bill requires.

Tribal contributions to Heinrich’s committees should not be read as an endorsement of BAAJA or as a proxy for the views of other Nations.

scraped.title: Yukon court dismisses lawsuit against Whitehorse shelter operator
scraped.description: The Supreme Court of Yukon has dismissed a lawsuit against a Whitehorse shelter by a father whose daughter died there in 2023.
scraped.author: Sara Connors
scraped.h1: Yukon court dismisses wrongful death lawsuit against Whitehorse shelter operator
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Father of Josephine Hager ‘quite upset’ by the decision says lawyer.

The Supreme Court of Yukon has dismissed a wrongful death lawsuit against the operator of the Whitehorse emergency shelter.

Chief Justice Suzanne Duncan said in a Nov. 6 decision that the lawsuit was brought after the one-year limitation period under the Yukon’s Fatal Accidents Act.

Josephine Hager, 38, a Selkirk First Nation citizen, died at the shelter on Feb. 1, 2023. Her father, Dale Joe, filed the lawsuit last October.

An inquest in April 2024 heard that Hager, who lived in a supportive housing unit at the shelter, died from a lethal mix of morphine and alcohol.

The lawsuit claims Connective, the non-profit organization operating the shelter, and five unnamed staff members were negligent in Hager’s death.

However, Connective argued in an application that Joe, who filed the suit more than two years after his daughter’s death, missed the one-year deadline under the act.

According to the decision, Joe said he wasn’t aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death and its potential wrongful nature until shortly after the 2024 inquest, more than a year after she died.

The decision also notes that his mother and brother died within a year of each other, adding to his grief.

An affidavit from Selkirk Elder and former chief Lucy McGuinty also states that traditional Northern Tutchone laws prevent those who follow them from interfering with matters of the deceased until a headstone potlatch is held, which she said typically takes one to two years.

The decision also notes that other jurisdictions, such as Alberta and Saskatchewan, give courts some discretion to consider personal circumstances.

Connective, meanwhile, argued that the act stipulates that the limitation period begins on the date of death, regardless of a plaintiff’s knowledge of the matter.

The organization also argued that even if Joe’s argument were allowed to proceed, the lawsuit was still filed more than a year after he became aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death.

The organization further contended that Indigenous customs or traditions provide no legal basis to extend or eliminate limitation periods.

It also noted that a headstone potlatch had not yet been held for Hager or Joe’s brother, which it said contradicts McGuinty’s statement that cultural tradition requires a headstone potlatch before the deceased’s affairs may be addressed.

Duncan said there was merit to Joe’s argument that the one-year limitation could begin when he became aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death.

However, she found that nothing in Yukon’s act allows a plaintiff’s personal circumstances to be considered grounds for an extension.

Duncan granted Connective’s application, effectively dismissing the lawsuit.

A spokesperson for Connective said in an email statement to APTN News that it was aware of the dismissal but had no comment.

Father disappointed lawsuit dismissed

Mark Wallace, Joe’s lawyer, said his client filed the lawsuit seeking justice for his daughter and was disappointed it was dismissed.

“(Joe) had really hoped that Justice Duncan would agree and let this go forward,” he said, noting his client was “quite upset by it.”

Wallace acknowledged that they knew there was a “reasonable chance” Connective would move to strike the lawsuit based on the limitation period, but said they hoped Duncan would agree with their arguments.

However, he said he didn’t disagree with the decision and that Joe wouldn’t be appealing.

“I think her interpretation of the law is correct,” he said.

Wallace said that while the outcome wasn’t what they wanted, Joe is hopeful the lawsuit will help raise awareness of the act’s limitation period for people in similar situations who might not be aware of it.

He also said he would like to see more flexibility under the act to account for personal circumstances, such as adopting wording similar to that in other jurisdictions.

The lawsuit is the 4th filed in recent years involving deaths at the shelter.

Two were settled last year , while another is still before the courts.

Sara Connors is originally from Nova Scotia and has a journalism degree from the University of King’s College in Halifax. After graduation she worked in South Korea for two years as an English language teacher and freelance journalist. After she returned home in 2019 she worked behind the scenes at CTV Atlantic in Halifax before joining APTN's Yukon bureau in July 2020.

scraped.title: Carney is the most ‘opaque, unaccountable person in politics’: May
scraped.description: Outgoing Green Party leader Elizabeth May says Prime Minister Mark Carney is not being held to account for his actions as leader.
scraped.author: Fraser Needham
scraped.h1: Outgoing Green Party leader says Carney is the most ‘opaque, unaccountable person in politics’
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Elizabeth May says Prime Minister Mark Carney is perhaps the most challenging party leader she has had to work with in more than four decades in politics.

“Accountability is really important and Mr. Carney is the most opaque, unaccountable person in politics I think I have ever seen,” the Green Party MP said.

May stepped down as Green Party leader earlier this month, making way for former Kitchener, Ontario MP Mike Morrice to take over the party’s reins.

She will continue on as the MP for the riding of Saanich-Gulf Islands in British Columbia.

One of the reasons May voted in favour of the 2025 budget was Carney’s pledge to respect Canada’s Paris commitments on climate change.

With the Liberal government’s continued backing of oil and gas projects, it is now highly unlikely Canada will meet these commitments.

Carney, a former governor of both the Bank of Canada and Bank of England, has often been touted as the right leader at the right time due to the country’s ongoing trade issues with the Trump administration in the U.S.

However, May said his credentials may not be as suitable as they seem.

“He comes with a very impressive resume and a lot of people assume he’s an economist and a banker,” she said. “He’s really a banker. Economists are capable of saying let’s take a project like pipelines and before we throw billions of public dollars at it, can we do a cost/benefit analysis?

“Is there a market for diluted bitumen in other countries around the world? Is there a reason we want to violate Indigenous rights and bulldoze these things through with bills like C-5 and C-39? He’s not held to account very much.”

In spite of it all, Carney and the Liberals continue to ride high in the polls. May has a theory of why this is the case.

“It’s like when you are on a highway and all the traffic slows down because you are rubbernecking an accident over there. If we keep our eyes on the road in Canada, we can see some flaws with Mr. Carney but if we’re rubbernecking and looking at, ‘Oh my God, the White House,’ it’s really easy for Mr. Carney not to be held to the same standards that previous prime minsters would have been for their actions.”

First Nations water

The head of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs says the organization has a number of issues with the Carney government’s First Nations Clean Water Act (Bill C-37) including the fact that it does not include access to clean drinking water as a human right.

“There needs to be a guarantee that the accountability does fall with the government,” Grand Chief Kyra Wilson said. “We always need to ensure that government is upholding the treaties. First Nations signed treaties with the Crown. It’s Canada’s duty and obligation to uphold those treaties. So, when we’re talking about safe drinking it’s not up to First Nations people to prove the case. It’s Canada’s obligation to uphold all of that.”

Wilson was in Ottawa this week to serve as witness before the House of Commons Indigenous and Northern Affairs Committee on Bill C-37.

She also said AMC takes issue with the fact the legislation was drafted without sufficient consultation from First Nations.

Arctic drilling

The minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs said oil and gas exploration off the coast of the Arctic will not move forward without the necessary consultation with Inuit organizations and environmental safeguards.

“We will be working hand-in-hand with the Indigenous groups in the north to understand whether we should move the Tariuq Accord (2023 co-management and revenue-sharing agreement for offshore petroleum resources signed between Canada, Inuvialuit Corporation and the Government of the Northwest Territories) forward,” Rebecca Chartrand said. “The governance is there, there’s still much work to do on making decisions.

“So, the decisions will rest on whether we have sound environmental assessments ensuring that we’re protecting the marine ecosystems and this comes directly from the early engagement meetings that I have held with the leadership in the north.”

The 2026 federal budget pledges $11 million over four years to support Arctic offshore governance which has led some to question whether or not the Carney government is going to lift the moratorium on offshore oil and gas activity signed between the previous Trudeau government and the Obama administration in the U.S. in 2016.

Fraser spent the last 20 years working in both print and radio in Saskatchewan – mostly in the northern part of the province. Before joining APTN’s Ottawa bureau, he was news director for the Missinipi Broadcasting Corporation working out of their Prince Albert office. He holds a bachelor of arts degree in political science from Carleton University and a diploma of journalism from Algonquin College.

Warning: this story discusses child abuse and suicide Manitoba’s youth advocate says more than half of serious injury reports involving kids are linked to sexual assault, and that 71 per cent of victims are Indigenous children. “It’s pretty telling,” said Sh...

scraped.title: Most of reported injuries to youth in Manitoba involve sexual assault
scraped.description: Report says more than half of 'serious injury' involving youth are linked to sexual assault, and 71 per cent of victims are Indigenous.
scraped.author: Emma Honeybun
scraped.h1: Majority of reported ‘serious’ injuries to Indigenous children in Manitoba tied to sexual assault
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Sherry Gott, the executive director of Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth (MACY), is pictured in 2024. Photo: APTN File

Warning: this story discusses child abuse and suicide

Manitoba’s youth advocate says more than half of serious injury reports involving kids are linked to sexual assault, and that 71 per cent of victims are Indigenous children.

“It’s pretty telling,” said Sherry Gott, the executive director of Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth (MACY) . “The numbers are pretty high, 53 per cent of our reports are a result of sexual assault or sexual exploitation, and the majority of those are Indigenous children.”

MACY is a non-partisan advocacy organization funded by the provincial government.

Alongside investigative work, it provides advocacy and social services to youth and families, which can result in safety plans, placements and post-release mental health and addictions support for children and young adults (aged 18 to 20).

Since 2000, her office has published annual reports which summarize trends, data and updates with respect to youth in Manitoba, as well as the organization’s recommendations to the province.

In 2023, the organization created its Serious Injuries Reviews and Investigations program, in response to a recommendation from the provincial Phoenix Sinclair Inquiry , created to examine the circumstances surrounding the neglect, physical abuse and eventual murder of the five-year-old girl in Fisher River Cree Nation almost a decade prior.

The inquiry resulted in amendments to provincial law, which aim to improve child welfare and investigations surrounding children both in and out of foster care.

According to the report, MACY received 506 referrals from April 2025 to March 2026. Only 300 of the referrals were able to be reviewed, according to the legal definition of a serious injury, according to the report. Five of the reviews were closed before completion because the youth died.

The report noted that the number of referrals received by MACY has been steadily growing over the last three years. The 2023-2024 report recorded 184, and 2024-2025 recorded 273.

Because of the demand, only 135 of the 300 referrals legally eligible for review have ended with complete serious injury reports, as of writing. Only 99 were assessed for potential investigation, and 36 of those assessments were reviewed further.

Just one case is currently being investigated.

Gott told APTN News that MACY doesn’t have the resources to keep up with the demand.

“There is a backlog, and we’ve actually redeployed some of our staff [from other departments] to do the work,” she said.

According to MACY, 53 per cent (71/135) of the injuries that received a report were a result of sexual assault, while 55 per cent of secondary injuries were also linked to the same cause.

Additionally, 25 per cent of cases involved drugs or alcohol; 22 per cent were linked to self-harm or attempted suicide; 20 per cent were bodily injuries, such as broken or fractured bones; 19 per cent involved gunshot or stab wounds; 15 per cent were head injuries; and accidental and “severe neglect” cases accounted for four per cent each.

Forty per cent of the injuries resulted in a hospital visit, and 35 per cent “were deemed life-threatening,” the annual report continued, and 71 per cent of all cases involved a youth who was First Nations, Inuit or Métis.

The report stated that, based on MACY’s data, 62 per cent of kids involved in serious injury reports have “experienced victimization in their lives.

“This fact alone highlights the importance of a targeted response and intervention by social services following any form of child victimization,” the report continued.

Additionally, “60 per cent experienced mental health concerns that were co-occurring, or combined with, substance use and suicidality.”

Gott recommended that the province should also pay attention to how many of the serious injuries occurred to a child in care.

“Either at the hands of caregivers, or foster parents, or their own families, so we need to highlight that quickly and implement some sort of strategy to support those children,” she said.

MACY also reviews and investigates the deaths of children, based on information received from the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) every time a death occurs.

In 2025-26, the OCME recorded 238 official child deaths; 195 of which involved children 17 and younger, and 43 involved young adults (18 to 20).

Almost half of the deaths were natural (44 per cent), and 36 per cent were undetermined. In most cases, the latter means it was a sleep-related infant death, and sometimes an overdose, according to the report.

Sixty of the deaths were eligible for review, and 68 per cent of the reviews involved an Indigenous youth.

According to the report, 98 per cent of the deaths which resulted in a review involved a child in foster care.

“When completing reviews, we identify factors which impact the young person, their family, or community,” the report stated. “These factors can impact or complicate the ways in which services are delivered to young people and their families. Many of these issues have a cumulative and enduring impact on the health and functioning of young people, families, and communities.”

Identified factors included adverse childhood experiences (23 per cent), historical or generational trauma (38 per cent), household safety challenges (35 per cent), and “inconsistent access to health and social services” (20 per cent), among others.

“I think it’s tragic,” Gott said. “The thing is, one child is too many deaths, and one of the things we’re requesting is to make sure that resources and supports are in place for families that need it, and especially the children in care.”

She said the “child welfare landscape is changing,” especially in the case of Indigenous Peoples, and that MACY supports the push to “make sure that children are being served by their own communities.

“And while they’re doing that, those supports and services and resources are needed in the community,” she said. “It is very unfortunate that there are a number of Indigenous children that have died.”

MACY has made several recommendations to the provincial government over the 26 years it has published annual reports. According to Gott, several remain incomplete.

In February 2026, the organization launched a new framework, The Promise of Seeds , which aims to better monitor how recommendations are being developed by Manitoba’s government.

In its first year, it gathered 29 recommendations made by MACY over the years, including the development of a “systems-navigation support” for families on foster care waitlists and improving resources “to support child trauma specialists in each of the ten family violence shelters in Manitoba,” among several others, and began to track how many were being reviewed or implemented by the province.

Currently, only four have come to fruition, but 16 are in progress and none have been completely ignored, according to MACY’s data.

Gott said that, even still, “there needs to be an improvement” on how long it’s taking.

“We will continue to advocate, to ensure that those recommendations that we’ve made, in all the systems, that includes justice, addictions, mental health, child welfare, be implemented,” she said.

In a written statement to APTN News, provincial Minister of Families Nahanni Fontaine said the Manitoba government “appreciates the critical work done by the Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth.

“We are currently in the process of renewing Tracia’s Trust , Manitoba strategy for sexually exploited youth . We have been engaging with survivors, service providers, Indigenous organizations, community providers and frontline professionals, including working directly with MACY on their concerns,” Fontaine said.

“We remain committed to working alongside survivors, families, Indigenous leadership, community organizations, law enforcement and more to prevent exploitation and ensure those affected have access to the support they need. We look forward to sharing more about the renewed Tracia’s Trust strategy in the coming months.”

In a written statement, progressive conservative MLA Jodie Byram said the findings in MACY’s 2025-26 report are “deeply concerning.”

“It shows that the total number of child deaths in Manitoba has risen by 15 per cent in 2026 to a total of 238 deaths. The independent office reviewed an additional 135 injuries to children and youth receiving services from child-welfare agencies — a 42 per cent increase from the last fiscal year,” she said. “This is heartbreaking.

“If children are being put in harm’s way, the province must undergo an independent inquiry to identify the systemic gaps facing these children”

You can find the entire 2025-26 annual report here.

With files from Justin Hardy in Winnipeg.

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

scraped.title: As Deb Haaland becomes first Indigenous woman governor in ‘US’ history, fellow Pueblo women face ongoing hurdles
scraped.description: As ‘New Mexico’ prepares to swear in the Kawaika (Laguna Pueblo) member – who already broke political barriers in Congress – women in her home community reflect on gender, colonization, and tribal governance
scraped.author: Savannah Peters, The Associated Press
scraped.h1: As Deb Haaland elected first Indigenous woman governor in ‘US,’ other Pueblo women still face hurdles
scraped.body_text:
As ‘New Mexico’ prepares to swear in the Kawaika (Laguna Pueblo) member – who’d already broken political barriers in Congress – women in her home community reflect on gender, colonization, and tribal governance

Savannah Peters, The Associated Press

●

●

This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press, and appears here with permission and minor style edits.

On the morning of Kawaika ( Laguna Pueblo )’s annual Feast Day, Ashley Sarracino knelt in her family home holding clothespins between her teeth.

She straightened her niece’s black cotton manta, a traditional one-shouldered dress, and tied a sash around her waist.

On these days, Sarracino is a caretaker, dressing relatives for the harvest dance and helping feed up to 150 guests. And as a former member of the Pueblo Council, she knows how to balance those traditional responsibilities with official duties.

“To me, those things aren’t in conflict at all,” she said.

Yet even as another Kawaika woman, former “U.S.” Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, is set to become the first Indigenous woman state governor , women with leadership aspirations such as Sarracino say they are swimming upstream in their Pueblo communities.

Sarracino said she was forced off the council after alleging she was paid less because she was a woman, a claim Pueblo officials deny.

In some of the 19 Pueblos in “New Mexico,” including Kawaika, tribal law and customs do not allow women to hold top government positions.

Haaland told The Associated Press she was once nominated to serve on her Pueblo council but did not make it past a primary. She quipped it was “easier to raise $1 million and run for Congress” than succeed in Pueblo politics.

“It’s still a man’s world in a lot of Pueblo communities, and certainly in mine,” she said.

Sarracino was offered a road map familiar to ambitious young Indigenous people: Leave the reservation to get an education, then return home to serve your community.

She built a career in non-profit work and political organizing, including as chair of her county’s Democratic Party.

In 2022, Sarracino was nominated by a Pueblo Elder to run for council secretary. She finished second but was appointed to the post after a resignation.

“Finally, I had an opportunity to use my skills to help my own community,” she said.

While reviewing budget documents, Sarracino discovered she was being paid US$14,000 less than her male predecessor. She asked the Pueblo governor for an explanation, sparking a bitter dispute that would end her tenure on council.

The council says Sarracino was paid less because she lacked experience and that she abandoned her post.

But Sarracino insists she was ousted and that the pay discrepancy reflects sexist attitudes embedded in tribal law.

Since 1996, the Pueblo’s election code has allowed women to run for council treasurer and secretary, but it does not explicitly allow them to serve as governor or lieutenant governor.

Its constitution, last amended in 2012, refers to the governor as “he” and “him.”

Sarracino’s dispute landed in tribal court but was dismissed this year on sovereign immunity grounds and she’s exhausted her appeals.

The case took a toll on her mental health. She said it’s been bittersweet to watch Haaland make political history.

“We all know she would never have the same opportunity here,” she said.

Yet Haaland’s ascent could help change attitudes at home.

Emily Hunt, who became Kawaika’s first woman elected official in the late 1990s with legal help from Haaland, believes the Pueblo will someday nominate a woman governor.

“Whether I’ll see it in my lifetime, I don’t know,” Hunt said.

Some Pueblos retain traditional theocracies, with government roles appointed by ceremonial Elders and reserved for men.

Charlotte Little, a citizen of Katishtya ( San Felipe Pueblo ), said women in those communities hold esteemed roles of their own.

A “New Mexico” state representative, Little never aspired to lead at home.

“It’s about respecting the culture that I come from,” she said.

Other Pueblos, under federal pressure in the 1930s, adopted secular constitutions and elections.

That includes Shiewhibak ( Isleta Pueblo ), where in 1986 Verna Teller overcame a contentious legal battle to become its first and only woman governor.

Council incumbents attempted unsuccessfully to strike Teller’s name from the ballot, arguing a woman could not hold office under Shiewhibak law. She won in a landslide.

Now in her 70s, Teller blames colonization for the patriarchy that she says persists in traditionally matrilineal Pueblo communities.

“When the Spaniards and the Catholics came here, they didn’t want to deal with the clan mothers. They threw women in the back seat,” Teller said.

“That has turned into this paternalistic attitude that men have to be in charge.”

That’s not the case at every Pueblo.

At Pʼohsųwą̈geh Ówîngeh ( Pojoaque Pueblo ), where council positions are open to all and candidates don’t need to be nominated, women have held all four executive positions since 2021.

Haaland is the most prominent among a wave of Pueblo women who have found success in mainstream politics, from school boards to state government and “U.S.” Congress .

She encouraged Pueblo women to look beyond their home communities for opportunities.

“We need more Native women everywhere,” she told The AP.

Sarracino has not ruled out a future Pueblo council run and, after attending Haaland’s election night celebration, now sees a potential path in state politics.

On Feast Day, as her family home sprang to life with visitors, Sarracino greeted friends and relatives with hugs, refilled their iced teas and later made sure they went home with oven bread and fruit pie.

She watched with pride as her nieces giggled over plates of enchiladas, their hands white with ceremonial clay from the morning’s dances.

She is planning her next move with those girls in mind.

“That’s the reason I couldn’t just let it go,” she said.

“Because I know they’re coming up behind me.”

This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press, and appears here with permission and minor style edits.

Savannah Peters, The Associated Press

Savannah Peters is an ‘Albuquerque’-based journalist covering Indigenous affairs at The Associated Press. She is a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.

Firekeepers tend to and protect the sacred fire. Your monthly contributions directly support IndigiNews’s Storytelling Lodge, helps sustain our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom, and ensures future generations of Indigenous storytellers have the resources they need to do the work.

As a registered Canadian charity, all eligible donations receive a charitable tax receipt.

If you believe Indigenous stories matter, if you value independent journalism, and if you want to help build a strong future for Indigenous media, we invite you to join our circle of Firekeepers today.

Together, we can keep the fire burning.

— Eden Fineday, Publisher, IndigiNews

Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

scraped.body_text:
ICT

The ICT Newscast for Friday, November 20, covers a historic powwow, street art, beading, fashion and Diabetes. Check out the ICT Newscast on YouTube for this episode and more.

Tribal members return to their original homelands in Massachusetts to reconnect with traditional sacred lands.

Chip Thomas, African-American and Lumbee, made his home on the Navajo Reservation to pursue a medical career. A neighbor gave Thomas his darkroom when he moved away. It started his career as a clandestine public artist, who shares his larger than life images in the desert.

Eliza Skenandore, an Oneida from Wisconsin, is the director of the Oneida Community Library and a citizen of the Oneida Nation. Learn how she began doing raised beadwork and how it influences her work as a librarian, teacher, and community builder.

Wisconsin Native Vote held its first ever Get Out The Vote fashion show on Oct. 30. ICT attended and heard from organizers about the unique tie in between fashion and civic engagement.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

It’s no secret that American Indians and Alaska Native lead statistics in high rates of diabetes and obesity. A new survey from the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine suggests many have not heard about one of the most effective dietary approaches to prevent and even reverse Type Two diabetes. Dr. Josie Howard is a psychiatrist and part of the committee’s Native Food for Life Program.

A good DJ makes all the difference at a fashion show. DJ AO, Austin Owen sets the beat. From weddings to community events, the Bdewakantunwan (Prairie Island) and Hopi recording artists becomes a chameleon with a turn table

scraped.title: Haudenosaunee citizens urge Congress to reject BAAJA - ICT
scraped.description: Threats to our lands and sovereignty often came through 'bipartisan' legislation for economic gain. Our Haudenosaunee nations have experienced years of infrastructure development by the US.
scraped.author: ICT Opinion
scraped.h1: Haudenosaunee citizens urge Congress to reject BAAJA
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Editor’s note: The 35-plus authors of this op-ed are listed at the end with their nations.

Haudenosaunee Confederacy citizens

As citizens of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, we urge Congress to reject the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in its entirety. BAAJA would speed federal permitting for energy and infrastructure projects by weakening the consultation process that protects our Indigenous lands. We are deeply concerned about the ongoing threats to the natural world and erosion of Indigenous sovereignty that this bill introduces. As Onkwehonweh (Original Peoples) of these lands, we stand against BAAJA. In unity, we join our relatives across Turtle Island, the tribal nations and Indigenous peoples who have spoken out against this bill.

On Nov. 19, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act by a vote of 62–33, despite strong opposition from tribal nations⁠, sending the legislation to the U.S. House of Representatives for consideration. BAAJA is not yet law. According to ICT , representatives from more than 100 Native Nations had already gathered at the U.S. Capitol to voice their opposition to the legislation⁠. We urge members of the House of Representatives to listen to Indigenous voices and consider the potential consequences for our lands, sovereignty, and the livelihoods of those who would be directly affected if this bill becomes law.

Our Haudenosaunee nations have experienced a long history of policies that have undermined our nation-to-nation treaty relationships and, by extension, attempted to erode our sovereignty. Many bills promised infrastructure, jobs, or opportunity, but Indigenous communities often bear the consequences of these so-called “bipartisan” economic development projects.

The dark legacy of the Kinzua Dam remains with Seneca Nation communities, whose 10,000 acres of Allegany Territory was stolen for the creation of a reservoir in 1965, in violation of the Treaty of Canandaigua⁠. The West Valley nuclear site, where fuel reprocessing operated from 1966 to 1972, released radioactive contamination into Cattaraugus Creek and its tributaries⁠. The creek flows through Seneca Nation’s Cattaraugus Territory before entering Lake Erie.

Just over a two-hour drive north of the Kinzua Dam, the Niagara Power Project took approximately 550 acres of Tuscarora Nation land for its reservoir⁠. These projects supplied flood control and electricity while our nations paid for them with our lands, a loss still felt today.

Among the Oneida, construction of the Erie Canal ⁠ between 1817 and 1825 increased trade and settlement across New York while Oneida Nation citizens lost their lands through deception and violation of their rights. The same canal was then used to transport Oneida people away from their homelands, with many descendants now living in Ontario and Wisconsin.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

In Akwesasne Mohawk Nation, the St. Lawrence Seaway and Power Project, developed during the 1950s, drastically changed the environment ⁠ through shoreline erosion and the industrial contamination that followed the availability of “cheap hydroelectric power.”

At Onondaga Lake, salt and chemical manufacturing left industrial waste in waters sacred to the Onondaga Nation and the entire Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Soda ash production along the lakeshore began in 1884 and continued until 1986⁠. The Jamesville Quarry expanded in 1909 to supply the Solvay Process manufacturing operation⁠, further altering Onondaga Nation lands.

In Cayuga Nation territory, industrial salt mining beneath Cayuga Lake ⁠ has raised concerns about environmental harm and the lake’s long-term protection. Development of the mine began in 1916, and Cargill acquired the mining rights in 1970⁠.

These projects have demonstrated how infrastructure development and US industry have stolen our lands, displaced our people, and threatened the waters that our communities forever depend on.

Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act ⁠, along with the related tribal consultation requirement ⁠, requires federal agencies to consider impacts on historic properties and consult with tribal nations that attach religious and cultural significance to those properties. This process gives tribal nations a way to raise concerns about federal projects that may impact sacred sites, burial grounds, and other places of cultural importance. Consultation is vital, as it provides Indigenous nations an opportunity to exercise our rights and requires the United States to honor tribal nation sovereignty, but BAAJA seeks to weaken this process.

Section 2301 of BAAJA would require an agency’s report to explain cases where an official decides against requiring measures to avoid, minimize, or mitigate harm because, “ in the sole discretion of the applicable Federal official and as otherwise allowed by law, other considerations outweigh the consideration of historic preservation as to any or all adverse effects of the undertaking”⁠ (p. 463, lines 17–24).

In other words, the federal official may decline to take measures to mitigate or avoid harm of a proposed project. If a tribal nation identifies a sacred site along a proposed work route and requests that the federal agency avoid that site, a written response does not offer much protection to the tribal nation community who may raise the concern. We uphold our nation-to-nation relationship with the United States and Indigenous self-governance. We expect the United States to engage in meaningful consultation while our concerns can still change an important decision about the wellbeing of our lands.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Supporters of the bill argue that faster permits could help build the transmission lines needed to bring more renewable energy onto the grid⁠. Congress should pursue that goal by developing any new permitting legislation alongside tribal nations at the beginning of proposed projects, giving the communities a proper amount of time to decide as sovereign nations. Federal agencies should consult tribal nation governments while routes and sites are still open to potential changes or adjustment.

We join the National Congress of American Indians ⁠, Native American Rights Fund ⁠, NDN Collective ⁠, Indigenous Environmental Network ⁠, and Water Protector Legal Collective ⁠ in opposing BAAJA. These organizations have raised concerns about tribal sovereignty, sacred places, and environmental protections, and have called on Congress to halt or reject the legislation.

We call on tribal nation leadership to speak out publicly and demand that members of the House of Representatives oppose the bill. We ask leaders in public health, environmental protection, historic preservation, higher education institutions, and local government to stand alongside tribal nations and make the same call.

To speak out against this bill, contact the U.S. Capitol switchboard at (202) 224-3121, ask to be connected to your U.S. representative, and urge them to vote against BAAJA. Readers can also find their representative and send a written message through their office’s website ⁠.

We carry forward the work of those who came before us and fought to defend Indigenous sovereignty. We uphold our treaty relationships so that future generations can exercise their rights and carry those teachings forward. Congress should honor those relationships and reject BAAJA.

Hugh Burnam, Mohawk Nation Cassandra Bean Minerd, Onondaga Nation Reesa R. Abrams, Seneca Nation Ryan Ransom, Mohawk Nation Spencer Lyons, Onondaga Nation Ansley Jemison, Seneca Nation Tammy Bluewolf-Kennedy, Oneida Nation Theresa McCarthy, Onondaga Nation Noelle Redeye, Seneca Nation Kalista Leaf, Mohawk Nation Nolie Anna, Mohawk Nation Ansley Hill, Mohawk Nation Lori V. Quigley, Seneca Nation Emerson Shenandoah, Onondaga Nation Cheyenne Oakes, Mohawk Nation Isaac White Jr., Mohawk Nation Yanenowi Logan, Seneca Nation Tesha Rourke, Mohawk Nation Logan Booth, Seneca Nation Kanyʌhtowa·nʌ Cheyenne Reuben-Thomas, Oneida Nation Clorissa Printup, Tuscarora Nation Cailey King, Mohawk Nation Danielle S. Smith, Onondaga Nation Michael Smoke, Mohawk Nation Brianna Carrier, Mohawk Nation Nicole Smoke, Mohawk Nation Scott M. Stevens, Mohawk Nation Jade Jackson, Mohawk Nation Aubrie Heron, Seneca Nation Morgan Huff, Seneca Nation Mac Schmidt, Onondaga Nation Cayde Lazore, Mohawk Nation Jake Cook, Mohawk Nation Walker Cook, Mohawk Nation Fantasy Jimerson-Kenjockety, Seneca Nation Darrin White, Onondaga Nation

scraped.title: Affordability and jobs act passes Senate - ICT
scraped.description: Bill aimed at streamlining energy projects slammed by tribes for stripping consultation requirements
scraped.author: Stewart Huntington
scraped.h1: Affordability and jobs act passes Senate
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Stewart Huntington

ICT

Tribal advocates looked ahead for ways to counter legislation they say erodes tribal sovereignty after the Senate Thursday approved a bipartisan bill aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure.

The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA, passed the nation’s upper legislative chamber by a 62-33 vote sending it to the House for consideration.

Title III of the BAAJA bill includes proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act that remove the current obligation to consult with tribes regarding certain projects. The changes have been bitterly opposed by tribal advocates including the National Congress of American Indians, the All Pueblo Council of Governors, the Great Plains Tribal Chairman’s Association, United South and Eastern Tribes, Rocky Mountain Tribal leaders council and others.

“The fight is not over,” said Wizipan Garriot, Sicangu Lakota and president of the NDN Collective, in a statement Friday. “The House still has the chance to do the right thing and vote against BAAJA, allowing the next Congress to take up permitting reform in a way that engages tribal leaders in meaningful consultation and gives the communities who would be most impacted by legislation like this a seat at the table.”

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

The effort to strip the bill of language seen as harmful to tribal sovereignty had supporters in the Senate, including Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., who sponsored an amendment that would have altered the bill’s language in favor of tribal interests.

Schiff decried Thursday’s vote in a statement: “As it stands, this bill achieves some critically important priorities, but falls short on others. I appreciate the bipartisan work on this bill and the support of the 36 Senators who joined me in pushing for an amendment that would have struck the legislation’s changes to the National Historic Preservation Act . In the new Congress, there will be a lot of opportunity to improve protections for tribal sovereignty, and I will continue consulting with California’s tribal leaders to ensure their voices are heard in the halls of Congress.”

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-California, also panned the vote.

“The bill threatens Tribal sovereignty, and I am deeply concerned that it could allow the destruction of ancestral lands, sacred places, and cultural resources without adequate legal recourse for the communities that have relied on them for generations,” he said in a statement issued Thursday after the bill passed.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer from New York, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Industry groups back the bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more. However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

Stewart Huntington is an ICT producer/reporter based in central Colorado. More by Stewart Huntington

scraped.title: GTA VI is finally here and filled with celebrity appearances. Here are some notable ones
scraped.description: From Janelle James and Michael Jai White to Denzel Curry and TLC and more, we round up the top guest appearances in Grand Theft Auto VI.
scraped.author: Kay Wicker
scraped.h1: GTA VI is finally here and filled with celebrity appearances. Here are some notable ones
scraped.body_text:
From Janelle James and Michael Jai White to Denzel Curry and TLC and more, we round up the top guest appearances in Grand Theft Auto VI.

The only people more eager for Grand Theft Auto VI than the players may have been the celebrities dying to be a part of it.

On Thursday, Nov. 19, some 13 years since the last installment and more than two decades since the franchise became a cultural phenomenon, Rockstar Games finally dropped GTA 6 , jam-packed with familiar mayhem, stunning graphics, and some surprising celebrity appearances—like actress and comedian Janelle James.

The “Abbott Elementary” star voices Tish, the host of the in-game radio show “She Got Assets,” but don’t get it twisted, she made it happen all on her own.

“It’s very important to me that everybody knows that not only is that me, I’m not simply ‘voice acting,’” she wrote on her Instagram Stories .

“I pursued, conceptualized, pitched, scripted, AND voice acted my radio show,” she continued, revealing, “Rockstar [Games] didn’t ‘choose’ me; I bullied my way to them. I’ve been playing this game since Vice City (was previously overcommitted to Metal Gear), and this is a literal dream come true!!”

The stand-up comedian also earned a writing credit on the game through the fictional talk show, which features an ensemble of characters voiced by fellow comedians and performers she brought into the fold, including Zainab Johnson, Liza Treyger, and Joanna Hausmann.

James said she’s been “told the response is already great,” before adding, “Hope to catch y’all in these online streets where I will promptly kick you square in your back then put 2 in your dome.”

Since its release, the game, which follows criminal partners Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval as they navigate a sprawling criminal conspiracy in the fictional, Florida-inspired state of Leonida, has been garnering rave reviews from gamers around the world and critics alike, as many praise its immersive world featuring music, visual art, graffiti, and some of culture’s biggest stars like James. However, she’s far from the only one.

There are potential tributes to late artists like Juice WRLD, real-life musical collaborations with artists like Travis Scott, and artist-hosted radio stations featuring the likes of PinkPantheress, among plenty of other surprises. As more players continue to discover the game, we’re rounding up some of our other favorite celebrity appearances.

Michael Jai White

After decades of kicking some serious butt on screen, Michael Jai White is bringing some of that action-star energy to Vice City . The actor and martial artist, best known for playing the titular hero in “Black Dynamite” and becoming the first Black actor to portray a major comic book superhero on film in “Spawn,” voices Kordell Grant, a fictional character in the game’s sprawling criminal underworld.

TLC

While scrubs may not be allowed in Vice City, a little creeping is just fine. And thank God because TLC’s Tionne “T-Boz” Watkins and Rozonda “Chilli” Thomas are lending their talents as hosts of “ Honey FM, ” an in-game R&B station players can jam to while cruising around, packed with nostalgic hits from the likes of Brandy, Monica, Jodeci, and Mary J. Blige. Naturally, their own classics like “Creep” are in heavy rotation.

Trina and Trick Daddy

Who better to welcome players back to Vice City than two of Miami’s finest? Trina and Trick Daddy have reunited as hosts of “ Dirty South Classics ,” another radio station, only this time celebrating the Southern hip-hop that helped put their hometown on the map. Players can cruise around listening to classics like Trick Daddy and 2Pac’s “Still Ballin’” and DJ Khaled’s “Born N Raised,” while hearing the two legends do what they do best: represent the 305.

Gucci Mane

Speaking of Southern hip-hop, Gucci Mane has never been one to miss an opportunity to remind folks who have shaped the region’s sound, and his GTA VI appearance is no exception . The Atlanta rapper joins Trina and Trick Daddy on “Dirty South Classics,” where he hosts a recurring segment titled “The Tap In.” His music also appears in the game’s soundtrack.

Burna Boy

Even in the middle of a high-speed police chase, there’s always time for a little Afrobeats. Burna Boy is helping bring the sounds of the African continent to Vice City as a host of “ AfroBank FM ” alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax. The station features a vibrant mix of, you guessed it, Afrobeats, but also amapiano, highlife, and even African classics, with music from artists including Asake, Uncle Waffles, Hugh Masekela, and, of course, none other than Burna Boy himself.

Denzel Curry and Freddie Gibbs

Of course, a game set in a fictionalized Miami wouldn’t be complete without some of the city’s own musical talent, and Carol City’s own Denzel Curry is right at home. The Florida rapper plays DWNPLY, a local artist who appears on the in-game podcast “Drunk Kings,” and contributes three songs to the soundtrack, including “PAX,” “Politik,” and “Bulletproof Ski Mask.” Meanwhile, Gary, Indiana’s Freddie Gibbs is bringing his own brand of hip-hop to Vice City, voicing a rapper named Freddie in “The Safe Trap,” one of the game’s fictional audio productions.

Charlamagne tha God

The longtime “Breakfast Club” co-host Charlamagne tha God has landed another morning radio gig, this time alongside Ivy Rivera on “ Early AF, ” a segment featured on Vice City Rap Radio. Together, the two bring some familiar morning-show banter to the fictional airwaves, giving players something additional beyond music to listen to between robberies, carjackings, and whatever other trouble they’ve gotten themselves into.

N.O.R.E. and DJ EFN

Somebody get the drinks because N.O.R.E. and DJ EFN have pulled up to Vice City and they brought their podcast mics. The longtime “Drink Champs” hosts appear as themselves on “Drunk Kings,” a fictional podcast that borrows plenty of inspiration from their irl show, right down to the boozy conversations and guests across hip hop. Among those joining the festivities are Denzel Curry’s fictional rapper DWNPLY and members of the game’s fictional female rap duo Real Dimez.

Sexyy Red

Of course, Sexyy Red found her way into GTA VI . The St. Louis rapper, whose music already sounds tailor-made for some of the game’s most outrageous moments, appears as herself and has several songs featured throughout the soundtrack, including “Pound Town,” “SkeeYee,” and “Hoochie Coochie.” She also links up with fictional rap duo Real Dimez for a remix of their song “Cooties.”

JT

It’s only right that a City Girl gets to run the radio in Vice City. Miami native JT, formerly one-half of the City Girls, has traded the recording booth for the DJ booth as one of the hosts of Vice City Rap Radio alongside producer DJ Stevie J. The station plays contemporary hip-hop from hit artists like Cardi B, Future, 21 Savage, and more, while JT’s own song “GMA” also makes the playlist.

Kodak Black

Kodak Black is representing Florida and making sure his Haitian roots get some love, too. The Pompano Beach rapper hosts “The Sniper of La Perle,” a hidden radio station players can unlock by scanning special posters throughout Leonida. Once discovered, the station is a celebration of Haitian music, featuring artists like Carimi, Emeline Michel, and Wyclef Jean, as well as several of Kodak’s own tracks.

Buddy Guy

Who says you can’t appreciate some good ‘ole blues while wreaking havoc across Vice City? After starring in “Sinners” made a whole new generation aware of him, at 90 years old, legendary guitarist Buddy Guy has added another unexpected credit to his already extraordinary career, this time as DJ Buddy, co-host of Gloriana Blues Radio alongside Rolling Stones guitarist Keith Richards . Together, the two introduce players to classics from B.B. King, Big Mama Thornton, Muddy Waters, and Sister Rosetta Tharpe, while Guy’s own “Stone Crazy” also gets some airtime. Even virtual criminals deserve a little musical education.

The weekly telecast is the first sports foray from Frazier and Smith's Straight Shooter Media Productions as they look to bring HBCU culture, traditions and more to a global audience.

Stephen A. Smith has long teased what his venture into broadcasting HBCU basketball would be. Now the ESPN personality and business partner, Kevin Frazier , have revealed their plans, and there’s a heavy emphasis on Howard University.

In partnership with BET, Smith and Frazier’s Straight Shooter Media Productions will bring HBCU basketball to a primetime audience beginning on Dec. 3 with a matchup between Grambling State University and Howard. The D.C.-based historically Black college and university will play in six other high-profile matchups against several HBCUs, including Morgan State, North Carolina A&T, Morehouse and Norfolk State.

The goal, according to Frazier and Smith, is to highlight the culture, traditions and student-athletes that makes HBCUs an integral part of college athletics, from the bands to the rivalries, school traditions and more.

For Smith and Frazier, the connection with BET adds to their HBCU athletic journeys: Smith played basketball at Winston-Salem State University, and Frazier spent time with Morgan State University’s basketball program while his father coached. Frazier also served as an assistant coach on those staffs for two seasons before graduating in 1989.

“Some of my fondest memories are from Morgan State where my father was head basketball coach,” Frazier said in a statement. “I grew up watching Hall of Fame players and sat beside him on the bench when Morgan won the 1974 National Championship. Producing these games on BET, the home of culture, in primetime is a dream come true. Before that first game, I’ll pause and think of my father, knowing this moment wouldn’t have been possible without him.”

Part of the showcase will include a halftime appearance from Nick Cannon and the cast of “Wild ‘N Out,” who will engage students during the Grambling State-Howard matchup on December 3.

Bringing HBCU sports back to BET was one of the key missions for outgoing BET President Louis Carr when he spoke to theGrio earlier this year.

“HBCU basketball represents the excellence, tradition and pride that have shaped generations of Black culture,” Carr said in a statement. “At BET, we have a unique platform to bring that experience to a national audience, celebrating not only the talent and competition on the court, but also the communities, school pride and rich traditions that make these institutions so special. Our partnership with Straight Shooter Media allows us to bring that full experience to viewers while continuing to spotlight the impact and legacy of HBCUs.”

Four of the first six games will be broadcast from Howard University, with the final two, slated to air in January, broadcast from Morgan State and Norfolk State. See the full schedule below.

The series premieres Thursday, Dec. 3, at 8 p.m. ET on BET.

But today, in the age of online shopping, Amazon and TikTok Shop, the tradition looks very different. Beyond most people being able to do their Black Friday shopping from the comfort of their homes, companies have begun launching their “Black Friday” sales days and sometimes weeks before your type A auntie has started preparing the collard greens.

scraped.title: L’Oréal Settles Hair Relaxer Cancer Lawsuit: What Black Women Need to Know Now – The Root
scraped.h1: L’Oréal Settles Hair Relaxer Cancer Lawsuit: What Black Women Need to Know Now
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

The settlement marks a new chapter in thousands of lawsuits raising questions about chemical relaxers and their potential health risks for Black women.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

Vicki Williams, owner of Hair Conspiracy for 21 years, works on Burnell Uchendu as they discuss the candidates for the democratic nomination on Tuesday, Jan. 22, 2008 in Houston, TX. African-American women are interviewed on what they think about the match-up between Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama. With the Democratic primary coming up in South Carolina, pundits are saying the election will hinge on the decisions of black women— will they vote their sex, their gender or neither? Most people polled said they would vote on experience, who is best for the job, or on the issues that are important to them. Photo by Mayra Beltran / Houston Chronicle (Photo by Mayra Beltran/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)

For generations, hair relaxers have been a fixture i n Black beauty culture. Now, a lawsuit alleging that L’Oréal’s chemical straightening products contributed to cancer in four women is bringing the potential health consequences of those products into sharper focus.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Four women have reached a confidential settlement with L’Oréal USA and other hair-care companies after alleging that years of using chemical relaxers contributed to their gynecological cancer diagnoses, according to Reuters . The agreement was reached Monday (Nov. 16), during what was set to be the first trial involving hair relaxer cancer claims in Chicago. The settlement amount was not disclosed.

The women, MaryAnne Lindsey, Surenthia Jenkins, Miranda Lofton and Sandra Simpson, filed lawsuits in 2023 and 2024. They are among thousands of women who have taken legal action against manufacturers, claiming prolonged exposure to chemical straighteners caused their illnesses.

L’Oréal, whose hair-care brands include Dark & Lovely and Optimum, maintains that its products are safe. A company spokesperson told Reuters that consumer health and well-being are their highest priority.

RELATED : A White Male TikToker Decided To Use Black Hair Relaxer… The Results Will Surprise You

“L’Oréal USA strictly follows all regulations in every market in which it operates, and its products are always subject to a rigorous scientific evaluation of their safety,” the spokesperson said.

Danielle Ward Mason, the attorney representing the four women, said she hoped the settlement would give her clients a sense of justice, according to Reuters.

The legal battle follows a 2022 National Institutes of Health study that found women who frequently used chemical hair-straightening products were more than twice as likely to develop uterine cancer as women who did not use them. The findings raised concerns about products that have long been marketed to Black women and used in households across generations.

L’Oréal argues that the study did not establish a direct causal link between its products and the health conditions alleged by plaintiffs. But the lawsuits aren’t stopping with the women who say they’ve been harmed.

According to Consumer Reports and Drug Watch, Arizona and Minnesota have also taken legal action against L’Oréal, raising concerns about whether the company properly warned consumers about the potential risks of its hair relaxers – products Black women have trusted for generations.

“It’s outrageous that L’Oréal marketed these products to Black women and girls as safe when they knew they were not and had a duty to disclose they were not,” Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said in a statement.

Additionally, there are more than 12,700 related cases consolidated in federal court in Chicago, according to court records.

While the latest settlement is not an admission of wrongdoing, activists say this is another reason Black women should be included in conversations about product safety, medical research and informed healthcare decisions.

Attorney General Kris Mayes wrote in a September statement . “Yet, instead of warning their consumers, they put profits over the safety of women and children. That is unacceptable, and we will hold them accountable for it.”

scraped.h1: Grieving D.C. Mom Fights for Son Accused of Killing His Twin
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Chantel Poe is mourning her 16-year-old son while fighting for his identical twin, who is accused of fatally shooting him.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

Screenshot from GoFundMe

Chantel Poe never imagined she would have to choose between comforting one son and protecting the other. But when Washington, D.C., police arrived at her home, she was cradling her 16-year-old son, Jabrell Young, who lay dying from gunshot wounds allegedly inflicted by his identical twin, Jamari, according to Fox 5 News. As she fought to stop the bleeding, she told Jamari to leave. Now, the mother is confronting the impossible: mourning one son while standing behind the other as he faces a murder charge.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

“This is an accident! This is an accident!” the grieving mother insisted outside the court on Thursday (Nov. 19), according to NBC Washington.

For Poe, the shooting was not the culmination of some longstanding feud between strangers. These were brothers who shared a childhood, a home and, according to their mother, an inseparable bond. She has repeatedly pushed back against portrayals of Jamari as a monster, maintaining that he never intended to kill his twin.

“My son and his brother are best friends. They love each other,” she continued.

RELATED : Not Again! A Twin Brother from Georgia Was Fatally Shot, and You’ll Never Guess Who Police Believe the Killer Is

It all started on Oct. 25 inside the family’s Northeast Washington home. According to court documents, the brothers had allegedly argued after Young entered Jamari’s bedroom and touched his belongings. The confrontation escalated into a physical struggle in the basement.

Poe told investigators that she and another witness went downstairs to separate the twins. Then came two gunshots, both of which struck Young in the chest, according to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

Jamari allegedly apologized to his mother, saying he didn’t mean for the gun to go off, court records say. Poe held Young, trying to stop the bleeding, and told Jamari to get out of the house.

The aftermath brought another devastating separation.

After Poe reportedly told the 16-year-old to leave, police issued a public alert seeking help locating him. It would take police more than three weeks to arrest him on Wednesday (Nov. 18). He was charged as an adult with second-degree murder while armed, NBC reported.

Poe has also spoken about the trauma of that night, including being prevented from saying goodbye as her son’s body was taken away. “They did not let me say my goodbyes,” she told WJLA. “They didn’t even let me watch my son leave out the door.”

Now, she is fighting another battle: raising money for legal representation for Jamari. In her GoFundMe appeal, Poe described herself as a grieving mother trying to secure a future for her surviving son while supporting the family members left to process Young’s death.

“I pray no mother ever has to watch their child fight for their life as you [try] your hardest to save them,” she said. “While I am still trying to process the unimaginable loss of my child, I am also fighting to protect and support my surviving son and their younger two siblings.”

She also alleged law enforcement harassment, intimidation, withheld devices and legal pressure while grieving her son’s death. Through it all, her position is complicated, but her plea is clear. She’s asking the world to remember Young, but not to give up on Jamari.

“I love you. I’m here to support you,” she said in a message to her son. He is set to return to court on Dec. 7.
