scraped.title: The Biggest Stories You Missed All Week
scraped.h1: A Lot Went Down This Week. Here Are the Biggest News Stories You Probably Missed
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

From United Airlines’ widespread system outage to the death of the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved Fiona the hippo, we’ve rounded up the biggest news stories you may have missed this week.

By

Angela Wilson

Published

(L-R) United Airlines 737 parked at the gate at Portland International (Photo: Getty Images) | Fiona the hippo (Photo: Cincinnati Zoo Twitter) |A steep residential street descends toward the downtown Los Angeles skyline at twilight, the financial district’s towers catching the last warm light beneath a soft orange-and-blue dusk sky (Photo: Getty Images)

If it felt like the universe was hitting every button on the chaos dashboard this week, you weren’t imagining things. Between cyber threats and major outages, the ground literally shaking in California , and the internet collectively mourning Cincinnati Zoo icon Fiona the hippo, a lot went down this week. If you were busy protecting your peace, don’t be left out of the loop! The Root gathered the biggest news stories from this week you may have missed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Mother Nature reminded California who was really in charge after a 5.0-magnitude quake struck overnight Thursday around Pinnacles—about 100 miles southeast of San Francisco–The New York Times reported. Less than five hours later, a 4.2-magnitude quake hit just outside of Los Angeles.

The shaking was reported across a wide area of Los Angeles, including communities well beyond the immediate epicenter one mile northwest of Commerce. According to USA Today , the Los Angeles Fire Department activated its earthquake response protocol, sending personnel to survey for potential damage to critical infrastructure.

Jim Beam announced it will temporarily halt production at its iconic flagship campus in Clermont, Kentucky, in December 2025 as demand for the liquor dried up. Nearly a year later, that halt has been extended indefinitely, according to The Independent .

This week, its parent company Suntory Global Spirits confirmed Jim Beam is extending the distilling pause, scrapping earlier plans to restart production in 2027 as demands for the bourbon whiskey continues to dwindle.

It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency. https://t.co/X0GVbDAiEQ pic.twitter.com/7wLF0uclWB

The internet is collectively mourning Fiona the hippo after the Cincinnati Zoo announced on Thursday that she had died at age nine—just shy of her 10th birthday, local news channel Fox 19 reported. A freak accident led to her death after a child tossed their knit hat in the air and a ceiling fan deflected it into her enclosure, where she swallowed it.

RELATED: 81-Year-Old Chris Brown Fan Speaks Out About Viral Dance Video

Veterinarians provided round-the-clock supportive care for Fiona, but 11 days later, the complications proved fatal . Born six weeks premature in 2017, Fiona became a global phenomenon inspiring merchandise and millions of fans, who continue to mourn her death online.

Barely three days after a nationwide FAA ground stop turned U.S. travel into a nightmare, United Airlines was hit by a widespread system outage that effected crew communications and messaging systems, as well as the airline’s ability to access crucial aircraft data needed for takeoff on Monday.

The glitch directly delayed nearly 150 departing flights before engineers got the system back online roughly 90 minutes later.

Silicon Valley just served up a plot twist straight out of a spy thriller after Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang abruptly resigned after 33 years. Explosive reports revealed he was involved in two extramarital affairs—one with a fellow Nvidia executive, and another with a former executive at a major Singaporean partner whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect is a Chinese spy. And Congress wants answers.

Three House committees have summoned Huang for a closed-door interview, according to CNN , and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was asked to testify to discuss “serious concerns about our national security.”

Georgia O’Keeffe’s ‘Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I’ from an East Village Private Collection achieves USD $4,878,000 in tonight’s sale. Follow along: https://t.co/CnGFBUCC5z pic.twitter.com/OsLSoAZkp2

Check your auntie’s closet, there just might be treasure there! That was the case in Manhattan, where a woman cleaning out her aunt’s East Village apartment found a long-lost 1930 Georgia O’Keeffe painting , Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I , stashed in its original box behind a rack of fur coats.

Purchased for $3,800 as a graduation gift in 1963, the painting had been hidden since the 1980s after a party guest stared at it a little too hard. Art historians had long listed the painting as “unlocated” until the niece’s discovery—and on Tuesday, it sold for a jaw-dropping $4.9 million at Christie’s New York .

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross—who oversaw cybersecurity policy and ⁠strategy across the federal government—exited his post this week following a string of outages that rattled major corporations like Microsoft, Apple, and JPMorgan Chase, according to The Guardian .

White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pressed for the shakeup because Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job” after a wave of back-to-back technology-related outages, including a nationwide halt to air travel and a temporary disruption to the US National Security Agency’s network.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” hits theaters Nov. 20 – an adaptation of Suzanne Collins’ bestselling prequel novel telling the origin story of District 12’s Haymitch Abernathy.

Set 24 years before Katniss Everdeen ever volunteered as tribute, the film drops audiences into the 50th Hunger Games, where the Capitol demanded twice the usual number of tributes. Rising star Joseph Zada steps into the shoes of a 16-year-old Haymitch, alongside Woody Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence, and Josh Hutcherson, who make their long-awaited returns.

Anthropic—an artificial intelligence corporation headquartered in San Francisco—broke the all-time record for the biggest initial public offering in history, per ABC News . The five-year-old startup behind the Claude chatbot made its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, raising $81.3 billion—unseating Elon Musk’s SpaceX—after pricing shares at $83.

The historic launch reportedly turned thousands of Anthropic’s roughly 5,300 employees into overnight millionaires.

Even in death, feminist icon Gloria Steinem refused to do anything the traditional way. On Nov. 18, hundreds packed Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory for a joyful celebration of life honoring Steinem, who died in September. She was 92.

Former first ladies Michelle Obama, Jill Biden, Hillary Clinton and stars like Cynthia Erivo, Emma Watson, and Cyndi Lauper gathered for a fitting send-off for a trailblazer who spent decades building a bigger table for women everywhere.

In a 62–33 bipartisan vote on Thursday, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a sweeping overhaul designed to force AI data center developers to shoulder an estimated $35 billion in grid infrastructure costs instead of passing them onto Americans, per The Guardian .

The measure now heads to the House after the Thanksgiving break, where the fight over who pays for—and lives next to—America’s AI power boom.

Your weekend binge just arrived! All eight episodes of “ The Altruists ” dropped on Netflix Thursday, following a couple’s ambitious attempts to revolutionize the catastrophic $8 billion collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX, leading to a $36 billion fraud.

Produced by Barack and Michelle Obama’s Higher Ground, the limited series stars Emmy winner Julia Garner (complete with prosthetic teeth and a fake nose) and Anthony Boyle.

President Donald Trump wrapped up a historic first-of-its-kind sit-down in China alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin of the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting this week.

Their discussion included joint declarations about nuclear risk reduction, increasing refined petroleum production and supply, promoting reform at the United Nations, and resolving disputes through dialogue. Despite the historic sit-down, no binding deals were put in place.

scraped.title: MAGA Demands DEI for White People After Keisha Lance Bottoms’ Black Team Photo Goes Viral, Then One of Their Own Drops a Receipt That Exposes Them
scraped.description: Keisha Lance Bottoms is facing MAGA backlash over the racial makeup of her transition team, but an unexpected voice is challenging the criticism.
scraped.author: Shelby Erdman
scraped.h1: MAGA Demands DEI for White People After Keisha Lance Bottoms’ Black Team Photo Goes Viral, Then One of Their Own Drops a Receipt That Exposes Them
scraped.body_text:
Keisha Lance Bottoms is facing MAGA backlash over the racial makeup of her transition team, but an unexpected voice is challenging the criticism.

Georgia’s new Gov.-Elect Keisha Lance Bottoms is fending off a MAGA attack over the early choices for her transition team.

A viral photo showing mostly Black people standing behind the mayor sparked accusations of racism and criticism from President Donald Trump’s voting base, even though white Republicans routinely ignore the same standards they’re now trying to demand from Bottoms.

The photo in question was posted by the X account End Wokeness. It shows Bottoms at a podium at the Georgia Capitol with her new staff members behind her. Of the almost 50 people pictured, eight are white.

As of Tuesday, Nov. 17, the post had more than a million views and reposts.

The caption above the photo accused Bottoms of ignoring the racial makeup of Georgia, as if she should hire her new team based on state demographics.

“Gov-elect Keisha’s new team: 73% black (Georgia is 31% black) 16% white (Georgia is 50% white) She says the goal is ‘representation.’”

It’s also striking that MAGA supporters would now demand equal representation from newly elected Black leaders after supporting Trump’s ongoing war on diversity, equity and inclusion policies. At the highest level of government, Trump has just one Black Cabinet member.

Social media erupted, criticizing MAGA’s double standard and calling out its demand for representation when it’s been clear that Republicans have no such concerns, certainly not based on population, when they’re in control of government.

Bottoms even had an unlikely ally defend her.

Longtime Georgia state lawmaker Vernon Jones, who switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party in 2021, posted a stark comparison between Bottoms’ early staff choices and outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp.

Jones, who lost his bid for Secretary of State in the Republican run-off this year, used an example of the Jekyll Island Authority as “100% White, with nine members.”

“Eight are appointed by the Gov. The ninth is on by virtue of being the Department of Natural Resources Director hired by the Gov,” Jones began .

“Georgia is 31% Black. Wonder how the other authorities and boards look?” he sarcastically pointed out.

They’re mostly all white.

“What if Keisha did what Kemp did and make appoint them all black? You would call her a racist. But not Kemp for appointing all white members. Is Kemp a racist? Well don’t infer that with Keisha if she did what he did,” he continued.

Then he added, “Now you want to look at race when you don’t like the shoe being on the other foot. Hmmmm!”

Others joined in pointing out the hypocrisy.

“Man, oh well. I’m in this photo. Be mad. LOL!!!!” tech entrepreneur and music artist Isaac Hayes III stated.

Another agreed, “You can talk about unfairness when you don’t just see it when its your people getting left out. I know it doesn’t make much sense right now, but when you’re all grown up you’ll understand.”

This commenter might have said it best. “You want DEI for white people snowflake?”

Bottoms beat Republican challenger Rick Jackson to become not only the first woman and the first African American elected governor of Georgia, but the first Black woman to win a governor’s race in the history of the United States.

And that’s after Jackson spent more than $200 million of his own fortune to try and beat her.

Bottoms has said she’s in the early stages of hiring her staff. And since she’s the first Democrat to win the governorship in Georgia in almost a quarter-century, there aren’t many seasoned Democrats on hand to help her.

The controversy grew after End Wokeness posted a clip of Georgia Secretary of State-elect Penny Brown Reynolds speaking at the state Capitol in Atlanta. The account framed her remarks as a response to criticism over how many Black people stood alongside her at the press conference.

“The diversity is intentional,” Reynolds said. She explained that she sought advice from people across Georgia who work in a range of professions.

Subscribe To The ABS Newsletter — Get our stories in your inbox.

We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

We know a request for support isn't why you came here. But without readers choosing to fund this work directly, the depth of reporting we can do at home and abroad shrinks along with everyone else's. If you're not in a position to give, that doesn't change how much we value you as a reader.

scraped.title: 'What Happened?': Karoline Leavitt Turns On Trump, Demanding Transparency as He Offers His Own Explanation for the Nationwide Outages
scraped.description: Karoline Leavitt admitted she worries about her bank account amid nationwide outages, then urged Trump’s White House to explain what’s happening.
scraped.author: Nicole Duncan-Smith
scraped.h1: ‘What Happened?’: Karoline Leavitt Turns On Trump, Demanding Transparency as He Offers His Own Explanation for the Nationwide Outages
scraped.body_text:
Karoline Leavitt admitted she worries about her bank account amid nationwide outages, then urged Trump’s White House to explain what’s happening.

America seems to be glitching. Since Nov. 13, flights have been grounded, banks have experienced outages, major websites have gone dark, and thousands of workers couldn’t log in to their emails. Officials haven’t tied the disruptions to a single cause.

But with one problem after another, Americans are wondering whether there’s more to the story than anyone is letting on.

Karoline Leavitt is one of many demanding more from the administration she once served. She spent 19 months defending Donald Trump from the White House podium.

But now Leavitt has her own concerns about money and funding, adding another layer to her criticism of the administration.

On Monday, Nov. 16, she appeared on “Fox & Friends,” with co-host Ainsley Earhardt asking how she would reassure Americans concerned about the recent technology and banking disruptions.

“Well, I am one of those Americans now, right?” Leavitt confessed. “No longer serving in government, no longer getting those classified briefings about what’s really going on behind the scenes. So as I’m here raising my family, I’m wondering the same thing, what’s happening?”

She added, “I’m checking my bank account with a little bit of worry. And what I would say to the White House is transparency is key.”

Leavitt even cited Vice President JD Vance’s recent interview with Laura Ingraham, in which he claimed, “We don’t see a crisis coming.”

Leavitt suggested the White House deliver that message “wide and loud.” She also encouraged Trump to provide “a message directly to the American people” when he returns from overseas.

Her comments drew little sympathy on Threads, where critics remembered her past enthusiasm for the administration’s transparency.

“She have some nerve!,” one Threads user exclaimed. Another asked, “What happened to the most transparent administration in history, hmm?”

“The irony of her calling for more transparency from the WH is astounding,” one person wrote. Another chimed in, “All of a sudden….after all the lying she did for them.”

“Because she KNOWS them enough to fully comprehend how serious this must be,” another person suggested, adding , “She’s scared because she no longer has a seat at the table, or is realizing she never did to begin with.”

Trump addressed the outages during a Friday White House briefing, in footage captured by C-Span. He seemed intent on separating the technology outages from the airport disruptions.

He called them “ separate events” and blamed some company outages on ongoing upgrades.

“But you’re going to have companies that go down, especially during these upgrading,” he said . “I have a very good feel of it because of my uncle—maybe genetically. I have a very good understanding of what we’re talking about.”

His comments came one day after he fired White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross amid the outages. Regarding the chaos in airports, he blamed the “ancient” air-traffic control system.

The criticism didn’t come out of nowhere. Leavitt spent much of her tenure promoting Trump’s accessibility.

In August 2025, after a reporter complained about being summoned to Trump’s lengthy Oval Office meetings, Leavitt posted: “President Trump is the most transparent and accessible President in American history!”

Days later, photos showing makeup covering dark bruising on Trump’s hand raised questions about his health. Golf footage appearing to show him dragging his leg prompted more speculation. Critics also questioned the administration’s handling of his financial records, medical information and the Epstein files.

She returned to the talking point in February 2026. That was weeks after Trump blamed his disappointing poll numbers on “bad public relations people” while she sat beside him.

She shared photos of the president with journalists, writing, “Honored to serve as the Spokeswoman for the most transparent President in history!” The post linked to a New York Post article about Trump’s press availability. Critics were hardly convinced.

Leavitt announced her resignation on Aug. 12, 2026, and departed Aug. 27. She cited a desire to spend more time with her two young children, including daughter Viviana, born in May. She called the decision bittersweet.

Meanwhile, speculation about the outages keeps circulating online.

“CONFIRMED: Apple is the latest. iCloud services are down for some users today, with sign-in problems listed on Apple’s own status page. Apple has not said why. This follows Microsoft 365 going down last week, the FAA grounding every US flight, banking systems going down, United grounding departures, malware hitting nearly 200 major websites, and the NSA’s internal communications network this morning. We’re beyond “coincidence” at this point, folks. We just are,” one person wrote .

There is no established evidence connecting those alleged incidents, despite the growing speculation.

Still, Leavitt’s concerns echo those of Americans demanding answers. After months of assuring the public that Trump was exceptionally transparent, the former spokeswoman now wants his administration to explain what’s happening.

Funny how transparency becomes a little more important when you’re no longer the one standing behind the podium.

scraped.title: ‘He Started Picking On Her’: Trump Reportedly Turned on Susie Wiles Mid-Cancer Fight, and What She Said About Him After Is Painful to Read
scraped.description: A new report reveals says Donald Trump’s treatment of former chief of staff Susie Wiles changed after she revealed her breast cancer diagnosis.
scraped.author: ArLuther Lee
scraped.h1: ‘He Started Picking On Her’: Trump Reportedly Turned on Susie Wiles Mid-Cancer Fight, and What She Said About Him After Is Painful to Read
scraped.body_text:
A new report reveals says Donald Trump’s treatment of former chief of staff Susie Wiles changed after she revealed her breast cancer diagnosis.

Susie Wiles was still showing up for work at the White House while undergoing treatment for breast cancer, determined to maintain her position as one of President Donald Trump’s most trusted advisers.

But according to a new account from a veteran journalist, her health battle may have marked the beginning of the end of that relationship, with Trump reportedly growing increasingly hostile toward the woman who helped him return to the White House.

Maggie Haberman of The New York Times says Trump began “picking on” Wiles after she disclosed her early-stage breast cancer diagnosis in March, reportedly viewing her illness as a sign of weakness.

The revelation offers a different perspective on the deterioration of their relationship, which culminated in Wiles leaving her position as chief of staff following Republicans’ disastrous midterm election losses and Trump’s reported fury over the results.

Haberman discussed Wiles’ departure Monday during an appearance on Jessica Tarlov’s “Raging Moderates” podcast. Tarlov asked whether the controversy surrounding Wiles’ daughter, Katie, who was accused of “trading influence” through her position at lobbying firm Continental Strategy, had contributed to the split.

Haberman said the situation was more complicated, describing a familiar pattern in Trump’s treatment of senior aides.

“In terms of why she left, there were a lot of reasons,” Haberman said. “The main one is that everybody has an hourglass timer with Trump on their own timeframe of how long they’re going to last. You know, the egg timer turns, and the sands start falling — it is literally true for everyone. And then they can end up coming back in some fashion.”

But Haberman pointed to Wiles’ cancer diagnosis as a significant turning point, saying people close to the White House had noticed Trump’s behavior toward her changing around that time.

“Susie was with Trump at his lowest point in 2021. He was with her at her lowest point when Ron DeSantis, after she had helped manage the late stages of his gubernatorial campaign, they had a huge falling out and it was over money-related issues,” Haberman said.

She then described how Wiles’ illness affected her ability to maintain a constant presence at the White House and how Trump reportedly responded.

“When Susie Wiles got sick — she’s been fighting cancer since February — she’s said publicly she’s cancer-free. But I don’t know anything more about her condition. A couple of people have said to us privately that you can trace the beginning of chaos becoming more visible — doesn’t mean it wasn’t there — but more visible and reverting to the Trump mean, around her diagnosis. She wasn’t physically as present, she tried working through it. People knew that she wasn’t there, and Trump does not like…illness. He sees it as weakness. And so, he started picking on her.”

Haberman also noted that Wiles was not the only person whose overlapping responsibilities and outside connections became an issue inside the administration. Some people were serving in multiple roles, including as special government employees while maintaining relationships with lobbying firms. Wiles’ daughter became part of that controversy, adding another source of tension.

“So, this was always going to end poorly this way,” Haberman added. “But it is true that Susie Wiles…she’s a transactional political figure in a way that Stephen Miller just is not.”

Wiles announced her breast cancer diagnosis in March, with Trump publicly disclosing the news. Despite undergoing treatment, she continued working as chief of staff, even making a rare trip to Capitol Hill in July to meet privately with Republican senators as the administration tried to break a legislative stalemate over Trump’s SAVE America Act.

In September, Wiles announced that she was cancer-free following treatment for early-stage breast cancer. She said pathology results came back after an appointment at the Mayo Clinic and thanked her family, doctors and supporters for helping her through the ordeal.

At the time, Wiles publicly praised Trump for his support. But Haberman’s account suggests the relationship had already begun deteriorating months earlier, reports said .

“Thank you to my family, friends, doctors, and everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way,” she said. “A special thank you to President Trump for his unwavering support. I am deeply grateful and will continue to work to advance his America First Agenda.”

The final break came after Republicans suffered major losses in the November midterms, handing Democrats control of both chambers of Congress. Trump was reportedly furious with Wiles and directed much of his anger at her, according to CNN reporting. Wiles offered her resignation Thursday evening, and Trump announced Friday that Stephen Miller would replace her as chief of staff.

Wiles said Friday would be her last day in the position, describing the experience as “the honor of a lifetime.” Trump said she would move to his political operation, although the precise nature of that role remained unclear.

Miller’s promotion also marked a significant shift in the administration’s leadership. A longtime MAGA hardliner, he has been a central architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown and other major policy initiatives.

scraped.title: Rejected Ballots Leave Mississippi HBCU Students Feeling Disenfranchised
scraped.description: A historic Senate election energized Black college students, but problems with voter registration and ballot counting left many frustrated.
scraped.author: Alecia Taylor
scraped.h1: Rejected Ballots Leave Mississippi HBCU Students Feeling Disenfranchised
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

On election night, as the country watched the margins shrink between Scott Colom and incumbent U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Muarib Abdul-Tawwab and his classmates sat on the edge of their seats.

In the weeks leading up to that day, excitement had been growing across Tougaloo College, a small, private, historically Black college of about 2,300 students in Jackson, Mississippi. Abdul-Tawwab had registered to vote over the summer, right after his birthday. In October, the 18-year-old and student leaders helped register at least 70 students to vote using their on-campus addresses.

Abdul-Tawwab said he and his peers were amazed: Colom really had a chance of winning. “We’re like, oh shoot, we are actually making a difference,” he recalled.

Then on Election Day, HBCU students from Tougaloo and Jackson State University found that hundreds of provisional, or affidavit, ballots weren’t counted due to errors ranging from incorrect counties on voter registrations to rejected ballots. Some students used student IDs, which is legal, according to the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, but those were still rejected.

Students were upset and questioned the process. Despite Colom’s victory, which makes him the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, Black students are grappling with thousands of tossed provisional ballots. They also told Capital B that their campus being split between two counties complicated the process. The dorms are in Madison County, but other parts of the campus are in Hinds County.

Many of the students didn’t even know the campus was split over two counties, said Aznii Welchlin, Tougaloo’s president of the student government association.

Welchlin, who is from West Jackson, said she never knew about the split. Although the 21-year-old graduating senior said she was shocked by the discovery, she wasn’t shocked that a small detail led to tossing out hundreds of Black students’ votes.

She said she’s seen how politicians have used tricks to stop Black and marginalized groups from voting. She pointed to the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision this year to gut parts of the Voting Rights Act, which opened the door for Republicans to redraw maps ahead of the midterms.

Still, when she spoke to her mentors who had attended Tougaloo, a college with a strong history in activism during the Civil Rights Movement, they had never heard of the split either.

In Mississippi, there is no online voter registration. Instead, student leaders attended training and leaned on local organizations like the state’s NAACP chapter to help register students on campus.

Abdul-Tawwab, Welchlin, and others persuaded their out-of-state classmates to register using their campus addresses. There was too much at stake, Abdul-Tawwab said. Across the state, anywhere Black people live, schools are underfunded, and there are too many food deserts, Abdul-Tawwab said.

His pitch was simple: “If you don’t think your vote matters, it does matter. But I say your vote matters more in Mississippi than it does where you’re from. … Where you’re from probably has a better, healthier voting practice than Mississippi does.”

“It’s all these issues, and most, if not all of them, can be traced back to having the wrong people in office,” Abdul-Tawwab said. “I was letting them know, like, if you don’t think your vote matters, it does matter.”

Tougaloo students weren’t alone in having their provisional ballots rejected.

In Hinds County alone, 2,426 affidavit ballots were received, yet officials rejected more than half of them, a county Resolution Board member told Mississippi Public Broadcasting Online . Lydia Grizzell, policy and advocacy manager of ACLU of Mississippi, said voter ID laws and inoperable machines fueled the more than a week delay with ballot counting.

“It is appalling the number of issues that we’ve seen, and we had on Election Day, and now we’re seeing the extension of that post-Election Day in a way that is not great,” she told Capital B .

There wasn’t a uniform way of counting ballots, she said, leaving it up to the local election boards. In some counties, counting votes happened behind closed doors, leaving questions for some.

Officials said many of the rejected ballots were due to error.

“Students who want to register have to write everything by hand, so when we think about that, we think about how things are spelled correctly,” Welchlin said.

Mississippians will cast their next votes in runoff elections for Mississippi State House District 70 and 77 on Dec. 1. In Hinds County, there’s a special general runoff for Mississippi 7th Circuit Court district attorney on Dec. 1.

In the meantime, Welchlin said students have learned their lesson and will make sure their registration has correct information.

She’s also working with the Mississippi Access Project , a student-led coalition focused on building access, advocacy and collective power in Mississippi. Jakari Holland, a Jackson State student activist, founded the organization. The group is pushing for the state to modernize its election process by allowing online voting and same-day registration.

She added that she hopes Colom’s win gives students hope instead of discouraging them from casting future ballots. On Nov. 11, Colom delivered his victory speech at the college. Welchlin said it warmed her heart that he chose Tougaloo.

”[For] many students, this was their first time voting and [they] were very discouraged,” Welchlin said. “They were really excited that they got to vote or tried to vote, and because of that, we’re going to get them re-registered.”

Alecia Taylor is the national education reporter at Capital B. More by Alecia Taylor

scraped.title: Hakeem Jeffries Moves Closer to Becoming First Black House Speaker
scraped.description: Even as Jeffries prepares for another historic breakthrough, some of his colleagues question whether he’s the right leader for this moment.
scraped.author: Brandon Tensley
scraped.h1: Hakeem Jeffries Moves Closer to Becoming First Black House Speaker
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

In the U.S. House’s more than 230-year history, it’s never had a Black speaker. But come January, that could change: House Democrats this week overwhelmingly voted to nominate U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York as the chamber’s next speaker.

“During the first 12 years of my life, my congresswoman, though I never met her, was Shirley Chisholm, trailblazer extraordinaire,” Jeffries said following the historic vote. “That young man was someone who was being so effectively represented by Shirley Chisholm. And now he has an opportunity, all of us, to try to do the same for the children of America at such a time as this.”

A native of Brooklyn, Jeffries’ political career began in 2007, in the New York State Assembly, before he won a seat in Congress in 2012. Jeffries has never shied away from drawing attention to his roots. In 2017, he paid homage to the Notorious B.I.G., another Brooklyn native, on the House floor, reciting some of the rapper’s lyrics before asking, “Where Brooklyn at?”

Since then, Jeffries has steadily climbed the Democratic ranks. He became chair of the House Democratic Caucus in 2019, and four years later, he became the House minority leader — the first Black lawmaker to lead a party in this position. Now, the 56-year-old is on the cusp of making history once more.

But Jeffries’ path to the speakership hasn’t been frictionless. Even as he prepares for another historic breakthrough, some of his fellow Democrats question whether he’s the right leader for this moment. Their objections snap into focus a much deeper tension between the symbolism of this milestone and the expectations of Black Americans confronting fresh threats to their rights and political power.

Securing the Democratic nomination was just the first step. Next, Jeffries must win a majority of votes cast by the full House — including Republicans — in a meeting scheduled for Jan. 3.

Following the “blue wave” in the 2026 midterm elections, Democrats will have a muscular majority in the House once lawmakers return. They’ve already won at least 257 seats, according to The Washington Post , which exceeds the 218 generally needed to elect a speaker. This means that Jeffries could lose dozens of Democrats and still claim the gavel.

Unlike U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York, who’s facing a challenge from U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland for Senate majority leader, Jeffries came up against no such opposition. Still, he won the vote 251-11, with the dissent springing largely from the party’s progressive wing, including newly elected Democratic Socialists.

Six of the incoming members who voted against Jeffries’ nomination — Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb, and Claire Valdez — joined Frederick Haynes III, who missed the vote due to unexpected illness but had intended to oppose Jeffries. They’re demanding stronger commitments on a variety of issues, including Medicare for All, immigration enforcement, and Gaza.

“Our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the members-elect said in a joint statement. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Because the ballots were cast in secret, not all of the members or members-elect who voted against Jeffries’ nomination are known.

Despite this tension, Jeffries has the backing of some of the most powerful Black lawmakers, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Long seen as a Democratic kingmaker, Clyburn is credited with reviving Joe Biden’s White House campaign in 2020.

“I thought we needed to have the kind of candidate that Hakeem Jeffries is — a very solid, no-nonsense guy who listens, who knows how to organize,” Clyburn told CNN. “What it takes is demonstrating that you’ve got the demeanor, that you’ve got the smarts, and with Hakeem Jeffries, you’ve got a very solid, substantive person. He’s gonna make a great speaker.”

In the role of speaker, Jeffries could give Black Americans a powerful ally when it comes to setting the country’s legislative agenda. In that position, he’d enjoy considerable influence over which bills receive votes and who leads key committees, among other things.

Already, Jeffries has outlined an agenda that emphasizes pursuing affordability and accountability. He’s vowed to lower the costs of groceries, housing, and healthcare, including by reversing cuts to Medicaid and by expanding Medicare benefits. These moves could have major implications for Black Americans, who disproportionately experience economic and medical insecurity.

“Our commitment is that we’re going to fight hard to make life better for everyone,” Jeffries said Wednesday. “We’re going to fight for small-town America. We’re going to fight for urban America. We’re going to fight for rural America. We’re going to fight for the heartland of America. We’re going to fight for Black and brown communities all across America.”

Voting rights could be another focus. With Black political representation under sustained attack following the U.S. Supreme Court’s redistricting decision this year, a Democratic-led House could revive efforts to strengthen the Voting Rights Act. Additionally, Jeffries has promised congressional investigations into the Trump administration, potentially giving Democrats a mechanism for scrutinizing how policies disproportionately burden Black Americans.

Still, Jeffries won’t be able to do everything as speaker. Even with Democrats in decisive control of both the House and the Senate, legislation could run into procedural obstacles or a veto from President Donald Trump.

scraped.title: Data Centers Flood Black Communities Without Residents Having a Say
scraped.description: Data centers are linked to dangerous air pollution that Black Americans die from at the highest rate in the U.S. But the health risks are only part of the concern.
scraped.author: Adam Mahoney
scraped.h1: Data Centers Flood Black Communities Without Residents Having a Say
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

This story was produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s AI Accountability Network and is the first of a yearlong Capital B investigation into how data centers are reshaping Black communities around the world.

By the time Zakiya Mabery learned that a $2 billion data center was planned just a 10-minute walk from her house, officials had already approved it.

The 200-acre facility in Augusta, Georgia, was first authorized in 2022 without a public hearing that would’ve allowed the community to voice their concerns.

Just months before the facility known as Project Eisenhower came to be, Mabery bought her home in a new housing development called Hayne’s Station. Since then, two-thirds of the people who’ve moved into the community have been Black.

“We would’ve never purchased a house if we knew a data center was coming,” she said about the project that began construction earlier this year.

Mabery’s experience exposes the racial divide in America’s data center boom — not just in where facilities are built, but in who gets a chance to question them.

Majority-Black communities are more than two times more likely to host a data center than majority-white ones and far less likely to receive the chance to hear about the projects before they’re approved or offer their opinion through public comment.

“It seems like [processes] are being built to silence citizens,” Mabery said at an Augusta Planning Commission meeting this past summer.

In recent years, dozens of AI data centers in communities home to hundreds of thousands of Americans have been approved without a public hearing .

For Black communities, the data center boom is extending a familiar pattern of environmental racism that has plagued families for generations.

Black communities are hosting infrastructure that generates wealth elsewhere. Meanwhile, they live with the pollution and disinvestment that undermines economic opportunity and contributes to poor health outcomes and premature deaths in their neighborhoods.

The stakes are growing as tech companies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into new infrastructure. President Donald Trump has pulled the levers of government in favor of these companies as he’s cast AI dominance as a competition the United States cannot afford to lose to China.

His administration has ordered agencies to exempt data centers projects from federal environmental review and to revise federal rules to accelerate their construction. At the same time, he has pushed federal agencies to limit the opportunities for public comment as the building boom reaches communities already carrying generations of industrial burdens.

The opportunity for residents to speak their mind is consequential to the outcome of a data center project.

On average, communities that have received a hearing before construction are nearly 80% white on average. Those without one are roughly 60% people of color.

When communities have received a public hearing, data centers have been blocked 66% of the time. When they don’t, they’re approved 80% of the time, according to Zoned Out, a tool created by researchers at Harvard University .

“We know disparities already exist in our communities, and now in the case of data centers, we’re seeing the targeting that happens without any say. It is systemic injustice,” said Aino Halonen, a former AI worker who led the Harvard study.

The racial disparities showed up during November’s midterm election . More than 40 jurisdictions nationwide allowed voters to decide if they wanted data centers in their communities via ballot measures. White residents made up an average of over 83% of the population in these places, compared with less than 5% for Black residents.

In Georgia, Mabery and her neighbors want a voice in what happens to their homes, health, and finances.

Data centers have increased PM 2.5 air pollution , which Black Americans die from at the highest rate in the U.S. The pollution can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer.

Carbon emissions from data centers are also connected to the intensification of climate change. America’s largest data centers are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of climate change-causing carbon dioxide emissions annually — more than emissions from entire countries like Kenya and Guatemala.

“These are not emotional concerns. This is where we live. We invested here. We live and bear the impact here,” Augusta resident Charles Zabel said about the data center. “We ought to have a voice in this. So far, we have not had a meaningful voice in this discussion. Representation does not mean protecting a project. Representation means protecting the people who already call this place home.”

Researchers at George Washington University Law School joined American University researchers to analyze the placement of more than 5,200 data centers in the U.S., finding the major racial divide in where they’re found.

Researchers accounted for income, population density, home values, and proximity to major power lines, and compared neighborhoods within the same state to test whether economics or geography explained the racial disparities in where data centers were located and the benefits the communities received.

Even after those adjustments, neighborhoods with larger Black, Latino, and Asian populations remained most likely to have these negative experiences with data centers.

“Even when you control for all of that, race stands out,” said Dhanaraj Thakur, director of the Fair Technology Initiative at George Washington University.

“I think it’s important to show that this is not some anecdotal thing that’s happening in a few cities like Memphis or elsewhere,” he added. “It’s actually happening across the country.”

The difference often comes down to zoning. Due to the long tentacles of segregation and redlining, Black people are far more likely to live in communities that are home to tracts zoned for industrial use.

When a data center requires rezoning from, say, commercial to industrial, the approval process generally includes public notice, a hearing, and a vote. But if the land is already zoned industrial, developers can secure permits through an administrative review without requiring opportunities for residents to intervene.

As Capital B has reported , there have been several incidents where developers have pursued projects in poorer, majority-Black neighborhoods with more lax public hearing requirements after encountering opposition in wealthier, whiter areas.

After a data center was proposed in a wealthy, 65% white community in North Carolina, for example, thousands of residents were able to submit signatures and comments against the project. Then, the developer withdrew the project.

Weeks later, that same developer moved the project to another county in North Carolina, where the closest neighborhood was predominantly Black and had a median income that was just one-third of the former community’s. Commissioners in the county quickly approved the project in a 6-1 vote.

Even as data centers are more likely to be in communities of color, these same communities are less likely to receive major economic benefits, Thakur’s study found. Campuses operated by tech giants such as Meta, Google, and Microsoft are more likely to generate property-tax revenue and implement community benefit agreements, but those campuses are more likely to be in majority-white neighborhoods than communities of color.

That pattern raises the prospect that communities of color are shouldering the financial and environmental burdens of data center development writ large without the same potential financial rewards, the researchers wrote.

“A lot of the rhetoric coming from industry is that there are lots of economic benefits from data centers — tax revenue and job creation,” Thakur said. “These are what the industry groups promise, even though we’ve seen a lot of contradictions to that. But even if you do accept that as fact, the research shows that communities of color are less likely to receive those benefits.”

According to some analyses, Black workers make up just 7% of AI workers compared to 13% of the general population.

As for construction, for one week last fall, Capital B spent every morning and evening outside the site for Meta’s data center in northern Louisiana, the largest project in North America. The two closest towns are over 80% Black. None of the workers Capital B spoke to or saw drive off in their Ford F-150s were Black.

As Black communities bear the brunt of this crisis, increasingly, they’ve also been left out of the imagined face of the opposition. Nationwide, roughly 70% of Americans opposed data centers. As such, the fight has been framed by advocates and politicians as one that crosses all racial and political boundaries.

But researchers found that the flattening of data center opposition to an “American problem” has erased the racial injustices permeating the boom.

Communities that have been highlighted via the media in resistance to data centers were about 79% white on average, compared with 53% white in communities without recorded opposition. They said that the disparity reflects unequal media coverage, political influence, and organizing resources.

“It’s interesting that only some communities are being highlighted as opposing it,” Thakur said. “It is erasing the nuance and racial inequality” at the heart of the boom.

At Capital B, we’ve highlighted Black communities fighting data centers everywhere from Memphis to Maryland and Mississippi .

In Augusta, where the community closest to the massive data center site is 67% Black, residents are committed to fighting for a say. This summer, the board of commissioners approved a temporary moratorium on data center development. The $2 billion construction project was not included in the blockage.

“We are asking for respect,” Mabery said.

In partnership with the Pulitzer Center and the Associated Press, Capital B is investigating the economic and environmental impacts of data centers on Black communities. Do you live near a data center? We want to hear about your experience, especially whether promises of jobs and local investment have materialized. Share your story with us here .

For nine months, the Rev. Edward Moultrie of St. Paul CME Church and his congregation filled county meetings, urging officials…

Americans don’t agree on much, but that’s not the case when it comes to data centers. ​Seven in 10 Americans…

Across a rural pocket of cotton and soybean fields in northeast Louisiana, Meta, the eighth most profitable company in the…

Adam Mahoney is the climate and environment reporter at Capital B. He can be reached by email at adam.mahoney@capitalbnews.org, on Bluesky, and on X at @AdamLMahoney. More by Adam Mahoney

scraped.title: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

For many people a trip to the zoo is an opportunity to see favorite animals like gorillas, giraffes and lions. But in Alburquerque, New Mexico, U.S., visitors can add spiders, scorpions and ants to their must-see list at the ABQ BioPark BUGarium . The facility also includes an aquarium, traditional zoo and botanic garden.

The BUGarium was closed for a year and reopened in October 2026 following a $1.45 million renovation.

Insects are the largest group of animals on Earth, and ecologically essential as pollinators and the base of many food chains. Famed entomologist E.O. Wilson once said: “If we were to wipe out insects alone — just that group alone — on this planet, which we are trying hard to do, the rest of life and humanity with it would mostly disappear from the land. And within a few months.”

The BUGarium exists to educate the public about the importance of insects. “Whether they’re pollinating plants, recycling nutrients, controlling pests, or supporting entire food webs, these animals are essential to healthy ecosystems,” said ABQ BioPark Associate Director Matthew Peterson in a statement.

Bugs are not always an easy sell. “Guests come to the BUGarium with a wide spectrum of attitudes ranging from disgust and horror to fascination and awe,” Alexandra Miller, the curator of entomology at the ABQ BioPark told Mongabay in an email. “We hope guests learn how important arthropods are to ecosystems around the world, what they can do to support native populations, and that arthropods require specialized care in the same way gorillas and elephants do.”

Along with spiders, scorpions, crabs and other animals with jointed exoskeletons insects are part of the taxonomic group Arthropoda.

A highlight of the insect-based zoo is a leaf-cutter ant ( Atta cephalotes ) colony from a rainforest in Trinidad. It shows the complex society of ants that farm fungus, their food, on leaves that they forage.

“The different chambers the ants live in are made out of blown glass, so guests have the opportunity to see how the entire ant colony operates and works cooperatively,” Miller said.

The BUGarium also exhibits insects and spiders from New Mexico’s Chihuahuan Desert.

“Connecting our guests to nature is a cornerstone of what we do at the BioPark, and at the BUGarium our focus is creating meaningful connections between guests and arthropods,” Miller said.

Other U.S. zoos like the San Diego Zoo and Cincinnati Zoo also have dedicated exhibits for connecting people with insects. However, insect and spider exhibits are not nearly as common as exhibits of popular vertebrate species.

“The BUGarium is part of a small group of facilities dedicated to live insects and arthropods in the United States. Our numbers may be small, but like the animals in our care, can have a huge impact,” Miller said. “We are proud to be a part of the story of connecting people to arthropods and promoting their conservation.”

Banner image : Leaf-cutter ants at ABQ BioPark BUGarium.

scraped.title: Indigenous protesters board soy and oil barges on Brazilian Amazon river
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Indigenous protesters board soy and oil barges on Brazilian Amazon river
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Hundreds of Indigenous protesters on several small boats and canoes stopped and boarded barges carrying soybeans and fuel on Brazil’s Tapajós River in the eastern Amazon. The demonstrations on Nov. 14 and 15 were to demand protection for the river amid industrial expansion and legal recognition of Indigenous territories in the region.

The two-day demonstration near Santarém, in Pará state, drew more than 650 protesters.

“Our children need this river, just as we need this river,” Jackson Tapajós, executive secretary of the Tupinambá Indigenous Council who participated in the protest, told Mongabay by phone. Smoke in the air from nearby forest fires was so thick that protesters could not see the barges approach until they were close, he said.

Indigenous women negotiated with armed security guards after approaching the fuel barge on Nov. 14, explaining that the group was peacefully protesting. The guards allowed them to board but stayed with them, Tapajós told Mongabay.

“We managed to talk to some of these guards … but they were by our side the whole time, the whole time with their guns, so that creates a lot of tension,” Tapajós said.

The Tapajós River is an export artery for the region, carrying large amounts of soybeans and corn from Brazil’s agricultural heartland to ports on the Amazon River, which ultimately connect to international trade routes via the Atlantic. According to the Ministry of Ports and Airports , 16.8 million metric tons of cargo was moved through the waterway in 2025, up 14.3% from 2024.

“ We fish in this river and use it to travel from one village to another. The river is part of our territories and our lives. That’s why we want to protect it,” Gilson Tupinambá, chief of the Tupinambá people, said in a statement published by nonprofit Amazon Watch.

For the Tupinambá people the river itself is sacred; its rock islands are considered the home of the encantados, or spiritual beings, Tapajós told Mongabay. Under a previous waterway decree those islands could have been blown up to accommodate heavier ship traffic, Tapajós said. However, the government repealed the decree in February, after a 33-day Indigenous blockade of a Cargill grain terminal.

None of the 12 Indigenous territories in the region has full legal recognition. In May, Brazil’s minister of Indigenous Peoples pushed to speed up the process following a technical visit to the region earlier in the month.

FUNAI, Brazil’s national Indigenous affairs agency, has yet to begin studying the land claims for five of the territories: Tupinambá do Baixo Tapajós, Encantados/Kumaruara, Sarambiá, Terra Preta and Arapyun. The other seven are at different stages of the land recognition process; some have been stalled for nearly two decades.

“We want to know what’s missing in each case, who’s responsible for moving it forward, and by when,” Lukas Tupinambá, coordinator of the Tapajós and Arapiuns Indigenous Council (CITA), said in a statement.

Banner image: Indigenous protesters board a soy barge on the Tapajós River in Brazil. All images courtesy of João Vitor Tupinambá.

items.title: What is BAAJA? Your permitting reform questions, answered
items.summary: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, aims to speed up permitting for big energy projects. Readers had a slew of questions about it.

scraped.title: What is BAAJA? Your permitting reform questions, answered » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, aims to speed up permitting for big energy projects. Readers had a slew of questions about it.
scraped.author: Sara Peach
scraped.h1: What is BAAJA? Your permitting reform questions, answered
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

We recently invited Yale Climate Connections readers to ask questions about the divisive Senate permitting reform bill moving through Congress. The result: More emails from readers on this topic than on any other subject in recent memory.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, aims to accelerate the permitting process for big energy projects like wind farms, fulfilling a longtime goal of the clean energy industry. But environmental groups and tribes have fiercely criticized the bill for substantially changing bedrock environmental laws and the federal process for consulting tribes.

We can't do this work without you. We've set an ambitious goal of raising $60,000 by the end of the year. Will you donate to support climate journalism today?

“The bill, the culmination of years of negotiations, is very good for the proponents of many kinds of energy projects (both clean and fossil), especially electricity transmission,” explained Michael Gerrard, founder and faculty director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University, in an analysis of the bill. “It is very bad for environmental groups and other project opponents who want to challenge these projects in court.”

Can proponents give examples of specific good projects needlessly held up? (I can think of plenty of bad projects pending, held up, or canceled.) – Yale Climate Connections reader BS

Bill sponsor Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico, points to the SunZia wind and transmission project in New Mexico and Arizona. It went online earlier this year – 20 years after it was proposed. Meanwhile, about 400 onshore wind projects are awaiting review by the Pentagon, which doesn’t have enough staff to get through the list, Utility Dive reported last week.

Supporters of permitting reform have also highlighted a transmission line in Oregon that took 17 years to get a permit. On average, it takes about 10 years to complete a new transmission line project, according to the U.S. Department of Energy .

Can you explain to us the more specific ways BAAJA weakens current environmental bills and tribal control of sacred lands? This would be very helpful to know to possibly improve the bill as it goes through the amendment process, and what to ask House representatives to amend as they take up the bill. – Reader MH

Many groups are worried about the ways that BAAJA weakens the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act, known as NEPA.

“BAAJA would pull NEPA’s principal teeth – the possibility of a court order blocking a project for violating NEPA,” wrote Michael Gerrard, the Columbia climate law expert. “If there are no serious consequences for violating NEPA, many may come to ignore it. Especially during a hostile administration, agencies might completely disregard NEPA, and everyone will lose the crucial information and public input that it provides.”

Earthjustice’s team of environmental lawyers put together a detailed guide to the potential implications of the permitting reform bill. See also the team’s analysis of an update to the bill called the manager’s amendment.

Native News Online provides this overview of impacts to tribes: “Tribal Nations and preservation advocates are fiercely opposing the fast-tracked Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) because its permitting reforms – written behind closed doors without tribal input – would strip away vital protections for sacred lands by narrowing required consultations, slashing legal challenge timelines, and preventing courts from halting unlawful energy projects.”

“It’s thorough and surgical – they knew exactly what they were doing,” one tribal advocate told Native News online. “It was such perfectly engineered legislation designed to strip tribes of their statutory protections that I can’t believe this is happening in 2026.”

Why does anyone supporting BAAJA as a climate action think that Trump will comply with this? Why does anyone think Trump won’t use BAAJA as a means to expand fossil fuel even more than he is doing now, with less control by law or by the public, and ignore wind and any other renewables? – Reader PH

We’ve reached out to Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse’s office for comment and will let you know what we hear. [ Update on November 20, 2026: Whitehouse’s office declined the interview request.] Inside Climate News summarized Sen. Heinrich’s argument this way: “the bill cuts permitting for a major power line from about two decades to about five years – still too slow for President Donald Trump to finish much, so the next president collects.”

Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, disagrees : “Over the next two years, BAAJA would create more legal runway for this president to make corrupt deals and greenlight harmful projects of all kinds, and it would constrain any future president from repairing the damage.”

I understand a key thing here is urgency: getting clean energy started sooner and lowering costs sooner. My question is: What if we wait for a different bill? Perhaps we could lobby to change this bill or create a new one? – Reader DK

I want to know if there are alternative pieces of legislation that would accomplish the fast-tracking of renewable energies without trashing existing environmental protections. Particularly if we just wait a few months for the new Senate and House to be seated. – Reader LR

Many prominent environmental leaders, including Ayana Elizabeth Johnson , are making a version of this argument: “YES, we need to permit clean energy faster. But, NO, not if that also means permitting dirty fossil energy faster – with major climate justice implications,” Johnson wrote this week. “And another NO if it means undercutting the authority of Tribes and State Governments to protect their water and land.”

But any future permitting reform bill would need to contend with the filibuster, which requires a 60-vote threshold to advance legislation in the Senate. (In theory, the Democratic majority could change the filibuster rule, but even Sen. Bernie Sanders doesn’t seem to like that idea .)

Policy veteran Jeff Navin argued (at length) on X and LinkedIn that a clean-energy-only bill would immediately run aground on the shoals of the filibuster. What’s more, Navin noted, many newly elected Democratic Senators support the oil and gas industry.

“Very few Democrats in the Senate support anything remotely close to a keep-it-in-the-ground agenda,” Navin wrote. “Next Congress, 19 members of the Democratic caucus who voted for cloture on the motion to proceed on this version of the permitting bill will return. They’ll be joined by James Talarico, who has endorsed all-of-the-above and vowed to protect oil and gas jobs. Mary Peltola has explicitly called for more oil and gas development. Scott Colom supports natural gas. Both Adam Hamilton and Annie Andrews endorsed an ‘all of the above’ strategy, which includes oil and gas.”

I’m following BAAJA closely as I’m worried it will preempt local control over a proposed new compressor station on the Mountain Valley Pipeline in my county in Virginia. How will it fare in the House if the Senate passes it? Any chance for a veto? – Reader ES

In politics, anything can happen. But here’s where things stood as of Thursday, November 19, according to The Hill : “While the bill appears highly likely to pass the Senate, its path in the House is a bit less certain. It has bipartisan House support, but it faces some opposition from progressive Democrats. Meanwhile, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) has raised pieces of the bill he’d like to change. [ Update on November 20, 2026: The bill has passed the Senate by a vote of 62-33.]

“It is competing with a crowded lame-duck agenda that includes a lapse in federal funding in December if Congress does not act. But the bill has support from the White House, which could help push it through.”

To what extent can state public utilities commissions balance the bad stuff in this bill? For example, if a new gas generation facility is proposed but isn’t the cheapest way to add capacity, can they still refuse to allow it? Can they block a pipeline from serving their state? Can they stop a project if it doesn’t follow state law (for example, the Minnesota clean electricity standard)? – Reader DH

“BAAJA affects only federal approvals,” said Michael Gerrard, the Columbia climate law expert, by email. “It does not prevent state and local governments from exercising their own authorities. So, for example, if a regulated electric utility receives federal approvals to build a new power plant in federal waters, it would still need approval from the state public utility commission, which would have the ability to disapprove the project.”

scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: Free online tool helps landowners understand growing threats to U.S. forests
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

As the climate changes, forests across the U.S. face many growing threats – from wildfires to pests, heat, drought, and storms.

Truettner: “But where the most vulnerability comes from for our forests is when a lot of these different risks are combined.”

So Charlie Truettner of the nonprofit American Forests says evaluating these risks all at once can help forest managers and landowners make better decisions about logging, conservation, or other activities.

But many do not have the bandwidth to collect and compile all of the various data sets.

So to help, his group developed a free online tool called the Forest Innovation Platform .

Truettner: “Our goal is to be able to combine some of the most important of those data sets … and instead of it taking months to years, you could do it in an afternoon.”

The tool allows users to zoom in on any forest area in the U.S. Then they can toggle between different layers to see current and future climate conditions and risks – like wildfire and insect damage.

Truettner says aggregating this data in one place will help landowners and forest managers assess and respond to emerging threats faster so they can better protect forests in the face of rapid change.

Reporting credit: Sarah Kennedy / ChavoBart Digital Media

scraped.title: Kyle could form off Florida as extensive, prolonged coastal flood threat grows » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: A developing storm could bring heavy rain, strong winds, and dangerous surf along the East Coast this weekend, with North Carolina’s vulnerable Outer Banks facing renewed flooding and erosion risks.
scraped.author: Irene Sans, Jeff Masters
scraped.h1: Kyle could form off Florida as extensive, prolonged coastal flood threat grows
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

If you thought the tropical season had wrapped up, don’t bet on it just yet! Hurricane season is still on, and a tropical or subtropical storm could develop as soon as Friday, November 20, just east of Florida. Hurricane hunter flights have been scheduled to investigate this system beginning at midday Friday. The next name on the Atlantic list is Kyle.

Torrential rainfall this week in Southeast Florida has already caused numerous headaches, school closures, changes to work schedules, and endless road detours. Many neighborhoods, including Plantation, a Broward County suburb, have received more than 16 inches of rain, with over a foot falling between Tuesday and early Wednesday. Rain continued across parts of the area Thursday morning. These heavy rains were tied to a frontal system that will remain across the Florida Peninsula as mid-level energy slowly moves north along it, bringing torrential rainfall along the Space Coast and the I-95 corridor into Southeast Georgia.

One major uncertainty is whether this system will intensify far enough offshore to organize into Tropical or Subtropical Storm Kyle.

Record-to-near-record warm ocean temperatures off Florida’s east coast have boosted extreme rains. Strong easterly surface winds have pushed very moist air from the Atlantic toward Florida’s east coast. According to Climate Central’s Ocean Shift Index , human-caused climate change made near-record warmth in waters within about 200 miles of Florida’s east coast two to seven times more likely.

Rain totals since 12a: 3.27" – Parkland 2.68" – Southwest Ranches 2.56" – Plantation 2.15" – Coral Spngs 2.05" – Weston 1.90" – Davie 1.67" – Cooper City None of this helps…only prolongs the situation while not invoking new areas of flooding. But no doubt, we are saturated.

As mid-level energy continues pushing north across the stalled front, a low-pressure system may develop near the surface over the unusually warm November waters just east of Florida. Assuming the system strengthens, it could become a subtropical or tropical storm while moving north-northeast, potentially hugging the Southeast U.S. coastline throughout the weekend.

Get news for people who love the planet. Sign up for our newsletters for the latest weather updates, tips, and inspiring stories

One factor supporting potential development this weekend is the warm Gulf Stream. This powerful ocean current transports warm tropical water northward along the western Atlantic from near the Bahamas. Sea surface temperatures just east of Florida remain in the low 80s, while offshore waters along the southeastern United States range from the upper 70s to the low 80s. These temperatures are more than adequate to support tropical or subtropical development. Other environmental conditions may also become favorable for development as early as Friday, including relatively low wind shear.

Whether this system receives an official name, it is likely to produce strong easterly winds, periods of heavy rainfall, rough surf, and potentially dangerous coastal conditions over an extensive area of the Eastern Seaboard. The greatest impacts could initially be felt along the I-95 corridor from Northeast Florida through Georgia and the Carolinas. The NOAA/NWS Weather Prediction Center has placed east-central Florida in and around the Space Coast in a high-risk area for Friday and Friday night (level 4 of 4) for potentially excessive rain leading to flooding.

For the period November 1-18, Melbourne International Airport had already racked up 17.25 inches of rain, and preliminary data shows that close to five additional inches had fallen by early afternoon on Thursday, November 19. If confirmed, this would not only push this month’s rainfall well beyond double the city’s record for any November (9.72 inches, set in 1963), but it would smash the city’s record for any month (21.06 inches, set in August 2018) – with 11 full days left in the month and more rain in the forecast.

Melbourne, FL up to over 20" of rainfall for November, doubling the prior record for the month — and unsurprisingly the St. Johns River has reached record levels in the area. Bay Area of CA also setting rainfall records — and more to come in both regions. balancedweather.substack.com/p/heavy-rain…

A HIGH risk is in effect in our Day 1 Excessive Rainfall Outlook. More details: https://t.co/cfgBoWyKla pic.twitter.com/7CGjdiAtT6

As this coastal storm tracks north-northeastward, heavy rainfall and gusty winds could eventually spread into the Northeast and New England throughout the weekend. Although models agree on this system’s general trajectory, a slight left or right shift could bring the center onshore along the Carolinas or keep it well offshore. Thus, residents along the Southeast coast should keep monitoring the forecast, as the system’s exact track, strength, and timing will determine where the most significant impacts occur.

By October 2, the Atlantic basin averages its 11th named tropical system. By November 19, the basin typically has experienced approximately 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes. To refresh our memories, the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has produced only 10 named tropical storms. Only one has become a hurricane, Isaias, which was also the season’s only major hurricane.

Strong onshore winds and 10-15-foot waves are expected to cause repeated rounds of minor to moderate coastal flooding and moderate to locally major beach erosion from Florida’s east coast north of the Bahamas into early Saturday, then extend northward into the coastal Carolinas over the weekend. If the storm hugs the North Carolina coast, this coastal flooding is likely to be particularly problematic in the Outer Banks, where coastal storms in September and October already washed out the only road connecting the vulnerable barrier island chain to the mainland, NC-12.

The September nor’easter brought the fifth-highest water level since records began in 1979 at the NOAA tide gauge at Duck , located in the northern Outer Banks. The storm’s erosion caused multiple home collapses, with the Island Free Press reporting that the National Seashore beach in North Carolina suffered “a significant amount of private beach stairs and boardwalk decking, septic system parts, and wooden and metal debris from houses littering the beach.” The beach was closed because of human waste from the destroyed septic systems fouling the water.

The September and October nor’easters caused 16 home collapses; before these storms, 32 houses collapsed into the ocean along the Outer Banks from 2020 to February 2026, for a total of 48 home collapses from 2020 to October 2026. The October nor’easter shut NC-12 for 10 days, and the road currently has just one lane open at the washout spot . A similar washout of NC-12 is possible from this weekend’s storm. Even if the Outer Banks escape a washout from this weekend’s storm, another coastal storm capable of inundating NC-12 is likely on Wednesday or Thursday, according to recent runs of the European and GFS models. This storm will be striking during the full moon king tide period, which will have unusually high tides. During the coming winter, we can expect that multiple strong nor’easters will affect the mid-Atlantic, and the prospects of multiple washouts of NC-12 through spring 2027 appear high.

Storm erosion problems for the Outer Banks will get much, much worse in the next few decades. Between 1979 and 2025, sea level increased by about 9.4 inches at Duck, in the northern Outer Banks. About 33% of this increase can be confidently attributed to human-caused global warming, according to Climate Central. This acceleration in sea level rise has led to a sharp increase in high tide flooding over the past 20 years. What would have been a one-in-10-year flood in 1979 (2.64 feet above high tide) has already occurred on five days at Duck in 2026 .

As I (Jeff Masters) wrote in my 2023 post, 30 great tools to determine your flood risk in the U.S. , a periodicity in the moon’s orbit causes much higher rates of sea level rise for different portions of the coast at different times during the next 18.6 years. An inflection point in this cycle came for Duck in 2023, and as a result, the next 10 or so years will see a sharp increase in the relative rate of sea level rise for the North Carolina Outer Banks.

At a time when the National Weather Service and climate science are under attack, Yale Climate Connections meteorologists Jeff Masters and Bob Henson are sharing life-saving news about extreme weather. Will you chip in to spread the word about hurricanes?

The forecast for coastal flooding in North Carolina’s Outer Banks is truly intimidating. Over the past five years, Duck has averaged about 15 days per year with “minor” coastal flooding, as defined by the National Weather Service. Under an “Intermediate” scenario (the path that most closely approximates sea level rise at Duck over the past few decades), NOAA and NASA predict that by 2045, the Outer Banks will see 80 flood days per year — over one day per week. And if sea level rise increases to the “Intermediate High” range, by 2065, 90% of all days are predicted to see flooding.

Sea level rise is predicted to continue to accelerate into the next century. In past eras when sea level rise was as high as is expected by 2080-2100, barrier islands were rare because erosion was too high. In just a few years, it’s likely to become prohibitively expensive to maintain a road into the Outer Banks will likely become prohibitively expensive. Not long after, these barrier islands are likely to suffer unofficial, gradual abandonment as rising sea levels and stronger storms fueled by human-caused climate change pound the coast. With a permanent population of around 57,000, the Outer Banks don’t have the tax base needed to fund the kind of adaptation efforts that will be needed to keep up with accelerating sea level rise.

In past eras when sea level rise was as high as is expected by 2080-2100, barrier islands were rare because erosion was too high. Trying to keep a road open to the Outer Banks is already getting very expensive. coastalreview.org/2026/11/barr…

Beginning around 2033, the 18.6-year lunar cycle will significantly increase the rate of sea level rise and rapidly increase high-tide flooding along most of the Gulf of Mexico coast, portions of the Southeast Coast, the West Coast, and Hawaii. The rapid acceleration in coastal flooding simultaneously along a huge swathe of heavily developed U.S. coast by the mid-2030s will be sure to significantly stress the coastal housing market.

Bob Henson contributed to this post.
