scraped.title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.
scraped.author: Simon Evans
scraped.h1: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
scraped.body_text:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.

Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.

Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew , a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO .

It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.

Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

Membership

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.

There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.

Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions , the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.

This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.

This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño . However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

The burning of fossil fuels since the industrial revolution is the largest contributor to this.

Since there is a direct link between each tonne of CO2 and each fraction of a degree of warming, historical fossil-fuel emissions can be tied to responsibility for current climate change.

This is typically calculated on the basis of historical territorial CO2 emissions, according to where in the world the fossil fuels are burned. It is also possible to assign historical responsibility on a “consumption” basis, according to where goods are used.

Historical emissions are often counted by country, but this puts the focus on populous nations. Alternatively, responsibility can be assigned per capita, based on today’s populations.

A less-familiar way to look at the question of historical responsibility is to consider where fossil fuels are extracted. This puts the spotlight on major fossil-fuel exporters.

The figure below shows that Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the largest CO2 exporters of all time, based on emissions from exported fossil fuels since 1850.

(The allocation is based on extraction taking place within current national borders. Emissions under the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among constituent countries, based on their share of emissions at the time of separation.)

Other major CO2 exporters, based on their overseas sales of fossil fuels since 1850, include Venezuela, Iran, Norway, the United Arab Emirates and Canada.

Between them, these major coal, oil and gas producers have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 over the past 175 years, according to Carbon Brief’s analysis.

The analysis shows that overall, the US and China retain the largest responsibility for historical warming under extraction-based accounting, despite having been net CO2 importers since 1850.

The US has large resources of coal, oil and gas, but was nevertheless a major oil importer until after the shale revolution in the early 2000s.

China remains a major oil and gas importer, describing itself as “rich in coal, lacking oil and gas”.

Russia remains in third place, as shown in the figure below, despite gaining responsibility for an extra 69bn tonnes of CO2 from exported fossil fuels.

The UK becomes the fourth-largest historical emitter, climbing above Germany due to the latter’s reliance on fossil-fuel imports.

Saudi Arabia becomes responsible for the world’s fifth-largest share of historical warming when including its fossil-fuel exports, which increase its cumulative emissions more than fourfold.

Australia also climbs up the rankings, becoming one of the top-ten largest emitters when including its fossil-fuel exports. This more than doubles its share of historical emissions.

Nations that drop down the rankings under extraction-based accounting, due to their reliance on fossil-fuel imports, include Germany, India, France and COP31 host Turkey.

Japan is a particularly notable example, as it is almost completely reliant on fossil-fuel imports. The nation is the sixth-largest emitter on a territorial basis and the 34th-largest on an extraction basis.

When considering population sizes, major fossil-fuel exporters have the highest extraction-based CO2 emissions since 1850, as shown in the figure below.

Small nations that export large amounts of oil and gas are particularly prominent on this list, including Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar, Norway and Trinidad and Tobago.

Andrew tells Carbon Brief that while the extraction-based accounting offers an alternative perspective on historical responsibility for warming, it also raises complex questions. He explains:

“At the end of the day, it’s not solely the responsibility of extracting countries that fuels are combusted; it’s joint responsibility between extractors, producers and consumers.”

He adds that responsibility for past decisions is shared by many actors. For example, he notes that oil production in the Middle East was historically “ developed by and for western powers”.

Free weekly newsletter

National emissions under extraction-based accounting come from a dataset developed by Robbie Andrew and covering the period from 1850-2025.

Emissions are allocated to the country that extracted the relevant fossil fuels, regardless of where the coal, oil or gas was burned.

The allocation is based on current national borders. Emissions that took place within the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among their present-day constituent countries, based on the relative shares of emissions at the time of separation.

Andrew notes that the dataset is a draft release, based on available data.

Population data for 2025 is taken from the UN Population Fund .

scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

20 November 2026

This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

Solar for All has been through the ringer, but its fight is nowhere near done.

The Trump administration on Tuesday appealed a court ruling that sought to restore the low-income solar program, sparking criticism from not only the typical clean energy proponents but a coalition of Republican allies, too.

The novel program was first envisioned in 2022 as part of the Inflation Reduction Act, with the EPA in 2024 picking winners who’d split a $ 7 billion pot to bolster solar power access for low-income and disadvantaged households. States, local governments, territories, tribes, and nonprofits all got a piece of the pie, and were developing plans to build community solar, rooftop solar, and battery storage when the program first came under attack.

In August 2025 , the EPA announced it was killing Solar for All — one of many blows in the Trump administration’s attempt to tear down the Inflation Reduction Act. Advocates, solar installers, and a labor group challenged the decision in court and secured a major victory this September as a federal judge ruled the EPA ’s rollback was illegal and that its reasoning for terminating the program was unjustified. A second judge ruled in favor of protecting Solar for All not long after. Some lawsuits seeking to recoup individual grants remain ongoing.

Still, the EPA never resumed grant handouts, and this week, it formally appealed the first of those rulings. Clean energy advocates immediately pushed back, saying that the Trump administration’s continued crusade against Solar for All doesn’t track with its promises to curb power prices.

“ Instead of getting out of the way of a program that will lower energy bills, the Trump administration is continuing its obstruction and delay,” Adam Kent, senior director for green finance at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in a statement .

A group of six Republican Congress members made a similar case in a letter they sent EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin this week.

“ At a time when energy costs are rising across the country, Solar for All is capable of quickly providing meaningful relief to Americans,” wrote the representatives from Guam, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. ​ “ We respectfully urge EPA to swiftly reinstate the Solar for All program and ensure projects move forward to implementation as planned.”

The letter is highly unlikely to change the Trump administration’s mind, especially since four of its six signatories will be replaced by Democrats in the next Congress. And slim Republican support aside, the administration doesn’t have a reputation for backing down from its many fights against clean energy.

Permitting reform clears the Senate

The U.S. Senate voted Thursday to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a bill aimed at speeding up energy project permitting.

The final vote to advance the bill was 62 - 33 , with Republicans almost unanimously voting in its favor. Fewer Democrats meanwhile voted for the bill’s final passage than elected to bring it to the Senate floor last week. Two Democratic senators authored the bill alongside two Republicans, but many Democrats and climate advocates are worried about how it will benefit fossil fuel projects alongside clean energy. Democrats also voiced concerns that the bill would weaken tribes’ input on energy projects that impact their land.

The bill now heads to the U.S. House, where Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said his party — which retains control of the chamber for now — will rally enough votes to pass it.

Democrats take on COP as Trump makes more gas deals

As Democrats try to convince the world that U.S. climate action isn’t dead, the Trump administration is trying to cement its fossil fuel legacy.

The federal government sent no official delegation to the COP 31 climate talks in Turkey this month. But a wave of Democratic Congress members, governors, mayors, and former officials did make the journey . Emboldened by their party’s Election Day sweep, they brought promises that the U.S. won’t be sidelined from international climate collaboration for much longer.

President Donald Trump is meanwhile meeting with global leaders to further his pro-fossil fuel agenda, Politico reports . The administration is looking to finance pipeline networks, liquefied natural gas import terminals, and other projects around the world, with a goal of locking countries into importing U.S. gas for decades.

Both COP 31 and Trump’s deals center on a global energy system in flux. Will the world continue to move away from fossil fuels and toward clean energy it can produce at home, like some countries have amid war in the Middle East? Or will an eventual end to the conflict return oil and gas to its former dominance? Only time will tell — though the latest International Energy Agency report forecasts what either scenario might look like.

Carbon paradox: Carbon dioxide emissions from the U.S. power sector are set to drop this year compared to last, suggesting that the Trump administration’s pro-coal policies haven’t been able to stave off the fuel’s decline. ( Canary Media )

Data centers reinstated: Texas allows environmental regulators to resume permitting data centers after a two-month pause, with officials already granting an air pollution permit to a SpaceX gas power plant and data center complex since the restart. ( Texas Tribune , Politico )

Emissions reality: The biggest data centers in the U.S. are responsible for a combined total of 25 . 7 million metric tons of carbon emissions each year — about as much as some small countries’ entire economies. ( New York Times )

Getting creative: Enfield, North Carolina, is pushing the developer of a local data center to fund a thermal energy network that would provide clean, cheap heating and cooling to buildings in town and potentially take advantage of the computing facility’s waste heat. ( Canary Media )

VPP policies get an F: The nonprofit Institute for Local Self-Reliance grades how welcoming states are to virtual power plants and other community-centered power systems, giving most a failing grade and only a few higher than a C. ( Utility Dive , report )

Fathom that: Ford begins shipping lithium iron phosphate EV battery cells from its Michigan factory to its Louisville, Kentucky, assembly plant, where the cells will be used in the forthcoming Fathom electric pickup truck. ( CNET )

Gas rule gets moving: A New York law ending the practice of utilities paying to hook up new homes to the gas system goes into effect next month, though regulations implementing it aren’t likely to be ready in time. ( New York Focus )

New York state is upgrading its ports for what it hopes will be a return to U.S. offshore wind development in the years after President Donald Trump leaves office.

On Friday, Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) announced over $ 228 million in state funding for five projects to bolster maritime infrastructure along New York’s rivers and harbors, Canary Media is first to report. The investments will enable companies and port operators to expand cargo-handling capacity, add heavy-lift equipment, and boost manufacturing capabilities — all things that could help offshore wind but aren’t limited to that.

The projects ​ “ will make our state prepared to support offshore wind in the future, but it also will ensure the investments produce jobs and economic benefits in the near term,” Doreen Harris, president and CEO of the New York State Energy Research Development Authority, said in an interview.

“ Port facilities and their upgrades tend to be capital-intensive, they tend to have long lead times. So our investments today are long-term in nature,” Harris said. She called the projects ​ “ strong infrastructure development for the state of New York, irrespective of their final use.”

The five awards draw from $ 200 million in grant funding that was initially earmarked to support offshore wind manufacturing and logistics but has been repurposed for maritime infrastructure more broadly. The money all stems from a $ 500 million initiative that Hochul announced for offshore wind in 2022 , during a far more optimistic time for the now-beleaguered industry.

In 2019 , New York set a target of building 9 gigawatts of offshore wind capacity by 2035 — enough to power roughly 6 million homes — to help meet its larger efforts to decarbonize the state’s electricity sector. As part of that push, state leaders sought to transform ports into job-creating hubs for making, assembling, and servicing the turbines that would spin in the Atlantic Ocean.

NYSERDA provisionally awarded $ 300 million in grant funding to GE Vernova and its subsidiary LM Wind Power in late 2023 to produce offshore wind turbine parts at the Port of Coeymans, along the Hudson River. At the nearby Port of Albany, local authorities began planning a $ 600 million facility that would supply steel tower pieces for offshore wind turbines.

Neither of those projects came to fruition, owing to economic headwinds and a series of supply chain problems , all of which were exacerbated by Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025 . Since then, his administration has made continual attempts to halt construction of in-progress wind farms, rescind approvals for planned projects, and thwart prospects for new development.

New York has led the legal fight against many of those actions — including Trump’s stop-work orders for the New York–based Sunrise Wind and Empire Wind projects, which have resumed construction — and the federal government’s unusual strategy of paying offshore wind developers to abandon their leases.

Still, state officials acknowledge that damage has been done to the state’s project pipeline. It is now ​ “ increasingly unlikely” that New York will meet its 9 -GW target in the next decade, owing to the ​ “ significant federal policy uncertainty” around offshore wind, according to the state’s 2025 energy plan .

Analysts have questioned whether developers will try again on American offshore wind projects anytime soon. Given that projects can take nearly a decade to build, it’s unlikely that any new offshore wind farms will move forward before 2035 without significant policy changes under future administrations, experts say.

New York currently has one operating offshore wind farm, the 132 -megawatt South Fork Wind. The state is expected to add another 1 . 7 GW in capacity next year when Equinor’s Empire Wind and Ørsted’s Sunrise Wind projects both come fully online. A total of nearly 6 GW is operational or near completion in the U.S. today.

The grants announced on Friday include $ 100 million to help the Port of Coeymans build a new heavy-lift wharf, expand its existing assets, and develop a facility to support ​ “ fabrication and industrial operations,” according to NYSERDA . The Port of Albany will receive $ 94 . 8 million to transform Beacon Island — the 85 -acre site that was supposed to host a turbine tower manufacturing facility — into a ​ “ multi-use marine terminal” that can support ultra-heavy-capacity cargo handling and staging needs.

In Mamaroneck, which abuts the Long Island Sound, Derecktor Shipyards was awarded $ 16 . 7 million so it can build and maintain vessels for a range of uses, including offshore wind operations, ferry services, and short-sea shipping. In Brooklyn, the firm Kalypso Offshore won $ 11 . 8 million to help build a subsea cable operations and maintenance hub, while the manufacturer Ionic Order received $ 5 million to expand its waterfront facility for making precast concrete products.

Harris said NYSERDA intends to issue additional awards to enable port upgrades across the state. She added that the agency is also soliciting grant proposals for ​ “ offshore wind predevelopment activities,” which could include community outreach, conducting transmission-interconnection studies, and other initiatives that lay the groundwork for future offshore wind farms.

“ We certainly have had to adjust our planning to reflect the realities of the day,” she said. ​ “ We have to be clear-eyed about the challenges this industry is facing that are illegal and unprecedented.”

Still, she added, ​ “ We remain committed to offshore wind in the mid- and longer term, so this port investment is reflective of that.”

scraped.h1: Senate OKs permitting bill that would boost clean and dirty energy
scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

20 November 2026

A bipartisan bill that would make it easier to build energy infrastructure — both dirty and clean — has passed the Senate by a 62 to 33 vote.

The sprawling Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would streamline permitting for energy and infrastructure projects by enacting significant changes to federal environmental regulations and introducing new policy mechanisms around data centers and the transmission grid. It would also provide developers with greater protections once a project is greenlit.

The House of Representatives will now take up the legislation, which was co-written by Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich (N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.) — two vocal supporters of clean energy — and Republican Sens. Mike Lee (Utah) and Shelley Moore Capito (W.Va.). The bill’s supporters aim to pass the current version now, while it has bipartisan momentum, rather than risk holding out for a better deal under the Democratic-led Congress next year.

Analysts widely expect that the legislation would accelerate the deployment of renewable energy — already the nation’s fastest-growing source of electricity. Critically, the bill would also help speed up the construction of transmission lines, which are needed to bring new energy generation online but notoriously difficult and slow to build in America. It would also ease permitting for fossil-fueled power plants, pipelines, and data centers.

The bipartisan bill has attracted a wide coalition of supporters that includes utility and fossil fuel groups as well as the clean-energy industry and many decarbonization advocates. But several major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, have come out against the legislation. A number of tribal groups have voiced concerns as well. Most Democratic senators ultimately voted against the bill.

Within the climate world, the key point of disagreement is whether the bill would drive an increase or a reduction in planet-warming emissions.

Different models have arrived at different conclusions. Energy analysis firm Rhodium Group has found that the bill would cause greenhouse gas emissions to fall. Think tank Resources for the Future also predicts it would reduce emissions . But other energy modelers have found the bill would spur so much construction of fossil fuel infrastructure that it would cause emissions to rise.

Despite the difficulty in projecting the bill’s impact, climate-minded supporters of the legislation say the U.S. energy transition can’t happen without major changes to federal permitting processes like those included in the bill.

Power lines offer a bracing example. The U.S. must double to triple its current transmission capacity to decarbonize the power grid by the mid- 2030 s, according to a study from Princeton University’s Repeat Project, but the pace of power line construction remains sluggish . Experts widely agree that the bill would accelerate the grid buildout.

Nevertheless, the bill’s opponents — many of whom support faster construction of clean energy and transmission — say it would give too much away to the fossil fuel industry. In particular, they warn that the bill’s modifications to the Federal Power Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act would let bad actors ram through fossil fuel and data center projects. They also fear that the Trump administration would continue to attack renewable energy projects even with the new law in place.

Opponents are now hoping the House, where Republicans hold a slim majority, will block the measure.

“ While a rogue president is waging a war on clean energy, the Senate rushed a deeply flawed bill that furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands, and endangers wildlife,” said Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford in a statement, adding that the House ​ “ must reject the Senate’s fast-tracked bill and demand debate and consideration to deliver for the people, not corporate polluters and Donald Trump.”

Permitting reform has been a live discussion for years, but over and over again, legislation has stalled out. This is the first time in recent years that a permitting reform bill has passed the Senate. Decarbonization advocates who support the bill argue that this is the best chance to enact reforms that are necessary for the energy transition — even if it requires some significant trade-offs.

Lena Moffitt, executive director of Evergreen Action, a climate advocacy group that’s come out in favor of the permitting bill , acknowledged in a statement that the legislation ​ “ includes many painful compromises,” but nevertheless her group is urging the House to pass it, too.

“ For years, our broken permitting system has stalled the power lines, clean energy projects, and public transit that make life more affordable,” she said. ​ “ While no single bill will solve the climate crisis or cost of living crisis on its own, this one will help us build cheap, clean energy faster and at scale and open the floodgates to the climate solutions we know are needed to save millions of lives.”

scraped.title: Why We’re Fighting Trump on Multiple Fronts to Protect the Arctic
scraped.description: The administration wants to maximize oil and gas drilling in Arctic regions of the U.S. We’re in court to stop them.
scraped.author: Earthjustice
scraped.h1: Why We’re Fighting Trump on Multiple Fronts to Protect the Arctic
scraped.body_text:
Congress is considering BAAJA, a permitting package that could fast-track fossil fuel projects and weaken bedrock environmental laws. Our Analysis

Congress is considering BAAJA, a permitting package that could fast-track fossil fuel projects and weaken bedrock environmental laws.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Our Stories

The administration wants to maximize oil and gas drilling in Arctic regions of the U.S. We’re in court to stop them.

By Earthjustice / Alaska Office

For the past two years, the Trump administration has relentlessly rolled out an all-out assault on public lands and waters in Alaska’s Arctic to maximize oil and gas drilling for the benefit of corporate polluters.

Earthjustice has spent decades fending off oil and gas drilling proposals in the region’s most sensitive landscapes to protect irreplaceable ecosystems, traditional ways of life, and our planet. Currently, we have two lawsuits pushing back on this administration’s attacks.

One challenges an extreme management plan and sweeping lease sale held by the administration this year in the Western Arctic that illegally granted oil companies leases to expand drilling into areas that have long been protected from industrialization. The second challenges the government’s decision to open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge’s entire Coastal Plain to oil and gas extraction and offer leases there, including in some of the most important habitat for threatened polar bears.

By fighting to keep fossil fuels in the ground in Alaska and elsewhere, we are helping to rein in a worsening climate crisis that is warming the Arctic nearly four times faster than anywhere else. Alaska needs ways to power its economy that respect its lands and people – not this.

Now this work is more urgent than ever. Across the Western Arctic and to the east in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, the Trump administration and fossil-fuel allies in Congress have opened more than 19 million acres for oil and gas extraction. Lease sales were held this year in both areas, and more than a million acres of globally significant wildlife habitat, including sensitive areas that have never been developed or targeted for drilling, were sold to highest-bidding fossil fuel companies.

In addition to these lease sales, the Trump administration is also seeking to change the rules in the Western Arctic to essentially rubber stamp oil and gas production projects and similarly cut out the public and limit environmental review for oil exploration.

As the Trump administration moves to aggressively expand fossil fuel development in the Arctic and change the rules to favor the oil industry, Earthjustice is engaging supporters like you to speak out and fighting back in court.

Arctic Ocean

Beaufort Sea

Nuiqsut

Chukchi Sea

Prudhoe Bay

Coastal Plain

Teshekpuk Lake

Western Arctic (National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska)

Arctic National Wildlife Refuge

Russia

Peter Hoey for Earthjustice

The Western Arctic (also called the "National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska" or NPR-A) is home to many millions of acres of specially designated lands because of their ecological and cultural importance. This includes Teshekpuk Lake, a wetlands area critical for migratory birds from around the world.

The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge is the country’s largest national refuge and home to diverse wildlife and Indigenous communities. Within the Arctic Refuge’s Coastal Plain are the calving grounds of the Porcupine Caribou herd.

At the beginning of this year, we restarted our long-running legal fight to protect the 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain of the Arctic Refuge from unlawful oil drilling. We originally sued the first Trump administration in 2020 when it opened this sacred area to oil drilling and held a lease sale. We’re back in court after the second Trump administration in October 2025 issued a decision reopening the entire Coastal Plain to oil leasing and reactivated the oil drilling leases sold during the first Trump administration.

When it opened the Refuge’s Coastal Plain to oil and gas development and subsequently held a lease sale, the administration failed to ensure that threatened Southern Beaufort Sea polar bears and the habitat they depend on will not be harmed. The administration’s actions violate several core environmental laws, including the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Our lawsuit — filed with NRDC, who is co-counsel, and representing NRDC, the Center for Biological Diversity, and Friends of the Earth — challenges these illegal leasing programs under NEPA, the ESA, the National Wildlife Refuge Act, the Wilderness Act, the Alaska National Interest Lands Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act.

Polar bears on the coast of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. (Florian Schulz / protectthearctic.org)

The Coastal Plain is irreplaceable wildlife habitat and sacred Indigenous land.

This leasing program poses considerable risks to polar bears, including the loss of important denning habitat, disturbance of denning mothers, and increased human-bear conflicts. The government acknowledges that the program is likely to lead to the death of dozens of polar bear cubs. Yet it gave its stamp of approval and declined to impose adequate protective measures for the bears.

The Coastal Plain is also the calving ground for the Porcupine Caribou Herd and supports millions of migratory birds, marine mammals, muskox, fish, and more. For the Gwich’in people who have relied on the caribou herd since time immemorial, this land is spiritually and culturally essential. The leasing plan would threaten these irreplaceable resources.

Caribou on the coastal plane of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska. (Florian Schulz / protectthearctic.org)

In the Western Arctic, a vast public land area west of the Arctic Refuge, we are suing the federal government over the BLM’s 5.5-million-acre lease sale announced in February and held in March 2026. The sale offered oil companies ecologically and culturally significant lands around Teshekpuk Lake and along the Colville River that have long been protected from oil and gas extraction. In March, 11 oil companies bid on 187 tracts totaling about 1.3 million acres. The suit also challenges the sale’s underlying management plan, re-adopted from the first Trump administration, that would open 82% of the Western Arctic to oil and gas leasing.

Two terns in the Western Arctic, near Lake Teshekpuk. (Kiliii Yuyan for Earthjustice)

The Western Arctic is the nation’s largest intact tract of public land, and it remains largely undeveloped. The region is home to iconic and imperiled wildlife species like polar bears and seals that depend on sea ice and includes habitat for caribou and other species that are central to the cultural practices and food security of nearby Indigenous communities. The Western Arctic also attracts migratory birds from around the globe, and hosts some of the highest densities of breeding shorebirds in the world.

By approving a management plan that allows oil and gas leasing on most lands in the Western Arctic — including in ecologically sensitive areas that have previously been off limits to oil drilling — and then holding an expansive lease sale and approving large-scale industrial exploration activity in those areas , this administration is prioritizing fossil fuel production over all other uses of these lands .

Earthjustice will continue fighting in court to keep oil and gas interests from destroying the Arctic and fighting fossil fuels that are driving the climate crisis. We stand ready to defend against unlawful actions by this administration.

Take action, and add your voice today:

Alaska Office

Opened in 1978, our Alaska regional office works to safeguard public lands, waters, and wildlife from destructive oil and gas drilling, mining, and logging, and to protect the region's marine and coastal ecosystems.

We’ve received your feedback — thank you!

“We cannot develop the vast majority of already known oil reserves, let alone Arctic Ocean oil, if we are to avoid the worst climate change consequences.”

Stay informed on how we hold accountable those who break our environmental laws.

As financial markets increasingly look to be buckling under the weight of the AI industry’s accounting and economic model contradictions, the Revolving Door Project is renewing our call for Democrats to preemptively reject any consideration—under any circumstance—of public funds to bail the industry out of its financial precarity. In August, we wrote that lawmakers must “take the simple and clear public stance of opposing any bailout for an “industry” that has generated far more arrogance and distress than productivity or happiness.”

Revolving Door Project Executive Director Jeff Hauser issued the following statement:

“As Anthropic’s founders are already cashing out, SpaceX (which now contains XAI) continues to slide, and as a regulatory gift basket for the industry is jammed through Congress, bypassing regular procedure and ignoring Democrats’ mandate from the midterm elections , it is more important than ever to brace for corporate America’s imminent dusting off of the “now is not the time to oppose moral hazard” playbook.”

“The AI industry did not consult the public in its disastrous financing, in fact it often aggressively obscured the details from communities and sought to trample democratic oversight. This disastrous speculative bubble has siphoned off enormous amounts of public money already, poisoned communities, eroded cyber infrastructure , and derailed the work of moving to a green economy. The public has already subsidized more than its fair share of the costs of this boondoggle. So when the industry comes hat in hand begging for us to save them from themselves, the message must be unequivocal: not one dollar more.”

U.S. home insurers took in an estimated $113 billion in excess underwriting profit from 2021 through 2025, according to a new report from Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, Revolving Door Project , and Public Citizen .

Drawing on data from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, the report, Home Insurers Are Ripping People Off Amid the Climate Crisis , shows soaring insurance costs cannot be fully explained by rising climate impacts, increased cost of reinsurance, or construction costs. Excessive industry spending on overhead like executive compensation, advertising, and shareholder dividends, and record high profits are also to blame for climbing insurance prices. Meanwhile, insurers are aggressively denying and delaying claims, leaving homeowners without the protection they paid for. The report also highlights at the state level how much climate adaptation could be paid for with the industry’s ill-gotten gains.

Key Findings

“Home insurers are simultaneously overcharging and short-changing households as the fossil fuel-driven climate crisis intensifies,” said Kenny Stancil, deputy research director at the Revolving Door Project. “Relentlessly hiking rates and denying ever more claims has enabled insurance companies to generate billions of dollars in excess underwriting income, which they waste on lavish CEO pay packages and endless ads, and funnel into financial markets to boost investment returns for shareholders. Public officials must use every tool at their disposal to curb industry profiteering and insist that these ill-gotten gains be used instead to help communities adapt to increasingly frequent and severe weather.”

“Insurance companies are maximizing profits by raising rates, withdrawing from communities, and closing a staggering number of claims without payment,” said Elyse Schupak, policy advocate with Public Citizen’s Climate Program. “After spending years pointing to climate change and rising disaster costs to justify offering policyholders less protection at a higher price, the insurance industry is reaping record profits. Insurance companies preach about protecting households, but the numbers reveal that the industry is actively padding its bottom line at their expense.

“Families are paying too much for home insurance and getting less back when climate disasters strike. In 2025, insurers paid just 55 cents in claims for every dollar they collected in premiums, far below the historical average of 70 to 80 cents in the 1990s,” said Alex Martin, climate finance policy director at Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. “ Insurance regulators and policymakers at every level of government should take action now to stop families from being forced to pay more for less.”

Along with these findings, the report also includes policy recommendations that prioritize climate adaptation and transparency for consumers: Strengthening oversight of insurer rate increases and considering loss ratio trends, requiring insurers to invest in and reward climate resilience, and increasing transparency over insurer underwriting, pricing, and claim decisions are among the report recommendations to address the industry’s profiteering.

scraped.title: Authors Sue LA Library Over Anti-Palestinian Discrimination After Talk Cancelled
scraped.description: Even institutions meant to be dedicated to free speech and inclusion are censoring Palestinian writers.
scraped.author: Marianne Dhenin
scraped.h1: Authors Sue LA Library Over Anti-Palestinian Discrimination After Talk Cancelled
scraped.body_text:
Even institutions meant to be dedicated to free speech and inclusion are censoring Palestinian writers.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Two authors have filed a lawsuit against the City of Los Angeles, alleging that the Los Angeles Public Library engaged in anti-Palestinian discrimination and violated their free speech rights after the library’s leadership canceled an online event last December where the two were slated to speak to teens about their books, which feature Palestinian characters. This lawsuit against one of the largest public library systems in the nation comes at a time when anti-Palestinian racism and censorship are growing more entrenched across the country, now more than three years into the U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza.

“The stakes are really high, and it’s about so much more than the rights of the authors or even the rights of the readers,” Nora Lester Murad, one of the authors and plaintiffs in the case, told Truthout . “If kids and adults can’t be exposed to representation of Palestinians that’s diverse and nuanced and human and complex and multifaceted, [that erasure] converges with the anti-Palestinian and anti-Muslim narratives that are being used to justify genocide.”

Murad and Palestinian American author Jenan Matari filed the lawsuit in the Superior Court of Los Angeles in late September to demand accountability for the Los Angeles Public Library’s cancellation of their event and to draw attention to anti-Palestinian censorship in the arts.

Matari is the author of the picture book Everything Grows in Jiddo’s Garden , about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather. Murad was slated to discuss Ida in the Middle , her young adult novel about a 13-year-old Palestinian American girl. The two were scheduled to speak at an online event on December 6, 2025, as part of Read Palestine Week , a global weeklong program highlighting Palestinian authors and stories celebrated in late November and early December each year.

The Los Angeles Public Library’s teen council, a youth volunteer group, voted to host a Read Palestine Week event, and the library’s Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group invited Murad and Matari and acted as liaisons between the authors and library administration in the lead-up to the scheduled event, according to the legal complaint.

But just three days before the event was scheduled to take place, the group notified Murad and Matari that the library administration had canceled it. The notice provided no further explanation for the cancellation, according to the legal complaint.

Records obtained by Los Angeles Public Press in a public records request and cited in the legal complaint later revealed that a staff librarian had emailed library leadership in mid-November 2025, accusing Murad and Matari of having “strong terrorist ties and virulently antisemitic views.” The email said it was sent on behalf of a group of Jewish library staffers and referenced an article from the right-wing Washington Free Beacon and profiles of the authors on Canary Mission , a pro-Israel doxxing platform. It also accused the Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group of having “deeply antisemitic views” and showing “racist behavior to me and others in our Heritage group.”

“This attack was not from outside but from inside the library.”

Later in December 2025, City Librarian John Szabo sent an internal email to staff claiming Murad and Matari’s event had been canceled because the library “has a responsibility to remain nonpartisan and apolitical” and that doing so was “necessary to uphold the Library’s commitment to an inclusive environment free of hate, discrimination, and harassment,” according to a copy of that email obtained by The LA Reporter in a public records request.

Szabo did not respond to Truthout’s request for comment before deadline. A member of the library’s public relations team told Truthout that the library cannot comment on pending litigation.

Murad told Truthout the accusations and cancellation follow a familiar pattern in which criticism of Israel is conflated with antisemitism in order to silence Palestinian speakers like Matari, anti-Zionist Jewish speakers like Murad, or others who speak out to criticize Israel or in support of Palestinian liberation. But, she added, the Los Angeles Public Library case is also unique because the pressure to censor Palestine-related speech came not from outside pro-Israel pressure groups but from inside an institution mandated to oppose censorship.

“People assume that when an institution like a library caves into anti-Palestinian racism that the attack was from outside, and this attack was not from outside but from inside the library,” Murad told Truthout . “You have to address those things differently. One is you’re telling the library, ‘Please don’t cave into external pressure,’ and the other one is ‘Hey, Library, you are the censor.’”

Neither Murad nor Matari is unfamiliar with anti-Palestinian censorship. Murad has published about the silencing of Palestinian narratives in libraries and children’s books. Matari has had events canceled before: Two private bookshops had already canceled planned readings with her before the Los Angeles Public Library event, and she told The Guardian that a New York library canceled a scheduled event with her after the Los Angeles news broke last year.

After the cancellation of Murad and Matari’s scheduled talk last December, more than 100 Los Angeles Public Library workers signed a letter condemning the move and emphasizing the library’s mission to oppose censorship. “Restrictions placed upon Palestinian voices are in direct opposition to the mission of the library,” the letter read. “It is the mission and the mandate of the Library to collect stories and protect them from censorship.”

The American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California and the National Coalition Against Censorship also called on the library to reschedule Murad and Matari’s talk in a joint letter in February 2026. That letter argued that the library “likely violated the First Amendment” when it canceled the event. It also criticized Szabo’s assertion that the library should remain “nonpartisan and apolitical,” calling it “absurd.” “If the library were to interpret its mission … to require it not to invite any author who has expressed strong political opinions, it would be hard pressed to find a single author to participate in its programming,” it read.

An Action Network campaign has since also resulted in more than 7,300 protest letters being sent to the Los Angeles Public Library from concerned patrons and community members. “The cancellation of an event that the youth of Los Angeles put the time and effort into putting on feels particularly antithetical to the mission of their library, both in their stated mission as well as the social function of the library as a space that fosters learning and exploring for youth,” Summer, a Los Angeles–based Palestinian artist and library patron who joined that campaign, told Truthout . “The library must be accountable to both the artists that they invited as well as the patrons who do not agree with that cancellation.”

“I don’t want to see any more authors experience the racism and discrimination I have faced at the LA Public Library, simply because I’m Palestinian and have continued to speak out against an ongoing genocide.”

Murad told Truthout that after such an outpouring of support failed to move library administrators, and after several unsuccessful attempts to engage them in conflict resolution talks, she and Matari felt they had little choice but to file a lawsuit. Their case alleges free speech violations, discrimination, and breach of contract, and seeks compensatory damages and an injunction that would require the library to reschedule the canceled event.

“When a library communicates through their actions that certain books and people are dangerous, so dangerous we can’t even let them come to the library and talk to us, it puts the weight of a public institution, so the government, behind a dangerous and racist message — it’s not just that our rights are being violated,” Murad told Truthout . “For Palestinians and for everyone’s right to learn from Palestinians and learn about Palestinians, we felt that we were doing a lawsuit for more than just us.”

Matari, in a press release announcing the lawsuit, said: “We need to hold public institutions accountable in order to protect free speech for all people, including the right to speak out for Palestinian freedom … I don’t want to see any more authors experience the racism and discrimination I have faced at the LA Public Library, simply because I’m Palestinian and have continued to speak out against an ongoing genocide.”

The city attorney’s office told Truthout it could not comment on pending litigation.

While it will take time before a resolution is reached in Murad and Matari’s case against the City of Los Angeles, Murad said she hopes the filing will send a message to other institutions that discrimination and silencing of Palestinian and other marginalized authors and narratives have consequences. “This isn’t just happening to us; Palestinians are being targeted by anti-Palestinian racism, and it’s affecting readers, and institutions have to be held accountable,” she said.

As Read Palestine Week approaches again, beginning November 29 this year, Summer told Truthout she hopes other arts institutions will reject the example set by the Los Angeles Public Library and that community members will advocate for those institutions to uplift Palestinian voices. “One of the ways people can support the blossoming of Palestinian art within public libraries is by requesting books and events by Palestinians,” she said. “All it takes is letting your desire to learn from them and read with them be known to your library branch.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

scraped.body_text:
“I do not bear good news,” Panama’s environment minister said. “We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change.

“This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on Democracy Now! by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries.

“At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, [are] saying is, ‘There is no money at home.’ But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from Turkey on the final scheduled day of the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31.

Climate advocacy groups and Indigenous organizations from across the world have slammed this gathering as the “worst COP ever” and rejected the latest draft text as a “disaster,” urging developing countries to reject the latest draft text.

Meanwhile, at a news conference just before our broadcast, Panama’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro has threatened to block any final agreement if it doesn’t include a cap on oil production. Earlier this week, he spoke out forcefully against the role of what he described as the “petroleum mafia.”

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: I do not bear good news. We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.

AMY GOODMAN: And this is Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s environment minister, speaking just before we went to air, flanked by representatives from Finland and Vanuatu, Belgium, Ivory Coast, France, Guatemala and other countries.

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: We have come together because we feel that the COP can still be saved if we focus on six key issues for our final declaration that clarifies for the world where we must go.

The first is that science must be the foundation. Everything we do must be based on science.

Second, we need a clear transition away from fossil fuels. It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly. We must transition away from fossil fuels in an orderly manner, if we are to confront climate change.

The third point for us, which is very important, is that fair contributions to climate finance must come from those with greatest responsibility. You pollute, you pay. It’s actually rather simple. You cause the problem, you must help to fix it. If you are the biggest emitter of CO2, if you are the biggest producers or consumers of petroleum, then you must contribute to solve this problem and these issues.

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier today, in a packed room for the press, the Climate Action Network, which encompasses over 2,500 civil society groups worldwide, as speakers detailed the failures of the COP, there were activists in the room, journalists and many others representing this COP31. The activists on the stage called out the European Union and other developed nations for their obstruction. The room repeatedly broke out into chants of “shame.” The moderator of CAN called the draft text a “disgrace” and introduced speakers.

DANNI TAAFFE: Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International.

TASNEEM ESSOP: There is nothing on the table that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. … This COP has had the highest number of lobbyists — fossil fuel lobbyists, AI lobbyists, CCUS lobbyists, CDR lobbyists. So, what we’re leaving this COP with is decisions made to actually promote the interests of those culprits.

DANNI TAAFFE: Avantika Goswami from CSE India.

AVANTIKA GOSWAMI: The European Union have, in a way, taken on the mantle that the U.S. has left the vacuum of, the blocker that the U.S. was. Unfortunately, we expected them to be leaders, but they have disappointed us. … And these are the parties that posture the most in the media. They say they are committed to climate multilateralism, and they are concerned about 1.5°C and the breach of the Paris Agreement goals. … So, we want to let them know that we see them and the games they’ve played, and we will not stand for it.

DANNI TAAFFE: Anabella Rosemberg from CAN International.

ANABELLA ROSEMBERG: The COP is not dying. The COP is being killed, not because it’s bloated, not because it’s inefficient or useless. It’s being killed because it’s the last space where civil society, where developing countries can hold developed countries accountable. … We are now asked to accept more empty words. We say no. We will fight back. And we say thank you for nothing. … So, this is also an appeal for all of us, for all the movements, to keep working together and change the faces of who’s representing developed countries in this place.

DANNI TAAFFE: And Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa.

MOHAMED ADOW: I can tell you, without any doubt, that this has been the worst COP ever.

AUDIENCE: Shame! Shame! Shame!

MOHAMED ADOW: Communities living in drought, floods and failed harvest were promised action. They cannot survive on an annual renewal of promises. We’re effectively pushing poor, vulnerable countries into further debt to protect themselves from a crisis they did little to cause.

TASNEEM ESSOP: I want to just say two things. One, when you come into a COP and a commissioner of a very important regional bloc says, “We’re not coming with any finance. Finance is dead in the water,” think about that, “dead in the water.” For us in the Global South, dead in the water is very literal. So it’s a shameful way to come to a COP where we are going to be fighting for adaptation finance to protect people from being dead in the water.

Secondly, the pledges that they brought to this COP for adaptation finance, you would have seen totaled around $50 million, which we said in our ECO is half the cost of an F-35 Lightning fighter jet.

AUDIENCE: Shame! Shame! Shame!

TASNEEM ESSOP: And we’re not even going to measure that $50 million in relation to the $3 trillion that rich nations are spending on wars, a genocide and conflicts across the world. Put that into perspective.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Tasneem Essop, the executive director of CAN, Climate Action Network International, and others speaking at a news conference earlier today. She is from South Africa.

For more, we’re joined by several leading environmental justice advocates.

Harjeet Singh is strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, a social justice organization, also global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign.

Nafkote Dabi is the change policy lead for Oxfam International, where she works at the intersection of climate and inequality. She’s from Ethiopia, where the next COP, COP32, will be held, in Addis.

And Meena Raman is with us, head of programs at Third World Network and president of Friends of the Earth Malaysia.

We thank you all for being with us. We’re going to start with Harjeet. You, as well as Nafkote, were holding up a sign behind the speakers that said, ”ECO. End the Genocide,” with big letters, ”SHAME!” There was rage in this room. It was the most packed news conference I had seen, packed with activists. Talk about where we are at on this last scheduled day, though it’s clear it’s going to go further.

HARJEET SINGH: Well, it is a matter of shame, Amy. This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction. We have spent more time on talking about electrification, without any details whether it’s going to be green or is going to be accessible to people. We have removed the reference to —

AMY GOODMAN: Wait. Just to explain that, “electrification” is sort of the watchword here.

HARJEET SINGH: Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: And the idea was renewable electrification.

HARJEET SINGH: Exactly.

AMY GOODMAN: But that seems to be — “renewable” — being dropped.

HARJEET SINGH: Absolutely. And otherwise, why are we talking about electrification in this space, if it is not green? That’s the question we should be asking. We do not see any reference to fossil fuel phaseout. Now, only the words are not enough, and I can explain that later, but that being dropped from the previous draft is just not acceptable. Adaptation finance, there was a clear agreement to scale it to $120 billion annually for developing countries.

AMY GOODMAN: No one knows what “adaptation finance” means.

HARJEET SINGH: OK. So, adaptation means helping communities prepare to deal with climate impacts. It’s about retrofitting their homes. It’s about building dikes. It’s about making sure that their agriculture is resilient and we are food-secure. And if you do not provide money — let’s take the example of Nepal. The reason they faced such a catastrophic disaster, because they were not prepared. When we see people in Ethiopia —

AMY GOODMAN: More than seven — what? About 7,000 people dead or missing?

HARJEET SINGH: Exactly. That’s the number.

AMY GOODMAN: Because of a glacier that melted?

HARJEET SINGH: Absolutely. So, it was a glacial lake outburst floods. And the numbers are important. They lost — the destruction was to the tune of $2.6 billion, and they will need now $5 billion for recovery and rehabilitation, which is 10% of their GDP. Imagine.

AMY GOODMAN: Why should the wealthy countries give it to them?

HARJEET SINGH: Because glaciers melted because of the burning of fossil fuels, and they did not provide money to Nepal for adaptation, and they are facing now loss and damage. So, Nepal, we should see it as a report card of the climate inaction that we have seen over the last 30 years. We did not phase out fossil fuels in time. That resulted in melting of glaciers. And we did not even have a plan or support to Nepal to deal with these climate impacts. And it shows that how we are failing to deal with climate impacts. And that’s why we say “shame.”

AMY GOODMAN: Meena Raman, you are head of programs at Third World Network, head of Friends of the Earth Malaysia. You have been to so many of these conferences. You, too, have expressed rage on each panel you are at. What do you want to see happen here?

MEENA RAMAN: Well, at this particular point in time, it’s relatively empty. The most important aspect of the COP is money, whether it’s for emission reductions, whether it’s for adaptation, whether it’s for loss and damage. The developing world came together, and they said, “We need money on the table of provision of finance.” What the developing countries demanded was actually to ensure that we talk about this. It was about talking about how the developed world is going to do that.

But all we came here as, you know, the EU commissioner was saying anything about finance is dead in the water. Now, that is horror, because we just came out of Nepal, as we know, and you say, “dead in the water.” People are literally dying due to the historical —

AMY GOODMAN: In the water.

MEENA RAMAN: “Dead in the water.” That’s what Hoekstra said. It was — it was for us —

AMY GOODMAN: The EU negotiator.

MEENA RAMAN: The EU commissioner. The EU commissioner. So, even before this COP, he said it. So, when you go to the negotiating halls, what you saw was finance was dead in the water, nothing on finance. So there’s no point talking about having higher ambition in terms of emission reductions or developing countries having to do fossil fuel phaseout or having more targets on electrification. They’re not going to be able to do this, if what they say is the means to implement that is not available. So, this is where this COP always becomes a problem.

AMY GOODMAN: You are wearing a sign — you are wearing a sticker, Nafkote Dabi, on the back of your ID here that says “Make rich polluters pay.” You have said — you’ve talked about inequality. Oxfam International is known for their report , “Disaster Divide.” The richest 0.1%, or 8 million people, have more emissions than the bottom 3.5 billion people, and that their carbon emissions contribute to the increase of climate disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and food crises. Can you explain how you feel this can be remedied? And how close to a tipping point are we?

NAFKOTE DABI: So, at the heart of the negotiations right now lies money, because, ultimately, you know, to support communities to adapt to the climate crisis, they need finance. And what rich countries, especially the EU, is saying is, ‘There is no money at home.’ But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities. You know, just private jets alone, you can raise $45 billion a year. From the excess of profit of fossil fuel companies, you can raise $400 billion. So, this money is available, and you can support communities at home, whether in Europe or the U.S. And then you can commit to your international climate finance obligation and support communities in the Global South, especially, you know, in Africa, that are faced with droughts, floods, displacement and death.

AMY GOODMAN: You know, we just had a headline on a vote on war in the U.S. Senate, and the amount — the billions of dollars that are being spent on the war in Iran, which has also led the entire world to understand how dependent we are on fossil fuels.

NAFKOTE DABI: Exactly. You know, emissions from military is about 5%. This is something that we’re not talking about. There’s huge money, as you said, Amy, going towards militarization, when communities around the world are actually literally dying from escalating extreme weather events. For the first time, by the way, Amy, I’m feeling really desperate, because we’re being told next year is going to be the hottest year on record. It’s going to go up to 1.7. Right now as we’re speaking, communities around the world are faced with the worst El Niño on record, and there is no support. These are communities that have done the least to cause the climate crisis, but they’re being left alone to deal with this situation. So, it’s a very shameful COP.

AMY GOODMAN: Now, what are the NGOs going to do? We just have two minutes before we end with an 8-year-old child who spoke out. A few years ago, it was Greta Thunberg, when she was 15 years old. Now we’re going to Little Miss Environment Kenya, who is 8, who has something to teach her elders. But one last statement. Harjeet, where we go from here? Are the NGOs going to reject the text? And what does it matter? What role do you play?

HARJEET SINGH: So, we have already rejected the current text. And what we would like to see: the developing countries really standing up and reject this text. And we keep saying developing countries are here to represent their own citizens. They can’t accept a text which will not enable them to implement climate action back home because there is no money on the table. And that’s exactly the reason developing countries have now — need to be very loud and clear in saying this COP outcome is not going to help us, unless developed countries open their pockets. It’s all about money.

AMY GOODMAN: Meena, how can it be this is the largest COP, and you’re talking about it being the greatest failure? Pick up that mic.

MEENA RAMAN: Yeah. The problem is that when you have the developed world come here and say that they don’t have national budgets to put on the table, and they talk about leadership, I think it is really imperative that we work with our Global North to actually put the pressure on the developed countries. We can’t have COP after COP backsliding. We let alone scaling up our resources. The U.K. has cut its pledge to the Green Climate Fund. The Global Environment Facility, the worst replenishment ever. So, when they are backsliding, here we are asking for more top up.

AMY GOODMAN: And finally, Nafkote, if you can talk about next year? We’re going to Ethiopia for COP32. What is the point of these COPs?

NAFKOTE DABI: You know, Ethiopia is faced — is at the frontline of the climate crisis. Ethiopians know what it means to face drought. Ethiopians are the most resilient people. They have been through many droughts, droughts after droughts. Right now, as I said, we’re faced with El Niño. Next year, the Ethiopian COP presidency needs to deliver justice for communities at the frontline of the climate crisis.

AMY GOODMAN: We have to leave it there, Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International, Harjeet Singh of Fossil Food Treaty Initiative, Meena Raman of Third World Network.

Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. scraped.h1: Israel Uploaded 3.5M Photos of Palestinians to Amazon Facial Recognition Tech
scraped.body_text:
For years, Israel has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and restrict Palestinian movement.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A new report reveals that Israel uploaded 3.5 million photos of Palestinians to Amazon’s facial recognition platform shortly after it launched its genocide in Gaza — shining yet more light on the tech industry’s complicity in repression and human rights abuses around the world.

The report , written by Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham and published in The Guardian this week, documents how the Israeli military uploaded the images to Amazon’s cloud soon after the start of Israel’s invasion and bombardment of Gaza in 2023. The military told Amazon that they uploaded the images specifically for the purpose of using Amazon’s Rekognition platform for facial recognition, according to documents leaked to the Guardian .

For years, the Israeli military has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and enact harsh restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement. Soldiers use a smartphone app called Blue Wolf, for example, to scan and catalog the faces of Palestinians passing through Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank.

In Gaza, Israel has increased its use of facial recognition technology since the start of its 2023 assault. In early 2024, The New York Times called Israel’s facial recognition program in Gaza an “ experimental effort ” — acknowledging that the mass surveillance at times “wrongly flagged civilians as wanted Hamas militants.”

Davies and Abraham’s latest report builds on Abraham’s prior reporting for The Guardian and +972 Magazine , as well as the findings discussed in NAZA , a 2026 documentary co-directed by Abraham. The film highlights how Israel has used AI-based surveillance systems to facilitate Israel’s remote killings of thousands of civilians in Gaza since 2023.

The report also demonstrates how Israel has deepened its relationship with Amazon over the course of its genocide in Gaza. As noted by Who Profits , Israel awarded Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS) a large-scale tender in 2021, known as Project Nimbus , allowing Israel to transfer large quantities of data onto its services. Israel’s use of AWS has only expanded since then.

Last December, Mohammed Mhawish, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, wrote about how Israel has intensified its use of surveillance since the start of the genocide.

The Israeli military has used “artificial intelligence to generate kill lists, monitoring our social-media accounts, and storing in bulk the audio of our phone calls,” he wrote.

Israel used these technologies to target journalists specifically — both within their own homes and while they were reporting, Mhawish said. Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, as well as other companies like Palantir Technologies, provide the infrastructure for the Israeli military to store Palestinians’ phone calls, analyze their communication, and decide who to target with a drone strike and when.

Last year, an investigative report by Abraham revealed the extensive use of Microsoft’s Azure platform by the Israeli military in order to surveil Palestinians’ phone calls before identifying targets for aerial bombardment. The revelations prompted tech workers to organize to force Microsoft to end Azure cloud storage and AI services in a partial withdrawal of contracts with Israel, though activists say that the company still retains contracts with the country .

Activists, including tech workers in No Tech for Apartheid , continue to organize against Google and Amazon’s Project Nimbus, and campaigns have grown internationally against Palantir.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.
