scraped.title: The Trumps are enriching themselves. Here come the investigations.
scraped.description: Voters said corruption was a major issue in the historic congressional landslide.
scraped.author: Dan Friedman
scraped.h1: The Trumps Are Enriching Themselves. Here Come the Investigations.
scraped.body_text:
Dan Friedman and Russ Choma January+February 2027 Issue

Wesley Merritt

Wesley Merritt

In 2025, we asked an adviser to Donald Trump Jr. about the ethical issues posed by the presidential son’s business activities. “Write your ridiculous story. Literally no one cares,” he shot back . “We don’t actually give a fuck.”

That last sentence was clearly true. Since the 47th president returned to office, he and his family have added billions of dollars to their net worth, brazenly profiting from crypto deals, real estate projects, and other ventures. But it turns out that Americans actually care quite a bit. An October Financial Times poll found that 69 percent of respondents were very or somewhat concerned about “corruption, self-dealing, or conflicts of interest” in the Trump administration. Even a few GOP politicians are noticing. In September, Sen. John Curtis of Utah urged his colleagues to haul Don Jr. before Congress and investigate the “use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit.”

Curtis’ request went nowhere. On November 3, however, Republicans lost control of the House and Senate in a landslide. Exit polling showed that government corruption was a major issue for 90 percent of voters, and Democrats will now have the power to launch investigations, hold hearings, and issue subpoenas. The White House did not respond to detailed questions for this story. But as the 120th Congress gets underway, here are eight examples of Trumpian money-making schemes and conflicts of interest that lawmakers might finally get to the bottom of.

Last May, Don Jr. celebrated his wedding with a bash on a private island that can rent for $100,000 per night. Guests, along with a five-tier funfetti cake, were flown in by helicopter. You might think that given his growing wealth, the president’s son would have covered the bill. But as his father would say , “Wrong.” ProPublica later reported that Umar Kremlev, an oligarch close to Vladimir Putin, helped finance the extravagant event—a gesture the happy couple insisted was nothing more than an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend.” Following an uproar, Kremlev told reporters that Don Jr. eventually paid him back. As it turned out, that wasn’t the extent of the two men’s travels. In August, according to the Financial Times , Don Jr. joined Kremlev on a hunting expedition in Mongolia and bagged a rare wild sheep.

In 2024, the Trumps launched World Liberty Financial—a crypto platform billed as an alternative to the banking system. Its main creation was the USD1 stablecoin, which can be used for digital transactions and whose value is pegged to the dollar. What’s in it for the Trumps? When you turn actual dollars into USD1 coins, their company gets to invest your money and keep the profits. So when Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the national security adviser for the United Arab Emirates, conducted a $2 billion crypto transaction using USD1, that was a pretty good deal for the first family. And Tahnoon isn’t just a client, he’s an owner! Four days before President Donald Trump returned to office, Tahnoon’s business empire reportedly purchased 49 percent of the company. He paid half a billion dollars, of which almost $200 million may have gone directly to Trump family entities, according to a lawsuit . (World Liberty says it has “complied with all applicable” laws.)

Unlike World Liberty’s crypto offerings—which at least purport to have a real-world use—the separately run $TRUMP meme coin seems to have no purpose other than signaling one’s fealty to the president. The company behind the coin has a licensing deal with the president, who has appeared at events for $TRUMP’s top investors. The coin can’t be used to buy anything; it’s simply a tool for speculation. The good news, for Trump, is that every time the coin is bought or sold, he collects transaction fees. In all, he appears to have earned a whopping $635 million from “royalties” related to the coin. The bad news, for you, if you bought into $TRUMP, is that investors have lost a lot of money—an estimated $3.8 billion as of last summer, according to the analytics firm Nansen.

Donald Trump’s Twitter knockoff, Truth Social, has been limping along with relatively few users and unimpressive revenues. But it does boast one power poster of note: the president himself. It’s the place to go if you want Trump’s unfiltered thoughts and policy announcements, which he apparently sees as a business opportunity. For the low price of up to $100,000 per month, you can purchase nearly instantaneous access to Trump’s pronouncements—a valuable resource for high-frequency traders —rather than having to wait a few moments like the rest of us. The company’s CEO has bragged that “markets already move on Truth Social posts.” So now, if you pay enough, you can be among the first to know which way Trump will be moving those markets.

In a particularly dystopian example of how Trump’s kids are cashing in, Eric and Don Jr. have built up investments in drone companies — plural!— seeking business with the US government and foreign states. Space-Eyes, a firm pursuing federal contracts, gave Eric an ownership share that The Wall Street Journal said was poised to be worth around $12 million, in exchange for using his “network of contacts” to help land business. An investment firm tied to the Trump sons backed another outfit, Powerus, as it tried to sell drones to Gulf states facing threats from Iran. That positions the Trumps, as the Associated Press put it , “to potentially benefit from a war that their father began.”

In a statement to Mother Jones, a spokesperson for Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump disputed the idea that they’re profiting from their dad’s presidency. The sons “are private citizens who have spent decades building, operating, and investing in successful businesses across a wide range of industries, long before their father first ran for public office,” said Kimberly Benza, who works for the Trump Organization. “Neither holds a government position, has broken any laws, or has ever sought to influence government policy, regulatory decisions, or the award of government contracts for personal financial gain.”

Benza added that Eric’s and Don Jr.’s “business careers did not begin with their father’s presidency, nor should they be expected to end because of it and any attempt to portray their lawful business activities as evidence of corruption, without identifying any actual misconduct, is baseless and fundamentally misleading.”

The Trumps aren’t the only nepo babies trying to cash in. As Steve Witkoff, Trump’s roving envoy, pursued a short-lived ceasefire between Israel and Hamas in 2025, his son Alex unsuccessfully solicited real estate investments from Gulf states involved in the peace process. While Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick arranged US government financing for mining in Kazakhstan, both families moved to profit off the deal. Eric and Don Jr. were investors; Brandon and Kyle Lutnick, who in 2025 took over their father’s investment firm, earned big fees arranging private financing. And Continental Strategy—where Katie Wiles, the daughter of Trump’s former chief of staff, is a partner—has nabbed contracts from clients like Republika Srpska, a Serbian nationalist enclave seeking US support to secede from Bosnia.

The president has spent much of his second term seeking to rebuild Washington in his image: the triumphal arch , the Reflecting Pool , the Kennedy Center , a championship golf course . All this costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and to pay for it, his aides have used a constellation of organizations to raise cash from companies and oligarchs whose fortunes could be affected by the administration’s policies. There’s Freedom 250 , a National Park Foundation subsidiary that used corporate donations and public money to fund Trump’s self-aggrandizing semiquincentennial celebrations . The Trust for the National Mall is funneling donations to his White House ballroom. And a new foundation is raising money for Trump’s “National Garden of American Heroes,” a maze of statues to be built on a site where new construction is currently illegal. Trump knows which special interests are paying for him to rip up DC. But in many cases, Congress does not .

Trump’s presidential library—to be built on pricey Miami real estate gifted by the state of Florida—doesn’t sound like it will have many books. But he’s suggested it will include a hotel , a golden statue of himself, and the $400 million Boeing 747 donated by Qatar for use as Air Force One. Presidential libraries face few rules , and Trump’s has already pulled in millions from his personal lawsuits , corporations , and even the proceeds two advisers earned from foreign interests. So when Trump prepares to go back up the golden escalator—a replica of which is also planned for the facility—the library may well be his last grift standing.

scraped.title: The AI safety community is increasingly freaked out. Should they be?
scraped.description: “I am scared, sad, and angry.”
scraped.author: Satchel Walton
scraped.h1: The AI Safety Community Is Increasingly Freaked Out. Should They Be?
scraped.body_text:
Digital billboards advertise Anthropic on the day of its IPO in Times Square Seth Wenig/AP

Here are some interesting quotes from the last few weeks, pulled from some of the most alarmed and influential voices in the AI safety world:

To be clear, the idea that government-overthrow could happen this coming May remains an outlier. The term “AI safety” has become near-monopolized by a circle of nonprofits that primarily fear existential risks from AI. They remain a small world (Cotra and Christiano are married, for instance), and many premises of their arguments on the future remain hotly contested . The consensus even among this community is that such extreme risks are more likely to be a few years away, rather than a few months away—and that while these are worries to take seriously even for next year, they are certainly not inevitabilities.

But the above quotes do reflect a general trend. Among those who foresee risks like AI takeover, the tenor of warnings has, in relatively short order, gone from quite worried to totally alarmed to, over the last few weeks, urgently-utterly-freaked-the-f**k-out-in-the-short-term . With variation from prognosticator-to-prognosticator, the most extreme fear of rogue superintelligence used to be reserved for perhaps a decade down the line. Now, it’s the next few years . Some watchers of the industry who were previously more skeptical of such arguments have partially changed tune .

If those who see shorter timelines for huge risks are right, we don’t have much time to wait for more definitive evidence.

The most influential new evidence is a report from the research group METR. Released on November 5 amid a midterms-dominated news cycle, the report concluded that the pace of AI development at Anthropic—as measured by scores on well-specified tests—is already, very roughly, twice as fast as in previous years, mostly due to the help of AI models themselves. In Anthropic’s leading statement on the report, co-founder Sam McCandlish wrote that he agreed with many of its conclusions: “AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much.”

Four METR researchers spent 11 weeks at Anthropic to reach that conclusion, but how convincing is the data they used? For the most part, no one knows. Anthropic redacted the most important evidence, with McCandlish saying it was proprietary and could have helped competitors speed up their own AI research.

Thus, a skeptic of intelligence explosion scenarios wrote that the report “is missing too much,” while Cotra agreed that what the discourse most urgently needs is “a far greater quantity and quality of concrete evidence.”

The selective release of data was especially frustrating to critics who have questioned METR’s ability to serve as a check on Anthropic due to the nonprofit’s reliance on the company’s cooperation.

As requirements for independent auditing of AI slowly take shape in the form of state laws, agreements with the White House, and congressional wrangling, access for organizations like METR is at the discretion of company policies. In addition to one-off reports like this one, Anthropic has said it is giving six METR staff “employee-like” access to its premises and researchers.

But so far, this rapidly-evolving arrangement is far from the rigorous standards of independence applied to the bank examiners Anthropic invokes in analogies. METR disclosed in its R&D report that one co-author received and declined a job offer from Anthropic during the project, but that such situations would now require recusal after updates to its conflict of interest policy. It also said that no METR employees at the time had equity in Anthropic, but it acknowledged in May that some of its staff “have strong social ties to employees of AI companies.”

“We think it is extremely important to minimize pressures we might face to adjust our reports or actions due to professional, material, or social connections to frontier labs,” a METR staff member told Mother Jones in an email. That, he said, is why METR doesn’t take money from the AI labs and tries to be transparent about the terms of its investigations.

The report’s findings on Anthropic played into fears that once AI development is continually sped up enough by the models themselves, it will catapult towards a superintelligence that could act in ways drastically out of step with human values.

That has long been a theory of how AI will develop—and parts of it have gained more credence this year. Frontier AI models have already become superhuman at math and parts of theoretical physics, have developed incredible cybersecurity capabilities, and have demonstrated a tendency—prominently displayed in the Hugging Face attack —to prioritize scoring well on evaluations over fulfilling the wishes of their designers. Just today, one of Anthropic’s in-house mathematicians claimed to have used Claude to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, perhaps the most famous and important unresolved problem in all of math.

But OpenAI research released on Wednesday contained richer data than the report on its arch-rival, and it came to a much more modest conclusion about how its models are speeding up AI research. On a metric similar to the main one METR used to publicize the 2x speedup at Anthropic, OpenAI found only a small increase in the rate of progress of its models. Still, its researchers found AI assistance to be quite valuable, with many OpenAI employees using AI resources worth tens of thousands of dollars per day to help with their work.

The OpenAI report bolstered critics who take AI capabilities and risks seriously while downplaying the possibility of a runaway intelligence explosion. For instance, the last few years of capabilities gains have come alongside huge infusions of money and computing power that are not certain to continue . Capabilities are usually measured on simulated tests, and it’s sometimes harder to see the effects of AI in data on real-world applications. And increasing models’ abilities in AI research might not be enough to lead to exponential danger. That evidence points towards a world where AI could still have transformative implications and surpass human abilities in many domains, but things don’t get so sci-fi so quickly.

But if those who see shorter timelines for huge risks are right, we don’t have much time to wait for more definitive evidence. Ready or not, we’ll find out pretty soon.

Disclosure: The Center for Investigative Reporting, the parent company of Mother Jones , has sued OpenAI for copyright violations . OpenAI denies the allegations.

scraped.title: The Melania series has one accidental purpose
scraped.description: The same slog of airbrushed nothingness now inadvertently tells a very different story.
scraped.author: Inae Oh
scraped.h1: The Melania Series Has One Accidental Purpose
scraped.body_text:
MediaPunch/AP

It’s hard to evince the logic of Melania, The Series , the two-episode follow-up to the first lady’s documentary film. The opening scenes are nearly identical to the slog of airbrushed nothingness we saw in January, leaving the viewer reeling from a mix of deja-vu and irritation. Was I really going to need another round of breakfast wine to endure this? Thankfully, the episodes were relatively short, each clocking in at under 40 minutes.

Which made the series a perfect vehicle for ambient viewing, allowing me to make coffee and check in on Melania’ s New York premiere on Thursday, where a parade of MAGA’s D-listers attended: Pam Bondi, Katie Zaccharia, Kellyanne Conway, and George Papadopoulos, to name a few. Notably absent this time around were Tim Cook and Jeff Bezos, both of whom attended private screenings ahead of the Melania release. Even President Trump didn’t show up to his wife’s premiere. (To Trump’s credit, he was flying back from a humiliating trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.) It is this accidental showcasing of just how far the Trump administration has plunged from January to the November elections that Melania, The Series proves its singular worth.

“What I’m hearing from my friends’ daughters is that they love Barron. That they want to go to NYU to meet him.” The remark is yet another reminder of just how rotten this whole Melania-on-film exercise is.

When my eyes did wander back to the television, some scenes did manage to break through my stupor. We finally hear Melania’s father talk after saying virtually nothing in the movie; Melania also makes a pointed dig at the plastic surgery procedures that surround her husband’s political party—”Women should honor the all-natural beauty which evolves as we age,” the first lady says over narration, as she is seen walking to the spa facilities of Mar-a-Lago. “All Authentic, never alteration.” Then there’s the rare scene of Melania discussing her son, Barron, while confirming speculation that he introduced his father to some manosphere podcasts. But even that small insight is spoiled when a sycophantic Brett Ratner tells his subject, “What I’m hearing from my friends’ daughters is that they love Barron. That they want to go to NYU to meet him.” The remark is yet another reminder of just how rotten this whole Melania-on-film exercise is.

After I finished the two episodes, my mind returned to Bezos. The Amazon founder, who denied having any involvement in Melania but called it a “ very wise business decision ,” claims to have had a major role in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond after paying $8.45 billion for the franchise in 2022. It was a rare comment, and an alarming admission that a billionaire tech titan was heavily involved in the creative process for the storied franchise. As for Melania , Bezos said nothing this week.
